francis-of-assisi.history:
St. Francis of Assisi, founder of the Franciscan Order, was born at Assisi in Umbria in 1181 or 1182, the exact year being uncertain. His father, Pietro Bernardone, was a wealthy cloth merchant; of his mother, Pica, little is known, though she is said to have belonged to a noble family of Provence. Baptized Giovanni, the child was renamed Francesco by his father, apparently out of fondness for France. The legend that he was born in a stable arose only in the fifteenth century.

As a youth Francis received elementary instruction from the priests of St. George's at Assisi, but he was not studious, and his literary education remained incomplete. Though associated with his father in trade, he showed little liking for a merchant's career. His early life gave no presage of sanctity: he loved pleasure, sang merrily, and delighted in fine clothes, becoming the favourite of the young nobles of Assisi and the leader of its revels. Yet even then he showed an instinctive sympathy with the poor.

At about twenty he rode out with the townsmen against Perugia, was taken prisoner, and was held captive for more than a year. A low fever contracted there appears to have turned his thoughts to eternal things, yet with returning health his eagerness for glory reawakened, and he prepared to join Walter of Brienne, then in arms in the Neapolitan States. A dream of a vast hall hung with armour all marked with the Cross, and a second illness at Spoleto followed by another dream bidding him return at once, sent him back to Assisi in 1205.

His demeanour changed, though he still joined at times in the revels of his former comrades. Asked jestingly whether he meant to marry, he answered that he was about to take a wife of surpassing fairness: Lady Poverty, whom Dante and Giotto later wedded to his name. He gave up his gay attire and wasteful ways, seeking in prayer and solitude the meaning of his call. Meeting a poor leper on the Umbrian plain, he overcame his instinctive disgust, dismounted, embraced the man, and gave him all the money he had. On a pilgrimage to Rome he emptied his purse at the tomb of St. Peter and, having exchanged clothes with a tattered mendicant, stood fasting that day among the beggars at the basilica door.

While praying before an ancient crucifix in the forsaken wayside chapel of St. Damian's below the town, he heard a voice saying, 'Go, Francis, and repair my house, which as you see is falling into ruin.' Taking the words literally, he sold horse and drapery at Foligno to raise money for the church's restoration; when the priest refused the gold, he flung it from him. His father's wrath drove him to hide for a month in a cave near San Damiano, and when he emerged, emaciated and squalid, he was pelted with mud and stones and mocked as a madman. In time Francis renounced his inheritance, embraced poverty, and gave himself to repairing churches and serving lepers.

Followers gradually gathered around him and became the Order of Friars Minor; with St. Clare he inspired the community known as the Poor Clares. He preached to all creatures: tradition holds that he preached to the birds and tamed a wolf. In 1224 he is said to have received the stigmata, the wounds of Christ. His Canticle of the Sun praises God through creation.

Francis died at the Porziuncola near Assisi on 3 October 1226 and was canonized in 1228. In the centuries since, a vast literature has grown up around him; modern study has recovered important early texts and has re-edited and translated his own writings. His feast is kept on 4 October, and he is venerated as the patron of animals and ecology.

anthony-of-padua.history:
Anthony of Padua was born at Lisbon in 1195 and received in baptism the name of Ferdinand. Later writers traced his line to Godfrey de Bouillon and to the kings of Asturias, but all that is known of his parents is that they were noble and God-fearing people living near the Cathedral of Lisbon. Educated in the cathedral school, he joined the Canons Regular of St. Augustine at the convent of St. Vincent outside the city walls at the age of fifteen, and in 1212 moved to the convent of Santa Croce in Coimbra to avoid distraction from visitors. There he spent eight years chiefly in study and prayer, gathering from Scripture and the writings of the Fathers a treasure of theological knowledge.

In 1220, when the bodies of the first Franciscan martyrs, put to death at Morocco that January, were brought to Santa Croce, he was inflamed with the desire for martyrdom. He received the Franciscan habit, left the Canons Regular for the Order of Friars Minor, and took the new name of Anthony, hoping to preach the faith to the Saracens. Severe illness compelled him to sail for Portugal in the spring of 1221; his ship was driven by a storm upon the coast of Sicily, where he regained his health, and he then traveled to Assisi for the general chapter of May 30. When the chapter was over he remained entirely unnoticed, saying nothing of his studies, and sought a place of solitude and penance; the provincial, Father Graziano, sent him to the hermitage of Montepaolo near Forli to celebrate Mass for the lay brethren.

His public career began at an ordination at Forli. When the assembled Franciscan and Dominican friars one after another declined to preach, Anthony, whom his brethren supposed able only to read the Missal and Breviary, was commanded by obedience to speak. He began slowly and timidly, but soon explained the hidden sense of Scripture with such profound erudition and sublime doctrine that all were astonished. St. Francis, informed of his learning, wrote to him in 1224 directing that he teach theology to the brethren, provided that the spirit of prayer and devotion not be extinguished. After conferring with the Abbot Thomas Gallo at Vercelli, Anthony taught at Bologna and Montpellier, and later at Toulouse; nothing of his teaching survives, but his writings show a doctrine of an entirely seraphic character.

It was as an orator that he reaped his richest harvest. A clear voice, a winning countenance, a prodigious memory, and profound learning were joined, in the eyes of his contemporaries, to the spirit of prophecy and an extraordinary gift of miracles. He combated the vices of luxury, avarice, and tyranny, and labored against the heresy of the Cathars and Patarines, while tradition holds that he once preached a sermon to the fishes. At Padua in 1229 and 1230 he wrote the Sermones de tempore and the Sermones de Sanctis, the only works he left.

He died at Arcella near Padua on June 13, 1231, at about the age of thirty-six, and was canonized in 1232, less than a year after his death. In 1263 his relics were transferred to the magnificent church the people of Padua had raised in his memory, in the presence of St. Bonaventure, Minister General of the order. When the vault was opened after thirty years, the flesh was found reduced to dust, but the tongue was uninjured, fresh, and of a lively red colour, which Bonaventure venerated with the words, "O Blessed Tongue that always praised the Lord."

The fame of his miracles has never diminished, and he is acknowledged as the greatest wonder-worker of his time. He is especially invoked for the recovery of things lost, as the old responsory of Friar Julian of Spires recalls, and he is honored as a patron of travelers; his feast is kept on June 13. Some of the wonders recorded by later biographers are regarded as legendary, though others rest on authority difficult to set aside.

dymphna.history:
St. Dymphna, also written Dympna or Dimpna, is venerated as a virgin and martyr. The earliest historical account of her veneration dates from the middle of the thirteenth century, when Pierre, a canon of the church of Saint Aubert at Cambrai, wrote a life of the saint under Bishop Guy I of Cambrai (1238-47). Pierre states that he drew his biography from oral tradition, and records that Dymphna had already been honored for many years in a church dedicated to her at Geel, in the province of Antwerp, Belgium.

According to that traditional narrative, Dymphna was the daughter of a pagan king of Ireland and became a Christian, receiving baptism in secret. After the death of her mother, a woman of remarkable beauty, her father sought to marry his own daughter, who was said to resemble her. Dymphna fled with a priest named Gerebernus, landing at Antwerp and taking up residence beside a chapel of St. Martin at Geel. Her father's messengers discovered the fugitives, and the king himself followed and renewed his proposal; when Dymphna refused, he commanded his servants to slay the priest and struck off his daughter's head. The two bodies were placed in sarcophagi and entombed in a cave, where they were later found; the body of Dymphna was buried in the church at Geel, while the bones of Gerebernus were transferred to Xanten.

This narrative, however, is judged to lack historical foundation: it follows a folkloric motif, found frequently in popular legend, of the king who seeks to marry his own daughter, so that nothing certain can be concluded from it about Dymphna's life or the era in which she lived. Nor can her identification with St. Damhnat of Ireland be proved. At Geel, nonetheless, fragments of two simple ancient sarcophagi are preserved, in which tradition holds that the bodies of Dymphna and Gerebernus were found, together with a quadrangular brick bearing two lines of letters read as DYMPNA; the discovery of the sarcophagus with the corpse and the brick may have given rise to her veneration.

In Christian art, Dymphna is depicted with a sword in her hand and a fettered devil at her feet. Her feast is celebrated on 15 May, the date under which she also appears in the Roman martyrology.

From time immemorial the saint has been invoked as patroness against insanity, and she is honored today in particular as patroness of those suffering from mental illness and anxiety. The Bollandists published numerous accounts of miraculous cures, especially between 1604 and 1668. From this devotion grew a distinctive tradition of care at Geel, which became famous for its humane treatment of the mentally ill. Those brought to the town in hope of healing were at first placed in an institution for observation, and later given shelter in the homes of the inhabitants, where they shared in agricultural labors and were treated kindly while being watched without their knowledge. Even at present there are sometimes as many as fifteen hundred persons whose relatives invoke St. Dymphna for their cure, and this arrangement has long been noted for its good results.

The old church of St. Dymphna at Geel was destroyed by fire in 1489; the new church, consecrated in 1532, still stands. On her feast day and on the Tuesday after Pentecost, numerous pilgrims visit her shrine, and a fraternity under her name has long existed in the town.

fabiola.history:
Saint Fabiola was a Roman matron of patrician rank, a member of the family of the Fabia, who died at Rome on 27 December, 399, or possibly 400. She belonged to the company of noble Roman women who came under the influence of Saint Jerome and gave up all earthly pleasures for Christian asceticism and charitable work. During Jerome's stay at Rome from 382 to 384 she was not yet part of the ascetic circle that gathered around him; only at a later date, after the death of her second consort, did she take the decisive step of entering upon a life of renunciation and labor for others.

Her first marriage was marked by grave suffering, for her husband led so vicious a life that to live with him was impossible. Fabiola obtained a divorce from him according to Roman law, and, contrary to the ordinances of the Church, she entered upon a second union before her first husband's death. Following the death of her second consort, she appeared on the day before Easter at the gates of the Lateran basilica, dressed in penitential garb, and did penance in public for her sin, an act that made a great impression upon the Christian population of Rome. The pope then formally received her again into full communion with the Church.

From that time Fabiola renounced all that the world had to offer and devoted her immense wealth to the needs of the poor and the sick. She erected a fine hospital at Rome and waited on its inmates herself, not even shunning those afflicted with repulsive wounds and sores. To the churches and religious communities at Rome and in other places in Italy she gave large sums, and all her interests came to be centered on the needs of the Church and the care of the poor and suffering.

In 395 she went to Bethlehem, where she lived in the hospice of the convent directed by Paula and applied herself, under the direction of Saint Jerome, with the greatest zeal to the study and contemplation of the Scriptures and to ascetic exercises. An incursion of the Huns into the eastern provinces of the empire, together with the quarrel that broke out between Jerome and Bishop John of Jerusalem over the teachings of Origen, made residence at Bethlehem unpleasant for her, and she returned to Rome. She remained, however, in correspondence with Jerome, who at her request wrote a treatise on the priesthood of Aaron and the priestly dress.

At Rome Fabiola united with the former senator Pammachius in carrying out a great charitable undertaking; together they erected at Porto a large hospice for pilgrims coming to Rome. She continued her usual personal labors in aid of the poor and the sick until her death. Her funeral was a remarkable manifestation of the gratitude and veneration with which the Roman populace regarded her, and Saint Jerome wrote of her a eulogistic memoir in a letter to her relative Oceanus. The Church keeps her memory on 27 December, the day of her death. She is honored as a patron of divorced people and of those in difficult marriages, of widows, and of hospitals, the sick, and those who nurse them.

john-chrysostom.history:
John, called Chrysostom or 'golden-mouthed' on account of his eloquence, was born at Antioch about 347 and died at Commana in Pontus on 14 September 407. The surname first appears in 553, in a constitution of Pope Vigilius, and reflects the standing he came to hold as the most prominent doctor of the Greek Church and the greatest preacher ever heard in a Christian pulpit. He is honored as a Doctor of the Church, and his feast is kept on 13 September.

His youth fell in troubled times. Antioch, the second city of the Eastern Roman Empire, echoed the religious struggles of the fourth century: pagans, Manichaeans, Gnostics, Arians, Apollinarians, and Jews all made proselytes there, while the Catholics were themselves divided by the schism between the bishops Meletius and Paulinus. His father Secundus, an officer of high rank in the Syrian army, died soon after John's birth, and his mother Anthusa, only twenty years old, raised him and an elder sister alone. She sent him to the best schools of Antioch, where he followed the lectures of the philosopher Andragatius and of Libanius, the most famous orator of the age and a tenacious adherent of the declining paganism of Rome. There he gained considerable Greek scholarship and classical culture, which he never disowned; his alleged hostility to classical learning rests on a misunderstanding of passages in which he defended the philosophy of Christianity against the myths of the heathen gods.

About 367 he met Bishop Meletius, a decisive turning point. Drawn by the bishop's earnest and winning character, he withdrew from profane studies to an ascetic life, studied Scripture, frequented Meletius' sermons, received baptism and ordination as lector about three years later, and joined an ascetic society near Antioch directed by Carterius and by Diodorus, later Bishop of Tarsus. Prayer, manual labor, and Scripture study were his chief occupations, and his earliest writings, nearly all ascetic, probably date from this period. Four years later he withdrew to a cave near Antioch as an anchorite for two years, until his health, ruined by watchings and fastings in frost and cold, forced him back to the city and his office as lector.

Probably early in 381 Meletius made him deacon, shortly before departing for Constantinople, where he died as president of the Second Ecumenical Council. Under the new bishop Flavian, John assisted at the liturgical functions, cared for the sick and poor, and probably taught catechumens. Toward the end of this period, about 386, he composed his most famous book, On the Priesthood, possibly occasioned, though the sources leave room for doubt, by the request that he and his friend Basil accept bishoprics about 372. Ordained priest by Flavian in 386, for the next twelve years his chief task was preaching, and the larger part of the popular religious instruction of Antioch devolved upon him.

His power as a preacher first showed itself in the Lent of 387. The people of Antioch, excited by the levy of new taxes, had thrown down the statues of the emperor Theodosius, and in the panic that followed Chrysostom preached a series of twenty or twenty-one sermons, the nineteenth probably not authentic, full of vigor, consoling and tranquilizing, until Flavian brought back the emperor's pardon from Constantinople.

Raised to the archbishopric of Constantinople in 398, he reformed the clergy and the imperial court and made powerful enemies. His preaching on the dignity of the poor and the duties of the wealthy is preserved in his most celebrated homilies. Twice exiled, he died in 407 on a forced march.

The Divine Liturgy bearing his name is still celebrated throughout the Byzantine East, and well over a thousand editions of his works have appeared, the oldest being Latin incunabula printed before 1500. He is invoked as a patron of preachers, teachers, and theologians, and of all who suffer from epilepsy or endure persecution for the sake of righteousness.

kilian.history:
Kilian, honored as the Apostle of Franconia, was born about 640 of noble parents, probably in Ireland, though some accounts have placed his origin in Scotland. Distinguished from youth for his piety and love of study, he is said by the later narrative to have embraced the monastic life, and later writers describe him as a monk of the celebrated monastery of Hy (Iona), and even as its abbot; this, however, cannot be proved. The older narrative states that he was consecrated a bishop before leaving his native land, a detail generally accepted as trustworthy; in keeping with the Irish custom of that age, he held no fixed diocese but served as a travelling bishop.

Resolved on missionary work, he left his native country with eleven companions, travelled through Gaul, crossed the Rhine, and reached the castle of Würzburg, the seat of the Thuringian (Frankish) Duke Gozbert, who was, like his people, still pagan. Before preaching there, Kilian went with his companions to Rome for missionary faculties. Pope John V, whom he had expected to find, had died on 2 August 686, and the faculties were obtained from his successor, Conon. The missionaries reached Würzburg in the summer of 686 and were in Rome in late autumn of the same year; on the return journey the party divided, and Kilian came back to Würzburg with the priest Coloman and the deacon Totnan.

Taking the town as the base of his activity, Kilian preached through an ever-widening area of East Franconia and Thuringia and converted Duke Gozbert, together with a large part of his subjects, to Christianity.

The early documents record the circumstances of the martyrdom. After the duke had become a Christian, Kilian told him that his marriage with Geilana, his brother's widow, was unlawful under the Christian dispensation, and the duke promised to separate from her. Geilana plotted vengeance and, in the duke's absence, had Kilian and his two companions secretly murdered; their bodies were buried at the scene of the crime together with the sacred vessels, vestments, and holy writings. This is generally held to have taken place on 8 July 689, although opinions differ as to the exact year. The same accounts add that the murderer later went mad, confessed his crime, and died miserably, while Geilana also died insane; details of this kind rest on the narrative tradition. Some modern critics have questioned parts of this story, but Kilian's missionary labors in East Franconia and his martyrdom are accepted without question.

Although the work was not carried on after his death, St. Boniface, on arriving in Thuringia, found evidence of his predecessor's influence. After wonderful cures at the burial place had brought it renown, the relics of the three martyrs were transferred in 743 by St. Burchard, first Bishop of Würzburg, to the Church of Our Lady; when Burchard had obtained Pope Zachary's permission for their public veneration, they were solemnly translated, probably on 8 July 752, to the newly finished Cathedral of the Savior. Later they were buried in St. Kilian's vault in the new cathedral, built, as tradition affirms, on the spot where the martyrdom took place. A New Testament belonging to Kilian was kept among the treasures of Würzburg Cathedral until 1803 and has since rested in the university library.

Kilian is the patron of the diocese of Würzburg, where his feast is kept on 8 July with great solemnity. He is also venerated as a patron of missionaries, martyrs, and bishops, of Germany, and of those who suffer chronic pain.

melania-the-younger.history:
Melania the Younger was born at Rome about 383, a member of the famous family of the Valerii; her parents were Publicola and Albina, and her paternal grandmother was the saint known as Melania the Elder. Little is known of her childhood. Through obedience to her parents, and against her own wishes, she was married in her thirteenth year to her kinsman Valerius Pinianus, a patrician. During seven years of married life she bore two children, both of whom died young. After their deaths her early longing for a celibate life returned, and with Pinianus's consent she resolved to live in continence and to walk the path of evangelical perfection. Pinianus thereafter stood toward her as a brother and was her companion in all her efforts toward sanctity, as together they parted little by little with their immense wealth, freeing their slaves and bestowing the proceeds of their estates on the poor and on the Church.

In 408, because of the Visigothic invasions of Italy, Melania left Rome and for two years lived near Messina in Sicily, where a life of monastic character was shared with some of their former slaves. In 410 she went to Africa, where she and Pinianus lived with her mother for seven years. There she became well acquainted with Saint Augustine and his friend Alypius, devoted herself to works of charity and piety and to the care of souls, and founded a nunnery of which she became superior, together with a cloister for men placed under Pinianus's charge.

In 417 Melania, her mother, and Pinianus traveled to Palestine by way of Alexandria. For a year they lived in a hospice for pilgrims at Jerusalem, where Melania met Saint Jerome, and she made further generous donations when she received the money from the sale of her estates in Spain. About this time she traveled through Egypt, visiting the principal places of monastic and eremitical life, and upon her return to Jerusalem she lived for twelve years in a hermitage near the Mount of Olives.

Before her mother's death in 431 a new series of monastic foundations had begun. Melania began with a convent for women on the Mount of Olives, whose maintenance she assumed while refusing to be made its superior. After her husband's death she built a cloister for men, then a chapel, and later a more imposing church. In November 436 she went to Constantinople, where she aided in the conversion of her pagan uncle Volusian, ambassador at the court of Theodosius II, and in the conflict with Nestorianism. Her later years included the journey of the Empress Eudocia, wife of Theodosius, to Jerusalem in 438; soon after the empress's return, Melania died in that city on 31 December 439, renowned for her humility, her generosity, and her wise counsel to monks and nuns. She is honored as a Desert Mother and as a model of the renunciation of wealth for the sake of the Kingdom.

The Greek Church began to venerate her shortly after her death, but she remained almost unknown in the Western Church for many years, her memory long obscured by confusion with her grandmother. Accurate knowledge of her life became possible only with the discovery of two manuscripts: a Latin life found by Cardinal Rampolla in the Escorial in 1884, and a Greek biography preserved in the Barberini library, both of which Rampolla published in Rome in 1905. Interest in the saint grew thereafter, and in 1908 Pope Pius X granted her office to the congregation of clergy at Somascha. She is venerated as a patroness of widows, nuns, monks, the poor, and contemplatives, and her feast is kept on 31 December, the day of her death.

sidonius-apollinaris.history:
Caius Sollius Modestus Apollinaris Sidonius, better known as Sidonius Apollinaris, was a poet, diplomat, and bishop of the fifth century, born at Lyons on 5 November in about 430 and died at Clermont about August 480. He came of a noble Christian family of the Gallo-Roman aristocracy, his father and grandfather both having served as prefects of the pretorium of the Gauls.

About 452 he married Papianilla, daughter of Avitus, who was proclaimed emperor at the end of 455 and honored his son-in-law with a statue in the Forum of Trajan. Sidonius wrote a panegyric in honor of Avitus, who had become consul on 1 January 456, the first of his three panegyrics. Within a year Avitus was overthrown by Ricimer and Majorian; Sidonius at first resisted, then yielded, and in 458 composed a second panegyric on the occasion of Majorian's journey to Lyons. After Majorian's fall he supported Theodoric II, King of the Visigoths, and after Theodoric's assassination he hoped to see the empire arise anew under the consulate of Anthemius. He went to Rome, eulogized Anthemius's second consulate in a panegyric dated 1 January 468, and became urban prefect of the city.

About 470 he returned to Gaul and, contrary to his own wishes, was elected Bishop of the Arveni at Clermont in Auvergne, chosen as the only one capable of maintaining Roman power against the attacks of Euric, Theodoric's successor. With the general Ecdicius he resisted the barbarian armies up to the time when Clermont, abandoned by Rome, fell in 474. He was for some time a prisoner of Euric and was later exposed to the attacks of two priests of his diocese; after the city's conquest he regained his position as bishop, finally returning to Clermont, where he remained until his death.

His works form two groups, the Carmina and the Epistulae. The poems comprise the three panegyrics with their appendixes, two epithalamia, a poem of acknowledgment to Faustus of Riez, a eulogy of Narbonne offered to two of its citizens, and a description of the castle of Leontius. The letters are divided into nine books with approximate dates: the first in 469, the second in 472, books five through seven between 474 and 475, and the ninth in 479; though written in prose, they contain several metrical pieces. After his conversion to Christianity, Sidonius ceased to write profane poetry.

The poems show a fairly pure latinity and correct prosody, but frequent alliterations and short verses in lengthy compositions betray the poet of a decadent period, whose chief inspiration was drawn from Statius and Claudian. Such defects are atoned for by powerful description, most evident in the letters, composed on the models of Pliny the Younger and Symmachus. Most of the letters are genuine correspondence, only somewhat retouched before insertion in the collection; more mannered than the poems, they abound in archaic words, antitheses, and plays upon words, and foreshadow the artificial diction of the Hisperica Tamina. Yet the artistic skill of the painter and story-teller makes up for these defects, and the letters preserve a highly colored and unique picture of the times, with sketches of the barbarian races, landscapes, and details of court intrigue.

Sidonius wished to unite the service of Christ with that of the Empire. By his works as well as by his career he strove to perpetuate the ancient culture of Gaul under the aegis of Rome, as its last representative, and when that became impossible he had to be content with saving its last vestiges under a barbarian prince. His letters and poems are among the most important surviving witnesses to late antique Gaul. He is venerated as a saint in the Catholic and Orthodox churches, with his feast kept on 21 August, and he is invoked as a patron of writers, scholars, bishops, and theologians, and for protection.

crispin-and-crispinian.history:
Saints Crispin and Crispinian are honored as martyrs of the early Church, put to death by beheading during the reign of Diocletian, the date of their execution being given as 25 October 285 or 286. It is stated that they were brothers, though the fact has not been positively proved. The legend relates that they were Romans of distinguished descent who went as missionaries of the Christian faith to Gaul and chose Soissons as their field of labor.

In imitation of St. Paul, they worked with their hands, making shoes, and earned enough by their trade to support themselves and to aid the poor; tradition presents them as devoting their days to preaching and to the service of those in need. In time they came to be venerated as patron saints of those who work in leather, with the shoemakers, saddlers, tanners, and cobblers claiming their patronage, as do weavers and workers generally.

The legend tells that, in the Diocletian persecution, the two were brought before Maximianus Herculius, whom Diocletian had appointed co-emperor. Maximianus first sought to turn them from their faith by alternate promises and threats, but they answered: 'Thy threats do not terrify us, for Christ is our life, and death is our gain. Thy rank and possessions are nought to us, for we have long before this sacrificed the like for the sake of Christ and rejoice in what we have done.' When Maximianus saw that his efforts were of no avail, he gave them into the hands of the governor Rictiovarus (Rictius Varus), a most cruel persecutor of the Christians. Under the order of Rictiovarus they were stretched on the rack, thongs were cut from their flesh, and awls were driven under their finger-nails. A millstone was then fastened about the neck of each, and they were thrown into the Aisne; the legend says they swam to the opposite bank unhurt, just as they suffered no harm from a great fire in which Rictiovarus, in despair, sought death himself. Afterward the two saints were beheaded at the command of Maximianus.

This narrative, which the Bollandists incorporated into their great collection and which is likewise found in various breviaries, appears to be a later composition. Its own statement that a large church had been built over the graves of the two saints suggests that the legend could not have arisen until a later age, and it contains many details of little probability or historical worth, seemingly compiled from various fabulous sources.

The cult of the martyrs nevertheless has ancient foundations. In the sixth century a stately basilica was erected at Soissons over their graves, and St. Eligius, the famous goldsmith, made a costly shrine for the head of St. Crispinian. Some of the relics of Crispin and Crispinian were carried to Rome and placed in the church of San Lorenzo in Panisperna, while other relics were given by Charlemagne to the cathedral he founded at Osnabrück, which was dedicated to the two saints. Their feast falls on 25 October.

pope-evaristus.history:
Pope Evaristus, known in the Liberian Catalogue by the name Aristus, succeeded St. Clement as bishop of Rome toward the close of the first century. The papal catalogues of the second century used by St. Irenaeus and St. Hippolytus list him as the fourth successor of St. Peter, immediately after St. Clement, and assign him a reign of about eight years, from about 98 or 99 to about 106 or 107; his death is placed about 107. Writing in his Ecclesiastical History, Eusebius says only that Evaristus succeeded Clement in the episcopate of the Roman Church, a fact already known from St. Irenaeus. The order of this early succession is considered certain, yet the earliest historical sources supply almost no authentic data about his life. His pontificate encompassed the end of the apostolic age, during which St. John the Apostle, the last of the Twelve, likely died.

Little is known of his origins. The Liber Pontificalis describes him as coming of a Hellenic family and as the son of a Bethlehem Jew; tradition further preserves the name of his father as Judah. Aside from this, the ancient records are silent concerning his life.

The same source credits him with allotting definite churches as tituli to the presbyters of Rome and with dividing the city into seven deaconries, although scholars judge that the Liber Pontificalis here refers a later Roman institution to his time. According to tradition he also decreed that marriages be celebrated publicly with the blessing of a priest. Two decretals ascribed to him by Pseudo-Isidore are recognized as forgeries, and no authentic legislation of his survives.

Though the Liber Pontificalis crowns him with martyrdom, that martyrdom, while traditional, is not historically proven. More trustworthy is the assertion of the same source that he was laid to rest in the Vatican, near the tomb of St. Peter. He is honored among the early saints of the Roman Church, and his feast is kept on October 26. In later devotion he has been invoked as a patron of engaged couples, brides, seminarians, and church unity.

anastasius-sinaita.history:
Anastasius Sinaita, also called Anastasius of Sinai, was a Greek ecclesiastical writer and priest, born at Alexandria in the first half of the seventh century. He was abbot of the monastery on Mount Sinai, later known as Saint Catherine's Monastery and counted among the most ancient monasteries in Christendom, at the foot of the mountain where Moses received the Law. He died after 700.

His life's work was the defense of orthodox Catholic teaching amid the controversies of the seventh-century Church. He proved so active an opponent of the Monophysites, the Monothelites, and the Jews that he was known as 'the new Moses'. His principal work, the Hodegos or Guide, was written in defense of the Catholic faith against these movements and became a popular manual of controversy among the medieval Greeks. He was also widely read in the East for his scriptural exegesis and for his instruction of monks and priests in the discipline of the spiritual life.

Other writings bear his name. The Questions and Answers on Various Theological Matters attributed to him are in part spurious. His Devout Introduction to the Hexaemeron, a treatise on the six days of creation, comprises twelve books, the first eleven of which have come down only in a Latin translation. These and other minor writings are published in volume LXXXIX of Migne's Patrologia Graeca. Le Quien likewise attributed to him the Antiquorum Patrum Doctrina de Verbi Dei Incarnatione, though without sufficient reason.

The Church keeps his feast on April 21, and he is honored as a patron of theologians, of monks, and of scholars devoted to the study of Scripture.

arialdo.history:
Arialdo was born of a noble family at Cutiacum, near Milan, and, after studies at Laon and Paris, became a canon of the cathedral chapter of Milan. When simony and clerical concubinage had spread through the Lombard church, he devoted himself to the reform of the clergy, joining the Pataria, the lay reform movement led by his kinsman St. Heribert, and preaching repentance to priests and people alike.

His denunciations of abuses aroused fierce opposition. The bishop, Guido, excommunicated him, but Pope Stephen reinstated him and bade him continue the work of reformation, which he afterward pressed on with the support of Pope Alexander II. Arialdo succeeded in having the bishop excommunicated for his repeated lapses, but a riot followed in which he was seriously injured. An earlier attempt had already been made on his life with a poisoned sword.

While on his way to Rome, Arialdo was set upon by the emissaries of Guido and slain; the year of his death is variously given as 1065 or 1066. Ten months afterward his body was found in Lake Maggiore, said to be in a state of preservation and giving off a sweet odour. It was carried to Milan with great ceremony, exposed in the church of St. Ambrose from Ascension to Pentecost, and interred in the church of St. Celsus; his relics were later enshrined in the city's cathedral. In 1067 Pope Alexander II declared him a martyr, and the people of Milan have venerated him as one who gave his life for the reform of the Church. He is remembered as a patron of church reform, of the persecuted, and of the laity.

bernard-of-menthon.history:
{"history": "Bernard of Menthon, also called Bernard of Aosta or Bernard of Montjoux, was born in 923, probably in the castle of Menthon near Annecy in Savoy. He was descended from a rich and noble family and received a thorough education, but he refused the honorable marriage proposed by his father and resolved to devote himself to the service of the Church. Placing himself under the direction of Peter, Archdeacon of Aosta, he progressed rapidly, was ordained a priest, and in 966, on account of his learning and virtue, was made Archdeacon of Aosta, entrusted with the government of the diocese under its bishop.

Bernard saw that ignorance and idolatrous observances still prevailed among the people of the Alps, and he resolved to devote himself to their conversion. For forty-two years he preached the Gospel to these mountain communities and carried the light of the faith into many cantons of Lombardy, laboring also against the local superstitions that had taken root among them; the account of his life credits this ministry with numerous conversions and many miracles.

The work for which his name has remained famous, however, concerned the pilgrim roads across the Alps. From the most ancient times a path had led from the valley of Aosta to the Swiss canton of Valais over the pass now known as the Great St. Bernard. Snow lies on the pass perpetually to a depth of seven or eight feet, and drifts sometimes accumulate to a height of forty feet; the crossing, extremely dangerous and especially so in the spring on account of avalanches, was nevertheless often used by French and German pilgrims on their way to Rome. For the convenience and protection of such travelers, Bernard founded in 962 a monastery and hospice at the highest point of the pass, eight thousand feet above sea level, and a few years later he established a second hospice on the Little St. Bernard, a mountain of the Graian Alps standing 7,076 feet above the sea.

After obtaining pontifical approval during a visit to Rome, he placed both houses in the charge of Augustinian monks, the community later known as the Canons Regular of the Hospitaller Congregation of Great Saint Bernard. The two passes came to bear the name of their founder, and the hospices were renowned for the generous hospitality extended there. At all seasons of the year, but especially during heavy snowstorms, the monks went out, accompanied by their well-trained dogs, in search of travelers who had succumbed to the severity of the weather; they offered food, clothing, and shelter to the unfortunate and took care also of the dead. Sustained by gifts and collections, the congregation numbered about forty members at the beginning of the twentieth century, the majority living at the hospice while others had charge of neighboring parishes. Tradition holds that the famous rescue dogs later bred by the canons took their name from the pass and its patron.

The last act of Bernard's life was the reconciliation of two noblemen whose strife threatened a fatal issue. He died at Novara, traditionally in 1008, though other accounts place his death around 1081, and was interred in the cloister of St. Lawrence. Venerated as a saint from the twelfth century in many places of Piedmont, including Aosta, Novara, and Brescia, he was not formally canonized until 1681, by Innocent XI. His feast day is observed on 28 May, and he is honored as the apostle of the Alps and invoked as a patron of travelers, mountaineers, skiers, and the poor."}

clement-of-alexandria.history:
St. Clement of Alexandria, properly Titus Flavius Clemens, was an early Greek Christian theologian who led the catechetical school of Alexandria in the late second and early third centuries. He is distinguished from Clement of Rome by the name by which he is commonly known. The date of his birth is unknown, but Athens was probably his birthplace, being given as the starting point of his travels. A convert to the Christian faith, he journeyed from place to place in search of higher instruction, attaching himself in turn to Greek masters of Ionia, Magna Graecia, and Coele-Syria, and then to an Egyptian, an Assyrian, and a converted Palestinian Jew. At last he met Pantænus in Alexandria, and in his teaching found rest.

Alexandria was well chosen. A center of culture and trade, it possessed a great university under the long-continued patronage of the state and a broad, tolerant intellectual temper in which Plato was the most favored of the old masters; it was also one of the chief seats of that mixed pagan and Christian speculation known as Gnosticism, in which Basilides and Valentinus taught. At an uncertain date in the latter half of the second century, a school of oral instruction was founded there as an official institution of the Church, its lectures admitting pagan hearers. Pantænus is the earliest teacher whose name has been preserved. Clement first assisted and then, about A.D. 190, succeeded him at the head of the school. He was already known as a Christian writer before the days of Pope Victor (188-199), and among his pupils were Origen and Alexander of Jerusalem.

His three major works, the Exhortation, the Tutor, and the Miscellanies, form a kind of progressive introduction to the Christian life. The Exhortation (Protreptikos pros Ellenas) is a persuasive appeal to the Greeks written in a lofty strain: it presents Christ as the noblest of minstrels, himself the New Canticle whose melody subdues the fiercest and hardest natures, and it ends with a description of the God-fearing Christian. The Miscellanies comprise seven entire books, the first four written before the Tutor; when he had finished the Tutor he returned to the Miscellanies, but he was never able to finish it, its opening pages are now missing, and the so-called eighth book known since Eusebius is only a collection of extracts from pagan philosophers. An earlier work, the Outlines (Hypotyposeis), in eight books, is no longer extant, though fragments survive; Eusebius describes it as an abridged commentary on nearly the whole Bible and on the Epistle of Barnabas and the Apocalypse of Peter. Photius charged it with impieties and fables, but conservative scholars are inclined to believe that his criticisms have thrown Clement's mistakes into undue relief; his style is difficult, and his extant writings show him in a better light.

Clement was influenced by Hellenistic philosophy to a greater extent than any other Christian thinker of his time, drawing in particular on Plato and the Stoics to illuminate the faith. He argued that Greek philosophy had its origin among non-Greeks, tracing Plato and Pythagoras back to Egyptian scholars, and his fragments suggest familiarity with pre-Christian Jewish esotericism and Gnosticism. On the Holy Ghost he says little, adhering closely to the language of Scripture. He acknowledges two natures in Christ and regards him as one Person, the Word, the Man-God who profits us both as God and as man. Photius accused him of Docetism, yet Clement clearly admits a real body in Christ, though he thought it exempt from common needs such as eating and drinking, and the soul of Christ exempt from the movement of the passions.

He died about the year 215. Remembered as a pioneer of Christian learning, he is honored as a patron of theologians, philosophers, scholars, and writers; his feast is kept on December 4.

corbinian.history:
Corbinian was born about 680 at Chartres, near Melun in France, and died on 8 September 730. Nothing is known of his youth. His father, Waldekiso, died before Corbinian's birth, and after the death of his mother, Corbiniana, he withdrew to live as a hermit at the church of Saint-Germain at Chartres; tradition holds that this solitude lasted fourteen years.

With some of his disciples he journeyed to Rome, a pilgrimage usually dated to 716, though 709 is also preserved in the sources. There he was consecrated bishop and given the pallium, and he preached with great success in the vicinity of his former home. In 723, some sources say 716, he again visited Rome with the intention of resigning his office, but the pope, Gregory II, would not listen to his request.

On the return journey Corbinian came to Mais in Tyrol, where messengers of Duke Grimoald induced him to go to Bavaria and settle at Freising. The dates of these Roman journeys are somewhat confused among the sources, but the people of Freising have long regarded 724 as the year of his arrival; the tenth centenary of the diocese's existence was celebrated in 1724 and the eleventh in 1824. There he labored as bishop in the evangelization of the Bavarian people.

Corbinian's fidelity to the Church's moral teaching brought him into conflict with the duke, whose marriage to Biltrudis, his brother's widow, was regarded as incestuous. After Grimoald's apparent repentance and subsequent relapse, Corbinian left Freising and remained away for a time. He returned in 729, at the invitation of Huebert, Grimoald's successor, and resumed his apostolic labors.

He died on 8 September 730 and was buried at Freising; his body was later transferred to Mais and in 769 was brought back to Freising by Bishop Arbeo, who also wrote an account of his life. Corbinian is remembered as a man of zeal and of strong feeling, not to say temper, who exercised great influence over all with whom he came in contact. His emblem is a bear. He is honored as a founding evangelizer of Bavaria and as patron of Freising and of the archdiocese of Munich and Freising, and he is invoked as a patron of bishops, hermits, pilgrims, and of Germany. His feast is kept on 8 September, with the translation of his relics commemorated on 20 November.

diodorus-of-tarsus.history:
Diodorus of Tarsus, bishop, monk, and theologian of the fourth century, was born of noble family, probably at Antioch. St. Basil calls him a "nursling" of Silvanus, Bishop of Tarsus, though whether it was at Antioch or at Tarsus is unknown. After studying at Athens he embraced the monastic life and became head of a monastery in or near Antioch, where St. Chrysostom was his disciple.

While Antioch groaned under Arian bishops, Diodorus did not join the irreconcilable party of Paulinus, yet stood unwaveringly for the faith of Nicaea. When Bishop Leontius made Aëtius a deacon, Diodorus and Flavian threatened to leave his communion and retire to the West, and the bishop yielded. Though not yet priests, the two taught the people to sing the Psalms in alternate choirs, first in the chapels of the martyrs and then, at Leontius's invitation, in the churches; the practice quickly spread throughout the Church. When the orthodox Meletius was appointed bishop in 361, Diodorus was made a priest.

He wrote against the pagans as early as the reign of Julian the Apostate, who declared that Diodorus had used the learning and eloquence of Athens against the immortal gods, whom, the emperor declared, had punished him with a hard and bitter life. During the persecution of Valens (364-378), while Meletius was in exile, the two priests kept the Catholics together, assembling them on the northern bank of the Orontes, since the Arian emperor did not permit Catholic worship within the city. Banished many times, Diodorus met St. Basil in Armenia in 372; on Meletius's return he was made Bishop of Tarsus and Metropolitan of Cilicia. The emperor Theodosius named Diodorus and St. Pelagius of Laodicea as norms of orthodoxy for the whole East. At the Councils of Antioch (379) and Constantinople (381), Sozomen credits him with proposing Nectarius as bishop and with helping to appoint St. Flavian as Meletius's successor, by which the unhappy schism at Antioch was prolonged.

When Diodorus came to Antioch in 386 or later, Chrysostom was already a priest. In a sermon Diodorus likened him to St. John the Baptist; the next day Chrysostom declared that it was Diodorus, his father, who was the true Baptist, a man who lived without possessions, had his food from alms, persevered in prayer and preaching, taught across the river as the Baptist had done, and was often imprisoned, indeed "often beheaded, at least in will, for the Faith."

His writings, once very numerous, survive only in a few fragments, chiefly in catenae. He wrote against some of the heresies and still more against heathen philosophy; Photius preserves a summary of his eight books "de Fato," and Leontius records that he composed commentaries on the whole Bible, which St. Jerome judged imitations of those of Eusebius of Emesa. Rejecting the allegorical interpretation of the Alexandrians, Diodorus adhered to the literal sense, an approach followed by his disciple Theodore of Mopsuestia and by Chrysostom himself.

As leader of the Antiochene School, Diodorus was later discredited by the heresies of Nestorius, of which Theodore was the precursor. St. Cyril of Alexandria declared him a heretic, but Theodoret wrote to exculpate him, the passages cited against him appear to belong to a work of Theodore, and he was not condemned at the Fifth General Council in 553. In opposing Apollinarius of Laodicea, who held that the rational soul in Christ was supplied by the Logos, Diodorus appears, in emphasizing the completeness of the Sacred Humanity, to have asserted two hypostases, going too far, yet not necessarily in a heretical sense. The praise of his contemporaries, especially Chrysostom, tends to exculpate him, and he is best regarded as the innocent source of Nestorianism, as St. Cyril is the unwilling origin of Monophysitism.

Diodorus died about 392. Remembered as a champion of orthodoxy and a father of monks, he is honored as a patron of theologians, monks, bishops, and church reform.

edmund-the-martyr.history:
Edmund the Martyr was King of East Anglia. He was born about 840 and died at Hoxne in Suffolk on 20 November 870. The earliest and most reliable accounts represent him as descended from the preceding kings of East Anglia; according to later legends, however, he was born at Nuremberg in Germany, the son of an otherwise unknown King Alcmund of Saxony.

Edmund was only about fifteen years old when he was crowned in 855, and he showed himself a model ruler from the first. He was anxious to treat all with equal justice, and he closed his ears to flatterers and to untrustworthy informers. In his eagerness for prayer he retired for a year to his royal tower at Hunstanton, where he learned the whole Psalter by heart, in order that he might afterwards recite it regularly.

In 870 the two Danish chiefs Hinguar and Hubba invaded his dominions, and Edmund bravely repulsed their first assault. They soon returned with overwhelming numbers and pressed terms upon him which, as a Christian, he felt bound to refuse. Desiring to avert a fruitless massacre, he disbanded his troops and himself retired towards Framlingham; on the way he fell into the hands of the invaders. His captors loaded him with chains and conducted him into the presence of Hinguar, whose impious demands the king once more rejected, declaring that his religion was dearer to him than his life.

His martyrdom took place in 870 at Hoxne in Suffolk. After beating him with cudgels, the Danes tied him to a tree and cruelly tore his flesh with whips. Throughout these tortures Edmund continued to call upon the name of Jesus. Exasperated at last by his constancy, his enemies began to discharge arrows at him, and the cruel sport was continued until his body had the appearance of a porcupine, when Hinguar commanded his head to be struck off. He thus died for the Christian faith he had refused to surrender, and his death was received as a martyrdom, his body being reverently buried at Hoxne.

From his first burial place at Hoxne his relics were removed in the tenth century to Beodricsworth, since called St. Edmundsbury, where arose the famous abbey of that name. There his shrine became one of the most celebrated pilgrimage sites of medieval England.

The memory of the royal martyr was preserved in a series of medieval narratives. The Passio S. Eadmundi of Abbo of Fleury, written in 985, is the earliest among these, and a later treatment of Edmund's infancy, the Infantia S. Eadmundi of Gaufridus De Fontibus, followed about 1150, while collections such as the Nova Legenda Angliae carried the story of his passion onward.

His feast is observed on 20 November. In Christian art he is represented with the sword and the arrow, the instruments of his torture. He is venerated as a martyr and honoured as a patron of kings, of the nobility, and of England, and he is invoked in times of plague; in the Middle Ages his intercession was also sought against the wolves that troubled the countryside.

epiphanius-of-salamis.history:
Epiphanius was born at Besanduk, near Eleutheropolis in Judea, after 310, and died in 403. While very young he followed the monastic life in Egypt, and on his return to Judea he founded a monastery at Besanduk and was ordained to the priesthood. In 367 his reputation for asceticism and learning led to his nomination as Bishop of Constantia, or Salamis, the metropolitan see of Cyprus, which he filled for nearly forty years.

His authority, grounded in zeal for the monastic life, in ecclesiastical learning, and in orthodoxy, reached far beyond his island. Probably in 376 he went to Antioch to investigate Apollinarianism and intervened in the schism there in favor of Paulinus, whom Rome supported, against Meletius, whom the episcopate of the East supported; in 382 he assisted at the Council of Rome for the same cause. About 394, carried away by an apparently excessive zeal, he went to Jerusalem to oppose the supposed Origenism of Bishop John, and in 402 he was at Constantinople to combat the same pretended heresy in St. John Chrysostom. He died on his return journey to Cyprus.

Writing at the instance of his correspondents, he produced the Ancoratus (374), or The Well-Anchored, which treats especially the Trinity and the Resurrection against the Arians and Origenists and closes with two symbols of faith, the shorter being the baptismal creed of the Church of Constantia. From a mere list of heresies in that work grew the Panarion (374-377), the Medicine Chest, a stock of remedies against the poisons of heresy: in three books comprising seven volumes it treats eighty heresies, twenty of them prior to Christ, three of which are the generic names Hellenism, Samaritanism, and Judaism, so that the true number is seventy-seven, the other sixty dealing with Christian doctrine. It ends with a long exposition of the Catholic faith.

Its value varies, for his ardour sometimes outran careful inquiry: he spoke of Apollinarianism on hearsay and at Constantinople told the Origenist monks he opposed that he knew neither their school nor their books. Yet the Panarion preserves much information found nowhere else, among it fragments on the Meletians of Egypt, two letters of Arius, the only account of the Audians, and a letter of Marcellus of Ancyra to Pope Julius. For the first three centuries he relied on literary sources alone, among them the preserved refutation of Irenaeus of Lyons and the lost Syntagma of Hippolytus, which lends exceptional value to his accounts of the Samaritans, the Jews, the Ebionites and their Gospel, and the Gnostics Valentinus and Ptolemaeus.

His character appears most clearly in the Origenist controversies, which showed disinterested zeal alongside a quickness to suspect heresy, a good faith easily taken advantage of by the intriguing, and an ardour of conviction that made him forget the rules of canon law and commit real abuses of power. He saw in Origen the chief cause of the heresies of his day, especially Arianism, opposing particularly the allegorical method and the doctrines concerning the Son, the pre-existence of souls, and the resurrection. Apart from the injustice of the controversy itself, he encroached on the jurisdiction of the bishops he opposed, hence his late conflicts with John of Jerusalem and with St. John Chrysostom, in which he was made use of by Theophilus of Alexandria. A circumstance well known in the history of images is his destruction of an image in the church of Bethel, recorded in his Letter to John of Jerusalem.

Despite such disputes, Epiphanius was revered as a saint and Church Father by the Eastern Orthodox and Catholic Churches and by other Christian traditions, and he is remembered for the unyielding love of orthodoxy that made him a pillar of the ancient faith. He is honored as a patron of church unity, bishops, theologians, and scholars, and his feast is kept on May 12.

eulogius-of-c-rdoba.history:
Eulogius of Córdoba was a Spanish martyr and writer who lived during the reigns of the Cordovan rulers Abd ar-Rahman II and Muhammad I (822-886). The date of his birth is uncertain, though it must have preceded 819, for by 848 he was a priest highly esteemed among the Christians of Catalonia and Navarre, and priesthood was then conferred only on men of thirty years of age. He was born into a noble family that had held land in Córdoba since Roman times and, like his five brothers, received an excellent education under the guardianship of his mother, Isabel. One brother, Joseph, held high office in the palace of Abd ar-Rahman II; two others, Alvarus and Isidore, were merchants trading on a large scale as far as Central Europe.

Among his teachers was Abbot Speraindeo, an illustrious writer of the age, and after completing his studies Eulogius continued to live with his family, both to care for his mother and to pursue learning with famous masters. He formed a close friendship with Alvarus Paulus, a fellow student, and together they cultivated every branch of sacred and profane science within their reach; their correspondence in prose and verse filled volumes, though they later agreed to destroy it as too exuberant and lacking in polish. Alvarus married, but Eulogius chose the ecclesiastical life and was ordained a priest by Bishop Recared of Córdoba. Alvarus has left a portrait of his friend: devoted from infancy to the Scriptures and growing daily in virtue, he surpassed all his contemporaries in knowledge and became a teacher even of his masters; poets, historians, philosophers, and above all the sacred writings were read and digested by him, while his humility remained remarkable, for he readily yielded to the judgment of others less learned than himself.

That humility appeared on two notable occasions. In his youth he resolved to make a foot pilgrimage to Rome, but gave up the project, yielding to the advice of prudent friends. Again, during the persecution of 850, after reading a passage of St. Epiphanius, he determined to refrain for a time from saying Mass so as to better defend the cause of the martyrs; at the request of his bishop, Saul of Córdoba, he set the scruple aside.

Under the Muslim rulers of Spain the Christians, though tolerated with some restrictions, felt the burden of subjection in financial exactions and military service. In this setting Eulogius became a leader of the Christian community in Córdoba and encouraged his fellow Christians to stand firm in their faith. He recorded the trials and deaths of those who confessed Christ before the Islamic courts, preserving the accounts that became the Memorial of the Saints and the Apologetic Book of the Martyrs. His extant writings give an account of nearly all that was most important in Spanish Christianity from 848 to 859, both within and beyond the Muslim dominions, and especially of the lives of the martyrs, of whom he himself proved a great part.

The circumstances of his own death are preserved by tradition: he was arrested for sheltering and defending converts to Christianity, and after refusing to renounce his faith he was beheaded on 11 March 859, the date of his feast. Shortly before his death he had been elected Archbishop of Toledo, though he never appears to have exercised that office. He is buried in the cathedral of Oviedo. Venerated as one of the most prominent of the Martyrs of Córdoba and remembered as a defender of conscience under persecution, he is honored as a patron of martyrs, scholars, and writers.

eusebius.history:
{"history": "Eusebius of Caesarea, known to tradition as Eusebius Pamphili, was born about 260 and died before 341. His birth date is argued in part from the events he himself narrates as belonging to “our own times,” which later scholars have taken to imply that he cannot have been born much later than that year. He spent his life in the Palestinian city whose see he would fill and whose church kept one of the great libraries of the early Christian world, formed in large part through the labors of the learned presbyter Pamphilus, whose devoted disciple he became and whose name he took as a mark of affection. Tradition holds that he received his first catechetical instruction and baptism at Caesarea and served there as a priest before his elevation to its episcopate, an inference drawn chiefly from the creed he presented at Nicaea, though how much biography that document can bear has been disputed among scholars.

Around 314 he became bishop of Caesarea Palaestina. When the Council of Nicaea propounded its Creed in 325, Eusebius wrote to his own diocese to explain his subscription, transmitting first the statement of faith he had presented to the council, which, read in the presence of the emperor Constantine, was found acceptable, and then the conciliar Creed as published with additions to his expressions. Many, though not all, modern scholars have understood the creed he read before the council to be the traditional baptismal creed of the church of Caesarea itself.

He stood in confidence with Constantine and took part in the great councils of the age. His Ecclesiastical History, the first comprehensive narrative of the Church from Pentecost to his own day, won him the title “Father of Church History,” and his Chronicon and On the Life of Constantine remain indispensable sources for the period. He was also a preacher on public occasions: orations at the dedication of the church of Tyre and at Constantine's Vicennalia, the latter thought to have served as the opening address of the Council of Nicaea; an address on the Sepulchre of the Saviour in 325, not extant; On the Paschal Festival, addressed to Constantine; and an In Praise of the Martyrs, preserved in the same manuscript as his Theophania and his Martyrs of Palestine. A treatise against the Manichaeans is perhaps implied by Epiphanius but not preserved.

Among his letters are those to Alexander of Alexandria and to Euphrasion, and one to the Empress Constantia, who had asked him for a likeness of Christ; his refusal of her request was made in terms that centuries afterward were appealed to by the Iconoclasts. At the Second Council of Nicaea part of that letter was read against him, with passages from the letters to Alexander and Euphrasion set alongside, to establish that he was, in the council's words, “of one mind and opinion with those who followed the Arian superstition.” Orthodox writers of later generations have likewise censured the theological sympathies by which his position at times inclined toward Arian views.

Whatever weight be given to this censure, his labors preserved the memory of countless martyrs and the story of the Church's earliest centuries for later generations. He is honored as a patron of scholars, writers, librarians, and theologians, who carry forward in their own measure the work of remembering."}

justus.history:
St. Justus carried the faith to the Anglo-Saxon peoples of England in the first generation of its conversion, serving first as a missionary, then as the first Bishop of Rochester, and at last as the fourth Archbishop of Canterbury. The particulars of his life depend almost entirely upon the Ecclesiastical History of Venerable Bede; the further details supplied by such medieval writers as William of Malmesbury and Elmham possess no historical authority. Through Bede, however, the general course of his career may be traced: reinforcement of the infant English mission, episcopal service at Rochester, exile and return beneath a heathen reaction, and government of the primacy in its early years.

He belonged to the second band of missionaries dispatched by Pope Gregory the Great from Italy, the company which arrived in 601 to reinforce St. Augustine and which conveyed the relics, books, sacred vessels, and other gifts sent by the pope for the support of the young English mission. Whether he was a secular priest or a monk cannot now be determined, for Bede is silent on the point; tradition holds him to have been a monk, but only the later monastic writers of Canterbury claim him as one of their own order.

In 604 St. Augustine consecrated him first Bishop of Rochester. On that occasion King Ethelbert bestowed upon the new see, by charter, a territory called Priestfield and other lands, though other charters in which Justus's name occurs are of dubious authenticity.

After the death of Augustine, Justus joined the new archbishop, St. Laurence, and Mellitus of London in addressing letters to the recalcitrant British bishops, but their appeal was without effect. A harsher trial soon followed. Upon the death of Ethelbert a heathen reaction swept the land, and Justus was expelled from his see, taking refuge for a year in Gaul. He was recalled by Eadbald, who had been converted by St. Laurence, and restored to Rochester.

When Mellitus, who had succeeded St. Laurence in the primacy, died on 24 April 624, Justus was elected to the vacant archbishopric of Canterbury. Pope Boniface sent him the pallium, and the pope's letter upon that occasion is preserved by Bede. Justus was already an old man, and little is recorded of his pontificate except that he consecrated Romanus as Bishop of Rochester and St. Paulinus as bishop for the North. The year of his death is uncertain, though 627, the commonly received date, would accord well with the period of about three years that the chroniclers assign to his archiepiscopate. His anniversary was kept at Canterbury on 10 November, his remains were laid with those of his predecessors at St. Augustine's Abbey in that city, and he is commemorated in the English supplement to the Missal and Breviary.

Justus's life thus belongs wholly to the first age of the English Church, reaching from the arrival of Gregory's missionaries to the earliest years of the see of Canterbury; yet of his archiepiscopate the record is almost bare, preserved in little more than Bede's notice of an old man's brief pontificate, marked by two episcopal consecrations and a pallium received from Rome.

macrina-the-younger.history:
Macrina the Younger, an early Christian consecrated virgin and a formative influence on the monastic and theological life of the Church, was born about 330 and died in 379. She is called the Younger to distinguish her from her grandmother, St. Macrina the Elder. As the eldest child of Basil and Emmelia, she was the sister of the Cappadocian Fathers Sts. Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa, and also of Naucratius and of Peter, who afterwards became Bishop of Sebaste.

She received an excellent intellectual training, though one grounded more in the study of the Bible than in that of profane literature. When she was twelve years old, her father had already arranged a marriage for her with a young advocate of excellent family. Soon afterward her affianced husband died suddenly, and Macrina resolved to devote herself to a life of perpetual virginity and the pursuit of Christian perfection. From that time she gave herself to prayer, to the reading of Scripture, and to the care of her family.

Her most enduring work was accomplished within her own household. She exercised great influence over the religious training of her younger brothers, especially Peter, and played a decisive part in their spiritual formation; it was through her that Gregory of Nyssa received the greatest intellectual stimulation.

After the death of their father, Basil took Macrina and their mother to a family estate at Annesi on the River Iris in Pontus. There, with their servants and other companions, they led a life of retirement, consecrating themselves to God; strict asceticism, zealous meditation on the truths of Christianity, and prayer were the chief concerns of that community. St. Gregory of Nazianzus and Eustathius of Sebaste were likewise associated with this pious circle and were stirred by it toward still further advances in Christian perfection. After the death of her mother, Emmelia, Macrina became the head of this community of virgins and widows, in which the fruit of an earnest Christian life matured; the form of communal life she shaped there is credited with influencing the later development of monasticism.

The principal source for her life is the biography Gregory of Nyssa composed of his sister, the Vita Macrinae Junioris, written in the form of a panegyric. In this celebrated account her brother described her sanctity, her asceticism, and her counsel concerning the soul and the resurrection.

Toward the end of 379, on his return from a synod of Antioch, Gregory visited his deeply venerated sister and found her grievously ill. In pious discourse the brother and sister spoke of the life beyond and of their meeting in heaven. Soon afterward Macrina passed to her reward, and her death was recorded as a passage of profound peace. From that conversation Gregory composed his Dialogue on the Soul and Resurrection, drawing on the words he had shared with his dying sister. In it Macrina appears as the teacher, treating of the soul, of death, of the resurrection, and of the restoration of all things; for this reason the work is known by the title ta Makrinia.

She is venerated as a patron of nuns, theologians, students, and single women, and she is remembered as an early exemplar of the consecrated virginal life within the Church. Her feast is celebrated on July 19.

mamertus.history:
Mamertus was Bishop of Vienne in Gaul during the fifth century; his birth is unknown, and he died shortly after 475. Of his early life nothing certain is recorded. The fact that his brother Claudianus Mamertus, afterwards known as a theological writer, received a sound training in rhetoric and enjoyed the personal acquaintance of Bishop Eucherius of Lyons suggests that the brothers belonged to a wealthy Gallic family from the neighbourhood of Lyons. Mamertus was likewise distinguished for his knowledge of profane subjects as well as of theology, and before his elevation to the episcopate appears to have been married. His election and consecration took place shortly before 462. As bishop he enlisted the services of his brother, who had withdrawn to a cloister, ordaining him priest of Vienne; the activity of the brothers is described in the letters of Sidonius Apollinaris, one of which is addressed to Mamertus himself.

Early in his episcopate he became involved in a dispute with Pope Hilarius over the privileges of the Bishop of Arles. Pope Leo I had regulated the boundaries of the ecclesiastical provinces of Arles and Vienne, leaving Valence, Tarentaise, Geneva, and Grenoble under Vienne and making all the other dioceses of the district subordinate to Arles. Regardless of this decision, Mamertus in 463 consecrated a bishop for the city of Die. King Gundiac of Burgundy complained to Pope Hilarius, who in October 463 directed Bishop Leontius of Arles to summon a synod from the different provinces to examine the matter. The synod decided against Mamertus, and in February 464 the pope declared that he and the bishop he had unlawfully consecrated ought really to be deposed; yet desiring clemency, he warned that unless Mamertus submitted to the regulations of Pope Leo he would be deprived of the four suffragan dioceses still subject to Vienne, while the bishop invalidly installed was to be confirmed by Leontius and might retain his see. Mamertus evidently submitted, since no subsequent reference to the incident survives.

During his episcopate the remains of St. Ferreolus were discovered, and Mamertus translated them to a church in Vienne built in honour of that martyr. He is remembered above all as the founder of the Rogation processions, the three days of penitential processions and litanies before the feast of the Ascension, a fact attested by Sidonius Apollinaris and by Avitus, his second successor. Tradition holds that, with earthquakes, fires, and other disasters threatening his people, he called the faithful to fasting, public prayer, and processions through the fields, and from this beginning the practice spread throughout the Western Church and endured for centuries. In connexion with these intercessory processions he summoned a synod at Vienne between 471 and 475. About 475 he attended a synod at Arles which dealt with the predestination teaching of the Gallic priest Lucidus; since this is the latest information preserved concerning him, he is believed to have died shortly afterwards.

After his death he was venerated as a saint. His name stands in the Martyrologium Hieronymianum and in the martyrology of Florus of Lyons under 11 May, the day on which his feast is still celebrated; in popular tradition he stands first among the so-called Ice Saints. He is honoured as patron of earthquakes and natural disasters and is invoked for good weather, patronages that reflect the intercessory processions he established, and he is counted among the patrons of bishops, remembered as a shepherd who governed his diocese with care and taught that the answer to calamity is not despair but humble, united prayer.

marcus-eremita.history:
Saint Marcus Eremita, known in Greek as Markos ho eremites, the Hermit, and also called Mark the Monk or Mark the Ascetic, was a theologian and ascetic writer of some importance in the fifth century. Various theories about his period and works were once advanced; these seem now to be supplanted by J. Kunze in his study Marcus Eremita, published at Leipzig in 1896. According to Kunze, Mark was superior of a laura, a settlement of hermit monks, at Ancyra, and then, as an old man, left his monastery to become a hermit, probably in the desert east of Palestine, near St. Sabas. He was a contemporary of Nestorius and died probably before the Council of Chalcedon in 451.

Among the earlier theories, the fourteenth-century historian Nicephorus Callistus, in his Historia Ecclesiastica, says that Mark was a disciple of St. John Chrysostom. Cardinal Bellarmine, writing in 1631, thought that this Mark was the monk who, in the year 900, prophesied to the Emperor Leo VI ten more years of life, an opinion refuted by Tillemont in his Mémoires. Another view, supported by the Byzantine Menaia, identifies him with the Egyptian monk mentioned by Palladius in the Historia Lausiaca, who lived in the fourth century. The discovery and identification of his treatise Against the Nestorians by P. Kerameus, published in his Analekta at St. Petersburg in 1891, made his period certain, confirming the dating defended by Kunze.

Ten works are attributed to Mark. Two are ascetic treatises for monks: Of the Spiritual Law, and Concerning Those Who Think to Be Justified Through Works. To these are added Of Penitence; Of Baptism; a letter To Nicholas on refraining from anger and lust; a Disputation Against a Scholar, directed against appearing before civil courts and on the subject of celibacy; the Consultation of the Mind with Its Own Soul, a work of reproach against the man who makes Adam, Satan, and other men responsible for his sins instead of himself; On Fasting and Humility; On Melchisedek, directed against those who hold that Melchisedek was an apparition of the Word of God; and Against the Nestorians, a treatise against that heresy, arranged without order. The first nine of these works are named and described in the Myrobiblion and are published in Gallandi's Bibliotheca veterum Patrum, printed at Venice in 1788, a collection reprinted with Gallandi's prolegomena in Migne's Patrologia Graeca. Further bibliographical notices of his works are found in the Bibliotheca Graeca of Fabricius-Harles and in the Institutiones Patrologiae of Jungmann and Fessler.

Mark is rather an ascetic than a dogmatic writer. He is content to accept dogmas from the Church, and his interest is in the spiritual life as it should be led by monks. Practical rather than mystic, he belongs to the Antiochene School and shows himself to be a disciple of St. John Chrysostom.

He is honored on May 20; in later devotion he has been invoked as a patron of hermits, theologians, writers, and contemplatives.

martin-of-braga.history:
Martin of Braga, also remembered as Martin of Dumio, was born about 520 in Pannonia and died in 580 at Braga in Portugal. After making a pilgrimage to Palestine he became a monk there, and there met Spanish pilgrims whose narrations induced him to go to Galicia, in northwestern Spain, with the purpose of converting the Suevi, some of whom were still half pagan and others Arian. He arrived in Spain in 550.

He founded various monasteries, among them that of Dumio, of which he became abbot and afterwards bishop. At the Synod of Braga, held in May 561, he signed as Bishop of Dumio. Later he became Archbishop of Braga, and in that capacity presided over the second Council of Braga in 572. He was successful in converting the Arian Galicians and in rooting out the last remnants of paganism among them. In later times he was honored with the designation Apostle to the Suevi.

His learning and piety were remarked upon in his own lifetime. Gregory of Tours, a contemporary historian, styles him plenus virtutibus, full of virtue, and relates that he was so steeped in letters that he was held second to none of his time.

Most of Martin's writings are moral, liturgical, and ascetical treatises. The best known of the moral works, the Formula vitae honestae, which Isidore of Seville also entitles De differentiis quatuor virtutum, sets out the Christian life chiefly for laymen through the four cardinal virtues and is believed to rest on a lost work of Seneca; his De ira is a compendium of Seneca's three books on anger. Three further treatises, Pro repellenda jactantia, De superbia, and Exhortatio humilitatis, set forth Christian morality.
