Of lasting importance in the history of medieval canon law is his collection of eighty-four canons, the Collectio orientalium canonum, or Capitula Martini, compiled after 561 and drawn mostly from Greek sources, with a few Spanish and African canons; its first part treats the ordination and duties of clerics, its second the duties and faults of laymen. He explained to the people why Easter is kept on variable dates in his little work De pascha, and answered a Spanish bishop who supposed the triple aspersion of baptism to be of Arian origin in his Epistola ad Bonifatium de trina mersione.

His ascetical works include the Sententiae patrum Aegyptiorum, a collection of narratives of Egyptian monastic life and sayings of Egyptian abbots translated from the Greek, and the Verba seniorum, a work of similar character rendered from the Greek by Paschasius, a deacon of Dumio, by Martin's order and with his help. A sermon, De correctione rusticorum, was directed against the pagan superstitions still prevalent among the peasantry of his diocese, and three poetical inscriptions also survive.

Martin is venerated as a saint, his feast kept on the twentieth of March, and is honored as a patron of bishops, missionaries, converts, and monks. No complete edition of his works has ever been published.

maurus.history:
Saint Maurus (c. 512-584) was a deacon, the son of Equitius, a nobleman of Rome, although several towns, among them Fondi, Gallipoli, and Lavello, have also claimed him. He was a disciple of Saint Benedict of Nursia and his chief support at Subiaco; Saint Gregory the Great, in the second book of his Dialogues, presents him as a model of the religious virtues, especially of obedience. Tradition holds that his noble Roman parents offered him to the monastery as a boy, so that he is honored as the first oblate, and that his obedience was so complete that, when sent to save a drowning boy, he ran across the surface of a lake, absorbed in prayer and unaware of the miracle that had carried him. He died in 584, and his feast is kept on 15 January.

According to the Vita ascribed to his supposed companion, the monk Faustus of Monte Cassino, Maurus went to France in 543 and became the founder and superior of the abbey of Glanfeuil, later known by his name; tradition further credits him with spreading the Rule of Saint Benedict through the Frankish lands. This narrative, however, rests on a disputed document. The Vita has been severely attacked by modern scholars: the Bollandist Delehaye judged it a forgery of Abbot Odo of Glanfeuil of the ninth century, while Adlhoch has made a zealous defense of it. Maurus's place at Benedict's side at Subiaco, attested by Gregory the Great, is therefore more securely established than the later account of his Gallic mission, which is best received as tradition rather than settled history.

In art he is represented as an abbot with crozier, or with book and censer, or holding the weights and measures of food and drink given him by his holy master. He is honored as the patron of monks and of cobblers, in Belgium of shoemakers, and also of charcoal-burners and coppersmiths, and he is invoked against epilepsy, gout, hoarseness, and other afflictions of the sick. The sick seek his intercession through the Signum Sancti Mauri, a blessing with invocation of the saint given in the Appendix of the Rituale Romanum.

pope-miltiades.history:
Miltiades, his name appearing also as Melchiades, a native of Africa, was elevated to the papacy on 2 July, in either 310 or, as most authorities judge, 311. The Roman See had stood vacant for some time after the banishment of Pope Eusebius, and the difficult questions raised by the apostates—Christians who had lapsed under persecution—remained unresolved at his accession. The year of his birth is unknown.

His pontificate opened amid a decisive turn of fortune. About 310 or 311 an edict of toleration issued by the Emperors Galerius, Licinius, and Constantine brought the great persecution to an end, and Christians were permitted to rebuild their places of worship, though persecution continued in the eastern provinces under Maximinus Daia; in 313 the Edict of Milan granted Christianity full legal standing. The emperor gave Miltiades the right to recover, through the prefect of the city, all ecclesiastical buildings and possessions confiscated during the persecutions, and the deacons Strato and Cassianus were charged with receiving them, making possible the thorough reorganization of the Church's administration and religious life in Rome.

Early in the pontificate Miltiades had the remains of his predecessor, Eusebius, brought back from Sicily and interred in a crypt of the Catacombs of St. Callistus. In the following year he witnessed the defeat of Maxentius and the entry into Rome of the Emperor Constantine, now converted to Christianity, after the victory at the Milvian Bridge on 27 October 312. Constantine afterward presented the Roman Church with the Lateran Palace, the palace once belonging to the Empress Fausta; it became the papal residence and the seat of the Church's central administration, and the basilica adjoining it, or afterwards built there, became the principal church of Rome.

The most consequential affair of the pontificate was the Donatist controversy. In 313 the Donatists appealed to Constantine, asking him to appoint bishops from Gaul as judges in the African dispute over the consecration at Carthage of the two bishops, Caecilian and Majorinus. The emperor wrote to Miltiades and to Marcus, requesting that the pope, joined by three bishops from Gaul, give the parties a hearing in Rome. On 2 October 313 a synod of eighteen bishops from Gaul and Italy assembled in the Lateran Palace under the presidency of Miltiades; after three days of deliberation it decided in favor of Caecilian, declaring his election and consecration as Bishop of Carthage legitimate, and thereby condemned the Donatist practice of rebaptizing apostate clergy and defended the sacramental integrity of the Church.

The Liber Pontificalis records that Manichaeans were found in Rome at this time, which was quite possible, since that sect was then beginning to spread in the West. The same source attributes to Miltiades a decree forbidding Christians to fast on Sundays or on Thursdays, because those days were said to be observed by the heathen as holy fasts, and another directing that the consecrated Oblation of the pope's solemn Mass be carried to the various churches of Rome. Such customs existed in Rome, but it is probably arbitrary to trace them to this pope.

Miltiades died on 10 or 11 January 314 and was laid to rest in the Catacombs of St. Callistus, where he was venerated as a saint. His feast is now observed on 10 December; a commemoration on 10 January is recorded in the fourth-century Martyrologium Hieronymianum. He is honored as a patron of bishops, of church unity, and of peace, and is invoked by those suffering persecution.

paul-the-simple.history:
Paul the Simple was an Egyptian hermit and a disciple of St. Anthony the Great, commemorated on March 7 and honored as a patron of hermits, monks, contemplatives, and the oppressed. The principal account of his life is found in Palladius of Helenopolis's 'De Vitis Patrum', which relates the story as Palladius heard it from men who had known Anthony, and in Tyrannius Rufinus's 'Historia Eremitica'.

According to this account, Paul was a husbandman, very simple and guileless. He had been married in his youth, and on discovering his wife's infidelity he left the world and set off to be a monk, presenting himself in the desert and knocking at the door of St. Anthony's cell.

Anthony at first refused him, judging him too old and too simple for the rigors of the eremitic life. In the dialogue the sources preserve, he told Paul it was quite impossible for a man of sixty to become a monk, bade him be content with the life of a laborer giving thanks to God, and, when Paul insisted, pointed him to a cenobium, saying that he lived there alone and ate only once every five days. With that he shut the door, and Paul remained outside. Tradition holds that he persevered there in fasting and prayer, lying by the cell, until on the fourth day Anthony, fearing the old man would die, took him in.

The episodes that follow show Anthony testing Paul's resolve. He set him to weaving a rope out of palm leaves, made him undo what he had done, and do it again. When evening came he asked whether Paul was ready to eat, and the reply was that it was just as Anthony liked. Anthony produced some crusts, took one himself, and, after a long grace in which a single Psalm was said twelve times over with as many prayers, gave the old man three. When each had eaten a crust, Paul was told to take another. "If you do, I will; if you don't, I won't," said Paul, and Anthony answered, "I am a monk, and one is enough for me." "It is enough for me," Paul replied, "for I am going to be a monk." There followed twelve prayers and as many Psalms, a little sleep until midnight, and Psalms recited until day. Paul finally obtained what he wanted.

After he had lived with Anthony some months, the saint gave him a cell of his own some miles away. Within a year, the accounts relate, the grace of healing and of casting out devils was bestowed upon him, and one story tells how he exorcized a demon over which even Anthony, it was said, had no power. Under Anthony's guidance he grew rapidly in holiness, in time surpassing many of the older monks in virtue and in the gift of discernment.

The Historia Monachorum preserves substantially the same facts as Palladius, though in a different atmosphere. In Palladius, Anthony is living quite alone and is reluctant to accept Paul, his purpose being to show him just what a hermit's life really was; in the Historia he appears as a kind of abbot of hermits who invites Paul to become a monk and subjects him to the ordinary tests an abbot might apply to any postulant. The difference seems chiefly to turn on whether the story is placed before or after Anthony began to have disciples. Other anecdotes concerning Paul are collected in Butler's Lives of the Saints and in the work of Tillemont.

Paul is a distinct figure from Paul of Thebes, the First Hermit, though the two were contemporaries. John, Abbot of Sinai, wrote of him: "Paul the Simple was a clear example for us, for he was the rule and type of blessed simplicity." He is remembered as a model of the holiness that comes not from learning but from a single-hearted love of God.

peter-igneus.history:
Saint Peter Igneus, whose proper name was Peter Aldobrandini, was an Italian monk of the Benedictine congregation of the Vallombrosians, a community in the hills above Florence shaped by the reforming zeal of Saint John Gualbert. He died on 8 February 1089. His life belongs to the great eleventh-century movement for the reform of the Church.

The struggle against simony, the purchase of ecclesiastical office, led in that century to violent scenes in several Italian cities. At Florence, Bishop Peter Mezzobarbo, known also as Peter of Pavia, was publicly accused of having acquired the episcopal dignity by simoniacal means. As he strenuously denied the charge, and as numerous and prominent supporters rallied to him, the controversy caused intense agitation in the city. The Vallombrosian monks were his chief accusers, and when the people insisted upon proof, recourse was had to the judgment of God through trial by fire.

In 1068, the Abbot Saint John Gualbert designated Peter Aldobrandini for the test. Tradition holds that before a vast crowd at Settimo he walked unharmed between two blazing pyres, and thereby successfully underwent the ordeal of fire. From this trial he took the name Igneus, meaning fire-tried, by which he is known to history. The triumph of the monks was followed by confession on the part of the bishop.

Peter Igneus subsequently became abbot, and in 1074 he was raised by Pope Gregory VII to be Cardinal-Bishop of Albano. He also founded the Abbey of Santa Maria in Montepiano in Tuscany. During the same pontificate he was entrusted with important missions: in 1079 he proceeded to Germany as papal legate, together with the Bishop of Padua, to mediate between the rivals Henry IV and Rudolf of Swabia, and when the excommunication of Henry IV was renewed at Salerno in 1084, Gregory VII designated him as one of the two envoys sent to France to promulgate the sentence.

He is honored as a patron of church reform, of monks, of Italy, and of conscience, and his feast is kept on 8 February, the anniversary of his death. His name remains joined to the struggle to rid the Church of simony.

peter-of-sebaste.history:
Peter of Sebaste was born about 340, the youngest child of Basil and Emmelia, a richly blest Christian family of Caesarea in Cappadocia from which likewise sprang St. Macrina the Younger, the jurist Naucratius, and the two great Cappadocian doctors, Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nyssa. Like his brothers, Peter took his usual designation from the city of his bishopric, Sebaste in Lesser Armenia. Though he has never received the celebrity of his siblings, he was not their intellectual inferior; his genius, however, proved practical rather than literary.

Macrina, his eldest sister, exercised a great influence over his religious training, acting as his instructress in the way of Christian perfection and directing him toward the spiritual and ascetic life. Renouncing the study of the profane sciences, Peter devoted himself to meditation on Holy Writ and to the cultivation of the religious life. After his father's death he aided Macrina and his mother Emmelia in their monastic establishment on the family estate by the river Iris, and Gregory of Nyssa, in his Life of Macrina, records that he assisted his sister toward the attainment of her life's object. Gregory's account is the principal source for these years.

Shortly after Basil's elevation to the episcopal See of Caesarea, Peter received priestly ordination from him. He subsequently withdrew from active affairs and resumed the life of a solitary ascetic.

About 380 or 381 he was elevated to the See of Sebaste. Without displaying any literary activity of his own, he took his stand beside Basil and Gregory in their fight against the Arian heresy, as the church historian Theodoret records, and he was present at the Ecumenical Council of Constantinople in 381. In his life and episcopal administration he displayed the same splendid characteristics as Basil, though no detailed account of his activity as a bishop has survived.

He did, however, carry forward the work of his brother Basil, bringing to completion the hospital Basil had founded at Caesarea. His close association with the ascetic foundations of his family continued alongside these labors, and in both the practical bent of his genius showed itself.

Peter followed his brothers' writings with the greatest interest and supported Gregory in the theological struggles of the age. It was at his advice that Gregory of Nyssa composed his great work Against Eunomius, in defense of Basil's similarly named book answering the polemical work of Eunomius. At his desire Gregory also wrote the Treatise on the Work of the Six Days, to defend Basil's treatise on the same subject against false interpretations and to complete it. Another work of Gregory's, On the Endowment of Man, was likewise written at Peter's suggestion and sent to him with an appropriate preface as an Easter gift. In this quiet way he shared in the defense of the faith during the Arian crisis, and the part he played in these commissions indicates the confidence reposed in his judgment by his brothers.

His episcopate lasted about a decade. Peter died in 391 and was venerated as a saint, honored as a bishop and confessor who served the Church with quiet fidelity in the shadow of his more famous kin. His feast falls on 9 January, and he is invoked as a patron of bishops, families, monks, and the sick.

pierius.history:
St. Pierius was a priest of the Alexandrian Church who flourished in the late third century, during the episcopate of Bishop Theonas. He is believed to have served as head of the city's celebrated catechetical school, probably conjointly with Achillas. Such a school prepared those approaching baptism for reception into the Church; there Scripture was expounded with the aid of philosophy, and there Pierius labored for years as teacher and catechist, forming catechumens in the faith.

His skill as an exegetical writer and as a preacher gained for him the appellation "Origen the Younger." He was renowned for his deep learning in Scripture and philosophy, and his treatises displayed the harmony of faith and reason in an age of great intellectual ferment. The comparison with his great predecessor at Alexandria testified to the esteem his learning enjoyed.

Pierius composed a work (biblion) comprising twelve treatises or sermons (logoi). In some of these he repeated dogmatic errors attributed by some authors to Origen, such as the subordination of the Holy Ghost to the Father and the Son, and the pre-existence of human souls. Both tenets figure among the speculative doctrines for which Origen was criticized, and their appearance in his work indicates his debt to the Alexandrian master. His known sermons include one on the Gospel of St. Luke (eis to kata Loukan); an Easter sermon on Osee (eis to pascha kai ton Osee); a sermon on the Mother of God (peri tes theotokou); several other Easter sermons; and a eulogy in honor of St. Pamphilus, who had been one of his disciples.

Philip of Side, Photius, and other ancient authors assert that Pierius was a martyr. St. Jerome, however, assures us that he survived the Diocletian persecution, after which he traveled to Rome and spent there the remainder of his life, dying at that city after the year 309. On this testimony, the term "martyr," as applied to Pierius, can only mean that he underwent sufferings, rather than death, for his faith. The precise occasion and nature of these sufferings are not recorded.

Only some fragments of his writings are extant. They were edited by Routh in his Reliquiæ Sacræ, printed again in the Patrologia Graeca, and republished with newly discovered fragments by Boor; an English translation appeared in the Ante-Nicene Fathers.

The Roman Martyrology commemorates him on November 4. He is remembered as a scholar-priest who gave his life to the exposition of Christian truth during the turbulent years before the peace of Constantine, and he is honored as a patron of scholars, catechists, philosophers, and teachers.

thomas-becket.history:
Thomas Becket, remembered as St. Thomas of Canterbury, was born in London around 1119 to parents who had come from Normandy and settled in England some years before. A legend that his mother was a Saracen cannot be relied upon; his parents were people of some standing rather than peasants, and their son was well taught from his earliest years and moved among gentlefolk. He learned to read at Merton Abbey and afterwards studied in Paris.

Leaving school, he took up secretarial work, first with Richer de l'Aigle and then with his kinsman Osbert Huitdeniers, Justiciar of London. About 1141 he entered the household of Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury, where he won his master's favour and became the most trusted of his clerks, entrusted with delicate negotiations. A portrait preserved in the Icelandic Saga describes him as slim and pale, dark-haired, winning in conversation, frank of speech yet slightly stuttering, and keen of discernment in making difficult questions plain. After a year spent in civil and canon law at Bologna and Auxerre, he was ordained deacon in 1154, his chief preferment being the Archdeaconry of Canterbury.

On King Stephen's death, Henry II appointed Becket Lord Chancellor in 1155, and he became, save perhaps for the justiciar, the most powerful subject in the king's dominions. Chroniclers spoke with wonder of the friendship between sovereign and minister, declaring that they had 'but one heart and one mind'; both were hard workers deeply concerned for the kingdom's welfare. Sent to France in 1158 to negotiate a marriage treaty, he travelled with such pomp that observers asked what the glory of the king himself must be. In 1159 he seems to have been the chief organizer of Henry's expedition to Toulouse; he pressed the collection of scutage, the money payment taken in lieu of military service, enforcing it against ecclesiastics to the bitter complaint of the Church. Though a deacon, he led the most daring attacks in person, the chronicler Garnier recording that in these encounters he saw Becket unhorse many French knights; yet no word was ever breathed against his personal purity, and foul speech and lying were hateful to him. More than once as chancellor he risked the king's displeasure, opposing Henry's project for the marriage of Mary, Abbess of Romsey, to Matthew of Boulogne.

Archbishop Theobald died in 1161, and the next year Henry resolved to advance his chancellor to the primacy in furtherance of his designs upon the Church. From the first Thomas drew back in alarm, saying, 'I know your plans for the Church; you will assert claims which I, if I were archbishop, must needs oppose.' Only when Cardinal Henry of Pisa urged acceptance upon him as a service to religion did he yield, still with misgivings. He was ordained priest and consecrated Archbishop of Canterbury in 1162. To the king's surprise, he took the office with total seriousness, defending the rights of the Church against royal power, and the conflict grew bitter. After years of exile he returned to Canterbury, and on December 29, 1170, four of the king's knights murdered him in his own cathedral near the altar.

His death shocked Europe, and he was canonized in 1173. His shrine at Canterbury became one of the great pilgrimage sites of the Middle Ages, and collections recording the miracles reported at his shrine were compiled. The fate of his relics is uncertain: a skeleton found in the crypt at Canterbury in 1888 was claimed by some to be his body, though the weight of learned opinion is adverse to the identification, and the tale that Henry VIII in 1538 summoned the archbishop to trial and had his remains burned is probably apocryphal. He is honored as a patron of priests, of martyrs, of England, and of church reform, and his feast is kept on December 29, the anniversary of his death.

vladimir-the-great.history:
Vladimir I Sviatoslavich, later called the Great, was born around 958, a son of the pagan prince Sviatoslav and grandson of St. Olga. His grandmother Olga had received the Christian faith, but she could not convert her son, who brought up Vladimir in the same heathen manner. Vladimir was given the rule of Novgorod, while his half-brothers Yaropolk and Oleg received Kiev and the Drevlian lands. Sviatoslav's death in 972 was followed by fratricidal war: Yaropolk overcame Oleg, and Vladimir, fearing a like fate, fled to the Varangians. He returned with a large force, retook Novgorod, took Polotsk, slaying its prince Ragvald and marrying his daughter Ragnilda, and then took Kiev, Yaropolk being slain upon his surrender. Vladimir thereby made himself ruler of Kiev and all Rus'.

As a heathen prince he kept several wives besides Ragnilda, raised statues and shrines to the Slavic gods in Kiev, chief among them Perun, and carried his wars against the Chervensk cities, the Yatviags of the Baltic shore, and the Bulgarians of the lower Volga. Yet the Christianity first planted among the eastern Slavs by Sts. Cyril and Methodius had been quietly advancing through his lands. The Chronicle of Nestor relates that he sent envoys to inquire of the faiths of his neighbors: they spoke unfavorably of the Muslims among the Bulgarians, of the Khazar Jews, and of the German Latin churches, but were deeply moved by the solemn Greek ritual of the Great Church of Constantinople, saying they could hardly tell whether they were in heaven or on earth, and they recalled that his grandmother Olga had embraced that faith.

In 988 he besieged Cherson in the Crimea, then within the borders of the Eastern Roman Empire, and took the city by cutting off its water. He sent envoys to Emperor Basil II to ask for his sister Anna in marriage, threatening to march on Constantinople if refused; the emperor answered that a Christian might not marry a heathen, but would sanction the alliance if Vladimir became a Christian prince. Vladimir, who had already studied the Christian doctrines, was ready to be baptized. Basil II sent his sister with clergy to Cherson, and there Vladimir was baptized by the Metropolitan Michael, taking the baptismal name Basil; tradition holds that he had been stricken blind and recovered his sight at his baptism. He then married Anna, put away his pagan wives, and returned in state to Kiev.

At Kiev he took upon himself the conversion of his subjects. He ordered the idols thrown down and broken to pieces, and the statue of Perun dragged through the mud and cast into the Dnieper. Impressed by the helplessness of their gods, the people gladly accepted baptism, wading into the river in crowds; some historians have read in this readiness evidence that the faith had already spread in secret. Vladimir urged all his subjects to become Christians and founded churches and monasteries at Kiev, Pereyaslav, Chernigov, and other cities. In 989 he built at Kiev the Church of St. Mary ever Virgin, commonly called the Cathedral of the Tithes, and in 996 the Church of the Transfiguration. Laying aside the warrior's career, he established schools and ecclesiastical courts and became known for his mildness and his care for the poor.

Anna died in 1011, leaving two sons, Boris and Gleb, afterward honored as Saints Roman and David. Vladimir had parceled his realm among his children, granting Novgorod in fief to his eldest son Yaroslav, who rebelled and refused both service and tribute. In 1014 Vladimir set out to march against his son, but fell ill and died on the way, at Berestova, on 15 July 1015.

The Church commemorates him on 15 July in the Russian Orthodox and Ruthenian Greek Catholic calendars under the title Ravnoapostol, equal to the Apostles, and venerates him as the baptizer of Kievan Rus'. He is honored as a patron of converts, of the nobility, and of the lands of Russia and Ukraine.

pope-gelasius-i.history:
Pope Gelasius I served as bishop of Rome from March 1, 492 until his death in November 496. He was Roman born, though the Liber Pontificalis calls him African in origin, taken by many to mean of African descent yet Roman born. Before his election he had been much employed by his predecessor Felix II (or III), especially in drafting ecclesiastical documents, which has led some scholars to confuse the writings of the two pontiffs.

Gelasius at once showed strength of character and a lofty conception of his office in his firmness toward the adherents of Acacius. Despite the efforts of the otherwise orthodox patriarch Euphemius of Constantinople and the threats and wiles of Emperor Anastasius, he would make no peace that compromised in the slightest the rights and honor of the Chair of Peter. He combated the pretensions of the New Rome, refused to make a city's temporal pre-eminence determine its ecclesiastical rank, and defended the rights of the second and third sees, Alexandria and Antioch. Nowhere in the period, it has been said, were stronger arguments found for the primacy of Peter's See than in his works, for he never wearied of teaching that Rome's princedom rests not on any council or civic importance but on Christ, who conferred the primacy on Peter and his successors. In his letter to Anastasius he set out the doctrine of the two swords: "There are two powers by which chiefly this world is ruled: the sacred authority of the priesthood and the authority of kings. And of these the authority of the priests is so much the weightier, as they must render before the tribunal of God an account even for the kings of men." His pontificate was too short to reconcile the Church of Byzantium; the East returned only under Hormisdas (514-23).

At home he finally abolished the Lupercalia, a superstitious and somewhat licentious vestige of paganism, after a long contest outlined in his letter to the senator Andromachus. He decreed the reception of Holy Communion under both kinds, the only effective way to detect the Manichaeans, who, feigning Catholicism and holding wine impure, refused the chalice; communion under the form of bread alone later returned with changed conditions. To him are owed ordinations on the ember days and the enforcement of the fourfold division of ecclesiastical revenues, for the poor, divine service, the bishop, and the minor clergy, a rule of older standing that he frequently inculcated upon bishops. At a Roman synod in 494 he published his celebrated catalogue of the authentic writings of the Fathers with lists of apocryphal and proscribed books, though the canon of Scripture long attributed to him is now more probably assigned to Damasus. In his zeal for the beauty of divine worship he composed hymns, prefaces, and collects and arranged a standard Mass-book, though the Sacramentary bearing his name belongs properly to the next century.

Though pope for only four and a half years, Gelasius exerted a deep influence on church polity, liturgy, and ecclesiastical discipline, and a large number of his decrees passed into Canon Law. In private life he was conspicuous for a spirit of prayer, penance, and study; he delighted in the company of monks and was a true father to the poor, dying empty-handed from his lavish charity.

As a writer he takes high rank for his period, vigorous and elegant in style though occasionally obscure, and is said to have been the most prolific of the popes of the first five centuries; there survive forty-two letters, fragments of forty-nine others, and six treatises, three on the Acacian schism, one against the Pelagians, one against the errors of Nestorius and Eutyches, and one against the advocates of the Lupercalia. Venerated as a saint from soon after his death, he is honored on November 21 as a patron of bishops, theologians, and writers, among the last of the great Latin Fathers of the Western Church.

pope-caius.history:
Pope Caius, also called Gaius, served as bishop of Rome from 17 December 283 until his death in 296, shepherding the Church through the last years before the great persecution of Diocletian. His feast is kept on 22 April. The Liber Pontificalis, the ancient register of the Roman pontiffs, preserves nearly all that is known of him, and this register, together with the traditions that gathered around his name, is the source of what follows concerning the pontiff. The encyclopedia article devoted to the name Caius does not deal with the pope; it is concerned with another man who bore the same name, a Christian author, whose account is set out below.

According to tradition, Caius baptized the men and women converted through the witness of Tiburtius and Castulus, and in a time of danger he took refuge in the catacombs beneath the city. There, the legend says, he suffered martyrdom, sealing his ministry with his blood. Much of this account is bound up with the legend of Saint Susanna of Rome, and it carries the character of pious story rather than of established history. He is honored nonetheless as a patron of bishops, of confessors of the faith, and of those who minister in times of peril, and he is invoked for protection.

The Caius of that article is a Christian author who lived about the beginning of the third century, of whose personal history little is known. Eusebius mentions him several times and records that he held a disputation with Proclus, a leader of the Montanists, at Rome in the time of Pope Zephyrinus (199-217), calling him a learned man and an ecclesiastic, a designation that need not imply that he was a priest; several extracts from his dialogue against Proclus are given by Eusebius. Jerome, Theodoret, and Nicephorus Callistus also mention him, all drawing their information from Eusebius. Photius gives some additional data drawn from a marginal note in a manuscript copy of the work on the "Nature of the Universe", in which Caius is said to have been a presbyter of the Roman Church and to have been elected "Bishop of the Gentiles"; but these indications, resting as they do on a confusion of the anti-Montanist Caius with Hippolytus, are absolutely valueless. Additional light has been thrown on the character of the dialogue by Gwynne's publication of some fragments from the work of Hippolytus "Contra Caium"; from these it seems clear that Caius maintained that the Apocalypse of John was a work of the Gnostic Cerinthus. The fragments of Caius are printed in Routh's Reliquiae Sacrae and in the Patrologia Graeca.

To the author alone is owed a very valuable evidence of the death of Saints Peter and Paul at Rome and of the public veneration of their remains there about the year 200. The passage comes from the disputation with Proclus and is transmitted by Eusebius: "But I can show the trophies of the Apostles. For if you will go to the Vatican or to the Ostian Way you will find the trophies of those who laid the foundations of this church." By "trophies" is understood the memorial chapel that preserved in each case the body of the Apostle.

The name Caius thus belongs to two distinct figures. The pontiff of 283-296, honored on 22 April as a patron of bishops and confessors, is known through the register of the popes and the legends that gathered around his name; the testimony to the trophies of the Apostles is left by the author, who disputed with Proclus under Pope Zephyrinus. The indications once offered for identifying the two men rest on a confusion with Hippolytus and are absolutely valueless.

abdon-and-sennen.history:
Abdon and Sennen, whose names appear in early calendars and martyrologies in various forms such as Abdo, Abdus, Sennes, Sennis, and Zennen, are honored as martyrs by both the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Churches, with a common feast on 30 July. Tradition holds that they were Persians of noble rank who came to Rome and suffered martyrdom during the persecution of Decius, about A.D. 250. The veneration paid them dates from as early as the third century.

Their Acts, written for the most part before the ninth century, preserve the memory of their witness but contain several fictitious statements about the cause and occasion of their coming to Rome and the nature of their torments, and so must be read with caution. These Acts relate that their bodies were buried by a subdeacon named Quirinus and transferred, in the reign of Constantine, to the Pontian cemetery on the road to Porto, near the gates of Rome. A fresco found on the sarcophagus supposed to contain their remains depicts them receiving crowns from Christ; according to Martigny, this fresco dates from the seventh century.

Several cities, notably Florence and Soissons, claim possession of their bodies, though the Bollandists judge that they rest in Rome. Their relics were venerated in a number of places, and they became patrons of several towns in Spain and Italy.

Devotion to them spread through popular veneration rather than detailed written accounts. The faithful invoked them for good harvests and for the protection of children, and they came to be honored as patrons of farmers, of children, and of souls in purgatory. They stand as quiet witnesses of the early martyrs of the Church.

pope-adeodatus-ii.history:
Adeodatus II, sometimes called Deodatus, was bishop of Rome from 672 until his death on the seventeenth of June, 676. The numeral distinguishing his name arises because his predecessor Deusdedit is in certain older sources occasionally styled Adeodatus I, and the two have sometimes been confused in older accounts of the popes. Before his election to the See of Peter, Adeodatus had been a monk of the Roman cloister of St. Erasmus on the Coelian Hill.

Little else is recorded of his pontificate. The notices of his reign identify two principal concerns: he was active in the strengthening of monastic discipline and in the repression of the Monothelite heresy, the teaching that Christ possessed only a divine will, which had troubled the unity of East and West. Of his correspondence, only the letters addressed to the Abbeys of St. Peter of Canterbury and St. Martin of Tours have been preserved, and this surviving exchange reflects the continued attention of the Roman see to the regular observance of monastic houses.

Ancient tradition recalls him as gentle and generous toward the poor, devoted to sacred worship, and mindful of the repair and adornment of churches. His feast is kept on the seventeenth of June, the anniversary of his death. He is honored as a patron of bishops and monks and of the work of church reform, and is remembered as a monastic pope who served peaceably and well in a comparatively quiet pontificate.

adrian-of-canterbury.history:
{"history": "Adrian of Canterbury, also spelled Hadrian, was born in North Africa around 630 and was of Berber descent; the historian Bede describes him simply as \"by nation an African.\" While still very young he became abbot of Nerida, a Benedictine monastery near Naples; little else is recorded of his early life.

When St. Deusdedit, Archbishop of Canterbury, died in 664, Pope Vitalian intended to raise Adrian to that see. Adrian, however, judged himself unworthy of so great a dignity and begged the Pope to appoint in his place Theodore of Tarsus, a Greek monk. Vitalian yielded, on condition that Adrian accompany Theodore to England, to support his mission and act as his adviser in the administration of the diocese of Canterbury.

The two left Rome in 668, but the journey was interrupted in France, where Ebroin, the Mayor of the Palace, detained Adrian for two years. Ebroin suspected that Adrian carried a secret mission from the Eastern Emperor Constans II to the English kings; only when the suspicion proved groundless was he allowed to continue. Adrian thus came to England only after a delay of two years.

Immediately upon his arrival, Archbishop Theodore appointed him abbot of the monastery of Saints Peter and Paul at Canterbury, a house founded by St. Augustine, the apostle of England, and afterwards known as St. Austin's. It was an office he held for the rest of his life.

Adrian accompanied Theodore on his apostolic visitations of England, and by his prudent advice and cooperation assisted the Archbishop in the great work of unifying the customs and practices of the Anglo-Saxon Church with those of the Church of Rome.

Well versed in all the branches of ecclesiastical and profane learning, Adrian made the School of Canterbury the centre of English learning. Under his leadership it flourished, producing a generation of learned clergy, and he established numerous other schools in various parts of England.

From these schools went out many of the saints, scholars, and missionaries who during the next century rekindled the waning light of faith and learning in France and Germany. In this work Adrian stood among the most learned teachers of his age, a renowned commentator on the Bible and a builder of the Church in England.

After thirty-nine years in England Adrian died on 9 January; the year is given as 710, though some accounts place it around 709. He was buried at Canterbury, and his feast is kept on 9 January, the day of his death. He is venerated as a patron of scholars and teachers and of the study of Scripture."}

aelia-flaccilla.history:
Aelia Flaccilla, known also by the Greek form Plakilla and remembered simply as Flaccilla, was a Roman empress of Hispanian descent and the first wife of the emperor Theodosius I, known as Theodosius the Great. Like her husband, she was of Spanish origin, and she may have been the daughter of Claudius Antonius, prefect of Gaul and consul in 382, though this parentage rests on conjecture. Her marriage to Theodosius probably took place in 376, the year in which his father, the comes Theodosius, fell out of imperial favor and Theodosius himself withdrew to Cauca in Gallaecia. Her eldest son, the future emperor Arcadius, was born toward the end of the following year, and in the succeeding years she bore two more children: Honorius, born in 384, who also became emperor, and a daughter, Pulcheria, who died in early childhood not long before her mother. Gregory of Nyssa states expressly that Flaccilla had three children, and for that reason a son named Gratian who is mentioned by Ambrose was probably not her child.

Like Theodosius, Flaccilla was a zealous supporter of the Nicene Creed. The church historian Sozomen records that she prevented a conference between the emperor and the Arian Eunomius. Ambrose described her as "a soul true to God", and on the throne she was an example of Christian virtue and ardent charity.

Theodoret in particular exalted her charity and benevolence, relating that she personally tended cripples and preserving a saying of hers: "To distribute money belongs to the imperial dignity, but I offer up for the imperial dignity itself personal service to the Giver." In these words she distinguished the generosity that belonged to her rank from the personal service she chose to render to God on its behalf. This same historian also praised her humility.

In the panegyric delivered at her death, Gregory of Nyssa bestowed on her the highest praise, portraying her as the helpmate of the emperor in all good works, an ornament of the empire, a leader of justice, and an image of beneficence, and commending her as filled with zeal for the faith, a pillar of the Church, and a mother of the indigent. Flaccilla died about 385 or 386 and was buried in Constantinople, Gregory of Nyssa delivering her funeral oration.

She has been venerated in the Greek Church as a saint, and her feast is kept on September 14. The Bollandists were of the opinion that she was not regarded as a saint but only as venerable, yet her name stands in the Greek Menaea and Synaxaria followed by words of eulogy, as is the case with other saints. Remembered for her charity toward the poor and for her motherhood, she is honored as a patron of the poor, of mothers, and of families.

afra.history:
Afra, martyr of the early Church, was put to death at Augsburg during the persecution of Diocletian, about the year 304, and from an early period her grave there was an object of great veneration. The city, known to the Romans as Augusta Vindelicorum, lay in the northern part of the province of Rhaetia on the river Lech, not far from its junction with the Danube. Raised to the rank of a municipium by the emperor Hadrian, it was an important Roman colony into which Christianity had already penetrated before the time of Constantine; the martyrdom of Afra is itself proof of that early Christian presence. That a Christian named Afra died at Augsburg for her steadfast profession of the faith is an indisputable historical fact.

The antiquity of her cult rests on early and independent witnesses. The Martyrologium Hieronymianum, a compilation from various calendars and lists of martyrs whose original form goes back to the fourth century, records that Afra suffered at Augsburg and was buried there, entering her under the fifth of August, with some manuscripts giving the sixth or the seventh. Venantius Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers in the sixth century, likewise names Augsburg as her burial place in his poem on St. Martin, and his testimony shows that her grave was held in great veneration in his day.

The more ancient part of the extant Acts of St. Afra, an account of her trial and death, is judged by critics to date from the end of the fourth or the beginning of the fifth century, and may therefore preserve not only the fact of her martyrdom but reliable details concerning her death. In this narrative Afra appears alone, without any trace of the exaggerations and fantastic embellishments that mark the later legends of the martyrs. According to this Passion, she was condemned to the flames because she professed herself a Christian and refused to take part in pagan rites; she was executed on a little island in the river Lech, and her remains were buried at some distance from the place of her death.

It is the later portion of the Acts, a legendary narrative of Carolingian times which most critics judge to have no claim to historical credibility, that tells of her early life; it appears to have been composed to connect the saint with the organization of the church of Augsburg. According to this account, her grandparents came from Cyprus to Augsburg and were initiated there into the worship of Venus, and Afra was given over to the service of the goddess as a prostitute by her own mother, Hilaria. The legend relates that during the persecution, Bishop Narcissus of Gerundum in Spain took refuge at Augsburg and found an asylum in the house of Afra, and that through his efforts the household was converted to Christianity and baptized. Before his departure, the account continues, he ordained Dionysius, a brother of Hilaria, as presbyter or bishop.

The same later narrative adds that, after the martyr's remains were laid in the tomb, her mother, Hilaria, and her three handmaidens, Digna, Eunomia, and Eutropia, themselves suffered martyrdom by fire.

Her remains are preserved at Augsburg in the church of Sts. Ulrich and Afra, beside which stands a Benedictine abbey. Her feast is celebrated on August 7. Later tradition honors her as a patroness of Augsburg and of converts, and as one of the patron saints of Germany.

aidan-of-lindisfarne.history:
Aidan was an Irish monk who had studied under St. Senan at Iniscathay, on Scattery Island. Early Irish writers such as Ware and Lynch place him as Bishop of Clogher, a see he resigned before becoming a monk at Iona about 630. His virtues led to his selection in 635 as the first Bishop of Lindisfarne, and in time he became known as the apostle of Northumbria, credited with the conversion of the kingdom's Anglo-Saxon population to Christianity.

St. Bede is lavish in praise of Aidan's episcopal rule and of his Irish co-workers in the ministry, recording that 'he was a pontiff inspired with a passionate love of virtue, but at the same time full of a surpassing mildness and gentleness.' Tradition holds that Aidan travelled on foot from village to village, founding churches and establishing schools, and lived austerely as the mission reached the Northumbrian nobility and poor alike.

Oswald, king of Northumbria, who had studied in Ireland, was a firm friend of Aidan and did all he could for the Irish missioners until his death at Maserfield, near Oswestry, on 5 August 642. Aidan died at Bamborough on the last day of August, 651, and his remains were borne to Lindisfarne.

His feast is celebrated on 31 August, and he is honored as a patron of missionaries, of firefighters, and of England.

aldhelm.history:
Aldhelm (c. 639-709), Abbot of Malmesbury and later first Bishop of Sherborne, was a kinsman of Ine, King of Wessex. Tradition makes him a son of Kenten and thus of the royal house of Wessex, though his eleventh-century biographer Faritius wrongly claimed him as the king's brother. He received his early education at Malmesbury, in Wiltshire, under an Irish Christian teacher named Maildubh, and himself attributed his progress in letters to Adrian, a native of Roman Africa and formerly a monk of Monte Cassino, who came to England in the train of Archbishop Theodore and was made Abbot of St. Augustine's, Canterbury. Since Theodore arrived in England only in 671, Aldhelm must then have been thirty or forty years of age, and the extravagance of his Latin style has been traced with some probability to that scholar's influence.

On returning to settle at Malmesbury, probably already a monk, he succeeded his former teacher both in the direction of the school and as Abbot of the monastery, though the exact dates given by some of his biographers rest on charters of very doubtful authenticity. As abbot his life was most austere, and it is particularly recorded of him that he recited the entire Psalter standing in ice-cold water. Under his rule the Abbey of Malmesbury prospered greatly, other monasteries were founded from it, and the chapel he built at Bradford-on-Avon, dedicated to St. Lawrence, is standing to this day. During the pontificate of Pope Sergius (687-701) he visited Rome and is said to have brought back from the Pope a privilege of exemption for his monastery, although the document which in the twelfth century passed for the Bull of Pope Sergius is undoubtedly spurious.

At the request of a synod held in Wessex he wrote a letter to the Britons of Devon and Cornwall upon the Paschal question, by which many of them are said to have been brought back to unity. When Hedda, Bishop of the West Saxons, died in 705 and his diocese was divided, Aldhelm, reluctantly, became the first Bishop of Sherborne, and his episcopate in the western portion of Wessex was brief. Some of the stone-work of a church he built at Sherborne still remains. He died at Doulting, in Somerset, in 709, and his body was conveyed to Malmesbury, a distance of fifty miles, crosses being erected at each halting place where the remains rested for the night. Many miracles were attributed to him both before and after his death, and in 857 King Ethelwulf erected a silver shrine in his honor at Malmesbury.

He is judged the first Englishman to cultivate classical learning with success and the first of whom literary remains are preserved, and scholars wrote to him from both Ireland and the Continent on points of learning. His chief prose work, a treatise on the praise of virginity, was dedicated to the Abbess and nuns of Barking, a community which seems to have included more than one of his own relatives; preserved in a large number of manuscripts, some as early as the eighth century, it was afterwards versified by the author himself in imitation of Sedulius, and the metrical version forms one piece with his poem on the eight deadly sins. Among his letters is a treatise on the laws of prosody addressed to Ealdfrith, King of Northumbria, illustrated with a large collection of metrical Latin riddles. He also composed poetry in his native Old English tongue, though no specimen survives.

His vocabulary is extravagant and his style artificial and involved, yet his writings throw light upon religious thought in England at the close of the seventh century, showing an earnest devotion to the Mother of God, veneration of the saints, notably St. Peter the key-bearer, and high esteem for the holy sacrifice of the Mass, prayer for the dead, and the monastic profession. Venerated after his death, he is honored by the Church with a feast on May 25, and is remembered as a patron of bishops, scholars, and writers, a scholar-saint who joined the love of letters to the love of God.

amphilochius-of-iconium.history:
Amphilochius of Iconium was a Christian bishop of the fourth century, born around 339 or 340 into a family of distinction in Cappadocia, perhaps at Caesarea. His father was an eminent lawyer, and his mother, Livia, was remembered for her gentleness and wisdom. Probably a first cousin of Gregory of Nazianzus, he was raised in the deeply religious atmosphere of the Christian aristocracy of his native province and came to stand within the circle of the Cappadocian Fathers.

He studied for the bar and practiced law at Constantinople, but soon retired from that career to lead a religious life near his friend and relative Gregory of Nazianzus, known as the 'theologian' of Nazianzus. He was soon drawn within the circle of Basil of Caesarea and appears to have spent a time in the Christian 'City of the Poor' that Basil had built at Caesarea for the care of the needy.

Early in 374 he became bishop of the important see of Iconium in Lycaonia, probably placed there by Basil himself, and he continued to aid Basil in the ecclesiastical affairs of Cappadocia until Basil's death in 379. Thereafter he remained closely associated with Gregory of Nazianzus, whom he accompanied to the Council of Constantinople in 381, where Jerome met and conversed with him. As bishop he defended the orthodox faith against the Arian and Macedonian heresies and worked for the unity of the Church.

In the history of theology he occupies a place of prominence for his defense of the divinity of the Holy Spirit against the Macedonians. It was to Amphilochius that Basil dedicated his treatise On the Holy Spirit. Amphilochius composed a similar work of his own, now lost, though it is known that he read it to Jerome on the occasion of their meeting at Constantinople.

A well-known anecdote illustrates his attitude toward Arianism: when the emperor Theodosius rebuked him for ignoring the presence of his son Arcadius during an audience, the bishop reminded the emperor that the Lord of the universe abhors those who are ungrateful toward His Son, their Savior and Benefactor. He was also energetic against the Messalians and contributed to the extirpation of that heresy.

His contemporaries rated him very highly as a theologian and a scholarly writer. Jerome, writing of the Cappadocian triad of Basil, Gregory, and Amphilochius, observed that their books were so filled with the lessons and sentences of the philosophers that one could scarcely tell whether their secular erudition or their scriptural knowledge deserved the greater admiration. In the next generation Theodoret described him in flattering terms, and he continued to be quoted by councils as late as 787.

Of his writings, only the Epistola Synodica is considered genuinely extant, according to Bardenhewer's assessment: a letter against the Macedonian heresy issued in the name of the bishops of Lycaonia and probably addressed to the bishops of Lycia. Works circulating under his name that are regarded as spurious include the Iambics to Seleucus, an early and important catalogue of the canonical books of Scripture, and various fragments drawn from scriptural discourses, dogmatic letters, and controversial writings.

He probably died some time between 394 and 403. Honored as a faithful bishop and defender of the faith, he is venerated on November 22 in the Roman Catholic Church and on November 23 in the Orthodox Church, and is invoked as a patron of bishops, theologians, and church reform.

andrew-the-scot.history:
St. Andrew the Scot, archdeacon of Fiesole, was born in Ireland, probably at the beginning of the ninth century, to noble parents. With his sister, St. Bridget the Younger, he seems to have studied under St. Donatus, an Irish scholar. When Donatus resolved to make a long pilgrimage to the holy places of Italy, Andrew accompanied him across the sea.

The two arrived at Fiesole in Tuscany as the people were assembled to elect a new bishop. Tradition holds that a heavenly voice indicated Donatus as most worthy of the dignity; once consecrated, he made Andrew his archdeacon. In that office Andrew served him faithfully through the forty-seven years of Donatus's episcopate. Apparently at Donatus's encouragement, he restored the church of St. Martin a Mensola and founded a monastery there, bringing to Italy the zeal for Scripture and monastic order that marked the Irish mission.

Andrew is commended for his austerity of life and his boundless charity to the poor. He died about 877, shortly after his master, St. Donatus, ending nearly half a century of service to that Tuscan see. His sister, St. Bridget, is believed by tradition to have been miraculously conducted from Ireland by an angel to assist at his deathbed; after his holy death she lived for some years as a recluse in a remote spot among the Apennines. Honored as a saint from an early period, before the formal canonization process, Andrew is commemorated on August 22 and is revered as a patron of scholars, teachers, and immigrants.

assicus.history:
Assicus, also recorded as Asicus or Assic, was bishop and patron of Elphin in Ireland and is venerated as the patron saint of that ancient see. He belongs to the first generation of Irish Christianity: the early sources present him as one of Saint Patrick's converts, and he is honored as the first bishop of Elphin, in County Roscommon, in the fifth century, in the generation of Saint Patrick and the first planting of the faith in Ireland.

Before his consecration he was a craftsman, remembered in early Irish sources as Saint Patrick's own metalworker. The Tripartite Life of St Patrick calls him Patrick's coppersmith, the maker of altars and square bookcases and of the saint's patens, and its compiler records that three square patens of his making could still be seen in his own day: one in the church of Patrick in Armagh, another in the church of Elphin, and a third in the great church of Donoughpatrick at Carns near Tulsk. He was an expert metalworker and was renowned also as a bellfounder, and tradition holds that his skill supplied chalices and sacred vessels for the new churches of Patrick's mission, so that his craft became the instrument of his ministry. Called from the workshop to the episcopate, he shepherded the young Christian community of Elphin.

Of his last days Archbishop Healy gives the following account. Assicus, in shame because of a lie told either by him, or, as others say, of him, fled into Donegal, and for seven years abode in the island of Rathlin O'Birne. His monks sought him out and, after much labor, found him in the mountain glens, and tried to bring him home to his own monastery at Elphin. But he fell sick on the way and died with them in the wilderness. They buried the venerable old man in the churchyard of Rath Cunga, now Racoon, in the barony of Tirhugh, County Donegal, on the summit of a rounded hillock near the road from Ballyshannon to Donegal, about a mile south of Ballintra, where the old churchyard, though long disused, could still be seen, though later visitors sought in vain for any trace of an inscribed stone. As that account puts it, he fled from men during life, and, like Moses, his grave is hidden from them in death. This withdrawal from company into solitude, first on the island of Rathlin O'Birne and then in the mountain glens of Donegal, has helped make him a patron of hermits.

His feast is celebrated on April 27, as the Martyrology of Tallaght records under that date. He is honored as a patron of bishops, of metalworkers, whose craft he exercised in the service of the altar, and of hermits.

auxentius-of-mopsuestia.history:
Auxentius was bishop of Mopsuestia, a city in Cilicia, and is honored as a saint in both the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches. Baronius placed him in the Roman Martyrology because of a story told by the historian Philostorgius, an account preserved through Suidas.

According to that story, tradition holds that Auxentius had at one time been an officer in the army of the emperor Licinius. When Licinius commanded his soldiers to lay offerings of grapes at the feet of a statue of Bacchus, Auxentius refused. Rather than obey an imperial order that would have compromised his faith, he gave up his commission and left the army.

He was later raised to the episcopate and served the Church in Cilicia. In the record of his veneration he is honored as a patron of soldiers, an association that recalls his early service in the imperial army, as well as a patron of bishops and of conscience.

Not all of the evidence concerning him speaks in the same direction. Tillemont was inclined to believe that Auxentius was an Arian, since he patronized the heretic Aetius, a patronage recorded in Philostorgius' Ecclesiastical History and considered by Tillemont to point to that conclusion. Whatever the truth of his theological sympathies, the story of his refusal to sacrifice to Bacchus endured in the tradition.

His feast day is December 18.

benignus-bishop-of-milan.history:
Saint Benignus served as Archbishop of Milan from 465 to 472, governing that great see in the decades following the death of its most famous bishop, Saint Ambrose. He inherited a church renowned throughout Christendom and shepherded it through a period of political upheaval, as the Western Roman Empire entered its final convulsions and new powers began to reshape the Italian landscape. Though the historical record preserves little of his deeds, his name and his office witness to the continuity of episcopal faith in a time of dissolution. He is honored as a saint in the Catholic Church, remembered as a patron of bishops and of church reform, and invoked for protection. His feast is kept on September 20.

He is to be distinguished from his Irish namesake, Saint Benignus of Armagh, who from 450 served as Saint Patrick's coadjutor in the See of Armagh and whose feast is celebrated on the 9th of November. The date of his birth is unknown; he died in 467. He was the son of Sesenen, an Irish chieftain in that part of Ireland which is now County Meath, and was baptized by Saint Patrick, becoming his favorite disciple. His gentle and lovable disposition suggested the name Benen, which has been Latinized as Benignus. He followed his master in all his travels and assisted him in his missionary labors, giving most valuable assistance in the formation of choral services. From his musical acquirements he was known as Patrick's psalm-singer, and he drew thousands of souls to Christ by his sweet voice. He is said not only to have assisted in compiling the Senchus Mor, the great Irish code of laws, but also to have contributed materials for the Psalter of Cashel and for the Book of Rights. He was present at the famous synod which passed the canon recognizing the See of the Apostle Peter as the final court of appeal in difficult cases, a canon preserved in the Book of Armagh. He resigned his coadjutorship in 467 and died at the close of the same year.

Even in Ireland his memory was long entangled with that of another namesake. Most authorities identified Patrick's psalm-singer with the Saint Benignus who founded Kilbannon, near Tuam, but it is certain, from Tirechán's collections in the Book of Armagh, that Saint Benignus of Armagh and Saint Benignus of Kilbannon were two distinct persons. The former is described as son of Sesenen of County Meath, while the latter was son of Lugni of Connaught, yet both were contemporaries. The Benignus of Kilbannon had a famous monastery, in which Saint Jarlath was educated, and he also presided over Drumlease; his sister, Mathona, was Abbess of Tawney, in Tirerrill.

The oldest lives of the Irish saint are those printed in Capgrave's Nova Legenda Angliae in 1516, and later accounts are found in O'Hanlon's Lives of Irish Saints, in Hardy's Descriptive Catalogue, and in Whitley Stokes's Rolls Series edition of the Tripartite Life of Saint Patrick; the Book of Rights, said to have been compiled by Benignus, was edited by O'Donovan for the Celtic Society in 1847. Such writings belong to the Irish namesake; of the archbishop of Milan, history records little more than the dates of his episcopate, from 465 to 472, and his office in the see once governed by Saint Ambrose.

burchard-of-w-rzburg.history:
Saint Burchard was born in England of Anglo-Saxon parents; the date of his birth has not been recorded. After the death of his father and mother he left his homeland to devote himself to the missionary labor then being carried on among the Germanic peoples, drawn by the great reputation of his countryman Saint Boniface, to whom he offered himself as an assistant. Since Boniface had already been raised to the archbishopric when Burchard joined him, the beginning of Burchard's work on German soil must be placed after the year 732. In the mission field he soon showed himself a competent and zealous messenger of the Faith.

When Boniface erected the ecclesiastical hierarchy in the mission territory of Thuringia, he consecrated Burchard Bishop of the new see of Würzburg. The year was probably 741, for on 22 October of that year Burchard took part, as a bishop and alongside Witta of Buraburg, in the consecration of Saint Willibald as Bishop of Eichstätt. Würzburg thus took its place among the sees through which the newly organized hierarchy of the German mission lands received its first bishops. In April of the following year Burchard belonged to the first German synod, and on 1 April 743 Pope Zachary confirmed the founding of the new diocese in a letter addressed to Saint Boniface. As first Bishop of Würzburg he devoted himself to spreading and confirming the Christian faith within his bishopric, and the see he governed became a center of Christian life in Franconia.

In the spring of 748 he undertook the journey to Rome, where he reported on the condition of the Church in Franconia and submitted various questions for decision. The confidence he enjoyed extended beyond the limits of his own diocese. Pepin the Short held him in high esteem, and in 749, when Pepin appointed an embassy to lay before Pope Zachary the question of who should be King of the Franks, he placed Burchard at its head, together with Fulrad, Abbot of Saint Denis. That the bishop of a recent missionary foundation was chosen for so important an errand indicates the standing he had acquired in the Frankish Church.

After his return from Rome Burchard was not able to continue his apostolic activity for any great length of time. He died in Germany most probably in the year 754, before the death of Saint Boniface. What is known of him must be read with some caution, for the principal biographical sources are late: the earliest life, written in the ninth or tenth century, is regarded as unreliable, while another account comes from the twelfth century. More than two centuries after his death, one of his successors in the see of Würzburg, Bishop Hugo (984-990), had Burchard's remains dug up and solemnly buried on 14 October, and that day has remained the feast of the saint.

Burchard is remembered as the first Bishop of Würzburg and as one of the Anglo-Saxon missionaries who, in the generation of Saint Boniface, built up the Church among the recently converted peoples of Germany. Working in lands that lay beyond the old frontiers of the Roman world, he belonged to the generation that planted the faith deep in the soil of central Germany. He is honored as a patron of missionaries, of bishops, and of Germany, and his feast is kept on October 14.

caesarius-of-arles.history:
Caesarius of Arles was born at Chalon-sur-Saône in Burgundy around 470-471 and died at Arles on 27 August 543. He entered the monastery of Lérins while quite young, but his health giving way, the abbot sent him to Arles to recuperate. There he won the esteem of Bishop Aeonius, who ordained him deacon and then priest. When the bishop died, Caesarius was unanimously chosen his successor in 502 or 503, and for forty years he governed the see with courage and prudence, standing out in a troubled age as the foremost bishop of Gaul.

His city, near the mouth of the Rhône and close to Marseilles, retained its ancient importance in Gaul, but as a political centre it passed through the rivalries of Visigoth, Ostrogoth, Burgundian, and Frank. More than once Caesarius fell under barbarian suspicion. Under Alaric II he was accused, without examination or trial, of intending to deliver Arles to the Burgundians and was exiled to Bordeaux; the king soon relented, leaving him free to summon the Council of Agde in 506. In 508, after the siege of the city, the victorious Ostrogoths caused him to be temporarily deported, and in 513 he was compelled to appear before King Theodoric at Ravenna, who was profoundly impressed, exculpated him, and treated him with distinction.

Profiting by the occasion, he visited Pope Symmachus at Rome. The pope conferred on him the pallium, said to be the first ever granted to a Western bishop, permitted the clergy of Arles the use of the dalmatic, confirmed him as metropolitan, and in June 514 renewed for him the dignity of Vicar of the Apostolic See in Gaul, whereby the Holy See gained a devoted co-operator who strengthened papal authority throughout southern Gaul.

He used that office to convoke a series of councils over which he presided and whose decrees were partly or entirely his own: Arles (524), Carpentras (527), Orange II and Vaison (529), and Marseilles (533). Provisions on church property, support for the parochial clergy, the education of clerics, and simple, frequent preaching, especially in country parishes, later entered the written law of the Western Church. He also compiled the 'Statuta Ecclesiae Antiqua', a summary of earlier canonical collections long misattributed by medieval copyists to the Fourth Council of Carthage but now recognized as his work. Add to these his own Council of Agde, the Spanish councils of Gerona, Saragossa, Valencia, and Lérida (516-524), and the Gallic councils of Epaone (517) and Orléans (538, 541), these last two influenced by Caesarius, completing a contemporary documentary portrait of a great Gallo-Roman ecclesiastical legislator and reformer.

The Second Council of Orange reflects special credit on him, for it condemned the false doctrine on grace known as Semipelagianism; its decrees are believed with good reason to preserve the substance of a lost treatise on grace and free will attributed to Caesarius by Gennadius and said to have been approved and circulated by Pope Felix IV.

Caesarius belonged to the last generation of Gallic church leaders who worked to integrate ascetic elements into the Western tradition, bridging monastic and pastoral ideals. He founded a monastery for women, and as a popular preacher of great fervor his sermons shaped the faith of clergy and laity; among those who most shaped his mind were Augustine of Hippo, Julianus Pomerius, and John Cassian. In his cathedral he was the first to introduce the Hours of Terce, Sext, and None, and he enriched the psalmody of every Hour with hymns.

His contemporaries revered him as a perfect monk in the episcopal chair, his Life describing him as a cleric in rank and office yet a monk in humility, charity, and obedience. A peaceful shepherd amid barbarism and war, he was generous and charitable to a fault, a great benefactor of his church, mindful of the helpless, and tactful in dealing with the powerful. He is remembered as a preacher, a reformer, and a shepherd of souls; his feast is kept on August 27.

chromatius.history:
Saint Chromatius, honored in the Church as a patron of bishops, theologians, and scholars, was one of the most celebrated prelates of the late fourth century. He was probably born at Aquileia, and in any case grew up there, becoming a priest of that church. About 387 or 388, after the death of Valerianus, he succeeded to the episcopal see of that important city, one of the leading churches of northern Italy, which he shepherded through a turbulent age of doctrinal controversy.

Chromatius stood at the heart of the intellectual life of the Church of his day through his active correspondence with illustrious contemporaries: Saint Ambrose, Saint Jerome, and Rufinus. Himself a scholarly theologian, he urged these friends to the composition of many learned works. Ambrose was encouraged by him to write exegetical treatises, while Jerome, writing at his suggestion, dedicated to him several translations and commentaries, among them translations of the Books of Paralipomenon (the Books of Chronicles), of Tobias, and of the books of Solomon, together with a commentary on the Prophecy of Habacuc.

When the bitter quarrel over Origenism set Saint Jerome against Rufinus, Chromatius attempted to make peace between the disputants. While rejecting the false doctrines of Origen, he maintained ecclesiastical communion with Rufinus and induced him not to answer Jerome's last attack, but to devote himself instead to new literary labors, especially the translation of the Ecclesiastical History of Eusebius.

Within his diocese, Chromatius opposed the Arian heresy with much zeal and rooted it out. He likewise gave loyal support to Saint John Chrysostom, Bishop of Constantinople, when Chrysostom was unjustly oppressed, writing in his favor to Honorius, the emperor of the West, who forwarded the letter to his brother Arcadius. This intercession, however, availed nothing.

Chromatius was active as an exegete in his own right. There are preserved seventeen treatises by him on the Gospel according to Saint Matthew, treating the passage of the Lord's baptism (Matthew 3:15-17) and the opening of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:1-6:24), besides a fine homily on the Eight Beatitudes, counted as an eighteenth treatise. He died around the year 407, and his feast is celebrated on 2 December. Through his learning, his patronage of biblical study, and his steadfast defense of the orthodox faith amid the storms of his era, he left a lasting mark on the Latin Church.

columba-of-sens.history:
Saint Columba of Sens, a virgin and nun honored as a martyr, is commemorated on December 31. She is said to have suffered toward the end of the third century, probably under the Emperor Aurelian. According to the traditional account, she was born to a noble pagan family in the northwest of the Iberian Peninsula and left Gallaecia for Gaul while still a child to avoid being denounced as a Christian; upon baptism she received the name Columba, meaning "dove."

She settled at Sens, where her beauty is said to have drawn the attention of Aurelian, who sought to compel her marriage to his son and cast her into prison upon her refusal. Tradition relates that she was preserved from death by fire through the intervention of a bear and a miraculous shower of rain; the account places her beheading near a fountain called d'Azon.

Tradition holds that her body was left on the ground until a man named Aubertus buried it, in thanksgiving for his restoration to sight upon invoking her. A chapel was afterwards built over her relics, and in time the Abbey of Sens rose on the site, at one period a place of pilgrimage in her honor. She was also honored as patroness of the parish church of Chevilly in the Diocese of Paris, and is invoked as a patroness of martyrs, single women, and the oppressed. Her history is somewhat legendary, and these details rest principally on later tradition rather than contemporary record.

columbanus.history:
Columbanus, abbot of Luxeuil and Bobbio, was among the most influential Irish missionaries of the early medieval Church. Born in West Leinster, Ireland, around 540, he died at Bobbio in Italy on 21 November 615. Nearly all that is known of his life comes from the biography written by Jonas, an Italian monk of the community at Bobbio, about 643, whose informants had been companions of the saint.

Well instructed from childhood, he struggled in youth against temptation until a religious woman counseled him that there was no safety for a young man except in flight. Resolving to leave the world despite his mother's opposition — tradition holds that she cast herself at the threshold to detain him — he departed and never returned. He first studied under Sinell, abbot of Cluaninis on Lough Erne, for whom he composed a commentary on the Psalms, and then entered the celebrated monastery of Bangor on the coast of Down, whose abbot was then St. Comgall. There he embraced the monastic state and for many years led a life conspicuous for fervor, regularity, and learning. At about the age of forty he seemed to hear the voice of God ceaselessly bidding him preach the Gospel in foreign lands, and his abbot, at first reluctant, gave consent.

Columbanus set out with twelve companions — among them St. Gall and Attala, who later became his immediate successor — passed briefly through Britain, and crossed to Gaul, arriving probably in 585. They made their way to the court of Gontram, king of Burgundy, who received them graciously, and Columbanus chose for his abode Annegray, a half-ruined Roman fortress in the Vosges Mountains, where the monks lived simply on forest herbs, berries, and the bark of trees. Crowds drawn by his reputation for sanctity made larger foundations necessary: in 590 he obtained from the king the Gallo-Roman castle of Luxeuil some eight miles away, and a third monastery followed at Fontaines, their superiors remaining subordinate to him. It is said that he then instituted the Laus perennis, a perpetual service of praise in which choir succeeded choir day and night, and for these communities he wrote his rule, embodying the customs of Bangor and other Celtic monasteries.

For nearly twenty years Columbanus remained in the Frankish kingdoms, observing the older Celtic computation of Easter. The Frankish bishops, uneasy at this stranger abbot's growing influence, objected to his Celtic Easter and to his exclusion of both men and women from the precincts of his monasteries, and in 602 they assembled to judge him. He declined to appear, lest, as he said, he "might contend in words," but addressed them a letter in which freedom, reverence, and charity were strangely mingled, admonishing them to hold synods more often. In his last years he left the Frankish kingdoms and crossed the Alps into Lombard Italy, where he founded the monastery of Bobbio and spent his remaining years.

He was a man of learning who continued his studies to the eve of his death. His works include a Penitential prescribing penances according to guilt, sermons, epistles, Latin poems, and a Monastic Rule of ten chapters, far shorter than that of St. Benedict. Its first chapters treat of obedience, silence, food, poverty, humility, and chastity, with fasting more rigorous than the Benedictine code, while later chapters regulate the choir offices and assign stripes or fasts for the smallest faults. His monks wore a tunic and cowl of undyed wool and devoted much time to manual labor. The rule was approved by the Council of Mâcon in 627, yet before the close of the century it was superseded by that of St. Benedict, and for a time the two were observed conjointly in some of the greater monasteries. In art he is shown bearded, wearing the cowl, holding a book with an Irish satchel, and standing among wolves. He is honored as a patron of monks, of missionaries, and of Europe, and as a father of Western monasticism; his feast is kept on 23 November.

constantine-the-great.history:
Constantine the Great, recorded on his coins as Flavius Valerius Constantinus, was born at Naissus, the modern Nis in Serbia, the son of Constantius, a Roman officer later raised to the imperial dignity, and of St. Helena, a woman of humble extraction but remarkable character. His birth year is uncertain, given variously as between 274 and 288. After his father became Caesar he appeared at the court of Diocletian and in 305 fought under Galerius on the Danube. Permitted at length to rejoin his father, he had only just distinguished himself in Britain when Constantius died on 25 July 306, whereupon the troops proclaimed Constantine Caesar, and Galerius yielded a reluctant acknowledgement. The event broke Diocletian's scheme of a four-headed empire, and was soon followed by the proclamation of Maxentius at Rome.

While rival claimants contended, Constantine stayed in his provinces, defending the frontier against the Germans. In 311 Galerius, the most violent persecutor of the Christians, died, and when Maxentius proclaimed him a tyrant, war became inevitable.
