Though far outnumbered, Constantine marched into Italy in the spring of 312, took Susa, defeated a strong force near Turin and forced the surrender of Verona. A vision, as the traditional account relates, had assured him that he would conquer in the sign of Christ, and his warriors bore the Christ monogram on their shields, though most were pagans. At the Milvian Bridge over the Tiber Maxentius' army was completely defeated on 28 October 312; the tyrant lost his life in the river. In gratitude to the God of the Christians the victor secured the toleration of Christian worship throughout the empire by the Edict of Milan in 313, and no bloody executions followed the victory. At Milan he allied himself to Licinius by marriage, secured protection for the Christians of the East, and in the same year Licinius defeated the last persecutor, Maximinus Daia.

Treachery soon compelled Constantine to war on Licinius; the campaign of 314, with his victory at Cibalae, ended in an armed peace that lasted ten years. About 322 Licinius, openly professing paganism, began to persecute the Christians and treated Constantine's rights with contempt, and war broke out anew. On 3 July 324 his well-disciplined troops defeated Licinius at Adrianople, and a siege of Byzantium followed; his rival's overthrow left Constantine sole ruler of the empire. He then founded Constantinople and made it the new capital, the city that was to remain for more than a thousand years the heart of Eastern Christianity.

Concerned earnestly with the affairs of the Church, Constantine occupied himself with the Arian controversy while avoiding direct interference with dogma, referring doctrinal decisions to the synods; when he appeared at an oecumenical council, it was less to influence the deliberations than to show his interest and impress the heathen. He banished bishops only to avoid discord, and opposed Athanasius from the belief that Athanasius sought to detain the corn-ships intended for Constantinople. Feeling the approach of death, he received baptism from the bishops assembled around him, declaring that he had desired, after the example of Christ, to receive the saving seal in the Jordan, but that God had ordained otherwise and he would delay no longer. Laying aside the purple, the emperor, in the white robe of a neophyte, peacefully and almost joyfully awaited the end, which came in 337.

Honoured at his death as a figure of faith, Constantine was venerated as a saint in both East and West, in an age before the formal process of canonization. His feast is kept on 21 May. He is remembered as the first Roman emperor to embrace the Christian faith, the ruler whom God raised up to give the Church peace and freedom after centuries of bloodshed, and he is honoured as the patron of converts, of church unity, and of peace.

cyril-of-jerusalem.history:
Cyril of Jerusalem, born about 315, was bishop of the holy city until his death, probably on 18 March 386. Little is known of his life beyond what his younger contemporaries, Epiphanius, Jerome, and Rufinus, and the fifth-century historians Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret record. Cyril himself dates his catechetical preaching to about 347, when he was held to be only a priest, ordained by his predecessor St. Maximus; he became bishop of Jerusalem in or about 350.

Accounts of his elevation differ. St. Jerome relates that Acacius of Caesarea, the metropolitan, and the other Arian bishops promised him the see on condition that he repudiate the ordination he had received from Maximus; that he agreed to serve only as a deacon. Socrates, by contrast, writes that Acacius drove out Maximus and installed Cyril in his place. A quarrel soon broke out between bishop and metropolitan over precedence and jurisdiction, and Cyril's adherence to the full Nicene teaching on Christ may have been the hidden ground of Acacius's hostility.

In 357 Cyril was exiled on the charge of selling church furniture during a famine, and took refuge with Silvanus, bishop of Tarsus. At the Council of Seleucia in 359 the Semi-Arian party was triumphant, Acacius was deposed, and Cyril seems to have returned to his see. In 360 he and other moderates were driven out again, returning only at the accession of Julian in 361. A decree of Valens in 367 banished the bishops restored by Julian, and Cyril remained in exile until the persecutor's death in 378. Through these repeated interruptions he remained a faithful shepherd of his flock.

In 380 St. Gregory of Nyssa came to Jerusalem on the recommendation of a council held at Antioch the year before; he found the faith in accord with the truth, but the city a prey to parties and corrupt in morals. In 381 Cyril attended the Council of Constantinople, at which the Nicene faith, now a law of the empire, was promulgated by order of Theodosius, and there formally accepted the homoousion, an act which Socrates and Sozomen call one of repentance.

Cyril's lasting gift to the Church is his Catechetical Lectures: an introductory address, eighteen Lenten instructions for those preparing for baptism, and five mystagogical instructions given in Easter week to the newly baptized. They appear to have been spoken extempore and written down afterwards; the style is clear, dignified, and logical, the tone serious and full of piety. They contain local references to the finding of the Cross, the position of Calvary and the other holy places, and the great basilica of Constantine in which they were delivered.

Their subject runs through the whole faith: sin and confidence in God's pardon, baptism, whose water cleanses the body as the Spirit seals the soul, and the Creed — the Father, the eternal Son born of a virgin, His passion, resurrection, ascension, and second coming, the Holy Ghost, and the resurrection of the body and the Catholic Church. The mystagogical sermons explain the renunciations of Satan before baptism, its effects, confirmation with blessed chrism, Holy Communion, and the Mass offered for the living and the dead. Under the disciplina arcani they were to repeat nothing of these mysteries to heathens or catechumens.

On the Eucharist his words are explicit: what appears bread is not bread, but the Body of Christ, and what appears wine is not wine, but the Blood of Christ, so that his teaching plainly contains the whole doctrine of Transubstantiation.

His extant works beside the lectures include a sermon on the Pool of Bethesda, a letter to the Emperor Constantius describing a cross of light that stretched from Calvary to the Mount of Olives, and three small fragments.

Venerated as a saint and Doctor of the Church, he is honoured as a guide for all who teach the faith and lead others into the mysteries of Christ, and as patron of catechists, theologians, and bishops.

pope-damasus-i.history:
Damasus was born about 304, probably at Rome, and it is certain that he grew up there in the service of the church of the martyr Saint Lawrence. His father, Antonius, was probably a Spaniard, while his mother, Laurentia, spent sixty years of widowhood in the service of God and died in her eighty-ninth year, as an epitaph discovered in the twentieth century records. In October 366 Damasus was elected bishop of Rome by a large majority, but adherents of the deceased Liberius rejected him, set up the deacon Ursinus as an antipope, and resorted to violence in his cause. The emperor Valentinian recognized Damasus and in 367 banished his rival, though the opposing party continued to persecute the pope; in 378 an accusation of adultery brought against him was dismissed by Emperor Gratian and by a Roman synod of forty-four bishops, which likewise excommunicated his accusers.

His pontificate fell in a time of grave doctrinal peril, which he met with vigor. In Roman synods of 368 and 369 he condemned Apollinarianism and Macedonianism, and he sent legates to the Council of Constantinople convoked against those heresies in 381. The Arian bishop Auxentius of Milan was excommunicated by a Roman synod, though he kept his see until his death in 374, when Saint Ambrose succeeded him. At a Roman synod Damasus also proclaimed an important canon of the New Testament. It was he who induced Saint Jerome to undertake his famous revision of the earlier Latin versions of the Bible, and for a time Jerome served him as confidential secretary. From the East, Saint Basil of Caesarea earnestly besought his aid against triumphant Arianism, though Damasus entertained some suspicion toward him. He lived to welcome the edict of Theodosius I, De fide Catholica, of February 380, which proclaimed as the religion of the Roman State the doctrine that Saint Peter had preached to the Romans.

When Illyricum was separated from the Western Empire in 379, Damasus safeguarded the authority of the Roman Church by appointing Ascholius, Bishop of Thessalonica, as his vicar, the origin of a papal vicariate of lasting importance. He strenuously maintained the primacy of the Apostolic See, teaching that the ecclesiastical supremacy of the Roman Church rested not on the decrees of councils but on the words of Christ himself.

He restored his own titular church, known today as San Lorenzo in Damaso, and provided proper housing for the archives of the Roman Church. At the Vatican he built a baptistery in honor of Saint Peter and drained the subterranean region near the apostle's tomb to protect the bodies buried there from stagnant water. In the basilica of Saint Sebastian on the Appian Way he raised the marble monument known as the Platonia, marking the place where the bodies of Saints Peter and Paul had been temporarily transferred in 258, and adorned it with a historical inscription.

Damasus is remembered above all for his devotion to the Roman martyrs. He restored the catacombs and composed epitaphs in honor of the saints buried there, executed by his friend Furius Dionysius Filocalus in the distinctive lettering known as the Damasan letters, and he also wrote brief epigrams on various martyrs and saints and some short hymns. Saint Jerome records that he treated the subject of virginity in prose and verse, but no such work has been preserved.

Damasus died on 11 December 384, and according to the Liber Pontificalis he was buried in the small church he had built on the Via Ardeatina, between the cemeteries of Callistus and Domitilla, together with his mother and sister; its ruins were discovered in 1902 and 1903. Venerated as a saint from antiquity, before the establishment of the Church's formal canonization process, he is honored on December 11 and invoked as a patron of scholars and theologians and of those who seek healing, remembered as a pope who loved the Scriptures and the martyrs.

didymus-the-blind.history:
Didymus the Blind was a Christian theologian of fourth-century Alexandria, born about 310 or 313 and dying about 395 or 398 at the age of eighty-five. Blind from the age of four, he nevertheless became one of the most learned men of his period. Rufinus relates that in his youth he prayed not for the sight of his bodily eyes but for the illumination of his heart. To St. Anthony he admitted that blindness grieved him, and the saint asked how a wise man could regret the loss of what he shared with ants and flies and gnats, and not rejoice in a spiritual sight like that of the saints and Apostles. St. Jerome habitually called him not the Blind but the Seer.

He studied not by reading but by listening, and kept long and frequent vigils; when his reader fell asleep, Didymus did not rest, but turned over what he had heard until it seemed inscribed on his mind. In this way he amassed a vast knowledge of grammar, rhetoric, logic, music, arithmetic, and geometry, with a perfect familiarity with Holy Scripture. He was early placed at the head of the catechetical school of Alexandria, over which he presided for about half a century.

St. Athanasius esteemed him highly, and the orator Libanius wrote that no one could be ignorant of Didymus unless he were ignorant of the great city wherein he had been night and day pouring out his learning for the good of others. Rufinus was his pupil for six years, Palladius visited him four times in ten years, probably 388-398, and Jerome spent a month with him to resolve his doubts on difficult passages of Scripture.

Didymus remained a layman all his life, leading an ascetic life in the city rather than the desert. The notion that he was married rests on a mistaken identification with a Didymus in a letter of St. Isidore of Pelusium. He told Palladius a story of a vision while dwelling on the thought of Julian as a persecutor: after taking no food he fell asleep and saw white horses whose riders cried out that Julian had died that day at the seventh hour, that he should eat, and that he should inform Athanasius the bishop. He noted the hour and the month, and found the event so.

A principal opponent of Arianism, he was perfectly orthodox in his Trinitarian and Christological doctrine, more explicit than St. Athanasius on the unity of the Trinity and the divinity of the Holy Ghost; combining the vocabulary of Athanasius with that of Basil and Gregory Nazianzen, he continually used the formula of three hypostases and one essence, though scholars differ on whether he invented it. His work on the Holy Spirit survives in Jerome's Latin translation; his three books De Trinitate, composed after 379, are preserved almost entire, and his treatise against the Manichaeans is nearly complete. His exegetical fragments on the Psalms are the most important, and a commentary on the Catholic Epistles is known through a Latin translation made for Cassiodorus, though in one place he declares II Peter spurious.

In his commentaries he shows the influence of Origen in care for the text and grammar and in wide allegorizing, but traces of Origenist heresy in his extant works are slight; he seems to have held the pre-existence of the soul. A follower of Origen who adopted many of his errors, he fell from favour in later ages; Jerome, when he made war on Origenism, ceased to boast of being his disciple. Though not named in the condemnation of Origen by Justinian, Didymus was anathematized together with Evagrius Ponticus in the edict of the Patriarch Eutychus of Constantinople, and was included in the condemnations of the Origenists by the sixth and seventh councils; this censure is to be taken as applying to his doctrine and not to his person. Since the works of a supposed heretic were not copied in the Middle Ages, most of his very numerous writings were lost, and later ages neglected him.

He was nevertheless honoured as a saint, and he is invoked as a patron of the blind, of theologians, and of scholars.

dionysius-of-alexandria.history:
St. Dionysius of Alexandria, whom Eusebius, St. Basil, and others called 'the Great', stands after St. Cyprian as the most eminent bishop of the third century. Born about the year 190 or earlier and said to have been of distinguished parentage, he became a Christian while still young. When a priest warned him of the danger in reading the books of heretics, a vision, as he himself relates, assured him that he was capable of proving all things, a faculty he credited with his own conversion. He studied under Origen, succeeded Heraclas as head of the famous catechetical school, and in December of 248 succeeded Heraclas again as the fourteenth Pope and Patriarch of Alexandria; he is thought to have retained the school's guidance even as bishop.

His pontificate opened amid violence. In the last year of the emperor Philip, 249, a riot at Alexandria, roused by a popular prophet and poet, had all the effect of a severe persecution, an event Dionysius described in his letter to Fabius of Antioch. He records how the mob beat and stoned the old man Metras; how the woman Quinta, refusing to sacrifice, was dragged along the pavement, dashed against millstones, and stoned; how the aged virgin Apollonia, her teeth knocked out, sprang of her own accord into the fire prepared for her rather than utter blasphemies; and how Serapion was dashed down from his own house with all his limbs broken. The houses of the faithful were plundered and no Christian could pass safely into the streets, yet so far as the bishop knew not one apostatized.

Decius instituted a legal persecution in January 250. Many at Alexandria conformed through fear, official position, or the persuasion of friends, but others bore witness with constancy. Julian and Kronion were scourged through the city on camels and then burnt; the soldier Besas, who protected them from insult, was beheaded; the aged Mercuria and Dionysia, a mother of many children, suffered by the sword; Nemesion was burnt between two robbers; and Dioscorus, a boy of fifteen, stood so firm under torture that the judge dismissed him for very shame. The steward Ischyrion was put to death by his own master for refusing to sacrifice. Many fled to deserts and mountains, perishing of hunger, thirst, cold, sickness, and wild beasts, while others were carried off as slaves. The prefect Sabinus sent a detective to search for Dionysius, who looked everywhere except the bishop's own house, where the saint had quietly remained; on the fourth day he departed by night with his household and certain brethren, passing through exile and barely escaping death.

Afterward he confronted the question of the lapsed. Some had been readmitted to fellowship by the martyrs, and Dionysius urged Fabius of Antioch, who inclined toward Novatian, to respect that judgment of men he called blessed martyrs, now seated with Christ and assessors in His judgment. Among the stories he preserved is that of the aged Serapion, who after a blameless life had sacrificed and could find no one to absolve him, yet received the Eucharist on his deathbed through his grandson and immediately expired. Like St. Cyprian he corresponded with the popes of his day, though neither mentions the other by name.

He was less a great theologian than a great administrator, and his writings took the form of letters; only one survives complete, preserved in Greek canon law, while Eusebius preserves many others in citation, and St. Athanasius quotes him for his defense of the divinity of the Word against heresy. Amid persecution and the plague that afterward devastated the city, he guided the Church of Alexandria with charity and clear doctrine.

Having grown old in the service of his see, he was obliged by age and infirmity to decline a summons to a synod at Antioch, sending a letter in his place. He died soon afterwards, in March of 264, after about fifteen years of shepherding the church through some of the fiercest trials Christians had known.

donatus-of-fiesole.history:
Donatus was an Irish teacher and poet who served as Bishop of Fiesole in Tuscany from about 829 to 876. The principal account of his life survives in an ancient collection of the Vitae Patrum, of which an eleventh-century copy is preserved in the Laurentian library of Florence. According to this Life, Donatus was born in Ireland of a noble family, and about 816 he visited the tombs of the Apostles in Rome. A later tradition, not recorded in the Life, adds that he made the journey in the company of his disciple Andrew.

The Life relates that, as Donatus traveled northward on his return, Divine Providence led him to Fiesole, and that he entered the city at the moment when the people were gathered about their altars, praying for a bishop to deliver them from the temporal and spiritual evils that afflicted them. He was raised to the see by popular acclaim.

As bishop, Donatus instituted a revival of piety and learning in the church entrusted to him. He did not disdain to teach the art of metrical composition himself, and the Life is interspersed with short poems by the saintly bishop. The best known of these is a twelve-line poem in which he describes the beauty and fertility of his native land and the prowess and piety of its inhabitants.

Donatus composed an epitaph for himself, in which he alludes to his birth in Ireland, his years in the service of the princes of Italy, Lothair and Louis, his episcopate at Fiesole, and his activity as a teacher of grammar and poetry. His feast day is observed on October 22, and he is honored as a patron of teachers, poets, and scholars.

edward-the-martyr.history:
Edward the Martyr was king of the English from 975 until he was killed on March 18, 979, though some accounts give the year of his death as 978. Born about 962, he was the eldest son of King Edgar the Peaceful and, through his younger half-brother Æthelred, uncle to St. Edward the Confessor. Edgar's death in 975 left the succession disputed between two children, so that the struggle, fought out among the great men of the kingdom, was in substance one between rival family alliances rather than between the young claimants themselves. A party headed by Queen Ælfthryth, Edward's stepmother and the mother of Æthelred, then a boy of about seven, sought the crown for her own son, and she was supported by Bishop Æthelwold of Winchester. Edward's claim, on the other hand, was upheld by St. Dunstan, Archbishop of Canterbury, by the clergy, by most of the nobles, and by Æthelwine, ealdorman of East Anglia. Having been acknowledged by the Witan, Edward was chosen as king and was crowned by Dunstan.

Though only about thirteen years old at his accession, the young king was already regarded as having given promise of high sanctity. His reign lasted three and a half years, yet he was remembered as one who won the affection of his people by his many virtues and who acted as a defender of the Church, in contrast with the party that had opposed his accession and that the old accounts describe as that of the irreligious. The queen, however, is said never to have abandoned her designs against him, and at the last she is held to have contrived his death.

On March 18, 979, while hunting in Dorset, Edward chanced to call at Corfe Castle, where his stepmother then resided. According to the traditional account, a glass of mead was offered to him as he sat drinking on horseback at the castle gate, and while he drank it he was stabbed in the body by an assassin, reportedly one of the retainers of his stepmother, the deed being laid to the contrivance of the queen's household. Edward rode away, but he soon fell from his horse, and tradition holds that, dragged by one foot in the stirrup, he was flung into a deep morass, where his body was afterward revealed by a pillar of light.

The king's body was first buried at Wareham. Three years later, it is said, his remains were found entire, and they were translated to Shaftesbury Abbey by St. Dunstan and by Earl Alfere of Mercia, who in Edgar's lifetime had been one of Edward's chief opponents. At his shrine many miracles were reported as obtained through his intercession. Queen Ælfthryth, tradition records, was in time struck with repentance for her crimes; she built the two monasteries of Wherwell and Ambresbury, and in the first of these she ended her days in penance.

The violence of Edward's end, joined to his own defense of the Church and to the character ascribed to the party opposed to him, obtained for him from the faithful the title of Martyr. He was venerated as a martyr immediately after his death, and his cult spread rapidly. His name is found in all the old English calendars on March 18 and is also recorded in the Roman Martyrology, and his feast is traditionally kept on that date. In later devotion he has been honored among the martyrs and as a patron of England and of the nobility, and he is remembered today among the royal saints of the English people.

eimhin.history:
Eimhin was abbot and bishop of Ros-mic-Truin in Ireland, probably in the sixth century. He came of the royal race of Munster and was brother of two other saints, Culain and Dairmid. Of the early part of his religious life little is known; his story comes into focus only when he is found at the head of the monastery of Ros-mic-Truin.

He became abbot in succession to the monastery's founder, St. Abban. Since it is recorded that a number of monks "followed the man of God from his own country of Munster", he was apparently connected beforehand with one of the religious houses of the south of Ireland. Ros-mic-Truin itself lies in South Leinster on the bank of the River Barrow, only eight miles by water from the confines of Munster, at the point where the Suir and the Barrow meet and in confluence enter the Atlantic. Although the abbey had been founded by St. Abban, it is said to have been colonized by Eimhin. So many religious and students from the south of Ireland came to dwell there that the place came to be called "Ros-glas of the Munstermen".

By some writers he is named as the author of the life of St. Patrick known as the Vita Tripartita, originally published by Father John Colgan and edited by Whitley Stokes. Of the lives of St. Patrick that are extant, this work contains a greater variety of details concerning the mission of the Apostle of Ireland than any other.

He was famous for many and great miracles. The date of his death has not been recorded, though competent authorities assign it to the earlier half of the sixth century.

Tradition holds that after his death his consecrated bell was held in great veneration and was used as a swearing relic down to the fourteenth century, oaths and promises made upon it being deemed inviolable. Among the manuscripts of the library of the Royal Irish Academy in Dublin are a prose tract entitled Caine Emine, that is, the tribute or rule of Eimhin, and a poem of several stanzas relating to the saint's bell. His name is preserved in the Irish calendars, and he is remembered as one of the early abbots and bishops of Ireland.

elias-i-of-jerusalem.history:
St. Elias I of Jerusalem (died 518) was, with Flavian of Antioch, one of the two Catholic bishops who resisted the attempt of the Emperor Anastasius I (491-518) to abolish the Council of Chalcedon (451). An Arab by birth and educated in a monastery in Egypt, Elias served as Bishop of Jerusalem from 494 to 513, years in which the imperial government sought to impose Monophysitism upon the church.

In 457 he had been driven from Egypt by the Monophysite Patriarch of Alexandria, Timothy the Cat. He made his way to Palestine, founded a laura at Jericho, and was ordained priest by Anastasius of Jerusalem. In 494 he succeeded Sallustius as Bishop of Jerusalem. He acknowledged Euphemius of Constantinople and refused communion to Macedonius, the intruder in that see, and he founded many monasteries throughout his patriarchate.

The emperor Anastasius, unlike his predecessors, who had favored Monophysitism chiefly as a political expedient for conciliating Egypt and Syria, pursued that policy apparently from religious conviction, under the influence of his chief adviser Marinus, himself a convinced Monophysite. At first he sought compromise, since the population of Constantinople and nearly all the European provinces were too Chalcedonian for an open attack on the council to be safe; but he went over wholly to the Monophysite cause, and in his chapel the Trisagion was sung with the Monophysite addition 'who was crucified for us.' The Acacian schism continued through his reign. In 511 Macedonius II, Patriarch of Constantinople, who had signed Zeno's Henotikon of 482 but refused to condemn the Council of Chalcedon, was deposed; his successor Timothy I began a fierce persecution of Catholics.

About 509 the Monophysite Xenaias of Hierapolis tried to make Elias sign a Monophysite formula, and the emperor ordered him to summon a synod that should condemn the Council of Chalcedon. Elias sent the emperor instead a Catholic profession of faith, but the document appears to have been falsified on the way. According to the historian Evagrius, the version delivered at court contained an anathema against those who speak of two natures in Christ; the bishop, saying that it had been tampered with, sent another without that anathema, and protested at once against the heretical formula brought to the emperor in his name.

A synod summoned at Sidon in 512 was expected to condemn the Council of Chalcedon and to depose Elias and Flavian of Antioch; it was chiefly Elias who prevented this result, as the two succeeded in persuading the assembled Fathers to do neither. The Monophysites continued to accuse the bishops of Nestorianism, and Anastasius deposed them in spite of the protest of Elias' legate, Sabas. Flavian was deposed first, and Severus, an open Monophysite, was introduced at Antioch; with him Elias and the monks of Palestine would have no communion.

The Count of Palestine, Olympus, then arrived at Jerusalem and offered Elias his choice of signing a Monophysite formula or being deposed. Elias refused to sign and was banished to Aila on the Red Sea in 513. His monks remained faithful to him to the end, and he died in exile in 518, remembered as a confessor of the orthodox faith.

The common presentation of Elias as a compromiser is unjust: he was steadfastly Catholic throughout. He is honored as a patron of bishops, of church unity, and of those who suffer persecution. His feast is kept on 20 July in the Eastern Orthodox Church, and with St. Flavian of Antioch he is named in the Roman Martyrology on 4 July.

emerentiana.history:
Emerentiana was a Roman virgin and martyr who died at Rome in the third century. Her cult is attested by the old Itineraries, the early guides to the graves of the Roman martyrs, which speak of her burial on the Via Nomentana near that of Saint Agnes. Over her grave a church was built which, according to these same Itineraries, stood near the church raised over the place of Saint Agnes's burial, though somewhat farther from the city wall. She was in fact interred in the coemeterium majus in that vicinity, not far from the cemetery of Agnes, and the archaeologist Armellini believed that he had discovered her original burial chamber there.

Tradition holds that she was the foster-sister of Saint Agnes, a bond preserved in the legend of that saint. According to this account, only a few days after Agnes's burial Emerentiana went to the grave to pray. She was still a catechumen, not yet baptized, when a crowd of pagans attacked her as she prayed and killed her with stones. Her death at the tomb of her foster sister gave her the crown of martyrdom, and in Christian art she is represented with stones in her lap, and also with a palm or a lily.

Her feast is kept on 23 January. The Martyrologium Hieronymianum likewise records her, though it places her under 16 September and notes her grave in the coemeterium majus. In later devotion she has been honored as a patroness of those suffering from stomach ailments, a devotion rooted in popular piety, and she has also been invoked as a protector and as an intercessor for the oppressed. Her memory belongs to the earliest generations of Roman Christianity, a witness whose faith endured to the point of death at the tomb of a fellow martyr.

eucharius.history:
Saint Eucharius is remembered as the first Bishop of Trier, the ancient see on the Moselle that became one of the oldest centers of Christianity north of the Alps. He is placed in the second half of the third century, the period in which the faith first took root in the Rhineland, and modern historians generally hold that the first missionaries reached Gaul, to which Trier then belonged, not earlier than about 250, assigning the early bishops of Trier to the period following that date.

The account of his life rests largely on medieval tradition, preserved in the Gesta Treverorum, a chronicle compiled at the monastery of St. Matthias near Trier. According to this tradition, Eucharius was one of the seventy-two disciples of Christ and was sent to Gaul by St. Peter as bishop, together with the deacon Valerius and the subdeacon Maternus, to preach the Gospel. The three made their way to the Rhine and to Elegia, in Alsace, where Maternus died. Tradition holds that Eucharius and Valerius hastened back to St. Peter, who gave his pastoral staff to Eucharius; upon being touched with it, Maternus, who had lain forty days in his grave, returned to life. The legend relates that the Gentiles were then converted in large numbers, and that after founding many churches the three companions came to Trier, where the work of evangelization advanced so rapidly that Eucharius chose that city for his episcopal residence. The same tradition credits him with raising a dead person to life and relates that an angel announced his approaching death, pointing to Valerius as his successor.

He is said to have governed the see for twenty-five years, to have died on December 8, the day on which his feast is kept, and to have been buried in the church of St. John outside the city. Valerius, according to the same account, was bishop for fifteen years and was succeeded by Maternus, who in the meantime had founded the dioceses of Cologne and Tongres and governed as bishop for forty years in all.

The staff of St. Peter, with which Maternus had been restored to life, was preserved at Cologne until the end of the tenth century, when its upper half was presented to Trier and later taken to Prague by Emperor Charles IV. In the Middle Ages it was believed that the pope used no crozier because St. Peter had sent his episcopal staff to St. Eucharius, a view with which Innocent III concurred. More recent criticism interprets the staff rather as the distinctive mark of an envoy, especially of a missionary; missionaries of later centuries, such as St. Boniface, were occasionally called ambassadors of St. Peter.

Historians have found many contradictions and inaccuracies in these records. Medieval dioceses often claimed origins as early as possible to increase their reputation and perhaps their rights, and the more reliable earlier accounts were lost, especially through the ravages of the Normans; when the lives of the holy founders of ancient Trier came to be written anew, gaps in the tradition were filled with fanciful legends, and an amplification of the story is attributed to the monk Goldscher, who lived at St. Matthias about 1130. From the Gesta the narrative passed unchallenged into numerous medieval works.

Within that older tradition, Eucharius is honored among the earliest missionary bishops who carried the Gospel into the Germanic lands, and as the one who laid the foundations upon which later bishops of Trier would build. He is invoked as a patron of missionaries and priests, and of Germany.

eugenius-of-carthage.history:
Eugenius was a Christian prelate of North Africa in the wretched days when the Vandals had overrun the Roman provinces and imposed their Arian creed upon the conquered. The see of Carthage had stood vacant after the death of Deogratias in 456, for the Arian Vandal kings long opposed an election; permission was at last granted by King Huneric at the instance of the emperor Zeno and of Placidia, into whose family the Vandals had intermarried. Eugenius was unanimously elected in 480 to succeed Deogratias, and he undertook the care of a flock harried by heretical rulers. He died on 13 July, 505.

His episcopate was consumed by the struggle between Arianism and the Catholic faith. His wise government, charity to the poor, austerity of life, and courage under persecution won the admiration even of the Arians. In his uncompromising defense of the divinity of the Word he was followed by his flock, many of whom were exiled with him. Contrary to royal edict he admitted Vandals into the Catholic Church, and in debate he worsted the Arian theologians whom the king pitted against the Catholics. Both sides claimed the name Catholic, the Arians styling their opponents Homoousians.

A conference between the two parties, held at some time between 481 and February 484, ended with the withdrawal of the chief Arian bishop on the plea that he could not speak Latin. The enraged Arians provoked a persecution under Huneric: forty-six bishops were exiled to Corsica and three hundred and two to the African deserts. Among the latter was Eugenius, who dwelt in the desert of Tripoli under the custody of a ruffian named Antonius. On setting out he addressed to the faithful of Carthage a letter of consolation and exhortation, still extant among the works of Gregory of Tours.

Gunthamund, Huneric's successor, allowed Eugenius to return to Carthage and permitted him to reopen the churches. After eight years of peace Thrasamund came to the throne, revived the persecution, arrested the bishop, and condemned him to death, though the sentence was commuted to exile at Vienne near Albi in Languedoc, where the Arian Alaric was king. There Eugenius built a monastery over the tomb of the martyr St. Amaranthus and led a penitential life until his death. He is said to have miraculously cured a man who was blind.

His writings include the Expositio Fidei Catholicae, demanded of him by Huneric and probably the statement submitted by the Catholic bishops at the conference, which proves the consubstantiality of the Word and the divinity of the Holy Ghost; the Apologeticus pro Fide; the Altercatio cum Arianis, fragments of which are quoted by Victor de Vita; and pleas for the Catholics addressed to Huneric or his successors, besides the letter to the faithful of Carthage.

Eugenius is revered as a saint who endured persecution with steadfastness, confessing the orthodox faith amid the exile of his brother bishops and laboring for the unity of the Church. He is honored as a patron of bishops and of church unity, and his feast is kept on 13 July.

florentina.history:
St. Florentina was born toward the middle of the sixth century in Cartagena, Hispania, during the period of Visigothic dominion, into a family remarkable for its holiness. Her three brothers—Leander, Isidore, and Fulgentius—all became Spanish bishops, and she with them was canonized by the Church. Leander, older than Florentina, was Archbishop of Seville; Isidore, her younger brother, succeeded Leander in the same see; and Fulgentius was bishop of Ecija (Astigis).

Tradition holds that Florentina was widowed while still young. Consecrating her virginity to God, she embraced the ascetic life through the influence of Leander, who before his elevation to the episcopate had been a monk. She gathered about herself a number of virgins who likewise desired to forsake the world and formed them into a religious community under her brother's guidance. Later sources place the residence of this community in the convent of S. Maria de Valle near Ecija, the city over which Fulgentius presided as bishop. In any case, it is certain that she had consecrated herself to God before the year 600.

Leander, who died in 600 or 601, wrote for his sister's guidance a work that still survives, the "Regula sive Libellus de institutione virginum et de contemptu mundi ad Florentinam sororem", on the rule of life owed by a nun and on contempt for the world. In it he lays down the manner in which cloistered virgins consecrated to God should order their lives: they are to avoid intercourse with women living in the world and with men, especially youths; to practice strict temperance in eating and drinking; to give careful attention to the reading and meditation of Holy Scripture; to hold equal love and friendship for all who live together in community. He earnestly exhorts his sister to remain true to her holy state, and Florentina regulated her life by this counsel and entered with fervor into the spirit of the religious life.

Her younger brother Isidore dedicated to her his work "De fide catholica contra Judaeos", which he composed at her request.

Florentina died early in the seventh century, probably about 612, and was honored as a saint after her death. Few details of her life survive, yet her veneration endured in Spanish tradition. She is venerated as the patroness of the diocese of Plasencia and is honored as a patroness of nuns, contemplatives, and widows. The Roman Martyrology records her name as Florentia, although Florentina is considered the correct form.

fructuosus-of-braga.history:
St. Fructuosus of Braga, an archbishop who died on 16 April around the year 665, was the son of a Gothic general, a dux whose lands lay in the region of Bierzo. He studied at Palencia, and after the death of his parents he withdrew as a hermit to a desert place in Galicia, renouncing the noble life into which he had been born. He had earlier accompanied his father on journeys across the family estates before resolving to leave the world.

The example of his retirement drew numerous pupils, and from this gathering arose the monastery of Complutum, or Compludo, over which Fructuosus at first presided as abbot. In time he appointed another abbot over the house and withdrew again into solitude. He went on to found nine further monasteries, as well as a community for eighty virgins placed under the abbess Benedicta, remembered as saintly. He is remembered as a model of the nobleman turned monk and bishop.

In 654 he was called to the bishopric of Dumium, and on 1 December 656 to the archbishopric of Braga. There he labored to reform the Church and to guide the clergy, and he came to be regarded as the greatest of the Spanish monastic bishops.

Two monastic rules remain from his hand. The first, in twenty-five chapters, was written for the monastery of Complutum and bears an appendix, called the pactum, containing the formulas of consecration and the vows. The second, known as the common rule, concerns a union of monasteries governed by an abbot-bishop and is addressed chiefly to the superiors of monasteries.

His life was written by Abbot Valerius, who relied on the accounts of his pupils. In 1102 his relics were transferred to Compostela, and his feast is kept on 16 April. He is depicted with a stag which, tradition holds, had been devoted to him after he saved it from the hunters. He is honored as a patron of bishops, monks, and hermits.

fulbert-of-chartres.history:
Saint Fulbert of Chartres, bishop and master of the cathedral school, was born between 952 and 962 and died on April 10, 1028 or 1029. His birthplace is uncertain: earlier scholars, following Mabillon, thought that he came from Italy, probably Rome, while his most recent biographer, Pfister, assigns his origin to the diocese of Laudun in the present French department of Gard. He was of humble parentage and was educated at the school of Reims, where his teacher was the famous Gerbert of Aurillac, who ascended the papal throne in 999 as Sylvester II.

In 990 Fulbert opened a school at Chartres that soon became the most famous seat of learning in France, drawing students not only from the remotest parts of that kingdom but also from Italy, Germany, and England. He served at the same time as chancellor of the church of Chartres and as treasurer of St. Hilary's at Poitiers. His pupils esteemed him so highly that they called him "venerable Socrates". In his teaching he opposed the rationalistic tendencies that had infected some dialecticians of his day, often warning his students against those who exalted dialectic above the teaching of the Church and the testimony of the Bible; it was nevertheless one of his own pupils, Berengarius of Tours, who went farthest in subjecting faith to reason.

In 1007 Fulbert succeeded the deceased Rudolph as Bishop of Chartres and was consecrated by his metropolitan, Archbishop Leutheric of Sens. He owed the episcopal dignity chiefly to the influence of King Robert of France, who had been his fellow student at Reims. Even as bishop he continued to teach in his school and retained the treasurership of St. Hilary. About 1020, when the cathedral of Chartres was destroyed by fire, he at once began to rebuild it in greater splendor, an undertaking financially assisted by King Canute of England, Duke William of Aquitaine, and other European sovereigns.

Although Fulbert was neither abbot nor monk, as some historians have wrongly asserted, he stood in friendly relations with Odilo of Cluny, Richard of St. Vannes, Abbo of Fleury, and other monastic figures of his time. He advocated the reform of the clergy, severely rebuked bishops who spent much of their time in warlike expeditions, and opposed the practice of granting ecclesiastical benefices to laymen.

His literary remains comprise 140 letters, two treatises, 27 hymns, and parts of the ecclesiastical Office. The letters are of great historical value, above all for the light they shed on the liturgy and discipline of the Church in the eleventh century, and they reveal a pastor both learned and tender, guiding clergy and laity alike. His two treatises take the form of homilies: one expounds the passage in the Acts of the Apostles describing Herod's persecution of the Church, while the other, the Tractatus contra Judaeos, shows that the prophecy of Jacob, that the scepter would not depart from Judah, had been fulfilled in Christ. Five of his nine extant sermons concern the Blessed Virgin Mary, toward whom his devotion was great, and he is credited with promoting the feast of her Nativity.

A life of St. Aubert, bishop of Cambrai, sometimes ascribed to him, was probably not his work. His letters were first printed at Paris in 1585 by Papire le Masson, and his complete works were edited by Charles de Villiers at Paris in 1608.

Fulbert is remembered as one of the most celebrated teachers of his age, a wise bishop who made the cathedral school of Chartres a center of learning and piety and a father of scholars. His feast day is April 10, and he is honored as a patron of bishops, teachers, and scholars.

gilbert-of-sempringham.history:
Gilbert of Sempringham was born at Sempringham, on the border of the Lincolnshire fens between Bourn and Heckington, around 1085; the exact date of his birth is unknown. His father, Jocelin, was a wealthy Norman knight holding lands in Lincolnshire; his mother, whose name is unknown, was an Englishwoman of humble rank. Because he was ill-favored and deformed, he was not destined for a military or knightly career, but was sent to France to study, where for a time he became a teacher before returning to his Lincolnshire home as a young man.

He was presented to the livings of Sempringham and West Torrington, churches in his father's gift, and shortly afterwards became a clerk in the household of Robert Bloet, Bishop of Lincoln. Alexander, who succeeded Robert in 1123, retained Gilbert in his service and ordained him deacon and priest, much against his will. The revenues of Sempringham sufficed for his maintenance in the bishop's court; those of West Torrington he devoted to the poor. Offered the archdeaconry of Lincoln, he refused it, saying that he knew no surer way to perdition.

When his father died, Gilbert became lord of the manor of Sempringham, and in 1131 he founded the Gilbertine Order, a double monastery of canons regular and nuns unique in England, becoming its first Master. With Bishop Alexander's help he built a dwelling and cloister for his nuns to the north of the church of St Andrew. His life thenceforth was one of extraordinary austerity, its strictness not diminishing with age despite the labor of governing the order.

In 1147 he traveled to Cîteaux in Burgundy, where he met Pope Eugene III, St Bernard, and St Malachy, Archbishop of Armagh; the pope expressed regret at not having known of him some years earlier, when choosing a successor to the deposed Archbishop of York. Because his foundation included women, the Cistercians refused to help, and Gilbert persevered in governing the order himself. Under his direction it eventually numbered twenty-six houses.

In 1165 he was summoned before Henry II's justices at Westminster, charged with having sent help to the exiled St Thomas Becket. Invited to clear himself by oath, he refused, for although in fact he had sent no help, such an oath might make him appear an enemy of the archbishop. He was prepared for a sentence of exile, but letters came from the king in Normandy ordering the judges to await his return, and he was found innocent.

In 1170, when Gilbert was already a very old man, some of his lay brothers revolted and spread serious calumnies against him. After some years of fierce controversy, in which Henry II took his part, Pope Alexander III freed him from suspicion and confirmed the privileges granted to the order.

Advancing age at length led Gilbert to resign the government of the order, and he appointed Roger, prior of Malton, as his successor. Very infirm and almost blind, he then made his religious profession, for though he had founded an order and ruled it for many years, he had never become a religious in the strict sense. He died at Sempringham in 1189, reputedly at the age of 106.

In 1202, at the earnest request of Hubert Walter, Archbishop of Canterbury, Gilbert was canonized by Pope Innocent III, and his relics were solemnly translated to an honorable place in the church at Sempringham, where his shrine became a center of pilgrimage. Besides compiling the rule of his order, he left a short treatise entitled De constructione monasteriorum. His feast is kept on February 4 in the current Roman calendar; the Catholic Encyclopedia, however, gives the date as 11 February. He is honored as a patron of church reform, of monks, and of the laity.

gildas.history:
Gildas, surnamed the Wise, was a sixth-century British monk, born about 516, who died at Houat in Brittany in 570. By his own account he was born in the year of the Britons' famous victory over the Saxons at Mount Badon, a battle the sources date to 493 or 516, whence the surname Badonicus; he is also known as Gildas fab Caw, after his father. His life is known chiefly through two medieval biographies, one by an unknown Breton monk of the Abbey of Rhuys in the eleventh century and the other by the Welshman Caradoc in the twelfth. Both contain unchronological and misleading statements; some early critics rejected them outright, and others posited two saints of the same name to reconcile them, but the more general opinion is that there was but one St. Gildas, the discrepancies arising because the lives were compiled in separate countries centuries after his death. Caradoc's statement that Gildas died at Glastonbury has been met with reserve, commentators noting that Glastonbury laid claim to many saints besides him.

Both narratives agree in their broad outline. He was born in Scotland on the banks of the Clyde, possibly at Dumbarton, of a noble British family; his father was named Cau or Nau, and his brother Huel or Cuil. He was educated in Wales under St. Iltut and was a companion of St. Samson and St. Peter of Léon. Embracing the monastic state, he crossed to Ireland, where he was advanced to the priesthood and is said to have lived at Armagh. The biographies recount a mission to North Britain in which his teaching was confirmed by miracles, and a return to Ireland at the invitation of King Ainmire, where he strengthened the faith of many and built monasteries and churches. Irish annalists associate him with St. David and St. Cadoc in giving a special liturgy to the second order of Irish saints, and tradition holds that he also made a pilgrimage to Rome.

His love of solitude led him, on the homeward journey, to the Isle of Houat off the coast of Brittany, where he lived a life of prayer, study, and austerity. When his retreat became known, the Bretons induced him to establish a monastery on the mainland at Rhuys, the community afterwards known as Saint-Gildas-de-Rhuys, and multitudes flocked to him. It was there that he composed his famous epistle to the British kings. His relics were venerated at Rhuys until the tenth century, when they were carried for safety into Berry; in the eighteenth century they were said to be preserved in the cathedral of Vannes. His feast is kept on 29 January, and a second observance on 11 May commemorates the translation of his relics.

Gildas's authentic work, the De Excidio et Conquestu Britanniae, is at once a history and a rebuke. It is usually divided into three parts: a preface; a sketch of British history from the Roman invasion to the author's own time; and an epistle of severe invective addressed to five petty British kings, Constantine, Vortipor, Cyneglas, Cynan, and Maelgwn, in which he also reproaches a clergy he accuses of sloth and simony. Both a record of events and a call to repentance and reform, it reveals a writer of no ordinary culture and sanctity, thoroughly acquainted with the Sacred Scriptures. Regarded as the earliest British historian and one of the best-documented figures of the Christian Church in the sub-Roman British Isles, Gildas is quoted by Bede and Alcuin, and two manuscript copies of his writings are preserved in the Cambridge University library; his work remains a foundational source for the history of early medieval Britain. He is honored as patron of several churches and monasteries in Brittany and elsewhere, and is invoked as a patron of scholars, writers, and church reform, and by tradition also of historians and bell founders.

pope-gregory-i.history:
Born at Rome about the year 540, Gregory came of a noble family: his father, Gordianus, was a wealthy patrician with large estates in Sicily and a mansion on the Caelian Hill, and his mother, Silvia, is honored as a saint, as are two of his aunts, Tarsilla and Æmiliana. His boyhood was passed amid the calamities of the Gothic wars, when Rome was successively captured, abandoned, and besieged, and the tinge of sadness that pervades his writings, together with his clear expectation of the world's approaching end, is traced to the impression these disasters left upon him. Gregory of Tours records that he was so skilled in grammar, rhetoric, and dialectic as to be thought second to none in Rome, and he seems also to have studied law; he loved above all to meditate on the Scriptures and was devoted to God from his youth up. Following the natural course of a patrician's career, he held subordinate public offices and, about the year 573, while still in his early thirties, became prefect of the city of Rome, an office shorn of much of its ancient splendor but still the highest civil dignity in the city.

After long prayer and inward struggle he resolved to abandon everything, most probably in 574, and become a monk. His Sicilian estates were given up to found six monasteries, and his home on the Caelian Hill was converted into a seventh under the patronage of St. Andrew, where he himself took the cowl, so that one who had gone about the city aglow with silk and jewels now served the altar of the Lord in a humble garment. Whether his community followed the Rule of St. Benedict was long disputed; the view that it did not has been practically abandoned. For about three years he lived in retirement, a period he often referred to as the happiest portion of his life, though the austerities he practiced then are believed to have caused the poor health that beset his later years.

His seclusion was broken in 578, when the pope, much against his will, ordained him one of the seven deacons of Rome. The Lombards were advancing rapidly on the city, and the only hope of safety seemed to lie in help from the emperor at Byzantium; Pope Pelagius II accordingly sent Gregory, in 579, as apocrisiarius, or permanent ambassador, to the court of Tiberius, where he remained some six years. Nothing could have been more uncongenial to him than the worldly atmosphere of the Byzantine court, and he maintained the monastic life there as far as circumstances permitted.

He became Bishop of Rome on 3 September 590, the sixty-fourth to hold the see, and governed the Church until his death on 12 March 604. His most famous act of evangelization was the dispatch of Augustine of Canterbury and his monks to England; his episcopate was likewise marked by a reforming care for the liturgy and practical charity toward the city's poor. His writings, especially the Pastoral Care and the Dialogues, exercised a momentous influence on the doctrine, organization, and discipline of the Church, and the chant tradition associated with his name made him patron of musicians and singers; he is also honored as patron of students and teachers.

Venerated as Gregory the Great, he is counted among the four great Latin Doctors of the Church. Later historians have found the religious situation of the Middle Ages almost inexplicable without his work, and a modern scholar has judged that the leading principles of later Catholicism are found, at any rate in germ, in his life and writings.

pope-gregory-ii.history:
Gregory II, a Roman, the son of Marcellus and Honesta, known to the West as Gregory the Younger, reigned as bishop of Rome from 19 May 715 until his death on 11 February 731, and is ranked among the greatest popes of the eighth century. Marked out for the Church while very young, he was placed in the schola cantorum, made subdeacon and sacellarius, or almoner, of the Roman Church by Sergius I, and entrusted with the papal library, of which he is the first known curator by name. As a deacon, Pope Constantine chose him for the journey to Constantinople to treat with Justinian II over the canons of the Quinisext Council; the emperor's every objection was met by the deacon's admirable answers.

Early in his pontificate he set about repairing the walls of Rome, threatened alike by the Lombards and by the Saracens; a flood of the Tiber and other hindrances kept the work unfinished. He sent tokens of encouragement to the Frankish leaders who were stemming the Saracen advance in Gaul. He upheld the monastic order, turning his parental mansion into a monastery after his mother's death and restoring many others, among them the celebrated abbey of Monte Cassino. Distinguished pilgrims came to him: Abbot Ceolfrid, who brought the Codex Amiatinus; King Ina, who founded the Schola Anglorum; and Duke Theodo of Bavaria, who sought preachers for his land. Gregory sent missionaries thither, among them Corbinian, one of the apostles of Bavaria, and above all the English monk Winfrid, afterwards called Boniface, whom he consecrated bishop in 722 to preach among the wild nations of Germany, winning Charles Martel's interest in that work and watching it unremittingly.

His early good relations with the Lombards, whose king drew up his laws under the pope's influence, were shadowed by their dukes' seizure of Byzantine possessions in Italy and by the weakness of the Greek exarch at Ravenna; Gregory appealed to Charles Martel and the Franks, who could not or would not come. Greater commotion followed in 727, when the decrees of Leo III, the Isaurian, against the sacred images were published in Italy. Although Greek officials plotted against his life, he resisted both the emperor's illegal taxes and his interference in ecclesiastical authority; thereupon the Lombards became for a time his defenders, and nearly all the Byzantine districts of Italy turned against the emperor, who would have been answered with a rival had the pope permitted it.

When Eutychius, the last exarch, drew the Lombard king Liutprand into an alliance to bring the pope to his knees, Gregory's personal influence over Liutprand dissolved it, and the pope, loyal in political matters to the emperor throughout, even furnished the exarch with troops to quell a rebellion. What he would not surrender was doctrine. By letters sent in all directions he warned the faithful against Leo's teaching, and in a council at Rome in 727 he proclaimed the true doctrine on the veneration of images. He stood by Germanus, Patriarch of Constantinople, and threatened Anastasius, who had supplanted that saint, with deposition unless he renounced his heresy. The old claim that he separated Rome and the West from subjection to Byzantium is an exaggeration of his resistance to the illegal taxes and iconoclastic edicts.

About the year 730 Ravenna fell for a brief space into Lombard hands and was recovered through the exertions of the pope and the Venetians, though the sources leave it uncertain whether Gregory II or his successor Gregory III wrought this service. Gregory also recognized the rival patriarchs of Cividale and Grado as joint heirs of the see of Aquileia and kept them for a time at peace. He died on 11 February 731, was buried in St. Peter's, and is honoured as a saint in the Roman and other martyrologies; the Church keeps his feast on that day, and he is remembered as a resolute pastor, a friend of monks, and a defender of sacred tradition.

gregory-of-nazianzus.history:
Gregory of Nazianzus, honored as Gregory the Theologian, was born at Arianzus in Asia Minor and died at the same place in 389. He was one of three children of Gregory, Bishop of Nazianzus, and of Nonna, whose influence converted her husband from the heretical sect of the Hypsistarii. Educated first at Caesarea in Cappadocia, Gregory there began the friendship with Basil that would shape both their lives and the theology of their age. He pursued rhetoric at Caesarea in Palestine, at Alexandria, and for some ten years at Athens, where he renewed his studies with Basil and numbered among his fellow students Julian, later called the Apostate. He was not baptized in infancy, though dedicated to God by his mother; some biographers infer that he received baptism during a violent storm at sea on the voyage to Athens, though the fact is not certain, and another account places it on his return to Nazianzus. He left Athens in 356, about thirty years of age.

At home he weighed a secular career in law or rhetoric against the monastic life, and after consulting Basil joined him for a time in Pontus, first at Tiberina and then at Neocaesarea, where he shared in the brotherhood of cenobites, helped edit Origen's exegetical works, and assisted in the compilation of Basil's rules. Summoned home, he was instrumental in restoring his aged father to orthodoxy after the bishop had subscribed the creed of Rimini, and was forced, over his scruples, to accept ordination, probably at Christmas 361. Grieved, he fled to his solitude but soon returned, preaching his first sermon on Easter Sunday and writing an apologetic oration on the priestly office that became a foundation for later treatises such as Chrysostom's De Sacerdotio and Gregory the Great's Cura Pastoris. The deaths of his brother Caesarius and his sister Gorgonia drew from him two of his most eloquent funeral orations, still extant.

When Basil became Bishop of Caesarea and Metropolitan of Cappadocia, the Emperor Valens divided the province, and Basil's jurisdiction was disputed by Anthimus of Tyana. To strengthen his position Basil founded a new see at Sasima and had Gregory consecrated its first bishop, greatly against his will. Gregory reckoned himself utterly unsuited to the place, and the place to him, and soon abandoned it to return as coadjutor to his father, who died early in 374. The episode left an estrangement with Basil that was never wholly removed, with no extant correspondence thereafter.

With Arianism then in the ascendancy, Gregory was called to Constantinople, where he preached in a chapel named the Anastasia and witnessed the restoration of orthodox worship; he served as Archbishop of the city from 380 to 381. His celebrated orations on the Trinity, marked by combined subtlety and lucidity of thought and rare beauty of expression, summed up and closed, as one critic observed, the controversy of a whole century. While he nowhere formulated the doctrine of the Double Procession, many passages anticipate the fuller teaching of the Quicumque vult, and for fourteen centuries these discourses have been a mine from which the greatest theologians of Christendom have drawn wisdom. Widely considered the most accomplished rhetorical stylist of the patristic age, he infused Hellenism into the early Church and set the paradigm for the Byzantine theologians who followed him.

Honored as a Doctor of the Church, he is remembered with Basil and Chrysostom as one of the Three Holy Hierarchs. He is venerated as a patron of theologians, preachers, and scholars, and his feast is kept on January 2.

hegesippus-chronicler.history:
Hegesippus, commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on 7 April, was a Christian writer of the second century whose work is known almost entirely through the citations of Eusebius. Eusebius records that he composed, in five books and in the simplest style, an account of the true tradition of the apostolic preaching, under the title Hypomnemata, or Memoirs. The work was written against the new heresies of the Gnostics and of Marcion, and appealed above all to the tradition embodied in the teaching handed down in the Churches through the succession of bishops. St. Jerome was wrong in supposing him to have composed a history; the Memoirs were nonetheless among the earliest attempts at church history.

According to Eusebius, Hegesippus was a convert from Judaism: he quoted from the Hebrew, was acquainted with the Gospel according to the Hebrews and with a Syriac Gospel, and cited unwritten traditions of the Jews. This does not make him a Judaeo-Christian in any sectarian sense, however; he was clearly an orthodox Catholic writer. He seems to have belonged to some part of the East, possibly Palestine.

The Memoirs recount a journey that took Hegesippus to Corinth and Rome, in the course of which he met many bishops and heard from all of them the same doctrine. He remained many days with the Corinthians, whose church had remained in the true word until Primus was bishop there; in Rome he drew up a succession of bishops up to Anicetus, whose deacon was Eleutherus, and in each succession and in each city all was, he wrote, according to the ordinances of the law and the Prophets and the Lord. The phrase by which he describes compiling this record has been disputed, but the best scholars accept the manuscript text: succession then bore the technical sense of a list of the bishops of a church, and the argument resembles that of St. Irenaeus against the heretics.

Lightfoot traced this list in the writings of St. Epiphanius and in the poem of Pseudo-Tertullian against Marcion, and it appears to stand at the base of the earlier part of the Liberian Catalogue, though several scholars have rejected his view. It seems fairly certain that Irenaeus, Africanus, and Eusebius drew upon it in forming their own catalogues, and it is probable that Eusebius borrowed his list of the early bishops of Jerusalem from Hegesippus.

Fragments preserved by Eusebius include an account, apparently legendary in its transmitted form, of the death of St. James the brother of the Lord; the story of the election of his successor Symeon; and the summoning of the grandsons of St. Jude to Rome by Domitian, whose names Hegesippus gave as Zoker and James. Eusebius also cites a list of the heresies against which Hegesippus wrote. Lawlor has shown that these passages were connected in the original and belonged to the fifth book of the Memoirs.

Eusebius probably took from Hegesippus the statement that St. John was exiled to Patmos by Domitian, and Hegesippus appears to have mentioned the letter of Clement to the Corinthians in connection with the persecution under Domitian. The dating of heretics by papal reigns in Irenaeus and Epiphanius, and the assertion that Hermas was the brother of Pope Pius, may likewise derive from his work.

His own notices fix his date: the death and apotheosis of Antinous fell within his own time, about the year 130; he came to Rome under Anicetus; and he was writing in the time of Eleutherus. The Memoirs are otherwise lost, though Zahn showed that the work remained extant in three Eastern libraries as late as the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Hegesippus is remembered as a faithful guardian of the tradition handed down from the beginning, and is honored as a patron of theologians, writers, and scholars.

hesychius-of-sinai.history:
Hesychius of Sinai was a priest and monk of the Order of St. Basil at the Batos, or Thorn-bush, monastery on Mount Sinai, an ascetic author of the Byzantine period. Nothing definite is known concerning his career or the exact time at which he lived. The mountain itself is honored in Christian tradition as the place where Moses beheld God, and the Thorn-bush monastery there is traditionally identified with the great monastery of Saint Catherine. The manuscripts that transmit his works as a rule give him the honorary title of 'Our Holy Father' (tou hosiou patros hemon Hesychiou presbyterou), and where the authenticity of that title in a manuscript is certain it is by itself sufficient to distinguish him from others who bore the same name, above all from the celebrated Hesychius of Jerusalem.

A second criterion of equal importance is the examination of the biblical text underlying the treatises of one or the other Hesychius: Hesychius of Sinai, in his quotations of Scripture, regularly follows the version of the Codex Sinaiticus. Even with such tests, attribution remains only partly settled. Only a few small fragments of this almost completely forgotten author have been preserved, and they have still to be collected and separately criticized. The latest edition of these works of the Fathers appeared under the title 'Hesychius, Presbyter of Jerusalem' and was published without any attempt at critical selection; only monographic investigation can determine how much of what it prints belongs properly to the monk of Sinai.

The pivotal point of such an investigation is a collection of two hundred ascetic maxims on sobriety and virtue, which the Migne edition assigns to Hesychius of Jerusalem under a pseudonym but which should, without doubt, be credited to Hesychius of Sinai. The author of the maxims acknowledges, by a play on words (ho hesychias pheronymos), that his name is Hesychius and that he is a Basilian monk; a number of manuscripts support this internal evidence, among them the Bodleian Baroccian 118, of the twelfth to thirteenth centuries, the Laudian 21, of the fourteenth, and the Canonici 16, of the fifteenth, together with the British Museum Burney 113, of the fifteenth. The printed text, moreover, could be corrected and improved to particular advantage from the British Museum Additional 9347, of the twelfth century, and the Bodleian Cromwell 6, of the fifteenth.

The maxims are dedicated to a certain Theodulus, a circumstance that gave rise in some manuscripts to the erroneous statement that he was their author. It cannot be determined how many of the maxims were drawn from older ascetics and how many were adopted in turn by later ones, evidence that the maxims circulated among ascetics. It is probable, in addition, that the ascetic and Biblical-ascetic fragments found in two Turin codices of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, under the name of 'Our Holy Father Hesychius,' should also be attributed to him.

Later ascetic tradition has associated his name with the way of inner stillness that the Christian East calls hesychasm. His life, however, must be reconstructed almost wholly from the witness of manuscripts rather than from a continuous narrative; what remains is his voice as a spiritual writer: terse counsels on watchfulness, temperance, and virtue, formed in the desert tradition of Sinai.

hilary-of-arles.history:
Hilary of Arles (Latin: Hilarius) was born about 401, though the exact place of his birth is unknown, into a notable family of northern Gaul from which, in all probability, there also came his kinsman Honoratus, founder of the monastery of Lérins and Hilary's predecessor in the see of Arles. Learned and wealthy, with every prospect of worldly success, Hilary abandoned honors and riches at Honoratus's urgent urging, followed him to the hermitage of Lérins, and there devoted himself under the saint's direction to the practice of austerities and the study of Holy Scripture.

When Honoratus, by then archbishop of Arles, was near death (he died around 429), Hilary came to his side and assisted at his final moments. As he was about to set out for Lérins he was retained by force and proclaimed archbishop in Honoratus's place. Obliged to yield to this constraint, he undertook the duties of his heavy charge resolutely. As bishop he was a tireless preacher and a rigorous ascetic: he assisted at the councils held at Riez, Orange, Vaison, and Arles, founded monasteries, cared for the poor, and carried the discipline of Lérins through southern Gaul.

In 444 he presided over a reunion of bishops, attended by St. Eucherius of Lyons and St. Germain of Auxerre, which deposed a certain Cheldonius for incapacity on grounds provided against by the canons. Cheldonius went to Rome, pleaded his cause successfully, and was reinstated in his see by Pope Leo the Great. Hilary then sought Leo to justify his course, but was not well received and was obliged to return precipitately to Gaul; priests sent afterwards to explain his conduct met with no better success. Persons hostile to him took advantage of the juncture to bring accusations against him at the court of Rome, whereupon the pope excommunicated Hilary, transferred the prerogatives of his see to that of Fréjus, and caused the Emperor Valentinian III to proclaim the famous decree that freed the church of Vienne from all dependence on that of Arles. The episode became one of the celebrated quarrels in the history of the Gallican Church, but the documents bearing on it are too few for a definitive judgment on its causes and consequences. It evidently arose because the respective rights of the court of Rome and of the metropolitan were not clearly established at the time, and because the right of appeal to the pope was not explicitly enough recognized. There is every reason to believe that, the storm once passed, peace was rapidly restored between Hilary and Leo.

A number of writings are ascribed to Hilary, but far from all are authentic; Quesnel collected those attributed to him in an appendix to his edition of the works of St. Leo. Hilary died on 5 May 449, the date of his feast, and is venerated by the Orthodox and Catholic Churches. He is honored as patron of Arles and as patron of bishops, monks, and those who labor for the reform of the Church; tradition holds that he is also invoked against snake bites.

honoratus.history:
Honoratus was born about 350. It is believed that he was born in the north of Gaul and that he belonged to an illustrious pagan family, though authors differ concerning his birthplace. Converted to Christianity together with his brother Venantius, he resolved to live henceforth wholly for God.

About 368 the two brothers embarked at Marseilles under the guidance of a holy person named Caprasius, intending to visit the holy places of Palestine and to learn from the monks of the desert in the lauras of Syria and Egypt. The death of Venantius, which came suddenly at Methone in Achaia, prevented the travellers from going farther. They returned to Gaul through Italy, and, after a stay at Rome, Honoratus went on into Provence.

There, encouraged by Leontius, Bishop of Frejus, he took up his abode on the wild island of Lerins, off the Mediterranean coast near modern Cannes, with the intention of living there in solitude. Numerous disciples soon gathered around him, and in this way the monastery of Lerins was founded. The house came to enjoy so great a celebrity that during the fifth and sixth centuries it was a nursery of illustrious bishops and remarkable ecclesiastical writers; tradition holds that Vincent of Lerins and Faustus of Riez were among those formed there. Cassian, who had visited the monastery, dedicated several of his Conferences to Honoratus.

The reputation for sanctity that Honoratus earned throughout the south-eastern portion of Gaul was such that, in 426, after the assassination of Patroclus, Archbishop of Arles, he was summoned from his solitude to succeed to the government of the diocese, which the Arian and Manichaean heresies had greatly disturbed. He appears to have succeeded in re-establishing order and orthodoxy, while still continuing to direct from afar the monks of Lerins. Of his conduct as bishop little more can be said, for the acts of his brief pontificate are not known.

He died in January 429, in the arms of Hilary, one of his disciples and probably a relative, who was to succeed him in the See of Arles. Different authors give the day of his death variously as the 6th, the 14th, or the 15th of January; his feast is kept on 16 January. His various writings have not been preserved, nor has the rule which he gave to the solitaries of Lerins.

He is remembered above all as the founder of Lerins and as a bishop summoned from solitude to govern a see disturbed by heresy. In later devotion he has been honored as a patron of monks and of farmers, and he has long been invoked for rain and against drought.

irenaeus.history:
St. Irenaeus, Bishop of Lyons and a Father of the Church, was born in Proconsular Asia, or at least in some province bordering thereon, in the first half of the second century; the exact date is controverted, some placing it between the years 115 and 125, others between 130 and 142. While still very young, he had seen and heard the holy Bishop Polycarp (who died in 155) at Smyrna.

During the persecution of Marcus Aurelius, Irenaeus was a priest of the Church of Lyons, many of whose clergy were suffering imprisonment for the faith. In 177 or 178 the clergy sent him to Rome carrying a letter to Pope Eleutherius concerning Montanism, and on that occasion they bore emphatic testimony to his merits. Returning to Gaul, he succeeded the martyr Saint Pothinus as Bishop of Lyons. In the religious peace that followed, the new bishop divided his activities between pastoral and missionary duties and his writings, almost all of which were directed against Gnosticism, the heresy then spreading in Gaul and elsewhere. In 190 or 191 he interceded with Pope Victor to lift the excommunication which that pontiff had laid upon the Christian communities of Asia Minor that persevered in the Quartodeciman practice in the celebration of Easter.

Nothing is known of the date of his death, which must have occurred at the end of the second or the beginning of the third century. In spite of some isolated and later testimony to the effect that he suffered martyrdom, it is not very probable that he ended his career with martyrdom. His feast is celebrated on 28 June in the Latin Church, and on 23 August in the Greek.

Irenaeus wrote in Greek many works which have secured for him an exceptional place in Christian literature, for they exhibit the testimony of a contemporary of the heroic age of the Church, one who had heard Polycarp, the disciple of St. John, and who, in a manner, belonged to the Apostolic Age. None of these writings has come down in the original text, but two survive entire in ancient versions.

The first and chief is Against Heresies, a treatise in five books devoted, according to its true title, to the detection and overthrow of the false knowledge, that is, of Gnosticism. It has reached us in a very ancient Latin translation whose scrupulous fidelity is beyond doubt. It contains a profound exposition of the Gnostic systems and of the principal heresies which had sprung up in the various Christian communities, and it is an invaluable source of information on the most ancient ecclesiastical literature from its beginnings to the end of the second century.
