In refuting the heterodox systems Irenaeus often opposed to them the true doctrine of the Church, and in this way furnished positive and very early evidence of high importance, notably on the origin of the Gospel of St. John, the Holy Eucharist, and the primacy of the Roman Church.

The second work, written after Against Heresies, is the Proof of the Apostolic Preaching, which has come down complete in an ancient Armenian translation. Its aim is not to confute heretics, but to confirm the faithful by expounding Christian doctrine to them, notably by demonstrating the truth of the Gospel by means of the Old Testament prophecies. It is a document of the highest interest and a testimony of the deep and lively faith of Irenaeus.

Of his other works, which include a treatise against the Greeks, writings addressed to the Roman priest Florinus, a treatise on schism addressed to Blastus, and several letters to Pope Victor and others concerning the Paschal controversies, only scattered fragments exist, many known only through the mention of later writers such as Hippolytus and Eusebius. A few fragments published in 1715 were later proven to be apocryphal fabrications.

Irenaeus is honored as a patron of theologians, of writers, and of church unity, and was declared a Doctor of the Church in 2022.

isaac-of-armenia.history:
Isaac, known in Armenian as Sahak and also called Isaac the Great or Parthev on account of his Parthian origin, was Catholicos, or Patriarch, of the Armenian Church from about 387. He was the son of St. Narses and descended from the family of St. Gregory the Illuminator, who had converted the Kingdom of Armenia to Christianity in the early fourth century, and Isaac is remembered as the last patriarch directly descended from him. Left an orphan at a very early age, he received in Constantinople an excellent literary education, particularly in the Eastern languages. After his election as patriarch he devoted himself to the religious and scientific training of his people.

His patriarchate coincided with a grave crisis. In 387 Armenia lost its independence and was divided between the Byzantine Empire and Persia, each portion placed under an Armenian feudatory king. In the Byzantine territories the Armenians were forbidden the use of Syriac, until then the language of divine worship, and Greek was to be substituted for it; in the Persian districts, on the contrary, Greek was absolutely prohibited while Syriac was greatly favored. The ancient culture of the Armenians was thus in danger of disappearing, and national unity was seriously compromised. To save both, Isaac devised, with the aid of the monk St. Mesrop Mashtots, the Armenian alphabet and began to translate the Bible. The translation, made from the Syriac Peshito, was revised by means of the Septuagint and, it seems, even from the Hebrew text, between about 410 and 430. The liturgy, hitherto Syrian, was likewise translated into Armenian, drawing at the same time on the Liturgy of St. Basil of Caesarea so that the new service took on a national character.

To carry this work forward, Isaac established schools for higher education and sent disciples to study at Edessa, Melitene, Byzantium, and elsewhere; through them the principal masterpieces of Greek and Syriac Christian literature were translated into Armenian, including the writings of Athanasius, Cyril of Jerusalem, Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa, John Chrysostom, and Ephrem. Through his efforts the churches and monasteries destroyed by the Persians were rebuilt, education was cared for in a generous way, the pagan worship of Ormuzd that Shah Yezdigerd tried to set up was cast out, and three councils were held to re-establish ecclesiastical discipline. He is said to have been the author of liturgical hymns, and two letters written by him, to the emperor Theodosius II and to Atticus of Constantinople, have been preserved.

Although a share in the Council of Ephesus of 431 was later wrongly ascribed to him, Isaac took no part in it. When disputes arose in Armenia between the followers of Nestorius and the disciples of Acacius of Melitene and Rabulas, he and his church appealed to Constantinople and, through St. Proclus, obtained the explanations they sought. A third letter attributed to him, addressed to St. Proclus, dates in fact from the tenth century.

A man of enlightened piety and of a very austere life, Isaac owed his deposition by the king in 426 to his great independence of character; in 430 he was allowed to resume the patriarchal throne. In his extreme old age he seems to have withdrawn into solitude, dying at the age of 110. Neither the exact year nor the precise month of his death is known, but it seems to have occurred between 439 and 441, although some accounts place his death about 438. The Armenian Church consecrates several days to his memory, keeping his feast on September 8, and venerates him among her greatest saints; he is honored as a patron of linguists, scholars, and translators.

isidore-of-pelusium.history:
St. Isidore of Pelusium was born at Alexandria in the latter half of the fourth century and died not later than 449-450; he is occasionally designated through mistake as Isidore of Damietta. Leaving his family and possessions, he retired to a mountain near the city of Pelusium, whose name was thenceforth joined to his own, and embraced the religious life in the monastery of Lychnos, where he became remarkable for exactness in observing the rule and for his austerities. A passage in his letters gives reason to believe that he held the office of abbot, and he is called a priest by Facundus and Suidas, though perhaps he had no clerical charge and was only a priest of the monastery.

His activity is known chiefly through his correspondence. It shows him fighting against unworthy clerics whose elevation to holy orders was a peril and scandal to the faithful, and he complains that many laymen ceased to approach the sacraments to avoid contact with them. His veneration for St. John Chrysostom led him to press St. Cyril of Alexandria to render full justice to the doctor's memory. He opposed the Nestorians, and when conflict arose after the Council of Ephesus between St. Cyril and John of Antioch he judged there was too much obstinacy on Cyril's side, urging him not to make a private grievance the pretext for an eternal rupture. Still living when the heresy of Eutyches began to spread in Egypt, he opposed in many letters the claim that Christ possessed but one nature. His life scarcely extended beyond 449, for his letters do not mention the Robber Council of Ephesus (449) or the Council of Chalcedon (451).

Evagrius attributes numerous writings to him, and Isidore himself mentions a treatise 'Adversus Gentiles' and a work 'De Fato' that met with some success, both now lost. His only surviving works are his letters, more than two thousand, of which 2182 remain, arranged in five books; Nicephorus speaks of ten thousand. They treat dogma and Scripture, ecclesiastical and monastic discipline, and practical morality for laymen of every condition. The letter to Theologius answers the Nestorians by contrasting the mother of the gods of pagan fable with the Mother of Jesus Christ, who conceived without intercourse with any man; that to Hierax defends the veneration of relics; that to Tuba observes it was thought unbecoming for a soldier to carry a sword in a city in time of peace.

His letters to monks throw light on the intellectual life of the Egyptian monastic centres. He reproached the monk Thalelaeus for reading pagan historians and poets full of fables and uncleanness, and advised that those entering the monastic state should not at first feel all the austerities of the rule, lest they be repelled, nor be left idle, lest they acquire habits of laziness, but be led step by step to what is most perfect. Great abstinences, he held, serve no purpose without mortification of the senses, and he regarded monastic life as consisting chiefly in retirement and obedience, the monk governed by his superior rather than by his own will.

Though very brief, most of the letters contain much instruction, often set forth with elegance, and the style is natural and unaffected. Whether explaining or reprimanding, disputing or praising, Isidore keeps the same moderation and sincerity, and in interpreting Scripture he prefers the moral and spiritual sense as most useful for those who consult him, practicing the maxim he taught others, that the life should correspond with the words. The Church keeps his feast on February 4, and he is remembered as a scholar of the desert who wedded learning to holiness.

john-cassian.history:
John Cassian, a monk and ascetical writer who was the first to introduce the rules of Eastern monasticism into the West, was born about 360. His birthplace is uncertain: Gennadius calls him a Scythian, though this is regarded as erroneous, arising from his years in the desert of Scete. As a young man he visited the holy places of Palestine with an older friend, Germanus, and the two assumed the monastic life at Bethlehem. The desire to learn the science of sanctity from its most eminent teachers drew them to the Egyptian deserts; though they had promised a prompt return, they were absent seven years, and after extending their leave they remained several years more among the solitaries most famous for holiness. It was then that Cassian gathered the materials for his two principal works.

From Egypt he passed to Constantinople, where he became a favoured disciple of St. John Chrysostom, who ordained him to the diaconate and entrusted him with the treasures of his cathedral. After the bishop's second expulsion, Cassian was sent by the Constantinopolitan clergy as envoy to Pope Innocent I at Rome in Chrysostom's behalf; he arrived there still a deacon and was probably ordained priest in Rome. From this time Germanus is heard of no more, and nothing is known of Cassian for the next decade or more.

About 415 he settled at Marseilles, where he founded two monasteries: one for men, over the tomb of the martyr St. Victor, and one for women. The rest of his days were passed at or very near Marseilles, and he died about 435.

The Institutes, written between 420 and 429, treats of the rules governing the cenobitic life and, in its later books, of the eight principal obstacles to perfection: gluttony, impurity, covetousness, anger, dejection, accidia, vainglory, and pride. The Conferences, twenty-four books issued in three parts, record the conversations of Cassian and Germanus with the Egyptian solitaries on the interior life. Cassian said the former dealt chiefly with the outer man and the customs of the coenobia, the latter with the training of the inner man and the perfection of the heart.

His influence and writings did much to spread monasticism in the West. St. Benedict drew upon him in composing his Rule and ordered selections from the Conferences, which he called a mirror of monasticism, to be read daily in his monasteries; Cassiodorus likewise recommended the work to his monks, with reservations concerning its teaching on free will. At the request of the Roman archdeacon Leo, later Pope Leo the Great, he wrote about 430-431 the De Incarnatione Domini contra Nestorium, a defence of orthodoxy against Nestorius, with scriptural proofs of Our Lord's divinity and Mary's title as Mother of God; written hurriedly, it is of less value than his other works.

His own teaching on grace did not escape suspicion of error. He defended the role of free will in resisting temptation and attaining sanctity, yet held that after the Fall there remained in every soul some seeds of goodness implanted by the kindness of the Creator, which must be quickened by the assistance of God. His position has been summed up: St. Augustine regarded man in his natural state as dead, Pelagius as quite sound, Cassian as sick. Prosper of Aquitaine alluded to him with great respect, without naming him; Cassian took no part in the controversy, and Semipelagianism was finally condemned by the Council of Orange in 529.

Although never formally canonized, Cassian has been honoured as a saint: St. Gregory the Great regarded him as such, and tradition holds that Urban V, once an abbot of St. Victor, had the words Saint Cassian engraved on the silver casket containing his head. His feast is kept on 29 February; at Marseilles it was celebrated, with an octave, on 23 July. Remembered as a master of contemplation and spiritual direction, and as a bridge between Eastern and Western monastic traditions, he is honoured as patron of monks and of contemplatives.

john-climacus.history:
John Climacus, also surnamed Scholasticus and known as the Sinaita, was born about the year 525, doubtlessly in Syria, and died on Mount Sinai on March 30, probably in 606, though some give the year as 605. Although his education and learning fitted him for an intellectual life, he chose while still young to abandon the world for solitude. The region of Mount Sinai was then celebrated for the holiness of its monks, and there he trained himself in the practice of the Christian virtues under the direction of a monk named Martyrius. After the death of Martyrius, wishing to practice greater mortifications, he withdrew to a hermitage at the foot of the mountain and lived there in isolation for some twenty years, constantly studying the lives of the saints, and thus became one of the most learned teachers of the Church.

Around the year 600, when he was about seventy-five years of age, the monks of Sinai persuaded him to put himself at their head. He carried out the office of abbot with the greatest wisdom, and his reputation spread so far that Gregory the Great, then pope, wrote to recommend himself to John's prayers and sent money for the hospital of Sinai, in which pilgrims were accustomed to lodge. Four years later John resigned his charge and returned to his hermitage to prepare for death.

He is remembered chiefly for two works. The greater is the Scala Paradisi, or Ladder of Divine Ascent, from which his surname comes and by which he is known in English as John of the Ladder. It was composed at the request of John, abbot of Raithu, a monastery on the shores of the Red Sea, and is addressed to anchorites and cenobites, treating of the means by which the highest degree of religious perfection may be attained. Divided into thirty steps, in memory of the thirty years of the hidden life of Christ, the divine model of the monk, it presents a picture of the virtues, from renunciation to the summit of love, and is marked by many parables and examples drawn principally from monastic life. Since it is written in a concise, aphoristic form, it is at times somewhat obscure, and for this reason it was made the subject of commentaries even in very early times. His other work is the Liber ad Pastorem.

The Scala obtained immense popularity and became one of the most widely read guides to the ascetic and contemplative life in the Eastern Church. In some manuscripts it bears the title Spiritual Tables; the most ancient manuscript is preserved in the Bibliotheque Nationale in Paris and was probably brought from Florence by Catherine de' Medici. It was translated into Latin by Ambrogio the Camaldolese, and one early Latin edition carried a commentary by Denis the Carthusian. The Greek text, with the scholia of Elias, Archbishop of Crete, and the text of the Liber ad Pastorem, was published by Matthaeus Raderus at Paris in 1633. Versions also appeared in Spanish, Italian, modern Greek, and French. An ancient life of the saint, written by a monk named Daniel, also survives.

John Climacus is venerated as a saint by both the Eastern Orthodox and Catholic Churches, and his feast is kept on March 30. He is honored as a patron of monks, of contemplation, and of spiritual direction. He remains, through his Ladder, a teacher of all who seek to climb toward God.

john-of-beverley.history:
John of Beverley was an English bishop of the kingdom of Northumbria in the early eighth century. He was born at Harpham, in the East Riding of Yorkshire, and died at Beverley on 7 May 721. In early life he was placed under the care of Archbishop Theodore at Canterbury, who supervised his education and is reputed to have given him the name of John. He became a member of the Benedictine Order and was for a time an inmate of St. Hilda's monastery at Streaneshaleh, known today as Whitby. He won renown as a preacher, displayed marked erudition in expounding Scripture, and taught among other subjects, though the authenticity of certain works later ascribed to him is doubtful.

On 25 August 687 John was consecrated Bishop of Hexham, a district with which he was not unfamiliar, for he had for a period led a life of retreat at Erneshowe, on the opposite bank of the Tyne. He afterwards returned to that place for seclusion, especially during Lent, whenever the cares of his episcopal ministration permitted. In 705 he was present at the synod convened on the River Nidd by Osred, King of Northumbria, to decide the case of Wilfrid. On the death of Bishop Bosa, after eighteen years of labor in the see of Hexham, John was translated to the see of York, the most important religious see in the north of England; Wilfrid succeeded him at Hexham.

Of his activity at York little is known beyond that he was diligent in visitation, considerate towards the poor, and exceedingly attentive to the training of the students whom he maintained under his personal charge. Tradition holds that this little company of pupils included Bede, whom John ordained; Berethume, afterwards Abbot of Beverley; Herebald, Abbot of Tynemouth; and Wilfrid the Younger, John's successor in the see of York in 718. He exercised his office with quiet fidelity in an age of upheaval and conversion.

Having purchased a place called Inderawood, to which a later age has given the name of Beverley, John established a monastery there and handsomely endowed the place, which became even in its founder's day an important ecclesiastical center. By building the first religious house there he is regarded as the founder of the town of Beverley itself. After resigning the see of York to his pupil Wilfrid the Younger, John retired to this monastery and passed the remainder of his life with Abbot Berethume, a one-time favorite scholar.

John was associated with miracles during his life and after his death, and in 1037 he was canonized by Pope Benedict IX. His bones were translated by Ælfric, Archbishop of York, and placed in a costly shrine; a second translation took place in 1197, and the remains were discovered in 1664 and again brought to light in 1736. Because his canonization preceded the Great Schism of 1054, he is honored as a saint also by the Eastern Orthodox Church. His feast is kept on May 7.

The monastery he founded grew around his tomb into one of the great pilgrimage shrines of medieval England, and Beverley Minster, raised in his honor, drew countless pilgrims through the centuries and became a place of healing and refuge. He is honored as a patron of bishops and scholars, and as one of the patrons of England.

john-the-silent.history:
John the Silent, also called John the Hesychast (Hesychastes, Silentiarius), was born at Nicopolis in Armenia on January 8, 452. His parents, Encratius and Euphemia, were wealthy and honored, belonging to families that had rendered great service to the state and produced renowned generals and governors; they were also devout Christians who gave their son a holy upbringing. In time he became Bishop of Colonia in Armenia, though the episcopal office would occupy only one chapter of a life largely given to solitude.

After the death of his parents in 471, John distributed his inheritance among his relatives, retaining only a small share, with which he built a church and a monastery. There, with ten congenial companions, he began a life of mortification and self-denial, whose wonderful traits were recorded by his biographer. These early years already showed the bent toward solitude that would characterize the rest of his life.

His retirement was interrupted when the Bishop of Sebaste drew him out of his solitude and, against John's vain resistance, made him Bishop of Colonia (Taxara) in 481. In this new dignity he preserved the monastic spirit entire, continuing his austerities and exercises as far as was compatible with his duties. A grave difficulty arose when his brother-in-law Pasinius oppressed the Church to such an extent that John was compelled to call upon the Emperor Zeno for assistance; with the emperor's help the affairs of the Church were set in order.

As soon as matters had been properly arranged, John secretly abandoned his see and went to the laura near Jerusalem, placing himself under the obedience of St. Sabas without revealing his identity, and he lived there unknown for many years. In the course of time Sabas, who had subjected him to trials of all kinds and had found him ready to perform even the most common and menial labours, thought him worthy of priesthood, and for this purpose sent him to Elias, Patriarch of Jerusalem. John now revealed all, and Elias informed Sabas that John had confided to him things which forbade his ordination. Sabas at first felt very sad, but was comforted by a vision in which the true state of affairs was made known to him. John's life was written by his contemporary Cyril of Scythopolis.

With the permission of his superior, John then entered a hut built against the face of a rock in the desert, and there passed the remainder of his days in seclusion and perpetual silence, whence his surname. The name 'the Silent,' or Hesychast, testifies to his guard over the tongue and his devotion to recollection and the interior life; according to his biographer, John spent some seventy-six years in this solitude before his death in 558. His feast is kept on May 13 in the General Roman Calendar, and the Eastern Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches commemorate him on December 3. He is remembered as one of the great witnesses to the hesychast tradition of silence and unceasing prayer, and is honored as a patron of hermits, contemplatives, and the prayer life.

jonas-of-bobbio.history:
Jonas of Bobbio, also known as Jonas of Susa, was born near the close of the sixth century at Sigusia (Susa) in Piedmont and died after 659. He is remembered as a monk and hagiographer of the Columbanian tradition and stands among the principal Latin monastic authors of the early Middle Ages. In 618 he entered the monastery of Bobbio in the province of Pavia, a foundation associated with the Irish missionary Saint Columbanus, where he embraced the austere and learned monastic life that Columbanus and his followers had established on the continent. The Church keeps his memory on May 28, and he is honored as a patron of writers, monks, and scholars.

Within a short time of his arrival Jonas was appointed to a position of confidence in the monastery, probably that of secretary to the abbots Attala, who died in 627, and Bertulf. In 628 he accompanied Bertulf on a journey to Rome, and after his return he took up his permanent abode in Gaul.

His settlement in Gaul brought him into the continental mission. Saint Amandus appealed to him for assistance in his missionary work among the heathen, and Jonas labored in what is now Belgium and Northern France. His presence in that district gave occasion for the composition of his life of Saint Vaast, the first Frankish Bishop of Arras.

Jonas owes his literary fame chiefly to the Life of Saint Columbanus. During a short visit to Bobbio in 639 he made a promise to the local monks, and in fulfillment of it he wrote the work between 640 and 643. He had arrived at Bobbio only three years after Columbanus's death, and he grounded his account of the great Irish saint in the testimony of those who had known him intimately. His material was strengthened by personal acquaintance as well: he knew Eustace of Luxeuil, Attala, and Bertulf themselves.

The body of work on which his reputation rests comprises, besides the Life of Saint Columbanus, the lives of the abbots Attala and Bertulf of Bobbio, of Eustace of Luxeuil, and of the Abbess Burgundofara, or Fara, of Evoriac, now Faremoutiers. In 659, while abbot of a monastery that cannot now be determined, he was sent by the queen-regent Bathildis on a mission to Chalon-sur-Saône. On that journey he sojourned for a few days at the monastery of Saint John of Réomé, now Moutier-Saint-Jean, in the Diocese of Langres, and to comply with the request of the monks he wrote the life of their founder, Saint John. The Life of Saint Fara is chiefly an account of the miraculous events alleged to have occurred during her rule at Evoriac; in it tradition preserves what her community recounted, and the narrative should be read with that qualification in mind.

Jonas wrote in a bombastic style, yet his biographies of Columbanus and his successors contain invaluable historical information and are regarded as among the most influential works of early medieval hagiography. Through them the memory of Columbanus and the spirit of the Columbanian foundations were preserved for the Church, and they continue to shape the understanding of seventh-century monasticism. Their standing was recognized early: Bede incorporated these lives into his ecclesiastical history, and Flodoard turned the Life of Saint Columbanus into hexameter verse.

pope-julius-i.history:
Julius I, a native of Rome and the son of Rusticus, was elected bishop of Rome on 6 February 337 after a four-month vacancy of the papal chair. He governed the Roman Church for fifteen years, until his death on 12 April 352, and his pontificate is chiefly remembered for his firm and judicious intervention in the Arian controversy, the dispute over the divinity of Christ that then divided East and West.

After the death of Constantine the Great, the exiled Athanasius was permitted to return to his see of Alexandria, but the Arian party set up a rival bishop, Pistus, and sent envoys asking that Pistus be admitted to communion with Rome; Athanasius in turn sent deputies bearing a synodal letter of the Egyptian bishops in his defense. At the Arian envoys' own request, Julius convoked a synod at Rome to hear both parties. In the meantime the Eusebian bishops had George of Cappadocia intruded forcibly into Alexandria, and Athanasius, exiled once more, came to Rome, as did Marcellus of Ancyra and other bishops removed by the Arian party. The Eastern bishops, in a haughty letter, refused to attend the synod they had themselves proposed. Held in the autumn of 340 or 341 under the pope's presidency, the synod examined the documents and reinstated Athanasius and Marcellus in their episcopal rights. Julius announced the decision in a notable letter to the Eusebian party, asserting that disputed cases should first be referred to the Roman see: 'Can you be ignorant that this is the custom, that we should be written to first, so that from here what is just may be defined.'

At the request of Julius and other Western bishops, Emperor Constans interceded with his brother Constantius for the bishops deposed by the Arian party, and both rulers agreed to summon a general council to Sardica in 342 or 343; Julius sent two priests and a deacon as his representatives. Although the Arian Eastern bishops held a separate assembly and departed, the council accomplished its task, regulating the procedure against accused bishops and establishing the manner of papal intervention in the condemnation of bishops. Athanasius was not restored until 346, after the death of the intruded George, whereupon Julius wrote, in a letter still extant, to congratulate the clergy and faithful of Alexandria on the return of their pastor. Two Arian bishops deposed at Sardica, Ursacius of Singidunum and Valens of Mursia, made formal recantation of their error to Julius, who received their signed confession of faith and restored them to their sees.

Within Rome his pontificate was a time of quiet growth: the number of the faithful increased rapidly, and Julius built two new basilicas, the titular church of Julius, now Saint Mary in Trastevere, and the Basilica Julia, now the Church of the Twelve Apostles, together with three cemetery churches outside the walls, one of them at the tomb of the martyr Saint Valentine. Veneration of the martyrs' tombs spread rapidly, and catalogues of the feast days of saints came into use in this period. Through Athanasius, who remained in Rome for several years after 339, the monastic life of Egypt became known in the capital and found many imitators in the Roman Church.

Julius died on 12 April 352 and was buried in the catacombs of Calepodius; soon honored as a saint, his remains were later translated to Saint Mary in Trastevere, the church he had built. His feast is kept on 12 April, and tradition holds that it was he who established 25 December as the official observance of the Lord's Nativity in the Roman Church. Remembered as a defender of orthodoxy and a guardian of due process in ecclesiastical affairs, he is venerated as a patron of bishops and of church unity, the pope who kept the center of communion firm in a divided age.

pope-leo-ii.history:
St. Leo II was Bishop of Rome from August 682 until his death on 28 June 683, shepherding the Church in the difficult years of the Byzantine Papacy. A Sicilian and the son of a man named Paul, he was elected pope only a few days after the death of his predecessor, St. Agatho, on 10 January 681, yet was not consecrated until 17 August 682. The delay of a year and seven months arose most probably from continued correspondence between the Holy See and the emperor Constantine Pogonatus concerning the relations of the Byzantine court to papal elections. Constantine had already promised Agatho to abolish or reduce the tax which for about a century the popes had been obliged to pay to the imperial treasury upon their consecration, and under Leo's successor he made further changes in what had been required of the Roman Church at a papal election; on this matter the imperial confirmation of Leo's election, and hence his consecration, was long postponed.

The most important act of Leo's brief pontificate was his confirmation of the acts of the Sixth Ecumenical Council (680-81), which had been held at Constantinople against the Monothelites and presided over by the legates of Pope Agatho. By this confirmation he upheld the orthodox faith concerning the two wills of Christ. After Leo had notified the emperor that he had confirmed the council's decrees, he made them known to the nations of the West. His letters to the king and to the bishops and nobles of Spain have come down to us; in them he explained what the council had effected and called upon the bishops to subscribe to its decrees. At the same time he was careful to make clear that, in condemning his predecessor Honorius I, he did so not because Honorius had taught heresy, but because he had not been active enough in opposing it. In accordance with the papal mandate, a synod held at Toledo in 684 accepted the Council of Constantinople.

Leo also maintained the rights of the Holy See over Ravenna. Encouraged by their city's long standing as a residence of the emperors and of the exarchs, the archbishops of Ravenna had aspired to patriarchal privileges and to autocephaly, that is, freedom from the pope's direct jurisdiction as their primate, and, failing to obtain the popes' consent, had tried to secure their claims by an imperial decree. This decree did not prove sufficient, and Leo obtained from Constantine Pogonatus the revocation of the edict of Constans. For his part, he abolished the tax which the archbishops had customarily paid upon receiving the pallium, and, while insisting that archbishops-elect must come to Rome for consecration, he limited their required stay to eight days and permitted them to send an annual delegate to render homage in their own name.

Perhaps out of fear that the Lombards might again ravage the catacombs, Leo transferred many of the relics of the martyrs into a church which he built to receive them.

His contemporary biographer describes him as both just and learned, and he was known for his generosity to the poor and his care for the liturgy. He is commemorated as a saint in the Roman Martyrology on 28 June, the feast formerly observed on 3 July with the rank of a semi-double, and he is honored as a patron of bishops, scholars, and the poor, remembered as a gentle and wise pontiff whose short pontificate served the Church steadfastly.

pope-leo-iv.history:
Pope Leo IV, a Roman and the son of Radoald, reigned from 10 April 847 until his death in 855. The alarming Saracen attack on Rome in 846, which had desecrated the churches of the Apostles, struck fear for the safety of the city, and Leo was consecrated without awaiting the consent of the emperor. Educated at Rome in the monastery of St. Martin near St. Peter's, he had attracted the notice of Gregory IV, who made him a subdeacon, and Sergius II later created him Cardinal-Priest of the church of the Quatuor Coronati. Much against his will, he accepted election to succeed Sergius II and at once took precautions against a repetition of the raid of 846.

He put the city walls into a thorough state of repair, rebuilding fifteen of the great towers, and was the first to enclose the Vatican hill by a wall. With money from the emperor and help from the cities and agricultural colonies of the Duchy of Rome, the work took four years; when the fortifications were completed and blessed with great solemnity in 852, the newly fortified quarter was called the Leonine City after him. While the work was still in progress, a great Saracen fleet, seemingly from Sardinia, sailed against Rome, but it was completely destroyed off Ostia in 849 by the allied fleets of Rome, Naples, Amalfi, and Gaeta, aided by a tempest. When the rebuilding was accomplished, Leo rebuilt Portus and entrusted it to Corsican exiles whom the Saracen ravages had driven from their homes, and other cities of the Roman duchy were fortified either by the pope himself or at his exhortation.

Leo likewise made good the damage the raid had done to the churches. St. Peter's had suffered very severely, and though as a whole it never regained its former magnificence, he managed to make it in parts more beautiful than before. He also renovated St. Martin's, where he had been educated; the Quatuor Coronati, of which he had been the priest; the Lateran Palace; the Anglo-Saxon Borgo; Subiaco; and many other places in Rome and beyond. He built the church of S. Maria Nova to replace S. Maria Antiqua, which the decaying Palace of the Caesars threatened to engulf.

In 850 Leo associated Lothair's son Louis in the empire by imposing on him the imperial crown. Three years later, according to an old English historian, he hallowed the child Alfred to king by anointing, received him as his own child by adoption, gave him confirmation, and sent him back to England with the blessing of St. Peter. In 853 he held an important synod in Rome, which passed decrees for the furtherance of ecclesiastical discipline and learning and condemned the refractory Anastasius, Cardinal of St. Marcellus and sometime librarian of the Roman Church.

Rebellious conduct by John, Archbishop of Ravenna, forced Leo to journey to that city to restore respect for the law, and he died while engaged in a similar effort with Hincmar of Reims. Nomenoe, Duke of Brittany, defied papal authority until his death in 851, deposing bishops and erecting a metropolitan see of his own at Dol. When St. Ignatius, Patriarch of Constantinople, asked Leo to confirm his deposition of the turbulent Gregory Asbestas, Bishop of Syracuse, Leo declined, because Ignatius had assembled bishops and deposed others without the knowledge of the pope. Amid these tensions with Constantinople, Daniel, a magister militum, accused Leo to the Frankish Emperor Louis of wishing to overthrow the domination of the Franks by a Greek alliance; the pope had no difficulty in convincing Louis that the charge was groundless, and Daniel, condemned to death, escaped it only by the emperor's intercession.

Leo died on 17 July 855 and was buried in St. Peter's. His biographer and the Patriarch Photius credit him with working miracles, and his name is found in the Roman Martyrology; he has been honored as a saint from antiquity. Remembered as a shepherd who defended his people in body and in soul, he is venerated as a patron of bishops and sailors and for protection.

pope-leo-ix.history:
Pope Leo IX was born Bruno at Egisheim, near Colmar, on the borders of Alsace, on 21 June 1002, the son of Hugh, first cousin to Emperor Conrad, and of Heilewide, both remarkable for their piety and learning. Biographers relate that he refused to study from a beautiful book his mother had given him until it was found to be stolen from the Abbey of St. Hubert in the Ardennes and restored to its owners. At five years of age he was entrusted to Berthold, Bishop of Toul, who kept a school for the sons of the nobility.

Bruno became a canon of St. Stephen's at Toul in 1017, and in 1024 his relatives sent him to serve in the chapel of his kinsman, the new Emperor Conrad; his companions called him 'the good Bruno.' In 1026, still a deacon, he commanded the contingent of Toul on Conrad's Italian expedition, and when Bishop Herimann died he was elected to succeed him. Conrad, who destined him for higher things, was loath to allow him so modest a see, but Bruno prevailed and was consecrated in 1027, administering Toul for more than twenty years amid famine and war. Sent as envoy to Robert the Pious, he established so firm a peace between France and the empire that it endured under their sons, and he held his episcopal city against Eudes, Count of Blois. The deaths of his father, his mother, and two of his brothers shadowed these years; he found consolation in music.

When Pope Damasus II died in 1048, the Romans asked the Emperor Henry III to give them either Halinard, Archbishop of Lyons, or Bruno. Henry at once chose Bruno, who did all he could to avoid the honour, agreeing at length only to go to Rome and accept the papacy if freely elected by the Roman people, wishing to rescue the See of Peter from servitude to the German emperors. Presenting himself barefoot and in pilgrim's guise, in the company of Hildebrand, he was acclaimed with one voice, and, assuming the name of Leo, was solemnly enthroned on 12 February 1049.

He first put down a fresh attempt by the ex-Pope Benedict IX to seize the papal throne, and entrusted the depleted papal finances to Hildebrand, the future Gregory VII, with whom he worked closely. In April 1049 he held a synod that condemned simony and clerical incontinence, and he then carried the reform of the Church across Europe in a series of journeys, holding a council at Pavia, an important synod at Reims, joining Henry III at Cologne, and securing peace in Lorraine by excommunicating the rebel Godfrey the Bearded; for these travels he was styled Peregrinus Apostolicus.

The pontificate closed amid the quarrel with the Patriarch Cerularius of Constantinople. Never recovering his spirits after the battle of Civitella, Leo was overtaken by mortal illness, had himself carried to Rome in March 1054, and died there on 19 April 1054. The dispute outlived him: on 16 July 1054 the two cardinals acting as his legates excommunicated Cerularius, and the East was finally cut off from the body of the Church. In this rupture, in which legates and patriarch had exchanged excommunications, the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Churches were formally divided, the event known as the Great Schism.

Leo's concerns reached England, whose saintly King Edward he dispensed from a vow of pilgrimage to Rome on condition that he give alms to the poor and endow a monastery in honour of St. Peter. He authorized the translation of the See of Crediton to Exeter, forbade the consecration of the unworthy Abbot of Abingdon as Bishop of London, and, throughout the troubles between Archbishop Robert of Jumièges and the family of Earl Godwin, sent the archbishop the pallium and condemned Stigand, the holder of his see. King Macbeth is believed to have visited Rome during this pontificate.

He was buried in St. Peter's, and his biographers credit him with miracles both in life and after death. His name found a place in the Roman Martyrology, and he has been venerated as a saint, his feast kept on 19 April.

macrina-the-elder.history:
Saint Macrina the Elder belongs to the generation of Christians who carried the Church through the last of its great persecutions, and knowledge of her life rests mainly on the testimony of the great Cappadocian Fathers, Saints Basil, Gregory of Nyssa, and Gregory of Nazianzus. Saint Basil refers to her in two of his letters, Gregory of Nyssa in his Life of Macrina the Younger, and Gregory of Nazianzus in his panegyric on Saint Basil. Her home was at Neocaesarea in Pontus, in Asia Minor. As a child she was acquainted with Saint Gregory Thaumaturgus, first bishop of her native town, whose preaching had won Neocaesarea almost completely for Christianity; she has long been remembered as a disciple of his. Since that venerable doctor died between 270 and 275, Macrina must have been born before 270.

During the Diocletian persecution she fled her native town with her husband, whose name has not come down to us, and endured many privations. She was thus a confessor of the Faith in the last violent storm that burst over the early Church; tradition holds that she and her husband hid for years in forests to preserve both their lives and their confession of the Faith.

Macrina became the mother of Basil the Elder, whose children included Basil the Great, Gregory of Nyssa, Macrina the Younger, and Peter of Sebaste. On the intellectual and religious training of Saint Basil and his elder brothers and sisters she exercised a great influence, implanting in their minds the seeds of piety and that ardent desire for Christian perfection which was later to attain so glorious a growth. The tradition of faith and prayer she planted thus bore fruit across the generations that followed her.

Because Saint Basil was probably born in 331, Macrina must have died early in the fourth decade of the fourth century. In her the Church venerates a Christian matron whose courage as a confessor and whose formative care of her family passed to her descendants. Her feast is celebrated on 14 January. Honored as a model of widowhood and of trust in divine Providence, she is invoked by widows, the poor, and grandparents.

magnus-felix-ennodius.history:
Magnus Felix Ennodius, rhetorician and bishop, was born in 473 or 474, probably at Arles in southern Gaul, and died at Pavia in northern Italy on 17 July 521, the date kept as his feast. When quite young he went to Pavia, where he was educated, was betrothed, and eventually became a priest; it does not appear certain that the marriage was ever contracted, and his fiancée at the same time became a nun.

About 496, shortly after the death of his benefactor Epiphanius, he received minor orders at Milan, drawn there no doubt by his uncle Laurentius, bishop of that city, and was soon ordained deacon and taught in the schools. In 498 a disputed election left two claimants to the papacy, the deacon Symmachus and the archpriest Laurentius. King Theodoric favored Symmachus, and in 501 convened a council at Rome, the famous Synodus Palmaris, to settle the question and put an end to the scandal it caused. Ennodius acted as secretary to Laurentius of Milan, who was the first to sign the council's decrees. When partisans of the unsuccessful archpriest wrote against its decisions, Ennodius replied with a defense of the synod, still extant, often known as the Libellus pro Synodo. There he maintained that human judges cannot pass judgment on a pope: God, he wrote, consented that the affairs of men be settled by men, but reserved judgment upon the pontiff of the supreme see to Himself.

In 513 Ennodius was still at Milan; shortly afterwards he was made Bishop of Pavia, being consecrated in 514. In 515 and in 517 he headed two successive embassies sent by Pope Hormisdas to the Emperor Anastasius at Constantinople on behalf of the Roman see; both proved fruitless, and the emperor's unrelenting enmity endangered the envoys' lives in 517. Of the remaining years of his episcopate nothing is known; the date of his death is preserved by an epitaph found by accident.

Ennodius was one of the most distinguished Latin rhetoricians and poets of his age and is counted the last representative of the ancient schools of rhetoric. His works include poems for special occasions and epigrams, particularly inscriptions for churches and other religious monuments, an autobiography (the Eucharisticum), a panegyric on King Theodoric, a life of his predecessor Epiphanius of Pavia, a life of the monk Antonius of Lérins, and numerous letters which, despite their verbosity, preserve much information about the persons and customs of the time. His Paraenesis didascalica of 511 celebrates rhetoric as the foremost of the liberal arts, through which a guilty man can be made to appear innocent and vice versa, and his declamatory Dictiones treat themes once the delight of pagan rhetoricians, such as the grief of Thetis over the corpse of Achilles and the lament of Dido forsaken by Aeneas. With the same resources he denounced, for instance, a man who set up a statue of Minerva in a place of ill repute, and in an epithalamium he retained the old mythological apparatus, describing the beauty of the nude Venus and making Love argue against virginity; yet elsewhere he refuted the fables of the poets and pointed to the understanding of the Christian Scriptures as the highest intellectual ideal. In him are visible the two tendencies whose conflict is never quite absent from Christian life.

His diction is exuberant and florid, though it occasionally manifests vigour. He is honored as a model of the learned bishop and as a patron of bishops, of writers, and of Europe.

martial.history:
Martial, whose name is also rendered Marcial, Martialis, and Marcialis, was a bishop of Limoges in the third century and is venerated as the first occupant of that see. He is counted among the missionary bishops who carried the Gospel into Gaul in the earliest age of the Church, and he has long been known as the Apostle of the Gauls or the Apostle of Aquitaine. He was canonized in the pre-congregation era. No accurate information survives concerning his origin, the dates of his birth and death, or the acts of his episcopate; essentially all that is known of him derives from Gregory of Tours.

According to Gregory of Tours, under the consulate of Decius and Gratus seven bishops were sent from Rome to preach the Gospel in Gaul: Gatien to Tours, Trophimus to Arles, Paul to Narbonne, Saturninus to Toulouse, Denis to Paris, Austromoine to Clermont, and Martial to Limoges. Martial appears to have been accompanied by two priests whom he brought from the Orient, so that he himself may have been born in that region. He succeeded in converting the inhabitants of Limoges to the Christian faith, and his labors there made the city one of the cradles of French Christianity; his memory has always been venerated there.

Very early, popular devotion transformed this figure into an apostle of the first century. Tradition holds, in this later account, that Martial was sent into Gaul by Saint Peter himself, that he evangelized not only the province of Limoges but all of Aquitaine, and that he performed many miracles, among them the raising of a dead man to life by touching him with a rod that Saint Peter had given him. A Life of St. Martial attributed to Bishop Aurelian, his successor, is in reality the work of an eleventh-century forger; according to this account, Martial was born in Palestine, was numbered among the seventy-two disciples of Christ, was present at the resurrection of Lazarus and at the Last Supper, and was baptized by Saint Peter. These stories fill long pages and were received with favor for many centuries, not only among the unlettered but also among the learned, and even into modern times.

For a long time, nevertheless, the biography of Saint Martial was exposed to well-warranted discussion, since it was bound up with the great question of the apostolicity of certain Churches of Gaul. As far as Martial himself is concerned, it has been clearly proved that he must be honored not as one of the seventy-two disciples of Christ, but as the first preacher of the Christian faith in the Province of Limoges, and that veneration of him should not extend beyond this.

The matter reached its formal resolution in the nineteenth century. Mgr Buissas, Bishop of Limoges, petitioned the Holy See in 1853 that the most ancient of his predecessors should not be deprived of the honors so long accorded him as one of the seventy-two disciples of Christ. The Sacred Congregation, acting unanimously on 8 April 1854, and Pius IX in his decree of 8 May following, refused absolutely to bestow on Saint Martial the title of disciple of Christ, and confined themselves to declaring that the veneration accorded him was of very ancient origin.

Two epistles inserted in the Bibliotheca Patrum are attributed to Martial, but they are apocryphal. He is invoked as a patron of prisoners, and he has long been called upon in prayer in times of plague and of natural disasters. The Church keeps his feast on 30 June.

maximus-of-turin.history:
Maximus of Turin was a bishop and theological writer, probably born in Rhaetia about 380, who served as the first known bishop of Turin, then a suffragan see of Milan. Only two dates in his life are historically established. In 451 he was present at the Synod of Milan, where the bishops of Northern Italy accepted the celebrated dogmatic letter of Pope Leo I setting forth the orthodox doctrine of the Incarnation against the Nestorians and Eutychians; among the nineteen subscribers Maximus stood eighth, and since the order was determined by age, he must then have been about seventy years old. The second established date is 465, when he was at the Synod of Rome; his subscription there followed immediately after the pope's, showing that he was the oldest of the forty-eight bishops present. History does not mention him after 465, and he died shortly after that year.

The approximate time and place of his birth may be surmised from a passage in one of his sermons, in which he designates himself a witness of the martyrdom of three missionary priests in 397 at Anaunia in the Rhaetian Alps. His successor in the see of Turin was St. Victor.

As bishop, Maximus shepherded a Christian community only recently emerged from paganism, guiding his diocese through the turbulent years in which the ancient world gave way to the Christian age. His discourses speak of an impending barbarian invasion and of the destruction of the Church of Milan by the barbarians, and in many of them he fearlessly rebuked the survivals of paganism still prevalent among his people while defending the orthodox faith against the inroads of heresy. All his discourses manifest his solicitude for the eternal welfare of his flock, and through his preaching he made a great contribution to the spread and consolidation of Christianity in northern Italy, so that he is remembered as a father of the Church in Piedmont.

He is the author of numerous discourses, first edited by Bruni and published in 1784 at the Propaganda by order of Pius VI. The works ascribed to him comprise one hundred and eighteen homilies, one hundred and sixteen sermons, and six treatises. The homilies and sermons fall into discourses on the seasons and feasts of the ecclesiastical year, on the saints whose feasts were commemorated on the day they were delivered, and on exegetical, dogmatic, or moral subjects. Three of the treatises concern baptism, one is directed against the pagans and one against the Jews; these last two survive only in fragments, and their genuineness is doubtful, as is that of a sixth treatise of short discourses on twenty-three topics drawn from the Four Gospels. An appendix contains writings of uncertain authorship, among them two long epistles addressed to a sick friend, and many of the writings Bruni ascribes to Maximus are of doubtful origin. The discourses are usually very brief and couched in forcible language, though at times over-flowery; they touch on many facts of liturgy and history, among them abstinence during Lent, the absence of fasting and kneeling at prayer during paschal time, and fasting on the Vigil of Pentecost, and in several of them Maximus upheld the supremacy of St. Peter.

Maximus is honored as a confessor of the faith and is venerated as a patron of bishops, preachers, and theologians. His name is entered in the Roman martyrology on 25 June, and the city of Turin honors him as its patron.

According to a life of the saint written after the eleventh century and regarded as entirely unreliable, a cleric one day followed him with an evil intention to a retired chapel where he was accustomed to pray. The cleric suddenly became so thirsty that he implored Maximus for help, and a roe happening to pass, the saint caused it to stop so that the man could partake of its milk. This legend accounts for the fact that Maximus is represented in art as pointing at a roe.

meletius-of-antioch.history:
Meletius was born at Melitene in Lesser Armenia and died at Antioch in 381. Before his elevation to Antioch in 360 he had been bishop of Sebaste, capital of Armenia Prima, perhaps from 358 or 359; his stay there was short and troubled, for the people remained attached to his predecessor Eustathius. Antioch itself, once a stronghold of Nicene orthodoxy, had for a generation been rent by schism under a series of unequal bishops, several of them open to Arian influence. When Eudoxius, raised to Constantinople in 360, reopened the Antiochene succession, bishops assembled from every side for an election in which the Acacians were dominant. The choice fell on Meletius, who had resigned Sebaste and was a personal friend of Acacius; because he had given assurances to both parties, orthodox and Arians alike believed at first that he was their own.

His doctrinal position was so delicate that he passed at different times for Anomean, Homoiousian, Homoian, or Neo-Nicene. Yet when the reigning emperor, a militant Arian, arranged a conference to draw out his convictions on the disputed verse, 'The Lord possessed me in the beginning of His way,' Meletius answered that Scripture does not contradict itself and that the Son, begotten before all time, is like unto the Father, His image, creator of all, not an imperfect but an adequate image. He spoke without technical language, satisfied his hearers, and his profession of faith was recognized as orthodox, a severe blow to the Arian party. Saint Basil wrote of him that he was the first to speak freely in favour of the truth and to fight the good fight. For such teaching he was exiled from Antioch three times by imperial authority, and throughout the Meletian schism, in which Paulinus was set up as a rival bishop, he bore the division of his flock as a long-suffering pastor.

His virtues were genuine: a simple life, pure morals, sincere piety and affable manners. Men weary of interminable controversy saw in his kindly, gentle temper the promise of peace, and he held the affection of the large and turbulent population of Antioch. Saint Gregory of Nazianzus called him pious, simple and without guile, full of godliness, with peace shining on his countenance; fittingly, there was honey in his name as in his disposition. He was esteemed by Saint John Chrysostom, Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, Saint Gregory of Nyssa, Saint Basil, and even by his adversary Saint Epiphanius. He began his episcopate by reforming notorious abuses and instructing his people, and he laboured without ceasing for the unity of the Church. As early as 381 he recognized that the death of one of the rival bishops would leave the survivor in full authority, but his friendly, peace-making proposals were rejected by Paulinus, who refused every settlement.

In 381 a great council of Eastern bishops was convoked at Constantinople, and, the bishop of Alexandria being absent, the presidency fell by right to the bishop of Antioch, whom Emperor Theodosius received with marked deference. The council elected Gregory of Nazianzus bishop of Constantinople, and to the great satisfaction of the orthodox it was Meletius who enthroned him. As it proceeded to confirm the Nicene faith, Meletius died almost suddenly, having spent his remaining days re-emphasizing his eagerness for unity and peace. His death caused universal sorrow. The obsequies, at which Theodosius was present, were celebrated in the church of the Apostles with touching and magnificent panegyrics, and his body was transferred to Antioch, where, after a second solemn service, the aged bishop was laid beside his predecessor Saint Babylas. His name long remained for the Eastern faithful a rallying sign and a synonym of orthodoxy, and his meekness in controversy bore witness to the charity of Christ.

mellitus.history:
Mellitus, a leading member of the Gregorian mission sent from Rome to convert the Anglo-Saxons, served as the first Bishop of London in the Saxon period and as the third Archbishop of Canterbury, and is remembered as a founder of English Christianity. Bede, whose account is the most reliable record of his life, describes him as of noble birth; because Pope Gregory the Great styles him abbot, it is thought he may have been Abbot of the monastery of St. Andrew on the Coelian Hill in Rome, to which both Gregory and St. Augustine had belonged. In 601 Gregory sent a second band of missionaries from Rome to join Augustine at Canterbury, with Mellitus as its leader, furnishing the party with commendatory letters to the bishops of Gaul and with all things needed for divine worship: sacred vessels, altar cloths, vestments for priests and clerics, relics of the holy apostles and martyrs, and many books.

Mellitus was consecrated bishop by Augustine soon after his arrival in England, and his first missionary efforts were among the East Saxons. Their king, Sabert, nephew to Ethelbert, King of Kent, supported the work, and by this aid Mellitus established his see in London, the East Saxon capital, and built there the church of St. Paul. On the death of Sabert his sons, who had refused Christianity, gave their people permission to worship idols once more. Seeing Mellitus celebrate Mass one day, the young princes demanded that he give them also the white bread he had been accustomed to give their father; when he answered that this was impossible until they had received Christian baptism, he was banished from the kingdom. Mellitus withdrew to Kent, where the death of Ethelbert had brought similar difficulties, and about the year 616 he retired to Gaul.

After an absence of about a year, Mellitus was recalled to Kent by Laurentius, Augustine's successor in the see of Canterbury, matters having improved there through the conversion of the new king, Eadbald. He was never able, however, to regain possession of his own see of London. In 619 Laurentius died, and Mellitus was chosen archbishop in his stead. He appears never to have received the pallium, and though he retained the see for five years, the absence of the pallium may account for his consecrating no bishops; throughout this period he suffered constantly from ill-health. He consecrated a church to the Blessed Mother of God in the monastery of SS. Peter and Paul at Canterbury. Tradition has also attributed to him the foundation of the Abbey of St. Peter at Westminster, though this is almost certainly incorrect. Among the many miracles recorded of him is the quelling of a great fire at Canterbury which threatened to destroy the entire city. The saint, although too ill to move, had himself carried to the spot where the fire was raging and, in answer to his prayer, a strong wind arose which bore the flames southwards away from the city.

Mellitus died on April 24, 624, and was buried in the monastery of SS. Peter and Paul, afterwards St. Augustine's, at Canterbury; some of his relics were preserved in London as late as 1298. His feast is observed on April 24, and he is honored as a patron of bishops, of missionaries, and of England.

pope-nicholas-i.history:
Nicholas I was born at Rome of a distinguished family, the son of the Defensor Theodore; date unknown. Trained in piety, learning, and eloquence, he entered the service of the Church at an early age, becoming a subdeacon under Pope Sergius II and a deacon under Leo IV. After Benedict's death in April 858 the Emperor Louis II came to Rome to influence the election; on 24 April 858 Nicholas was chosen pope, consecrated, and enthroned in St. Peter's in the emperor's presence.

He governed at a time of grave disorder: the empire of Charlemagne had fallen to pieces, Christian territory was threatened from north and east, morality was widely despised, and many bishops were worldly and unworthy of their office. Against this decline Nicholas set himself as a conscientious representative of the Roman Primacy, resolved to vindicate Christian morality and defend the law of God even against powerful bishops.

His conflict with Archbishop John of Ravenna, who oppressed the papal territory, maltreated the legates, and forged documents to support his claims, ended in excommunication and, after repeated summons, in his submission to the pope, though he later relapsed and was excommunicated anew. A dispute with Hincmar of Reims over Bishop Rothad of Soissons, who had appealed to Rome after his deposition, established the right of the papacy to judge important causes, and Hincmar in the end yielded to the decrees of the Apostolic See in a quarrel over the see of Bourges.

The marriage laws were defended with the same zeal. Ingiltrud, wife of Count Boso, was excommunicated after ignoring a summons to the Synod of Milan in 860. The most stubborn struggle was with Lothair II of Lorraine, who had cast off his lawful wife Theutberga for Waldrada; synods at Aachen in 862 and Metz in 863, where the papal legates had been bribed, sanctioned the union, but Nicholas brought the case before his own tribunal and at the Lateran Synod of October 863 deposed the archbishops who had upheld it. When Louis II took the side of the deposed bishops and Lothair laid siege to Rome, the pope was confined for two days in St. Peter's without food, yet he did not waver; the emperor was reconciled and withdrew, and the archbishops were sent home. Nicholas sought to reconcile Lothair and Theutberga until his death, but without effect, and he urged leniency toward Judith, who had married Baldwin, Count of Flanders, without her father's consent, to protect the freedom of marriage.

In the East, after Patriarch Ignatius of Constantinople was deposed in violation of ecclesiastical law, Nicholas asserted the authority of the Apostolic See and labored to keep the Eastern and Western Churches in communion. When Bulgaria, converted by Greek missionaries, sent an embassy from its ruler, Prince Boris, bearing one hundred and six questions on Christian teaching and discipline in 863, Nicholas answered in his celebrated Responsa Nicolai ad consulta Bulgarorum and sent envoys to foster Christian life among the converts, though Boris ultimately joined the Eastern Church. He likewise confirmed to St. Anschar, Archbishop of Bremen, and his successors the office of papal legate to the Danes, Swedes, and Slavs.

At Rome he rebuilt and endowed several churches and encouraged religious life, living in austere piety, and he was highly esteemed by the citizens of Rome and by his contemporaries. A long-discussed question, whether he made use of the forged pseudo-Isidorian decretals, was resolved by later investigation, which concluded that he was not acquainted with the collection as a whole and did not base his view of the law upon it.

Nicholas died on 13 November 867 and after death was honored as a saint, such veneration coming from antiquity rather than from formal canonization; his feast is kept on 13 November. He is remembered, alongside Leo I and Gregory I, as the last of the popes to bear the title 'the Great,' and he is honored as a patron of bishops and of church reform.

nilus-the-younger.history:
Nilus the Younger, also called Neilos of Rossano, was born at Rossano in Calabria around 910. He grew up in southern Italy, where the Greek-speaking Christian tradition had long flourished, and was for a time married; a daughter was born to him. An illness brought about his conversion, and with his wife's consent he entered religious life, becoming a monk and a propagator of the Rule of St. Basil in Italy.

His ascetic life, his virtues, and his theological learning won him renown. He lived for a time as a hermit and later passed certain periods at monasteries which he either founded or restored; he spent some time at Monte Cassino and at the monastery of St. Alexius in Rome. Traveling widely through southern Italy, he gathered disciples and did more than anyone to establish the Italo-Byzantine monastic tradition of the region.

When Gregory V (966-999) was driven out of Rome, Nilus opposed the usurpation of Philogatos (John) of Piacenza as antipope. Later, when Philogatos had been tortured and mutilated, Nilus reproached both Gregory V and the Emperor Otto III (993-1002) for the deed.

Nilus' chief work was the Greek monastery of Grottaferrata near Frascati, which he founded in 1004 and of which he is counted the first abbot; the abbey remains a living center of the Italo-Byzantine monastic tradition. Toward the end of his life he divided his time between Grottaferrata and a hermitage at Valleluce near Gaeta, and he died in 1005.

His feast is kept on 26 September in both the Byzantine calendar and the Roman Martyrology, and he is venerated in both the Eastern Orthodox and Catholic churches. He is honored as a patron of monks, of abbots, and of Italy.

olaf-haraldsson.history:
Olaf Haraldsson was born in 995, a son of King Harald Grenske of Norway, and reigned as king from 1015 until a rebellion drove him from the throne in 1028. Sources differ on his baptism: the saga-writer Snorre places it in Norway in 998, though it more probably took place around 1010 at Rouen in France, administered by Archbishop Robert. In his early youth Olaf went as a viking to England, where he took part in many battles and became earnestly interested in Christianity.

After many difficulties he was elected King of Norway and made it his object to extirpate heathenism and to make the Christian religion the basis of his kingdom. He is remembered as the great Norwegian legislator for the Church: like his ancestor Olaf Trygvesson, he made frequent and severe attacks on the old faith and customs, demolishing the temples and building Christian churches in their place. He brought bishops and priests from England, a few of whom are known by name, such as Grimkel, Sigfrid, Rudolf, and Bernhard, and on the whole he seems to have taken Anglo-Saxon conditions as a model for the ecclesiastical organization of his kingdom.

Resentment against Olaf grew strong, due not only to his Christianity but also in high degree to his unflinching struggle against the old constitution of shires and for the unity of Norway. The mighty clans rose in rebellion and applied to King Cnut of Denmark and England for help, which was willingly given; Olaf was expelled and Cnut was elected King of Norway. For this struggle Norwegians have regarded him as a great champion of national independence, honored alike by Catholics and Protestants, and he is venerated as the patron of soldiers, of conversion, and of the oppressed.

After two years of exile Olaf returned to Norway with an army and met his rebellious subjects at Stiklestad, where the celebrated battle took place on 29 July 1030. Neither King Cnut nor the Danes took part in the fighting. Olaf fought with great courage, but was mortally wounded; tradition records that he fell on the battlefield praying 'God help me'. Many miraculous occurrences are related in connection with his death and with his disinterment a year later, after belief in his sanctity had spread widely.

His friends Bishop Grimkel and Earl Einar Tambeskjelver laid the body in a coffin and set it on the high altar of the church of St. Clement in Nidaros, now Trondheim. Canonized barely a year after his death by Bishop Grimketel at Nidaros, Olaf received the title Rex Perpetuus Norvegiae, Norway's Eternal King, and became the patron of his nation. His feast is kept on 29 July. His cult spread widely in the Middle Ages, not only in Norway but also in Denmark and Sweden; even in London, St. Olave's Church on Hart Street was long dedicated to the canonized King of Norway. In 1856 a St. Olave's Church was erected in Christiania, the Norwegian capital, where a large relic of St. Olaf, a donation from the Danish Royal Museum, is preserved and venerated. The arms of Norway display a lion with St. Olaf's battle-axe in its forepaws.

optatus.history:
Optatus was Bishop of Milevis, in fourth-century Numidia, in the North African region corresponding to present-day Algeria, then among the most vibrant centers of Christian thought in the Latin-speaking West. He was a convert: St. Augustine ranks him with Cyprian, Lactantius, Victorinus, and Hilary among those who brought great riches out of paganism, and he had probably been a pagan rhetorician before his conversion.

He is remembered above all for his treatise against the Donatists, the schismatic movement that held the sacraments of clergy who had lapsed under persecution to be invalid. Written in answer to Parmenian, the successor of Donatus in the see of Carthage, it was recorded by St. Jerome as six books composed under the emperors Valens and Valentinian (364-75); seven books survive, its list of popes reaching Siricius (384-98). Internal indications date the first books to about 366-70 and a second edition, with a seventh book appended, to about 385-90.

The treatise addresses the whole controversy. Optatus distinguishes schismatics from heretics: the former, though they have rejected unity, retain true doctrine and true sacraments, and so ought not to be threatened with eternal damnation—a mild judgment compared with the severity of many of the Fathers, apparently motivated by the belief that all who have faith will be saved, though after long torments. Both sides agreed the Church is one; the dispute was where it is found. Optatus argues that it cannot exist only in a corner of Africa: it must be the catholic Church spread throughout the world. Parmenian had enumerated six properties of the Church, five of which Optatus accepts, contending that the first, the episcopal chair, belongs to the Catholics, who therefore possess all the others. Rather than defend the Catholic succession at Carthage, he traces the chair to Rome: upon Peter the bishop's chair was first conferred, the one chair in which unity was to be preserved, and his list of popes ends with Siricius, with whom the whole world agreed in one communion—after which he mocks the recent Donatist antipopes at Rome.

In the fifth book, Optatus argues against the doctrine the Donatists had inherited from St. Cyprian, that baptism conferred outside the Church cannot be valid, and he anticipates Augustine's argument that the faith of the baptizer does not matter, since it is God who confers the grace. His well-known statement of the objective efficacy of the sacraments declares that 'the sacraments are holy of themselves, not through men.' Rebuking the Donatists' sacrileges against the altars of God, he asks, 'what is an altar but the seat of the Body and Blood of Christ?' The seventh book adds a notable argument for unity: Peter had sinned most grievously in denying his Master, yet he retained the keys, and for the sake of unity and charity the Apostles did not separate from his fellowship; hence the readiness to receive the Donatists back without difficulty, for there must always be sinners in the Church, and charity covers a multitude of sins.

His style is vigorous and animated, more terse than flowing, yet marked by the gentleness and charity with which he insisted on calling the Donatist bishops his 'brethren.' An appendix preserves an important dossier of Donatist documents apparently collected between 330 and 347; it was already mutilated when copied, and the single manuscript containing it is incomplete, so that much material for the early history of Donatism has been lost.

Optatus apparently never received any ecclesiastical cultus; his name was inserted in the Roman Martyrology on the fourth of June, though it is unknown to all the ancient martyrologies and calendars, and his feast is kept on that day. He is honored as a patron of bishops, theologians, and church unity. His single work stands among the earliest Latin theological treatises on the nature of the Church, a monument of convincing dialectic, elegant literary form, and Christian charity.

osmund.history:
Osmund was a Norman noble who became one of the most influential churchmen of the English Church after the Norman Conquest. A late medieval document identifies him as the son of Henry, Count of Sées, and of Isabella, daughter of Duke Robert of Normandy, and tradition holds that he came to England with his uncle, William the Conqueror. He proved a trusted counsellor, was made chancellor of the realm, and served as one of the chief commissioners for the Domesday Book, being present at the Great Gemot at Old Sarum in 1086, when the survey was accepted and the great landowners swore fealty to the sovereign.

In 1078 he was made Bishop of Salisbury, the second bishop of the united see, by William's choice and with the authority of Pope Gregory VII, and was consecrated by Archbishop Lanfranc. The diocese comprised Dorsetshire, Wiltshire, and Berkshire, with its seat at Old Sarum, a fortress on a high hill rather than a city, which Peter le Blois described as the ark of God shut up in the temple of Baal. His work there was threefold. He oversaw the completion of the cathedral, consecrated on 5 April 1092, though five days later a thunderstorm destroyed its roof and damaged the fabric. He constituted the cathedral body on the Norman model, with a dean, precentor, chancellor, and treasurer, some thirty-two secular canons bound to residence, and a school for the clergy under the chancellor; his canons were renowned for their musical talent and zeal for learning, the cathedral was constituted the Mother Church of the diocese, and their influence shaped the foundation of other cathedral bodies.

The third work was the Sarum Use. Osmund introduced little that was new; he selected from the customs around him and arranged the offices and services of the Mass, the Divine Office, and the Calendar. The Ordinal of Osmund, intended primarily for his own diocese, spread within a hundred years almost throughout England, Wales, and Ireland, and entered Scotland about 1250, holding general approval until the reign of Mary. The Register of St. Osmund preserves the Consuetudinary, De Officiis Ecclesiasticis, together with documents and charters concerning the cathedral and its foundation.

William of Malmesbury records him as so eminent for chastity that common fame would itself blush to speak otherwise than truthfully of his virtue, stern to penitents yet no more severe to them than to himself, and free from ambition. Osmund gathered a good library for his canons and, even as a bishop, did not disdain to transcribe and bind books himself. He revered St. Aldhelm, his predecessor at Sherborne three centuries earlier, officiated at that saint's translation, and helped Lanfranc obtain his canonization; a relic of the saint kept at Sarum was, tradition holds, the occasion of miracles. He favored the king at the Council of Rockingham in 1095 in the investiture dispute, but after the Lateran Council of 1099 he boldly sided with Archbishop Anselm, and is said to have knelt before him on his way to Windsor to receive his forgiveness.

Osmund died in the night of 3 December 1099 and was buried at Old Sarum, the see remaining vacant for eight years before Roger succeeded him. In 1228 the bishop and canons petitioned Gregory IX for his canonization, and on 1 January 1457 Pope Callistus III issued the Bull confirming his cult. On 23 July of that year his remains were translated to New Salisbury, where his sumptuous shrine was destroyed under Henry VIII; a flat slab inscribed MXCIX now lies under the easternmost arch on the south side of the cathedral. Honored for his fidelity in royal and episcopal office alike, he is venerated as a patron of bishops, of England, and of church reform.

pammachius.history:
Pammachius was a Roman senator, a man of rank and learning. In his youth he frequented the schools of rhetoric together with St. Jerome, and the friendship between the two men endured for many years. In 385 he married Paulina, the second daughter of St. Paula of Rome.

In 390 he was probably among the men of noble birth and outstanding religion who denounced the teachings of Jovinian to Pope St. Siricius. Later, when Pammachius attacked St. Jerome's book against Jovinian for prudential reasons, Jerome replied with two letters thanking him; the first of these, a defense of the book, was probably intended for publication.

The death of Paulina in 397 marked the great turning point of his life. Pammachius became a monk: that is, he put on a religious habit and gave himself up to works of charity and prayer, an event testified to by St. Jerome and by Paulinus of Nola in their correspondence. Rather than seeking a second marriage, he devoted the rest of his life to the service of the poor.

With St. Fabiola he built a hospice at Porto, at the mouth of the Tiber, for the reception and care of poor strangers. In this work he devoted the resources of his station to the relief of the sick and of travelers far from home. The site has been excavated, and the excavations have disclosed the plan and arrangement of the building, described as the only one of its kind, with rooms and halls for the sick and the poor grouped around it.

In 399 Pammachius, together with Oceanus, wrote to St. Jerome asking him to translate Origen's work De Principiis and to repudiate the insinuation of Rufinus that Jerome was of one mind with Rufinus concerning Origen. St. Jerome answered them the following year in two letters. The exchange belongs to the disputes of that period concerning Origen. In 401 St. Augustine thanked Pammachius for a letter he had written to the people of Numidia, where Pammachius owned property, exhorting them to abandon the Donatist schism.

Pammachius was also a man of letters. Many of St. Jerome's commentaries on Scripture were dedicated to him. This association linked his name with the study of the Scriptures. The church of Saints John and Paul at Rome was founded either by Pammachius himself or by his father; it was known in ancient times first as the Titulus Bizantis and afterwards as the Titulus Pammachii.

Pammachius died about the year 409, some twelve years after the death of his wife.
