He is venerated as a saint in both the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic Churches, and he is honored as a patron of the poor, of widowers, and of the study of Scripture. His life is remembered for the way that personal grief and high station alike were turned into service. His feast is kept on 30 August.

pantaenus.history:
St. Pantaenus was a Sicilian theologian and one of the most significant figures in the intellectual life of the early Church. Trained in the Stoic philosophy, he came to Christianity after a career as a philosopher, bringing to the faith a disciplined mind and a persistent hunger for truth. According to Eusebius, he became head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria about the year 180 and was still living in 193; since he was succeeded by Clement of Alexandria, who left the city about 203, the date of his death is placed with some probability around the year 200.

The Catechetical School of Alexandria, the earliest such institution in the Church, became profoundly influential in Christian theology. The most important fact known concerning Pantaenus is that he anticipated both Clement and Origen in the study of Greek philosophy as an aid to theology, endeavoring to press the Greek philosophers into the service of Christianity. Origen, defending his own use of the philosophers, appealed to Pantaenus's example, recalling that he had benefited many before his time by his thorough preparation in such things.

Clement names Pantaenus by name as his teacher in his Hypotyposes. Eusebius conjectured that Clement also alluded to him in the Stromata, where the last of his teachers, unnamed, is described as a Hebrew of Palestine, the ablest of them all, whose hiding place in Egypt Clement sought out, and in whom he found rest. The identification has been doubted, since a Hebrew of Palestine was unlikely to have been trained in Stoic philosophy; in its favor are the facts that this teacher was met in Egypt and that Pantaenus turned Greek philosophy to Christian ends. It may well be that a mind like Clement's found rest in that feature of his teaching.

Through the Hypotyposes, a book largely made up of traditions received from the elders, opinions and traditions ascribed to Pantaenus appear to have been handed on, though it is not certain that Clement reckoned him among the elders he had known. Passages quoted under his name in later collections, such as the Eclogae ex Prophetis and the Scholia of Maximus Confessor, may derive from that work. Photius reports that the Apology for Origen composed by Pamphilus and Eusebius stated that Pantaenus had been a hearer of men who had seen the Apostles, and perhaps had heard the Apostles themselves; the stronger assertion may rest on conjecture, while the milder statement may go back to Clement.

Tradition holds that Pantaenus travelled as a missionary as far as India, though the land he reached may in fact have been South Arabia. There he is said to have found Christians already in possession of the Gospel of Matthew in Hebrew, which they had received from the Apostle Bartholomew. Eusebius hands on the account only as what was said.

No certain writing of his survives. Because Anastasius Sinaita singled out Pantaenus among the early Fathers as interpreting the six days of creation and the Garden of Eden as figures of Christ and the Church, a line of thought that appears in the closing chapters of the Epistle to Diognetus, Lightfoot and Batiffol conjectured that Pantaenus was the author of those chapters. The suggestion remains a conjecture.

Canonized in the pre-congregation era, Pantaenus is remembered with a feast on July 7. He is honored as a patron of philosophers, theologians, and teachers, and as a patron of those who seek to reconcile faith and reason.

perpetuus.history:
St. Perpetuus served as Bishop of Tours from about 460 until his death around 490. He belonged to an illustrious Gallo-Roman family closely bound to the episcopal see he would govern: St. Eustachius, who had been his predecessor, and St. Volusianus, who became his successor, came from the same lineage. His episcopate fell in the decades after the collapse of Roman authority in Gaul, a turbulent period in which the church in Touraine looked to its bishops for stability and leadership.

Perpetuus guided the Church of Tours for some thirty years, and it is apparent, from the little information that survives, that during his administration Christianity was considerably developed and consolidated in Touraine. Shortly after his elevation he presided over a council at which eight bishops, reunited in Tours on the feast of St. Martin, took part; at this assembly an important rule concerning ecclesiastical discipline was promulgated. He maintained careful surveillance over the conduct of the clergy of his diocese, and mention is made of priests who were removed from their office because they had proved unworthy.

He built monasteries and various churches, but the work closest to his heart was the veneration of St. Martin of Tours, the great soldier-bishop of the previous century, to whom he was especially devoted. Saint Britius had constructed a little chapel to protect the tomb of St. Martin, and Perpetuus desired to replace it with a beautiful basilica, completed about 470. In this way the humble shrine was transformed into one of the chief pilgrimage sites of medieval France.

Beyond his devotion to Martin, Perpetuus encouraged the cult of the saints and the liturgical life of his diocese more broadly, working to establish order in a time of political upheaval. The picture that emerges from the surviving evidence is of a conscientious shepherd who combined pastoral vigilance with an energetic program of building, and whose long episcopate coincided with a period of consolidation for the church in Touraine.

A valuable witness to his character is his last will and testament, a document belonging to the end of the fifth century that was published for the first time in 1661 by Dom Luc d'Achery in his Spicilegium. This curious historical monument gives an excellent idea of the sanctity of its author and remains an important source for his life.

Perpetuus died at the close of his long episcopate. The sources give differing dates, some recording 490 and others 8 April 491, and his feast is kept on April 8. He was honored as a faithful shepherd who guided the church of Tours through a difficult age, and he is venerated as a saint, invoked in particular as a patron of bishops, pilgrims, and church reform.

peter-chrysologus.history:
St. Peter Chrysologus was born at Imola in 406 and died there in 450. Nearly everything recorded of him derives from a biography first written in the ninth century by Agnellus in the Liber pontificalis ecclesiae Ravennatis, an account that gives only scanty information and preserves little beyond the broad outlines of his life and career.

He was baptized, educated, and ordained deacon by Cornelius, Bishop of Imola, and in 433 he was elevated to the bishopric of Ravenna, a see for which there are indications that it had previously held the rank of metropolitan. His advancement owed much to the influence of the Empress Galla Placidia, who, according to tradition, was guided to her choice by a vision of St. Apollinaris. The new bishop's piety and zeal won universal admiration, and his oratory was such that he received the surname Chrysologus, Greek for "golden-worded."

He stood in the confidence of Pope Leo the Great, with whom he maintained a humble correspondence, and he defended the orthodox faith against the heresies of his age. When the Monophysite Eutyches, after his condemnation by the Synod of Constantinople in 448, endeavored to win Peter's support, the bishop declined, and the endeavor met with no success.

For his preaching Peter is chiefly remembered. A collection of his homilies numbering 176 was made by Felix, Bishop of Ravenna (709-17), though some pieces in that collection are interpolations, and several homilies known to be genuinely his are found in other collections under different names. The sermons are in great measure explanatory of Biblical texts, brief and concise, and they were prized for their clarity, their devotion, and a warm pastoral concern for his people; for this reason he is honored as the Doctor of Homilies. Among his subjects he treated the mystery of the Incarnation, the errors of Arius and Eutyches, and the Apostles' Creed, and he devoted a series of homilies to the Blessed Virgin and to St. John the Baptist.

His works were first edited by Agapitus Vicentinus at Bologna in 1534, followed by the editions of D. Mita in 1634 and S. Pauli in 1775, the latter reprinted in the Patrologia Latina. In 1863 Fr. Liverani edited nine previously unprinted homilies from manuscripts in Italian libraries, together with variant readings of several others, and several homilies were translated into German by M. Held in 1874.

In honor of his enduring teaching he was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1729. He is honored as a patron of preachers, bishops, and theologians, and his feast is kept on July 30.

philastrius.history:
St. Philastrius was Bishop of Brescia in northern Italy during the late fourth century, an era in which the Church was contending with Arianism and other doctrinal divisions. He died before 397, and his feast is kept on July 18. He is venerated as a patron of bishops, of church reform, and of theologians.

His episcopal service was exercised amid the doctrinal struggles of the age. He was among the bishops who gathered at the synod of Aquileia in 381, convened under the authority of St. Ambrose to address heresy and to defend the Church's teaching on the Trinity. St. Augustine met him at Milan about 383, or perhaps a little later, as Augustine himself records in one of his letters.

Philastrius is also remembered as the author of a catalogue of heresies, the Diversarum Hereseon Liber, composed about 384. The work surveys deviations from the faith handed down from the apostles and reflects the same pastoral concern for doctrinal integrity that marked his episcopate. Its chief scholarly value lies in a circumstance discovered by Lipsius: for the Christian heresies up to Noetus, the compiler drew from the same source as Epiphanius, namely the lost Syntagma of Hippolytus. With the aid of Philastrius, Epiphanius, and the Pseudo-Tertullian treatise against heresies, scholars have been able to reconstruct in large measure that lost work of Hippolytus. The Catalogue was first printed at Basle in 1528, and the latest edition was published by Marx in the Vienna Corpus Script. Eccles. Lat. in 1898.

Much of what is related of Philastrius's earlier life rests upon a sermon among the writings of St. Gaudentius, purporting to have been preached on the fourteenth anniversary of Philastrius's death. According to this tradition, his life began with a great act of renunciation, for which the preacher compared him to Abraham. He was ordained a priest and travelled over nearly the whole Roman world, preaching against pagans, Jews, and heretics, especially the Arians. Like St. Paul, he was said to carry in his body the stigmata of Christ, having been scourged for his zeal against those heretics. At Milan he was a mainstay of the Catholic party during the episcopate of St. Ambrose's Arian predecessor. At Rome he held both private and public disputations with heretics, and is credited with the conversion of many. His wanderings ceased when he was raised to the see of Brescia.

The genuineness of this sermon has long been debated. Doubts were first raised by Dupin, and they were reiterated by Marx, the latest editor of Philastrius, who regarded the sermon as a forgery of the eighth or ninth century. Knappe defended its authenticity by linguistic arguments, and his Bollandist reviewer judged that he had made a strong case. Whatever position be taken on the sermon, the outlines of Philastrius's career rest on firmer ground: his presence at the synod of Aquileia, his writing against the heresies, and his meeting with Augustine are independently attested. He died before 397, leaving a reputation for doctrinal fidelity and steadfast episcopal service in a time of theological conflict.

plegmund.history:
Plegmund, a Mercian, spent his early life near Chester as a hermit on an island that came to bear his name, Plegmundham, the present Plemstall. His reputation for piety and learning caused King Alfred the Great to summon him to court, where he helped the king in his literacy work.

In 890 he was chosen Archbishop of Canterbury and went to Rome to receive the pallium from Pope Formosus. When the acts and ordinations of Formosus were condemned in 897, and the condemnation was confirmed in 905, Plegmund's own position became questionable. In 908 he paid a second visit to Rome, probably to obtain from Pope Sergius III confirmation of his acts as archbishop and to arrange a subdivision of the West Saxon episcopate. The subdivision was carried out the following year, when Plegmund consecrated seven bishops in one day, five for Wessex and two others.

He died in extreme old age on 2 August 914 and was buried in his cathedral at Canterbury. Venerated as a saint after his death, he is honored as a patron of hermits, translators, and scholars, and his feast is kept on August 2.

porphyrius.history:
Porphyrius, Bishop of Gaza and remembered for his part in Christianizing a city long attached to its pagan temples, was born at Thessalonica around 347. After five years as a monk in the Egyptian desert of Scete, he spent a further five years living in a cave near the Jordan. Although his health remained impaired, he frequently visited the scene of the Resurrection in Jerusalem, and it was there that he met the Asiatic Mark, who in time became a deacon of his church and his biographer. To effect the sale of the property Porphyrius still owned in his native city, Mark set out for Thessalonica; upon his return, the proceeds were distributed among the monasteries of Egypt and among the needy in and around Jerusalem. In 392 Porphyrius was ordained to the priesthood, and the relic of the Holy Cross was entrusted to his care.

In 395 he was consecrated Bishop of Gaza, a stronghold of paganism with an insignificant Christian community, a see then dominated by the worship of Marnas. The hostile attitude of the pagan population led the bishop to appeal to the emperor for protection, and he pleaded repeatedly for the destruction of the pagan temples. His episcopate became a long struggle against paganism, recounted by his deacon Mark in the Life of Porphyrius, which records the threats he endured; tradition holds that the imperial decree ordering the destruction of the temples was obtained through Empress Eudoxia. The great temple of Marnas, the Marneion, was razed, and a Christian church was raised upon its site.

In 415 Porphyrius attended the Council of Diospolis. He died at Gaza on February 26, 420, and was buried in the church he had built. Venerated as a zealous bishop, he is honored as a patron of bishops and of the causes of church reform and conversion, and his feast is kept on February 26, the anniversary of his death.

The principal source for his episcopate is the Vita S. Porphyrii of Mark the Deacon, for centuries known only in a Latin translation; the original Greek text was published in 1874 by M. Haupt, and a new edition was issued in 1895 by the Bonn Philological Society. The Bollandists printed his life in the February volume of the Acta Sanctorum (Paris, 1865), and a historical and grammatical study of Mark's text was published by Nuth at Bonn in 1897.

possidius.history:
Possidius, bishop of Calama in Numidia, was a close companion of St. Augustine of Hippo and is remembered chiefly as his friend and biographer. The dates of his birth and death are unknown. In his Life of Augustine he lets it be known, speaking of himself in the third person, that he belonged to the clergy of Augustine's monastery, and he records an unbroken friendship with the saint lasting forty years. According to Tillemont, he was raised to the episcopate about 397, and at Calama he followed Augustine's example by establishing a monastery of his own.

Much of his episcopate was spent in conflict with the Donatists. At a council held at Carthage, Possidius challenged Crispinus, the Donatist bishop of Calama, to a public discussion, which Crispinus declined. Shortly afterwards a presbyter of Crispinus's clergy, bearing the same name as his bishop, attempted to assassinate Possidius. When Crispinus refused to punish him, legal proceedings were instituted; the Donatist bishop was proved a heretic and heavily fined, but at Possidius's intercession the fine was not exacted, an episode recorded in the Life and in Augustine's correspondence.

Possidius served the African Church through successive controversies. In 407 he sat, with Augustine and five other bishops, on a committee appointed to adjudicate an ecclesiastical matter whose particulars have not survived. In 408 a riot stirred up by the pagans at Calama nearly cost him his life. In 409 he was one of four bishops deputed to go to Italy to obtain the protection of the emperor against the Donatists, and in 411 he stood among the seven bishops chosen to represent the Catholic party at the Collatio, the conference held that year between the Catholic and Donatist parties. In 416 he assisted at the Council of Milevum, where fifty-nine Numidian bishops addressed a synodal letter to Pope Innocent I asking him to take action against Pelagianism; Possidius joined Augustine and three other bishops in a further letter to the pope on the same subject, and he was present at the conference between Augustine and the Donatist Emeritus.

When the Vandals invaded Roman Africa, Possidius took refuge at Hippo and was present at Augustine's death in 430. His Life of St. Augustine, a short work composed before the capture of Carthage in 439, includes an account of that death, written by one who had shared the saint's friendship for four decades. It is included in all editions of Augustine's works and also printed in Hurter's Opusc. SS. Patr., and it remains an indispensable source for Augustine's later years and for the fall of Roman order in North Africa. To the same purpose Possidius compiled an indiculus, a catalogue of Augustine's writings, preserved in later editions of the saint's works.

Prosper's Chronicle records that in 437 Possidius and two other bishops were persecuted and expelled from their sees by the Vandal king Genseric, an Arian; this is the last recorded notice of him. His feast is kept on May 16, and he is honored as a patron of bishops, scholars, and theologians.

rimbert.history:
Rimbert was archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen from 865 until his death at Bremen on 11 June 888. It is uncertain whether he was by origin a Fleming or a Norman. He was educated at the monastery of Turholt near Bruges in Flanders, and it was there that St. Ansgar, the first Archbishop of Hamburg, became acquainted with him and later made him his constant companion.

When Ansgar died on 2 February 865, Rimbert was chosen as his successor, and in December of that year Pope Nicholas I sent him the pallium. Because Ansgar's missionary system was based on a connection with the Benedictine Order, Rimbert became a monk at Corvey shortly after his consecration. He subsequently undertook missionary journeys to West Friesland, Denmark, and Sweden, though concerning these journeys no detailed information has survived.

In 884 Rimbert succeeded in putting to flight the Norman marauders on the coast of Friesland, and in remembrance of this incident he was later held in special veneration in Friesland. Among his episcopal achievements, the foundation of a monastery at Bücken near Bremen and his care for the poor and the sick are especially emphasized.

Rimbert is chiefly remembered for his biography of St. Ansgar, known as the Vita Ansgari, a work distinguished by valuable historical information and a faithful portrait of its subject, for which historians remain indebted to him. Knowledge of Rimbert's own life, by contrast, is meager, for the biography of him written by a monk of Corvey, while very edifying, is poor in actual information.

Venerated on June 11, the anniversary of his death, Rimbert is honored as a patron of bishops, missionaries, and writers.

sabina.history:
Saint Sabina is honored as a martyr of the early Roman Church. She was the widow of Valentinus and the daughter of Herod Metallarius, and she suffered martyrdom about the year 126. Her feast is kept on 29 August.

The chief account of her life comes from the Acts of her martyrdom, a text that carries no historic value. According to this traditional narrative, she lived at Rome and was converted to Christianity by Serapia, her female slave. Serapia was put to death for her faith, and later in the same year Sabina herself suffered martyrdom. The details of the story thus rest on an uncertain source, and any retelling of Sabina's conversion and death should be received as tradition rather than documented history. Within that tradition, she is remembered as a Christian widow who followed her servant in the faith and shared in her witness, and she is invoked as a patron of martyrs, widows, and the oppressed.

Her memory is closely associated with the Aventine Hill in Rome. In the year 430 her relics were brought there, and the basilica called after St. Sabina, which is of considerable interest in the history of art, preserves her memory on that site. Originally the church was dedicated to both Sabina and Serapia, so that the two women of the traditional narrative were honored together in one place.

pope-stephen-i.history:
Stephen I served as Bishop of Rome from 12 May 254 until his death on 2 August 257, though some doubt attaches to the precise dates of his pontificate. The most ancient catalogues record that he was a Roman by birth and the son of Jovius. According to the Liber Pontificalis, his predecessor Lucius I, when about to be martyred, entrusted the care of the Church to Stephen, then his archdeacon. Much of what is known of Stephen is connected, directly or indirectly, with the severe teachings of the heretic Novatus and the controversies that followed.

Stephen's most important work was his defense of the validity of baptism administered by heretics, maintained against the contrary opinion of St. Cyprian of Carthage and other bishops of Africa and Asia. Newly discovered letters of St. Dionysius of Alexandria bearing on this controversy have since come to light, and Archbishop Benson of Canterbury judged that Stephen "triumphed, and in him the Church of Rome triumphed, as she deserved."

Early in his pontificate, Faustinus, Bishop of Lyons, frequently urged Stephen to take action against Marcian, Bishop of Arles, who had attached himself to the doctrines of Novatus and denied communion to the penitent lapsi. For reasons now unknown, the pope did not move, and the bishops of Gaul turned to Cyprian, begging him to write to Rome. Cyprian did so in a letter that remains the sole source of information on the affair, entreating Stephen to imitate his martyred predecessors and to instruct the bishops of Gaul to condemn Marcian and elect another in his place. As nothing more is said of the matter, it is supposed that the pope acted in accordance with these wishes and that Marcian was deposed.

The case of the Spanish bishops Martial and Basilides also brought Stephen into dealings with Cyprian. Condemned as libellatici by the bishops of their province for denying the faith, the two first acknowledged their guilt but afterwards appealed to Rome. Deceived by their story, Stephen exerted himself to secure their restoration. Some of their fellow bishops took their part, while the rest laid the case before Cyprian; an assembly of African bishops convoked by Cyprian renewed the condemnation of the two men and exhorted the people to enter into communion with their successors. The African bishops were careful to point out that Stephen had acted as he did because, situated at a distance and ignorant of the true facts of the case, he had been deceived.

Stephen was likewise anxious to preserve the tradition of his predecessors in practical charity as well as in faith, and is said to have relieved in their necessities all the provinces of Syria and Arabia. In his day the vestments worn by the clergy at Mass and other church services did not differ in shape or material from those ordinarily worn by the laity; the Liber Pontificalis credits him with ordaining that vestments which had been used for ecclesiastical purposes were not to be employed for daily wear.

The Liber Pontificalis further adds that Stephen finished his pontificate by martyrdom, but the evidence for this is generally regarded as doubtful; he is nonetheless honored as a martyr and invoked as a patron of bishops, priests, and martyrs. His feast is kept on 2 August. He was buried in the cemetery of St. Calixtus, whence his body was later transferred by Pope Paul I to a monastery founded in his honor.

theodorus-and-theophanes.history:
Saints Theodorus and Theophanes, called the Grapti — a name meaning 'written upon' and rendered in later memory as 'the Branded' — were brothers and natives of Jerusalem, remembered as bold proponents of the veneration of sacred images during the second Iconoclastic controversy in the East, when the emperors of Byzantium forbade the honoring of icons. Theodorus was born about 775 and Theophanes about 778; both were educated in the holy city and trained in the monastic life before being called to Constantinople.

Both entered the monastery of St. Sabas, near Jerusalem, at that time under the guidance of Michael, who would later serve as syncellus of the Patriarch of Jerusalem. There the brothers received an excellent theological training and distinguished themselves as zealous, strict ascetics. About 812 they made their way to Constantinople, entering a monastery there.

In the imperial capital they energetically defended the veneration of images in opposition to the Emperor Leo V (813-820), and were exiled in consequence. Under his successor, Michael II (820-829), they were brought into the monastery of Sosthenes on the Bosphorus. This first banishment began a pattern of exile and recall that would mark the rest of their lives.

Theophilos (829-842), a tyrannical and iconoclastic emperor, exiled the brothers once more but recalled them to the capital in 836, had them scourged several times, and finally had twelve lines of verse cut into their skin. From this punishment came the name Grapti, 'the written upon,' which has remained attached to their memory; tradition holds that the verses were satirical and that they were cut into the brothers' foreheads. They were then sent into exile once more, and in that exile Theodorus died, about 842 or 843.

Theophanes lived to see the close of the Iconoclastic controversy in 842, in the reign of the Empress Theodora. In that same year he was raised to the Archdiocese of Nicaea, which he administered until his death in 845. He composed a large number of religious poems, among them a poem on his dead brother, but these works have not yet been published.

The brothers are venerated as saints. Their feast is kept on October 11, the date on which the Greek Church observes the feast of Theophanes; the Greek Church keeps Theodorus on December 27, while the Roman usage recorded in the early twentieth century celebrated both brothers on that same date. Remembered as confessors, they are honored as patrons of those who suffer persecution for the faith and of the reform of the Church.

trudpert.history:
Trudpert was a missionary in Germany in the seventh century. He is generally described as a Celtic monk from Ireland, though some accounts consider him a German by birth. According to legend, he went first to Rome in order to receive from the pope the authority for his mission. Returning from Italy, he traveled along the Rhine into the country of the Alamanni in the Breisgau, in the region of modern Baden.

A person of rank named Otbert received him and gave him land for his mission about fifteen miles south of Freiburg. Coming as a stranger to these upland valleys, Trudpert cleared away the trees, built a cell for himself, and erected a little church, which Bishop Martinus of Constance dedicated in honor of Saints Peter and Paul. There he led an ascetic and laborious life, and the accounts describe him as gathering a small company of disciples about the place.

His death came by violence rather than by natural causes. According to the traditional account, while he was asleep he was murdered by one of the serfs whom Otbert had given him, in revenge for the severe tasks that had been imposed upon him. Otbert gave Trudpert an honorable burial. Tradition holds that his tomb became a place of pilgrimage and healing.

In the century after his death, the Benedictine Abbey of St. Trudpert was built on the very spot where he had been buried, and the monastery that grew from his witness bore his name through the following centuries. In the year 815 his bones were translated, and on that occasion the first biography of him was composed; this life was revised in the tenth and again in the thirteenth centuries, so that the account of his deeds reached its final form long after his lifetime.

The story of his life is so full of legendary details that no correct judgment can be formed of Trudpert's era, of the kind of work he accomplished, or of its success. The period of his residence in the Breisgau was formerly given as 640-643, while the scholar Baur assigns 607 as the year of his death. His day of death, 26 April, is kept as his feast day. Despite the obscurity that surrounds him, he is remembered among the Irish monks whose missionary labor brought the faith to the German peoples, and he is honored as a patron of Germany, of missionaries, and of monks.

ultan-of-ardbraccan.history:
St. Ultan of Ardbraccan was an Irish monk and abbot-bishop of the seventh century, known as Ultan the Scribe. The Irish Annals describe him as of the royal race of O'Connor, and he succeeded St. Breccan as Abbot-Bishop of Ardbraccan about the year 570. According to O'Clery's Irish Calendar, he educated and fed thousands of poor students from all parts of Ireland. Tradition holds that he composed writings in honor of children and of those afflicted with disease, and that he tended the sick with a father's tenderness. On account of this care, he has been invoked as a patron of children, of physicians, and of sick children. As a bishop he is also remembered for governing his monastery and diocese with wisdom.

He was a scribe who treasured the Word of God, and among the monuments of his literary powers are lives of St. Patrick and St. Brigid. He was the maternal uncle of St. Brigid, and he collected a life of that saint for his pupil, St. Brogan Cloen of Rostuirc, in Ossory. His exquisite Latin hymn in her honor, beginning "Christus in nostra insula," is incorporated in the Solesmes Chant books.

His chronology presents a difficulty. Since St. Brigid belongs to an earlier generation while his death is not chronicled until the seventh century, the assumption of his kinship with her would involve an extraordinary longevity of some 180 years; the scholar Windisch, however, has offered an explanation that resolves the seeming inconsistency.

The year of his death is uncertain, the various annalists giving 653, 656, 657, and 662, but the Annals of Ulster, wherein his obit is recorded under the year 657, are generally followed. He died on 4 September, on which day his feast has been kept in Ireland for centuries. St. Ultan's Well still remains at Ardbraccan, where his memory endures.

wilfrid.history:
Wilfrid (634–709) was born in Northumbria, the son of a thegn. Unhappy at home under a stepmother's unkindness, he was sent at fourteen to the court of King Oswy, where Queen Eanfleda, at his own request, placed him in the monastery of Lindisfarne. After three years she sent him to Rome with St. Benedict Biscop, where he studied under Boniface, the pope's archdeacon. On his way home he spent three years at Lyons, receiving the tonsure from its bishop, Annemundas, who wished him to remain and marry his niece; Wilfrid was determined to be a priest. When persecution arose at Lyons, Annemundas perished in it, and Wilfrid, spared as a Saxon, returned to England.

Alchfrid, Oswy's son and heir, gave Wilfrid the newly founded monastery of Ripon, where he introduced the full Benedictine Rule; its previous Columbite monks withdrew to the north. He was ordained a priest only after five years as abbot, and his principal work was the advancement of Roman usage in the dispute between the Holy See and the Scottish monks of Northumbria; at the Synod of Whitby in 664 his advocacy carried the majority. Colman and his monks withdrew, and Wilfrid was elected bishop in Colman's place. Refusing consecration from northern bishops whom he regarded as schismatics, he received it at Compiègne.

His return was delayed, and in 666 he was shipwrecked on the coast of Sussex, whose heathen inhabitants repelled him and nearly killed him; landing in Kent, on reaching Northumbria he found his see filled by St. Chad. He retired to Ripon and worked in Mercia, especially at Lichfield, and in Kent, until in 669 Archbishop Theodore of Canterbury secured Chad's withdrawal and Wilfrid once more became Bishop of York. He enforced Roman obedience more completely, founded many Benedictine monasteries, rebuilt the minster at York, acting with magnificence though his own life was simple and restrained.

Under Ecgfrid, Oswy's successor, Wilfrid lost favor, partly because Etheldrida, the king's bride, followed his advice in refusing to live with her husband and retiring to a monastery. When Theodore subdivided his diocese into sees at Lindisfarne, Hexham, and Witherne, Wilfrid rejected the archbishop's right to do so and appealed to Rome. By a singular confusion of names, Winfrid, Bishop of Lichfield, bound for Rome at the same time, was stopped in his stead, and Wilfrid arrived safely; a council summoned by Pope Agatho decided in his favor. He was to return to York, appointing coadjutors, but the king imprisoned him at Bambrough and then exiled him.

Driven from Northumbria, he preached as a missionary at Selsey in Sussex among the people who had once repelled him. A reconciliation with Theodore in 686 restored him to Northumbria under King Aldfrid; he became Bishop of Hexham and later occupied York again when it fell vacant. When he refused to recognize Theodore's annulled subdivision, he left York and appealed to Rome a third time in 704. After lengthy proceedings he was again victorious; taken ill at Meaux on the journey home, he recovered and was reconciled to Archbishop Brihtwald, whose synod restored to him Hexham and Ripon, though not York. Though unsatisfactory, he accepted it, the principle of Roman authority having been vindicated.

Throughout his life Wilfrid defended the rights of the Holy See, first against Colman and the Scottish monks from Iona, then against Theodore and his successor at Canterbury, spending much of his life in exile for that principle. To him is due in great measure the establishment of Roman authority in England, and for this he holds a high place among English saints. He spent his last days at Ripon and died at Oundle in Northamptonshire in 709. Eddius, brought from Canterbury in 669 to teach the Roman chant at York, wrote his life at the request of Acca, his successor at Hexham. He is honored as a patron of bishops, of England, and of church unity, and his feast is kept on April 24.

willehad.history:
Willehad, the first Bishop of Bremen, was born in Northumberland before 745. A friend of Alcuin, he probably received his education at York under St. Egbert. After his ordination, and with the permission of King Alchred, he was sent to Frisia between 765 and 774. Later tradition, noted by Baronius in the Roman Martyrology, numbered him among the disciples of St. Boniface, but this cannot be so, for Boniface had left England in 718 and had died in 754.

His first labors brought him to Dockum, where St. Boniface had received the crown of martyrdom in 754, and there his preaching won many conversions. Crossing the Lauwers, he met with little success at Hugmarke, now Humsterland in the Diocese of Münster, and was obliged to leave. He went on to Trianthe, Drenthe in the Diocese of Utrecht, where all at first seemed favorable but where he afterward made little progress.

In 780 Charlemagne sent him to Wigmodia, a region near the North Sea between the Weser and the Elbe. There God's blessing accompanied his labors, and he built many churches among a people long resistant to the faith. For some two years the work prospered; then, in 782, the Saxons under Widukind rose in insurrection, many of his companions were killed, and his churches were destroyed. Willehad escaped and made his way to Rome, where he was received by Pope Adrian I. He then retired to the Abbey of Echternach and gave himself to the copying of books, transcribing among others the Epistles of St. Paul. When the insurrection had been suppressed by Charlemagne, he returned to Wigmodia and resumed his labors, preaching amid the violence and upheaval of an age of conquest and conversion.

On 13 July 787 he was consecrated bishop at Worms, and he fixed his residence at Bremen. There he built a cathedral, dedicated on Sunday, 1 November 789, in honor of St. Peter. A few days later, while on a missionary tour, he was attacked with a fever and died at Blecazze, Blexen on the Weser, on 8 November 789. His body, first buried at the place of his death, was transferred by his successor, St. Willericus, to a stone church and there placed in a chapel.

Through years of labor marked by violence and exile, Willehad laid the foundations of the Church in northern Germany. The see he established at Bremen would become one of the great missionary centers of the medieval Church. He is venerated as a patron of missionaries and of bishops, and as a patron of Germany.

A feast on 13 July commemorates the date of his consecration. During the Reformation his relics were lost; the commemoration was in time neglected and forgotten, until by permission of the Sacred Congregation of Rites it was reintroduced in 1901 in the dioceses of Münster, Osnabrück, and Paderborn, to be kept on a vacant day after 8 November.

An account of his life was written by a cleric of Bremen after 838, perhaps before 860, and the account of his miracles was written by St. Ansgar.

william-of-gellone.history:
William of Gellone, also known as William of Orange, was born in 755 and died on 28 May, about 812. His father was Theoderic and his mother Aldana, and he was in some way connected with the family of Charlemagne, whom later memory describes as his cousin. As a youth he was present at the emperor's court, and he thus belonged to the highest circles of the Frankish aristocracy.

He attained in 790 the dignity of second count of Toulouse, remembered in some accounts as its second duke, and he is by other writers also styled Duke of Aquitaine; he held this rule until about 811. Charlemagne employed him against the Saracen invaders from Spain, whom he defeated at Orange, a victory associated with the name William of Orange by which he is also known. He served with distinction in the Carolingian campaigns.

William became the hero of the ninth-century Roman de Guillaume au court nez, but this romance belongs to legend rather than sober history. His life is told in more reliable form by an anonymous biographer whose account was written soon after the saint's death, according to Mabillon before the eleventh century, and according to the Bollandist Henschen during the eleventh century.

In 804 he founded a Benedictine monastery in the valley of Gellone, near Lodève in the diocese of Maguelonne, since known as Saint-Guilhem-le-Désert, and he subjected it to St. Benedict of Aniane, whose monastery stood close at hand. Two years later, in 806, he himself received the monastic habit at Gellone. After retiring from public life he spent his remaining years in prayer and penance within the community he had established. Two documents of his are preserved by Mabillon: a testament granting certain property to Gellone, and another instrument subjecting the monastery to the Abbot of Aniane.

William died on 28 May, the day on which his feast is kept. He was canonized in 1066 by Pope Alexander II. Remembered as a soldier who became a monk, he is honored for his valor in battle and his humility in retirement, and he is venerated as a patron of soldiers, of monks, and of the nobility.

pope-zachary.history:
Zachary served as bishop of Rome from 741 until his death in March 752, the last pope of the Byzantine Papacy. A Greek from Calabria, the son, according to the Liber Pontificalis, of a man named Polichronius, he most probably served the Roman Church as a deacon and signed the decrees of its council of 732. After the burial of Gregory III on 29 November 741, he was unanimously elected, consecrated, and enthroned on 5 December; his biographer there describes him as gentle, conciliatory, and charitable toward clergy and people. His feast is kept on March 15.

Soon after his election he notified Constantinople, addressing his letter not to the iconoclast Patriarch Anastasius but to the Church of Constantinople. His envoys reached the capital while Artabasdus, brother-in-law of Emperor Constantine V, held power after usurping it in 742, and papal letters were even dated by the usurper's reign; when Constantine V prevailed, the pope's letter urged him to restore the doctrine and practice of the Church in the worship of images, and the emperor received the envoys kindly, giving the Roman Church the Italian villages of Nympha and Normia, whose territories extended to the sea.

When he took office Rome was in danger: King Luitprand of the Lombards was preparing a new incursion, and Duke Trasamund of Spoleto failed to keep his promises of aid. Zachary abandoned that alliance and relied on personal influence, going to Terni, where Luitprand received him with honor; he obtained the return of Ameria, Horta, Polimartium, and Blera, restitution of the church patrimonies taken within the previous thirty years, and a twenty-year truce. When Luitprand next moved against Ravenna, Zachary sent envoys and then went himself to Pavia, where, keeping the feast of Sts. Peter and Paul, he persuaded the king to abandon the attack and restore the city's territory. Luitprand died soon after, and in 749 his successor Ratchis confirmed the peace; the same year Ratchis abdicated with his wife and daughter and took monastic vows before the pope.

In 743 he held a Roman synod of sixty bishops, which issued fourteen canons on church discipline and weighed marriage impediments within the fourth degree. With St. Boniface he kept up an active correspondence, confirming the missionary dioceses of Wurzburg, Buraburg, and Erfurt, authorizing the Frankish synod Karlmann wished to hold with Boniface as papal legate, confirming the metropolitans of Rouen, Reims, and Sens, and upholding the condemnation of the heretics Adelbert and Clement. To England his care extended in the Synod of Cloveshove of 747, held for the reform of discipline at his urging. Asked by Frankish churchmen whether it seemed right that one should be king who did not really possess the royal power, he answered that it did not, and on the pope's authority Pepin the Short had himself proclaimed King of the Franks in place of Childeric III, a decision that reshaped the political map of Europe and bound the papacy to the Franks.

He restored the churches of Rome with costly gifts, rebuilt the Lateran palace, established settled landed possessions (domus cultae) for the Roman Church, and built the original church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva. In the Lateran repairs the head of the martyr St. George was found and translated to the Church of St. George in Velabro. Alms were given regularly to the poor from the papal palace, and when Venetian merchants bought slaves at Rome to resell them to the Saracens of Africa, he purchased them all, lest Christians become the property of heathens. He translated Gregory the Great's Dialogues into Greek, a version widely circulated in the East, and was buried in St. Peter's. Canonized before the formal processes of later centuries, he is invoked as a patron of peace, of slaves and trafficking victims, and of those who labor to defend the poor and the vulnerable.

pope-zephyrinus.history:
Zephyrinus, born in Rome, died on 20 December 217 after governing the Roman Church for nearly two decades. He was elected after the death of Pope Victor I; his accession is placed in 198 or 199. Hippolytus, in the Philosophymena, describes him as a simple man without education, understood to mean that he had not pursued higher studies but devoted himself to the practical administration of the Church.

Shortly after his elevation, Zephyrinus summoned the confessor Callistus, then living at Antium, and entrusted him with oversight of the common burial ground on the Via Appia, acquired under Victor and thereafter named for Callistus. Callistus was evidently also made a deacon, became the pope's confidential counselor, and, in time, his successor. In these years the favorable position of the Christians under Septimius Severus steadily worsened, and in 202 or 203 an edict forbade conversion to Christianity under severe penalties; nothing is known of the edict's execution in Rome or of the Roman martyrs of the era.

The internal disputes of the Roman Church centered on the doctrine of the Trinity. The adherents of Theodotus the Tanner, excommunicated by Pope Victor, formed an independent community ruled by Theodotus the Money Changer and Aselepodotus. As Eusebius records, these men induced the Roman confessor Natalis, who had confessed the faith under torture before a pagan judge, to serve as the sect's bishop for a monthly payment of 170 denarii. Warned repeatedly in dreams and, as he believed, tortured by angels, Natalis cast himself one morning at the feet of Zephyrinus in a penitential garment covered with ashes, confessed his wrongdoing, and was received again into the communion of the Church. The Montanist Proclus published a defense of the new prophecies, which the learned Roman Christian Caius answered in a dialogue invoking the graves of Peter on the Vatican Hill and of Paul on the Via Ostiensis; Hippolytus answered Caius with the Capita contra Caium.

The most consequential conflict arose with Hippolytus himself, the foremost theologian among the Roman presbyters, who taught that the Divine Logos became man in Christ and, as distinct from God, is the mediator between God and the world of creatures. Cleomenes and especially Sabellius opposed the Theodotians firmly yet refused to acknowledge the incarnation of the Logos, stressing the absolute unity of God; for teaching that the Father, not the Son, had been crucified, they were called Modalists or Patripassians. Zephyrinus did not interpose authoritatively between the schools; the Modalist error was not yet clearly evident, while Hippolytus's doctrine raised difficulties against the Church's tradition. The pope taught simply that he acknowledged one God, the Lord Jesus Christ, and that it was the Son, not the Father, who died, which was the doctrine of tradition. Hippolytus pressed him to define the Person of Christ as distinct from the Father and to condemn the Monarchians and Patripassians; Zephyrinus would not consent, and Hippolytus grew embittered toward the pope and especially toward Callistus. After Zephyrinus's death, when Callistus was elected bishop of Rome, Hippolytus withdrew with his followers, caused a schism, and made himself a rival bishop.

Zephyrinus was buried in a separate sepulchral chamber above the cemetery of Callistus on the Via Appia. The Liber Pontificalis attributes to him two decrees, one on the ordination of the clergy and one on the Eucharistic liturgy in the title churches of Rome, but these ascriptions are judged arbitrary and without historical basis. He was succeeded by Callixtus I, who was himself venerated as a saint and martyr. Honored from antiquity as a saintly pope and a steadfast guardian of the divinity of Christ, Zephyrinus is invoked as a patron of church unity, of bishops, and of church reform; the date of his feast is not recorded in the sources.

chrysanthus-and-daria.history:
Chrysanthus and Daria were Roman martyrs buried on the Via Salaria Nova, where the ancient itinerary guides to the tombs of the Roman martyrs record that their graves were publicly venerated. A church was erected over their tomb near that of Saint Saturninus, which stood by the catacomb of Thraso, and the grave itself lay in a disused sandpit close at hand. Their veneration in Rome was already established in the fourth century, as the appearance of their names in the Martyrologium Hieronymianum attests.

The surviving Acts of the martyrs, however, do not date before the fifth century and are held to be without historical value; they exist in a longer Greek text later translated into Latin and in a shorter Latin account. According to the later tradition, Chrysanthus was the son of the noble Polemius of Alexandria and came to Rome with his father, where the presbyter Carpophorus converted him to the Christian faith, and everything was then done to make him apostatize. Daria, a beautiful and intelligent Vestal Virgin, was brought into contact with him, but she too was won to Christ, and the two joined in a virginal marriage. Many Romans and Roman ladies were converted through them, among them the tribune Claudius, his wife Hilaria, and their sons Maurus and Jason, all of whom, except the mother, were put to death for the faith. Chrysanthus and Daria themselves were condemned and stoned to death in a sandpit on the Via Salaria.

The Acts place their death in the reign of the emperor Numerianus, who ruled from 283 to 284, although because that ruler was never in Rome some historians have instead read the name as Valerianus and assigned the martyrdom to the persecution under that emperor, while others consider the indication to have been drawn from the legend of an Oriental martyr of the same name. The martyrdom itself and the veneration of the saints' tombs, however, are regarded as assured.

The Acts relate a further martyrdom closely connected with their tomb. After the saints' death, when many of the faithful of Rome had assembled there to celebrate the anniversary, the persecutors surprised them and filled the subterranean crypt with stones and earth, so that all within perished. When the tomb of Chrysanthus and Daria was later sought and found, the bones of the saints and even the silver liturgical vessels used for the celebration of the Eucharist were discovered. All was left as it was found, a wall was raised so that no one could enter, and through a window opening in the wall could be seen the tomb of the saints together with the bones of the Christians who had died there.

The tomb was embellished by Pope Damasus, who caused poems in praise of the martyrs to be engraved on marble and placed there, and Gregory of Tours describes the sanctuary in his De gloria martyrum. The shrine was desecrated during the invasions of the Goths and later restored, as a metrical inscription of that time, falsely attributed to Pope Damasus, records. In the ninth century the remains of the saints were brought to Prüm and thence transferred to Munstereifel in Rhenish Prussia, where they are still greatly venerated.

Saints Chrysanthus and Daria are commemorated on March 19, the day on which the Greeks celebrate their feast. The Martyrologium Hieronymianum names the martyrs on August 12 and November 29, and according to some manuscripts on other days as well, while the Roman Martyrology records the martyrs on October 25, a date also found in some martyrologies of the seventh century. Honored among the martyrs of the early Christian centuries, they are invoked as patrons of families and of conversion, a patronage recalling the tradition that many were brought to the faith through them.

pope-hormisdas.history:
Hormisdas belonged to a wealthy and honourable family of Frosinone in the Campagna di Roma; his date of birth is unknown. He had been married and was widowed before receiving higher orders, and his son Silverius later became pope (536-537) and is venerated as a saint. Under Pope Symmachus (498-514) he served as a deacon of the Roman Church, was one of Symmachus's most prominent clerical attendants during the schism of Laurentius and notary at the synod held at St. Peter's in 502. Ennodius of Pavia expressed the conviction that this deacon, eminent for piety and distinguished birth, would occupy the See of Rome.

The day after Symmachus's funeral on 20 July 514, Hormisdas was chosen and consecrated his successor, no divisions or disturbances being recorded at his election. One of his first cares was to remove the last vestiges of the Laurentian schism in Rome, receiving back into the Church such of its adherents as had not already been reconciled.

From the beginning of his pontificate the affairs of the Greek Church occupied his special attention. The Acacian schism, which had broken out over the "Henoticon" of the Emperor Zeno and had separated the Greek and Roman Churches, still held sway at Constantinople. The Emperor Anastasius (491-518) maintained the Henoticon, grew increasingly favourable to Monophysitism, and persecuted bishops who refused to repudiate the Council of Chalcedon; the patriarchs of Constantinople, Jerusalem, and Antioch had been driven from their sees. Eastern bishops had appealed to Rome under Symmachus, but were not then ready to submit to the condemnation of Acacius.

Amid the discontent aroused against Anastasius, Vitalian of Lower Moesia led a revolt demanding recognition of the Council of Chalcedon and unity with Rome. Anastasius was obliged to negotiate and in December 514 invited Hormisdas to a synod at Heraclea in Thrace, but the two hundred bishops who assembled there on 1 July 515 separated without result. Hormisdas convened a synod at Rome and sent an embassy of two bishops, a priest, a deacon, and a notary to Constantinople, together with a confession of faith for the Eastern bishops to sign. The mission brought no real result; Anastasius gave the envoys an evasive letter, and an imperial embassy of 516 failed to move the Senate, which, like King Theodoric, remained faithful to the pope. Meanwhile further bishops of Scythia, Illyricum, Dardania, and Epirus submitted to the condemnation of Acacius and signed his confession of faith.

A settlement was finally reached after Anastasius's death: the Formula of Hormisdas, a confession of faith drawn up in 519, secured the reunion of Rome and Constantinople, celebrated before a great crowd in the cathedral on 28 March 519, the fruit of patient diplomacy.

Hormisdas also caused a Latin translation of the canons of the Greek Church to be prepared by Dionysius Exiguus and issued a new edition of the Gelasian "Decretum de recipiendis libris", and sent letters to bishops in Spain and Gaul and directions on church administration. When the African bishop Possessor appealed to him concerning the Semipelagian views colouring the writings of the Bishop of Riez, he rebuked the quarrelsome spirit of the monks behind the inquiry, ruling that what was good in Faustus's works should be preserved and what was contrary to Church doctrine rejected. His relations with Theodoric were amicable, and shortly before his death came tidings that Thrasamund, the Vandal king of Northern Africa, had died (523), and that the persecution of Catholics in that region had ceased.

Hormisdas died at Rome on 6 August 523 and was buried at St. Peter's, where the text of his epitaph has been preserved. His feast is kept on 6 August. Remembered as a peacemaker of the Church and a steadfast defender of the faith of Chalcedon, he is honoured as a patron of church unity and church reform.

pope-siricius.history:
Siricius was born at Rome about 334, the son of a man named Tiburtius, and entered the service of the Roman Church in his youth, serving as lector and then as deacon under Pope Liberius, as the inscription on his grave attests. After the death of Damasus he was unanimously elected bishop of Rome in December 384 and consecrated probably on 17 December. Ursinus, an old rival for the see, was still alive and maintained his claims, but an imperial letter of February 385 consented to the election and praised the piety of the new bishop, and no difficulties arose.

Almost at once the pope had occasion to assert his primacy over the universal Church. A letter from Himerius, bishop of Tarragona in Spain, directed to Pope Damasus, had asked counsel on fifteen points of baptism, penance, church discipline, and clerical celibacy. Siricius answered it on 10 February 385 in the letter known as the Directa decretal, a letter of binding decisions rather than mere advice, issued in full consciousness of his supreme authority. This letter is the oldest completely preserved papal decretal. He directed Himerius to make the decrees known to the neighbouring provinces, so that they should be observed there as well.

Church discipline was his constant care. A Roman synod of 6 January 386, attended by eighty bishops, reaffirmed nine canons on points of discipline, among them the consecration of bishops and the celibacy of the clergy; its decisions were sent to the bishops of North Africa and to others who had not attended, with the command to act in accordance with them. Another letter dealt with the election of worthy bishops and priests.

Siricius also resisted heresy. About 390 to 392 a synod held at Rome condemned Jovinian, a monk who opposed fasts, good works, and the higher merit of the celibate life, together with eight of his followers; the decision was sent to Ambrose, bishop of Milan and a friend of the pope, who condemned them in synod with the bishops of upper Italy. Siricius and Ambrose also opposed Bonosus, bishop of Sardica, accused of errors on the Trinity and of denying that Mary was always a virgin; further proceedings against him were left to the bishop of Thessalonica and the Illyrian bishops.

In the Priscillian controversy the pope sharply condemned the bishops who had accused Priscillian before the secular court and prevailed upon the usurper Maximus to condemn him to death, and he excommunicated Felix, bishop of Trier, in whose city the execution had taken place. A letter to the Spanish bishops set out the conditions under which converted Priscillians were to be restored to communion. In the East he interposed in the Meletian schism at Antioch, which had outlasted the death of Meletius in 381.

A five-aisled basilica was dedicated by the pope in 390, and his name may still be read on one of its pillars preserved from the fire of 1823. Contemporaries judged him harshly: Paulinus of Nola spoke of the haughty policy of the Roman bishop after a reserved reception at Rome in 395, an attitude explained by irregularities in his own election and consecration, and Jerome blamed the pope's lack of judgment for the letter of communion given to Rufinus of Aquileia in 398. His known labours do not bear out these judgments.

Siricius died on 26 November 399 and was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria, where his inscription has been recovered; the Liber Pontificalis gives an incorrect date for his death. His name was inserted in the Roman Martyrology by Benedict XIV. He is numbered among the saints honoured before the formal canonization process existed, and his feast falls on 26 November. He is honoured as patron of bishops and of canon lawyers, and tradition holds that he was the first bishop of Rome to style himself pope. He is remembered as a pastor who gave shape to the law of the Church.

abdias-of-babylon.history:
Abdias of Babylon is remembered in Christian tradition as one of the Seventy Apostles whom the Lord Jesus sent forth in pairs to preach, as recorded in the Gospel of Luke. He is honored especially as the first bishop of Babylon. Tradition holds that Saints Simon and Jude consecrated him to this see, commissioning him to shepherd the fledgling church in the East. He is further associated with Saint Thomas and Saint Addai, and in Syriac Christianity he is connected with the first Patriarch of the Church of the East. Such traditions, though legendary in form, bear witness to the early spread of the Gospel beyond the frontiers of the Roman Empire, into Mesopotamia and Persia. Very little is otherwise known about him.

In written sources he appears chiefly as the reputed author of a work in ten books known as the Historia Certaminis Apostolici, which recounts the labours and deaths of the Apostles. The book purports to have been translated from Hebrew into Greek by Eutropius, a disciple of Abdias, and then, in the third century, from Greek into Latin by Julius Africanus, the friend of Origen. On this account, the work presented itself as a witness of great antiquity.

Critical study, however, has shown the Historia to be in reality a Latin work, for in it are cited the Vulgate of Saint Jerome, the Ecclesiastical History of Rufinus, and Rufinus's Latin translation of the Recognitiones of Clement; it therefore cannot date from the third century as claimed. According to the scholar R. A. Lipsius, it was compiled during the latter half of the sixth century in some Frankish monastery, for the purpose of satisfying the natural curiosity of Western Christians about the fate of the Apostles. Its compiler drew upon much older materials circulated under the names of the Apostles, which he abridged or excerpted to suit his purpose, and often revised or expurgated in the sense of Catholic teaching, since a number of the writings he used were originally Gnostic compositions, filled with speeches and prayers intended to spread that heresy. The lasting interest of the work lies in the ancient material its author claims to have drawn from the acts of the Apostles, and in the many ancient legends thus brought down to later ages.

Whatever conclusions are reached about the writings attributed to him, Abdias himself stands in Christian memory as a figure of the apostolic mission that carried the name of Christ to the ancient cities of Babylon and Edessa. His veneration belongs to the earliest centuries of the Church, before the formal canonization processes of a later age. His feast is kept on October 28, and he is honored as a patron of missionaries and preachers.

pope-adeodatus-i.history:
Pope Adeodatus I, also known as Deodatus or Deusdedit, served as bishop of Rome from his consecration on the nineteenth of October 615 until his death on the eighth of November 618. The date of his birth is unknown. He was distinguished for his charity and zeal.

He encouraged and supported the clergy, who had been impoverished in consequence of the political troubles of the time. When his diocese was visited by a violent earthquake and by the scourge of leprosy, he set an heroic example in his efforts to relieve the suffering.

The few decretals ascribed to him are unauthenticated. Tradition holds that he was the first pope to make use of leaden seals, or bullae, on pontifical documents; one example from his reign is still preserved, its obverse bearing the figure of the Good Shepherd among His sheep with the letters Alpha and Omega beneath, and its reverse bearing the inscription Deusdedit Papae.

His feast is kept on the eighth of November, the anniversary of his death. He is honored as a patron of bishops and of the poor.

pope-agapetus-i.history:
Agapetus I was bishop of Rome from 535 until his death on April 22, 536, after a reign of about ten months. The date of his birth is uncertain. He was the son of Gordianus, a Roman priest who had been slain during the riots in the days of Pope Symmachus. His first official act was to burn before the assembled clergy the anathema that Pope Boniface II had pronounced against his rival Dioscurus and had ordered preserved in the Roman archives.

He confirmed the decrees of the council held at Carthage after the liberation of Africa from Vandal rule, by which converts from Arianism were declared ineligible for Holy Orders and those already ordained were admitted only to lay communion. He likewise accepted an appeal from Contumeliosus, Bishop of Riez, whom a council at Marseilles had condemned for immorality, and ordered St. Caesarius of Arles to grant the accused a new trial before papal delegates.

Meanwhile Belisarius, after his easy conquest of Sicily, was preparing for an invasion of Italy. The Gothic king Theodahad, as a last resort, begged the aged pope to go to Constantinople and bring his influence to bear on the emperor Justinian. To meet the costs of the embassy, Agapetus was compelled to pledge the sacred vessels of the Church of Rome. Setting out in midwinter with five bishops and a large retinue, he reached the eastern capital in February 536, where he was received with honors befitting the head of the Catholic Church. As he likely foresaw, the mission failed of its object, for Justinian could not be turned from his resolve to re-establish imperial rule in Italy.

The visit nevertheless proved decisive for the Church. The patriarch of Constantinople, Anthimus, had left his see of Trebizond without canonical authority and had joined the crypto-Monophysites who, in concert with the empress Theodora, were working to undermine the Council of Chalcedon; over the protests of the orthodox, the empress had seated him on the patriarchal throne. Upon the pope's arrival, prominent clergy brought charges against Anthimus as an intruder and a heretic. Agapetus ordered him to make a written profession of faith and to return to his forsaken see, and when he refused, declined to hold any relations with him. Justinian, deceived by his wife as to the orthodoxy of her favorite, threatened the pope with banishment; Agapetus replied that he had come with eager longing to behold the Most Christian Emperor Justinian, but had found in his place a Diocletian whose threats did not terrify him. This firm answer made Justinian pause. Convinced at last that Anthimus was unsound in faith, the emperor raised no objection when the pope deposed and suspended the intruder and, for the first time in the history of the Church, personally consecrated his lawfully elected successor, Mennas. To clear himself of every suspicion of abetting heresy, Justinian gave the pope a written confession of faith, which Agapetus accepted with the proviso that, while he could not admit in a layman the right of teaching religion, he was pleased that the emperor's zeal accorded with the decisions of the Fathers.

Shortly afterward Agapetus fell ill and died in Constantinople. His remains were brought to Rome in a leaden coffin and deposited in St. Peter's. His memory is kept on September 20, the day of his deposition, and the Greeks commemorate him on April 22, the day of his death; East and West alike venerate him as a saint. Remembered for upholding the orthodox faith and the lawful order of the Church amid war and imperial pressure, he is invoked as a patron of church reform and of protection.

pope-agatho.history:
St. Agatho was born in Sicily towards the end of the sixth century and died in Rome in 681. Tradition holds that he was originally a Benedictine monk at St. Hermes in Palermo, and there is good authority that he was more than one hundred years old when, in 678, he ascended the papal chair as successor to Pope Donus. On this account he is said to have been the longest-lived pope in history.

Shortly after Agatho became pope, St. Wilfrid, Archbishop of York, arrived at Rome to invoke the authority of the Holy See in his behalf. Wilfrid had been unjustly and uncanonically deposed from his see through Theodore of Canterbury's division of the archdiocese. Agatho convoked a synod in the Lateran to investigate the affair, and Wilfrid was restored to his see, an early sign of the new pope's concern for justice among the bishops.

The chief event of Agatho's pontificate was the Sixth Ecumenical Council, held at Constantinople in 680. Agatho sent legates bearing a letter in which he confessed the orthodox faith, and at the council these legates presided. The assembly addressed the controversy of monothelitism and affirmed that Christ possessed two wills, divine and human, in one person, and by its decrees the Monothelite heresy was practically ended. Peace was thus brought to a Church long divided on the question. Before the acts of the council had reached Rome for the pope's approval, Agatho had died.

Agatho was buried in St. Peter's on January 10, 681, and his feast is kept on that day. He was remarkable for his affability and charity, and on account of the many miracles he is said to have wrought he was styled Thaumaturgus, or Wonderworker. His memory is celebrated by the Latin as well as the Greek Church, and he is venerated by Catholics and Orthodox alike.

His brief but consequential pontificate joined two pastoral concerns: the restoration of a bishop unjustly deprived of his see and the settlement of a dispute that had troubled the whole Church. On this account his patronage is invoked for bishops and for church unity.

alphonsus-liguori.history:
Alphonsus Liguori was born at Marianella, near Naples, on 27 September 1696, and was baptized two days later in the church of Our Lady of the Virgins in Naples. The eighteenth century was not remarkable for depth of spiritual life, yet it produced three of the Church's greatest missionaries, and Alphonsus was one of them. His family was old and noble, though the branch to which he belonged had become somewhat impoverished. His father, Don Joseph de' Liguori, a man of genuine faith and stainless life, served as a naval officer and Captain of the Royal Galleys; his mother was of Spanish descent. Alphonsus was the eldest of seven children.

Not sent to school, he was educated by tutors under his father's eye and made great progress in every kind of learning, practising the harpsichord three hours a day until at thirteen he played with the perfection of a master. Riding and fencing were his recreations. At sixteen, on 21 January 1713, he took his degree as Doctor of Laws, although the statutes fixed the age at twenty, and he began to practise at the bar at about nineteen. His confessor later declared that he preserved his baptismal innocence till death.

In eight years as an advocate, tradition holds that he never lost a case; whatever allowance such a report requires, by twenty-seven he stood among the leaders of the Neapolitan Bar. Success nevertheless drew him into society, and about 1722 he began to neglect prayer and the practices of piety, a period he later looked back upon with sorrow, though it involved no serious sin. In 1723 he appeared as one of the leading counsel in a lawsuit between a Neapolitan nobleman and the Grand Duke of Tuscany, in which property valued at 500,000 ducats was at stake. After a brilliant opening speech he learned that he had overlooked a document which destroyed his whole case, and he acknowledged his mistake at once. At twenty-seven he abandoned the bar.

He was ordained a priest in 1726. In 1732 he founded the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, known as the Redemptorists, to preach missions to the poor in the countryside around Naples. He became a bishop in 1762. He wrote more than a hundred works, devoted above all to moral theology, in which he steered a middle course between rigorism and laxity.

Alphonsus died at Nocera de' Pagani on 1 August 1787 and was canonized in 1839. In 1871 he was declared a Doctor of the Church, and his feast is kept on 1 August. He is venerated as a patron of confessors, moral theologians, and those who suffer from scruples.

pope-anacletus.history:
Anacletus, whose name appears in some sources as Anencletus, is honored as the second successor of Saint Peter and the third bishop of Rome, following the apostle and Saint Linus. He is traditionally described as a Roman by birth and is placed among the popes of the closing years of the first century, an era from which very little documentary evidence survives. He is numbered among the earliest martyrs of the Roman Church and was venerated as a saint long before the establishment of formal canonization processes.

The chief difficulty surrounding his life concerns his identity. Ancient Christian writers spoke of a pope called Cletus as well as one called Anacletus, and whether the two names belong to one man or to two has long been debated without resolution. Irenaeus, Eusebius, Augustine, and Optatus employ both names indifferently, as though they referred to a single pontiff, while Tertullian passes over him entirely. Even the order of the earliest bishops of Rome is unsettled: Irenaeus lists Linus, Anacletus, and Clement in that sequence, whereas Augustine and Optatus place Clement before Anacletus. Certain ancient catalogues, including the Catalogus Liberianus, the poem known as the Carmen contra Marcionem, and the Liber Pontificalis, distinguish Cletus and Anacletus as separate persons, and the Catalogus Felicianus even presents Anacletus as a Greek and Cletus as a Roman. Modern scholars have likewise been divided; the weight of later judgment, represented by historians such as Hergenröther, De Smedt, Döllinger, and Duchesne, has favored identifying the two as one, though other authorities have left the question open.

This uncertainty extends to chronology, and no exact dates for his pontificate can be given with confidence. Duchesne observed that precision concerning the earliest bishops is impossible and that the list of Irenaeus, running from Linus and Anacletus through Clement to Anicetus, who certainly reigned in 154, is essentially all that can be affirmed about primitive pontifical chronology. Tradition accordingly places his service as bishop of Rome in the last years of the first century.

Of his activity, the one point of positive record is that he ordained a number of priests for the Church of Rome. Later tradition amplifies this, crediting him with the ordination of a great number of priests and with the establishment of roughly twenty-five parishes, or titles, throughout the city. He is recorded to have died a martyr, perhaps around the year 91, though the circumstances of his death are unknown. His name is preserved in the Roman Canon of the Mass among the earliest popes who gave their lives for the Church, and he is invoked as a patron of priests and of martyrs. His feast is kept on April 26.

pope-anicetus.history:
Anicetus succeeded Pius as bishop of Rome about the year 157 and governed that Church until about 168, although the chronology of this early period is so confused that more exact dates cannot be verified. His episcopate fell within the reign of the emperor Marcus Aurelius, when the empire did not yet tolerate the name of Christian, and the young Church faced both outward pressure and inward division. He is remembered as a vigilant defender of the apostolic faith at a time when novel teachings threatened the Gospel in its first flowering.

Foremost among the events of his pontificate is the visit of Polycarp of Smyrna, who came to Rome between 160 and 162, in extreme old age, to confer with him on the paschal controversy. Polycarp and others in the East kept Easter on the fourteenth of the month of Nisan, whatever the day of the week; at Rome the feast was always kept on Sunday, and the day of the Lord's death was observed on Friday. The matter was discussed, but nothing was decided. According to Eusebius, "Polycarp could not persuade the Pope, nor the Pope, Polycarp. The controversy was not ended but the bonds of charity were not broken"; Anicetus permitted the aged bishop to continue keeping the day to which he was accustomed in the Church of Smyrna. The encounter stands as an early witness to unity preserved in charity, a concern for which Anicetus is especially honored.

At about the same time Hegesippus, a Christian historian whose testimony is valued because he lived so near the age of the Apostles, also came to Rome. Ecclesiastical authors record his visit as noteworthy, since many illustrious men repaired to Rome in that period, emphasizing very early the supreme dignity and authority of the Roman Pontiffs. Yet the same years brought trouble within the city: Marcion, Marcellinus, Valentine, and Cordo were at Rome disturbing the Church with their teaching, and Anicetus is remembered for his resistance to the Gnostic and Marcionite errors of the day.

The circumstances of his death are uncertain. Tradition holds that he suffered martyrdom; some accounts place it as early as 161, while his pontificate is otherwise traced to about 168, and the dates given vary between the sixteenth, seventeenth, and twentieth of April, the last of these preserved as his feast day. Recognized as a saint from before the formal canonization process existed, he is honored as a patron of church unity and of theologians, one who held fast to the apostolic faith while keeping the bonds of charity unbroken.

pope-anterus.history:
Pope Anterus served as bishop of Rome for a brief period, from November 21, 235, until his death on January 3, 236. He succeeded Pontian in the chair of Peter during a time of tension and uncertainty for the Church. His pontificate, lasting some forty days, was among the briefest in the early history of the papacy. He is said to have been a Greek by birth.

Apart from the length of his reign and the place of his burial, few details of his pontificate can be stated with certainty. Tradition holds that he was martyred, though the details of his death are obscure. The Liber Pontificalis records that he suffered death for having caused the Acts of the martyrs to be collected by notaries and deposited in the archives of the Roman Church, an undertaking by which the memory of those who had died for the faith might be preserved. This tradition appears old and respectable, but the Liber Pontificalis, compiled at a later date, remains its sole witness, and the best scholars have judged the account insufficiently guaranteed.

His burial is more securely attested. Anterus was interred in the papal crypt of the Cemetery of Callixtus at Rome, where the site of his sepulchre was identified by the archaeologist De Rossi in 1854. His tomb was closed by a narrow oblong slab bearing a Greek epitaph, of which broken remnants were recovered; these attest at once to his Greek origin and to the prevalence of the Greek language in the Roman Church up to that time.

A letter attributed to him, the Epistola Anteri, comes from the Pseudo-Isidorian forgeries and is not accepted as his own work. His feast is kept on January 3, the anniversary of his death, and he is honored as a martyr, remembered for a pontificate of brief duration marked by fidelity in a difficult age.

apollinaris-claudius.history:
Saint Apollinaris Claudius, also called Apollinaris of Hierapolis or Apollinaris the Apologist, was a Christian apologist and bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia in the second century.
