He became famous for his polemical treatises against the heretics of his day, whose errors he showed to be entirely borrowed from the pagans. He wrote two books against the Jews, five against the pagans, and two on "Truth"; none of these writings is extant.

In 177 he published an eloquent Apologia for the Christians, addressed to the Emperor Marcus Aurelius. In it he appealed to the Emperor's own experience with the "Thundering Legion", whose prayers, the appeal recounted, won him the victory over the Quadi. The exact date of his death is not known, but it probably occurred while Marcus Aurelius was still emperor.

With his works lost, knowledge of Apollinaris rests largely on Eusebius of Caesarea, who preserves fragments of his writings and commends his learning and zeal for the truth. He was one of the first to raise a defense of the faith against the calumnies that surrounded the young Church, standing among the early apologists who sought to explain the Gospel to the Greco-Roman world and to refute the Gnostic errors that pressed in on every side.

His feast is kept on January 8. His canonization belongs to the pre-Congregation era, and he is invoked as a patron of writers and theologians.

augustine-of-canterbury.history:
Augustine, first Archbishop of Canterbury and remembered as the Apostle of the English, was probably a Roman of the better class; nothing else is known of his youth. Early in life he became a monk at the monastery of St. Andrew on the Caelian Hill, which Gregory, afterwards Pope Gregory the Great, had built from his own patrimony. Amid the discipline of the Benedictine Rule his character was formed, and he in time served as the community's prior.

Gregory, raised to the papacy in 590, turned some five years later to the monastery he had once ruled. From among the monks he chose about forty for a mission to the pagan English and designated Augustine, then prior of St. Andrew's, as their representative and spokesman. The occasion came in 595 or 596, when a rumour reached Rome that the pagan inhabitants of Britain were ready to embrace the faith in great numbers if preachers could be found to instruct them. Gregory's first plan was to purchase English captive boys of seventeen and upwards, bring them up in the Catholic faith, ordain them, and send them back in due time as apostles to their own people; he asked Candidus, a presbyter administering Roman Church estates in Gaul, to set aside revenues for the purpose. The pope also deplored the lack of episcopal zeal among the Christian neighbours of the English, whether Gaulish prelates or the Celtic bishops of northern and western Britain.

The prospects of the mission rested on circumstances in Kent. Æthelberht, king there from 559 or 560, had established an overlordship reaching eastward to the sea and as far north as the Humber and the Trent, and was acknowledged as Bretwalda. Charibert of Paris gave him his daughter Bertha in marriage, stipulating that she should have the free exercise of her religion, and the Frankish bishop Luidhard accompanied her to Canterbury, where the ruined church of St. Martin, dating from Roman-British times, was set apart for her use. The marriage is thought to have taken place some twenty years before the plan of the mission arose.

The company set out in June 596, carrying letters to the bishops and Christian princes along the way, and instructed to provide themselves with Frankish interpreters before entering Britain. Discouragement overtook them early: tales of the uncouth islanders chilled their enthusiasm, and some of their number proposed to draw back, whereupon Augustine agreed to return in person to Gregory and lay the difficulty before him. He went forward in the end and landed in Kent in 597, where King Æthelberht, whose wife Bertha was already a Christian, received him kindly.

Tradition holds that Augustine baptized the king and many thousands of his subjects. He established his see at Canterbury and founded the monastery which in time became Canterbury Cathedral. In keeping with his commission from the Roman See, he sought also to reconcile the older British church with Roman customs, though his success in his own lifetime was limited.

Augustine died on 26 May 604. He was buried in Roman fashion outside the walls, in a grave beside the great Roman road from Deal to Canterbury over St. Martin's Hill, near the abbey church he had begun in honour of Sts. Peter and Paul and which was afterwards dedicated to his memory. When the monastery was completed, his relics were translated to a tomb in its north porch; a modern hospital is said to occupy the site of his burial. Later Canterbury legends enshrine memories of the mission, though their chronology does not withstand close examination. His feast is kept in late May, with the Roman Calendar and the proper of the English office assigning different days, the latter observing the true anniversary of his death. In art his symbols are the cope, pallium, and mitre as Bishop of Canterbury, and the pastoral staff and gospels as missionary. He is honoured as the Apostle of England and is venerated as a patron of missionaries and of England.

ava.history:
Saint Ava, commemorated on 29 April, was a German poet venerated as a saint in the Roman Catholic Church and traditionally invoked as a patron of the blind and of nuns. She was the first woman known to have written in German and is probably identical with a recluse of the same name who died in 1127 in the vicinity of Melk in Austria. Later tradition identifies her as a Benedictine abbess living under the rule of Saint Benedict and honors her as a model of the monastic virtues.

From a passage in her own work it is known that she was the mother of two sons, who helped her in procuring the material for her poems. These poems are metrical versions of stories from the New Testament and consist of the Life of Jesus, the Antichrist, the Gifts of the Holy Ghost, the Last Judgment, and John the Baptist. They are preserved in two manuscripts, one at Verona and the other at Gorlitz, the latter containing the only text of John the Baptist. Her authorship of that poem, as well as of the Life of Jesus, has been questioned, but hardly on sufficient grounds.

The poems are naive in tone and display deeply religious sentiments, though, except for occasional passages, they are destitute of poetic merit. Their technique is often crude, assonance taking the place of rhyme and alliteration being not infrequent. The chief source from which she drew her material was the New Testament, but she also made use of older German poems and possibly of other writings, such as the apocryphal Gospel of the Infancy of the Saviour by the Pseudo-Matthew.

Apart from the passage in which she speaks of her two sons, almost nothing is known of Ava's life or personality. Through these poems, preserved in the two manuscripts at Verona and Gorlitz, she is remembered as the first woman known to have written in German.

benedict-biscop.history:
Saint Benedict Biscop, also known as Biscop Baducing, was an English monastic founder of the seventh century, born about 628 into a noble Anglo-Saxon family. He spent his youth at the court of the Northumbrian king Oswy, and when he was twenty-five years old he set out on the first of five pilgrimages he would make to Rome. On his return to England he introduced, wherever he was able, the religious rites as he had seen them practised in the city.

A second journey soon followed. On his way home he stopped at Lérins, where in 666 he received the religious habit. Two years later he was again in Rome, and Pope Vitalian sent him, together with the monk Adrian, to accompany Theodore, the newly appointed archbishop of Canterbury, as an adviser. Benedict held this office for two years, resigned it in 671, and at once set out on another pilgrimage to Rome.

That journey and the two pilgrimages that followed were devoted in large part to collecting treasures for the monasteries of Wearmouth and Jarrow, which he founded in 674 and 682 respectively under the patronage of King Oswy: relics, books, and paintings gathered in the city of the Apostles. The books and images he carried home furnished the studies and churches of the twin houses, which became one of the great centers of learning in early medieval England. In these communities the Roman use shaped monastic worship, in keeping with the rites Benedict had learned in Rome. He engaged Abbot John, the arch-cantor of Saint Peter's in Rome, to teach his monks the chant of the Roman liturgy, and he brought masons and glassmakers from Gaul to raise stone churches with glazed windows. He was the first to introduce into England the building of stone churches and the art of making glass windows.

Benedict died on 12 January 690, sixteen years after the foundation of Wearmouth, and his feast is kept on that day. A Latin account of his life was written by Saint Bede, and his memory remains closely bound to the twin monasteries that he built and furnished.

He is honored as a patron of musicians, a patronage that recalls the Roman chant he established in his monasteries, and as a patron of scholars. He is remembered also as a father of the English Benedictine Congregation.

pope-benedict-ii.history:
The date of Benedict II's birth is not known. He was a Roman, the son of a man named John, and he died on May 8, 685, after serving for less than a year as bishop of Rome. While still a boy he was sent to the schola cantorum, and there he distinguished himself by his knowledge of the Scriptures and by his gift for singing. His early formation joined the chanting of the psalms to the study of the sacred text, and both remained marks of his later life.

Raised in time to the priesthood, he was remarkable for humility, for his love of the poor, and for generosity, and his generosity to the poor was joined to a ready care for the pilgrims who had come to Rome. After a vacancy of more than eleven months, he became pope on June 26, 684.

In that age the newly elected pope waited, before enthronement, upon confirmation from the emperor, and so the deaths of popes were followed by vacancies of many months. To abridge these vacancies of the Holy See, Benedict obtained from the emperor Constantine Pogonatus a decree that either abolished imperial confirmation altogether or made it obtainable from the exarch in Italy. The decree has come down through early Roman collections, and its exact terms have been weighed by later scholars. By its terms the choice made by the Roman church no longer had to await distant approval before its new bishop could take up his office, and the see of Peter could govern its own succession more freely. The emperor also sent Benedict locks of hair from his two sons, whom he received in adoption.

Benedict likewise gave attention to the decrees of the Sixth Ecumenical Council. He received the acts of the council and saw them promulgated in the West; to help suppress Monothelitism, he endeavored to secure the subscriptions of the Spanish bishops to the council's teaching, and he sought to bring about the submission to it of Macarius, former bishop of Antioch, whose acceptance had been wanting.

In the affairs of the English church, he was one of the popes who favored the cause of St. Wilfrid of York. At Rome, many of the city's churches were restored under his care, and his liberality extended to the church's servants: to its clergy, to its deaconries, which were maintained for the care of the poor, and to its lay sacristans. The generosity that had marked him as a priest thus continued to govern his conduct as bishop of Rome.

Benedict died on May 8, 685, and he was buried in St. Peter's. Brief as it was, his pontificate is remembered chiefly for the part he played in freeing the Roman succession from long imperial delay, and he is counted among the early medieval popes who tended the see of Peter with learning and pastoral care. He is honored as a saint in the Roman tradition; his feast is kept on May 7, and he is invoked as a patron of priests and of pilgrims, a patronage that recalls his learning in the Scriptures and his charity toward the poor and toward those who came to Rome from afar.

berach.history:
St. Berach of Termonbarry, who died in 595, was a disciple of St. Kevin of Glendalough and a celebrated Irish saint of the early medieval Church. His memory is still fresh in County Roscommon, where his name has endured across the centuries, and he is counted among the holy men who carried the monastic ideal across the Irish midlands. He belonged to the tribe of Cinel Dobtha, the O'Hanley of Doohey Hanley, to which the MacCoilidh family also belonged. Most of his long life was spent within the Diocese of Elphin, and there he built his church at Cluain Coirpthe, the place afterward known as Termonbarry or Kilbarry. He is honored as a patron of hermits and of students. Tradition holds that he first dwelt there as a hermit, and that his hermitage and later foundation gave the place its name.

His sister, St. Midabaria, was abbess of a nunnery at Bumlin, near Strokestown, where she is venerated as patroness on 22 February. Her ancient conventual church and graveyard are still to be seen there.

Under the title of Berach of Cluain Coirpthe, St. Berach is honored in several martyrologies, and his holy life drew pilgrims to Kilbarry from all parts of Ireland. His feast is kept on 15 February, the day assigned him by most martyrologists. Colgan and O'Hanlon alike record his celebration under that date, and the saint's memory is preserved also in the Annals of the Four Masters, the Annals of Ulster, and the early collections of the acts and lives of Irish saints.

The MacCoilidh family, whose name was anglicized to Cox in the early years of the seventeenth century, were hereditary custodians of St. Berach's crosier and served as coarbs, or lay abbots, of Kilbarry. The crosier is now preserved in the Dublin Museum. In 1890, Dr. M. F. Cox of Dublin, the lineal representative of the MacCoilidhs, unearthed St. Berach's boat and had it placed beside the present Catholic church of Whitehall, near Kilbarry.

His oratory at Cluain Coirpthe was in time replaced by a fine damhliag, or stone church, built by MacCoilidh and O'Hanley in 916, after which the site acquired the name Termon Barry, or Kilbarry, that is, the church of St. Berach. Kilbarrack Church in County Dublin was also called after the saint, for there, in his early days, he spent some time and performed many miracles, duly recorded in his Life, an account belonging to hagiographical tradition. His bell was long preserved at the Abbey of Glendalough, the monastery associated with his master St. Kevin, though it has disappeared since the sixteenth century.

Local tradition recounts signs and wonders associated with his prayer; such accounts rest upon his Life and upon local memory rather than upon contemporary record. As a disciple and a founder, Berach embodies the chain of holiness that linked one generation of Irish saints to the next, each teacher raising up disciples who carried the faith further into the land.

bernard-of-clairvaux.history:
Bernard of Clairvaux was born in 1090 at Fontaines, near Dijon, into the highest nobility of Burgundy. His parents were Tescelin, lord of Fontaines, and Aleth of Montbard, and he was the third of their seven children, six of whom were sons. Traditionally a devout man foretold his great destiny, and the child was educated with particular care. At nine he was sent to the renowned school of Chatillon-sur-Seine, kept by the secular canons of Saint-Vorles, where he excelled in literature and devoted himself for a time to poetry. He showed from youth a special devotion to the Blessed Virgin. His mother died when he was scarcely nineteen, and after the trials of his youth he began to think of withdrawing from the world to a life of solitude and prayer.

In 1113 Bernard sought admission to the abbey of Citeaux, founded in 1098 to restore the Rule of St. Benedict in all its rigour, and he entered with some thirty young noblemen of Burgundy. Three years later, St. Stephen, third Abbot of Citeaux, sent him at the head of a band of monks to found a new house in the Diocese of Langres, in a valley Bernard named Claire Vallee, or Clairvaux, on 25 June 1115. During the absence of the Bishop of Langres he was blessed as abbot by William of Champeaux, Bishop of Chalons-sur-Marne, who saw in him a predestined servant of God.

The beginnings of Clairvaux were trying. The regime was so austere that Bernard's health suffered, and only the influence of William of Champeaux and the authority of the General Chapter persuaded him to soften his austerities. Disciples flocked to the monastery; his aged father and all his brothers entered Clairvaux as monks, and his sister Humbeline, with her husband's consent, took the veil in the Benedictine convent of Jully. As the house overflowed, daughter foundations followed: Three Fountains in 1118, Fontenay in 1119, and Foigny in 1121. In 1119 Bernard attended the first General Chapter of the order, which fixed the constitutions and the Charter of Charity confirmed by Pope Callixtus II that December.

Bernard also acted in defense of the young order. At the request of William of St. Thierry he published his Apology, answering those who held the new order's rules impracticable; Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny, replied without wounding charity, and Suger, Abbot of St. Denis, was moved by the apology to restore discipline in his monastery. Bernard became the most influential churchman of his age, a reformer of monastic life, a counselor of popes and kings, and a preacher of the Second Crusade.

His works range widely. In 1120 he composed De Gradibus Superbiae et Humilitatis, the homilies De Laudibus Mariae, and the homilies on the Gospel Missus est; On the Conversion of Clerics followed in 1122, and in 1129 the De Laudibus Novae Militiae, addressed to Hughes de Payns, first Grand Master of the military order instituted in 1118. In De amore Dei he taught that God is to be loved without measure; the Book of Precepts and Dispensations (1131) answers questions on the Rule of St. Benedict; De Gratia et Libero Arbitrio upholds the Catholic dogma of grace and free will after the principles of St. Augustine; and the Book of Considerations was addressed to Pope Eugenius III. His preaching survives chiefly in eighty-six sermons on the Canticle of Canticles, together with eighty-six sermons for the whole year, sermons on Psalm 90, and some five hundred thirty letters. His sermons on the Song of Songs and his writings on the love of God shaped Western mysticism for centuries.

Bernard died at Clairvaux on 21 August 1153. He was canonized by Pope Alexander III on 18 January 1174, and Pope Pius VIII bestowed on him the title of Doctor of the Church. The Cistercians honour him as only the founders of orders are honoured, because of the widespread activity he gave to the Order of Citeaux. His feast is kept on 20 August, and he is venerated as patron of contemplatives and beekeepers and invoked by those seeking deeper prayer.

beuno.history:
{"history": "Beuno, sometimes anglicized as Bono, was a seventh-century Welsh abbot and confessor. According to the medieval life known as the Bucced Beuno, he was born in Powis-land, and tradition further holds that he belonged to the royal line of Powys. After education and ordination in the monastery of Bangor in North Wales, where according to tradition he studied under St. Deiniol, he became an active missioner.

His work in Gwynedd enjoyed the support of Cadvan, King of Gwynedd, who was his generous benefactor. Cadvan's son and successor, Cadwallon, deceived Beuno about some land, and when the saint demanded justice the king proved obdurate. Thereupon Cadwallon's cousin Gweddeint, in reparation, 'gave to God and Beuno forever his township', and there, around 616, Beuno founded the Abbey of Clynnog Fawr in Carnarvonshire. Eleven churches bearing St. Beuno's name, together with various relics and local usages, witness to his far-reaching missionary zeal.

Beuno became the guardian of his niece, the virgin St. Winefride, and the restorer of her to life; her clients still obtain marvellous favours at Holywell in Flintshire. He was relentless with hardened sinners, but full of compassion to those in distress.

Before his death, which occurred 'on the seventh day of Easter', he had a wondrous vision; the year of his death is given as about 660. Tradition holds that he was buried at Clynnog, and in later devotion he has been honored as a patron of sick children and of those who tend animals. He is commemorated on the 21st of April."}

boisil.history:
Saint Boisil was a monk in the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Northumbria who served as prior of Melrose Abbey and is remembered chiefly as the spiritual master of Saint Cuthbert. Almost all that is known of him comes from Bede, in the Ecclesiastical History and the Life of Cuthbert, and Bede derived his information from Sigfrid, a monk of Jarrow who had been trained by Boisil at Melrose. Though his fame rests largely on his connection with his great pupil, the master was plainly worthy of the disciple. Bede records that Boisil was learned in the Scriptures and of great purity of life, and his contemporaries were deeply impressed by his supernatural intuitions.

Melrose, an offshoot of Lindisfarne, was established in the late 640s, and Boisil belonged to its first generation of monks, rising in time to become its prior under Abbot Eata. When the young Cuthbert presented himself at the abbey, Boisil exclaimed, "Behold a servant of the Lord," and at once obtained leave from Eata to receive him into the community. He guided Cuthbert's early steps in the religious life, and tradition holds that he prophesied the future greatness of the youth committed to his direction.

Both master and pupil were tested by the great pestilence of 664. When Cuthbert was stricken down by the epidemic, Boisil declared that he would certainly recover, and he did. Boisil himself fell victim to it, as he had foretold three years earlier; before the end came, he predicted that Cuthbert would become a bishop and would effect great things for the Church, and he commended his pupil to the bishop's care. He died in the same year and was buried at Melrose.

Bede also relates that, after his death, Boisil appeared twice in a vision to his former disciple, Bishop Ecgberht. He has been credited, on somewhat dubious authority, with the authorship of certain theological works, but none of them have been preserved. The Roxburghshire town of Saint Boswell's commemorates his name, and his relics, like those of Saint Bede, were carried off to Durham in the eleventh century by the priest Ælfred.

His feast day is 24 February; the early calendars assigned his day to 23 February, while the Bollandists treat of him on 9 September. He is honored as a patron of monks and of spiritual direction. He is remembered less for recorded miracles than for the work of spiritual formation and the prophecies Bede attributes to him, above all for the disciple he formed.

pope-boniface-i.history:
Boniface I was elected bishop of Rome on 28 December 418 and served until his death on 4 September 422. Little is known of him before his election: the Liber Pontificalis calls him a Roman and the son of the presbyter Jocundus, and he is believed to have been ordained by Pope Damasus I and to have served as Innocent I's representative at Constantinople c. 405.

The death of Pope Zosimus opened one of the double elections that troubled the early Church. Just after Zosimus's obsequies on 27 December 418, a faction of the clergy, chiefly deacons, seized the Lateran basilica and elected the archdeacon Eulalius; the next day the higher clergy chose Boniface, an aged priest esteemed for charity, learning, and good character, much against his will. Both were consecrated on 29 December and each acted as pope. The Prefect Symmachus, hostile to Boniface, obtained from Emperor Honorius the confirmation of Eulalius, and Boniface was expelled. A synod of Italian bishops at Ravenna in early 419, unable to decide, ordered both claimants to withdraw pending a larger council. When Eulalius returned and seized the Lateran on Holy Saturday, imperial troops expelled him, and the emperor recognized Boniface as legitimate pope on 3 April 419. Boniface re-entered the city on 10 April after a schism of fifteen weeks; Eulalius was made bishop elsewhere, the sources differing on his see. In 420 a critical illness of the pope encouraged Eulalius's partisans to renewed efforts; on recovering, Boniface obtained from Honorius a law that in contested papal elections neither claimant should be recognized but a new election held.

His pontificate was marked by zeal for discipline. He reversed his predecessor's policy of extraordinary vicariates: Zosimus had given Patroclus, Bishop of Arles, extensive jurisdiction over Vienne and Narbonne, and Boniface curtailed these primatial rights and restored the metropolitan powers of the chief bishops. He sustained Hilary, Archbishop of Narbonne, in filling the vacant see of Lodeve against Patroclus's intruded candidate in 422, and in 419 insisted that Maximus, Bishop of Valence, be tried not by a primate but by a synod of the bishops of Gaul, whose decision he promised to sustain.

With the African Church he inherited difficulties over appeals to Rome, particularly the case of Apiarius. On 31 May 419 the Council of Carthage answered his predecessor's memorandum, stating it could not verify canons quoted by the legates as Nicene but later found to be Sardican; yet it promised to observe them, acknowledging the pope's office as guardian of the Church's discipline. In 422 he received the appeal of Anthony of Fussula, deposed by a provincial synod of Numidia at St. Augustine's instance, and decided that he should be restored if his innocence were established. He supported Augustine in combating Pelagianism; the two were friends and correspondents, and Augustine dedicated several of his works to Boniface.

He watched over the Illyrian church, insisting on obedience to Rome. Dissatisfaction among some bishops at his refusal to confirm Perigines as Bishop of Corinth unless Rufus recognized him became the pretext for Theodosius II to grant the ecclesiastical dominion of Illyricum to the Patriarch of Constantinople on 14 July 421. Boniface remonstrated with Honorius and prevailed on him to press for its rescission; the law was not enforced, but it passed into imperial codes and troubled succeeding popes. By a letter of 11 March 422 he forbade the consecration in Illyricum of any bishop whom Rufus would not recognize. He renewed Pope Soter's rules barring women from touching the sacred linens or tending the incense, and enforced laws excluding slaves from the clergy.

He was buried in the cemetery of Maximus on the Via Salaria, near the tomb of St. Felicitas, in whose honor and gratitude for her aid he had raised an oratory. The Church keeps his feast on 25 October, and he is honored as patron of bishops and of church unity.

bridget-of-sweden.history:
Bridget of Sweden, also called Birgitta, was born about 1303 and was the most celebrated saint of the Northern kingdoms. Her father, Birger Persson, governor and provincial judge of Uppland and one of the wealthiest landholders of the country, and her mother, Ingeborg Bengtsdotter, were both distinguished by deep piety, and St. Ingrid was a near relative of the family. Bridget received a careful religious training, and from her seventh year showed signs of extraordinary religious impressions and illuminations. After her mother's death, about 1315, an aunt took her mother's place, and to that influence Bridget owed the unswerving strength of will that afterward marked her life.

In 1316, at the age of thirteen, she was united in marriage to Ulf Gudmarsson, then eighteen. The happy marriage was blessed with eight children, among them St. Catherine of Sweden. Bridget's saintly life and great charity soon made her name known far and wide, and she was acquainted with learned and pious theologians, among them Nicolaus Hermanni, later Bishop of Linköping, and Matthias, canon of Linköping, who became her confessor, afterward succeeded in that office by Peter Magister. She later gained great influence at the court of King Magnus Eriksson. Between 1341 and 1343, in company with her husband, she made a pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostella; on the return journey Ulf Gudmarsson fell ill, recovered sufficiently to finish the journey, and died in 1344 in the Cistercian monastery of Alvastra in East Gothland.

Bridget then devoted herself entirely to prayer, asceticism, and religious undertakings. The visions she believed herself to have had from early childhood now became more frequent and definite, and she believed that Christ Himself appeared to her. These experiences, dictated to her confessors and collected as the Revelations, were translated into Latin by Matthias and by Peter, Prior of Alvastra, and were held in great repute during the Middle Ages.

She now founded a new religious congregation, the Order of the Most Holy Savior, known as the Brigittines, whose chief monastery at Vadstena was richly endowed by King Magnus and his queen in 1346. To obtain confirmation of her institute, and to seek a larger sphere of activity for her mission, which was the moral uplifting of the period, she journeyed to Rome in 1349 and remained there until her death, leaving the city only on pilgrimages, among them one to the Holy Land in 1373. In August 1370 Pope Urban V confirmed the Rule of her congregation. Bridget made earnest representations to Pope Urban, urging the removal of the Holy See from Avignon back to Rome. In Rome she accomplished great good by her pious and charitable life and by her earnest admonitions to others to adopt a better life, following the excellent precedents she had set in her native land.

She died in Rome on 23 July 1373. The year following her death her remains were conveyed to the monastery at Vadstena, and on 7 October 1391 she was canonized by Pope Boniface IX. Remembered for her Revelations and for the order she founded, she is venerated as a patroness of widows and as co-patroness of Europe, and her feast is kept on 23 July.

bruno-of-querfurt.history:
Bruno of Querfurt, also called Brun and Boniface, was a Camaldolese monk, missionary archbishop, and martyr remembered as the Second Apostle of the Prussians. He was born into the Saxon noble family of Querfurt, and it is commonly said that he was a relative of Emperor Otto III, though this has been disputed. Sent to Magdeburg at about the age of six to be educated in the cathedral school under the learned Geddo, he proved a diligent scholar, became a canon of the cathedral while still a lad, and was afterward received into the imperial court, accompanying the young emperor to Rome for his coronation in 996.

In Rome Bruno came to know St. Adalbert of Prague, who was martyred by the pagan Prussians a year later, and Adalbert's death kindled in Bruno a strong desire for martyrdom. Although he spent much time in the Aventine monastery where Adalbert had become a monk, he entered religious life in the Camaldolese monastery of Pereum near Ravenna, then under the guidance of St. Romuald. His training there was severe, embracing manual labor, fasting, and night vigils, and illness weighed heavily upon him, yet he found joy in the friendship of Benedict of Benevento, a brother of his own age who shared his cell.

Otto III hoped to convert the Slavic lands between the Elbe and the Oder through a monastery to be founded among Romuald's most zealous disciples. In 1001 Benedict and another brother went, laden with imperial gifts, to Poland, where Duke Boleslas received them kindly and taught them the language. Bruno remained in Italy awaiting his appointment: Pope Sylvester II made him archbishop over the pagan nations and granted him the pallium, but left his consecration to the Archbishop of Magdeburg, who consecrated him in February 1004. Because war had broken out between Emperor Henry II and Duke Boleslas, Bruno could not go to Poland at once; he went instead to Hungary, where he completed his life of St. Adalbert, a literary memorial of much worth.

His mission to the ruler Achtum and the principality called Black-Hungary met with opposition, including that of Greek monks, and bore no fruit; in December 1007 Bruno went to Russia. Grand Duke Vladimir entertained him for a month and then gave him a territory extending toward the Pechenegs, esteemed the fiercest and cruelest of the pagan tribes. Bruno spent five months among them, baptized some thirty adults, aided in bringing about a treaty of peace with Russia, and left one of his companions there whom he had consecrated bishop. About the middle of 1008 he returned to Poland, consecrated a bishop for Sweden, learned that Benedict and four companions had been killed by robbers in 1003, and wrote, from the accounts of eyewitnesses, the history of these Polish brothers. Toward the end of the year he sent Emperor Henry II a memorable, though ineffectual, letter exhorting him to clemency and peace with Boleslas.

Shortly afterward, with eighteen companions, Bruno set out to found a mission among the pagan Prussians. Finding the ground unfruitful, the party moved toward the borders of Kyivan Rus' and Lithuania, preaching courageously as they went, and there they were attacked and the whole company murdered. Bruno died on 14 February 1009, meeting death by decapitation with great composure. Duke Boleslas bought the bodies of the slain and had them brought to Poland, and tradition holds that the city of Braunsberg took its name from him.

Bruno and his companions were reverenced as martyrs soon after their deaths. He is commemorated on 15 October and is generally represented with a hand cut off. A legendary account of his martyrdom by one Wipert is of little value, while his fellow pupil Thietmar, Bishop of Merseburg, gives a brief notice of him in his chronicle. In his care to root the faith in native soil he provided the young churches with clergy, and he is honored as a patron of missionaries and martyrs.

caesarius-of-nazianzus.history:
Caesarius of Nazianzus was a physician and the younger and only brother of Gregory of Nazianzus, one of the Cappadocian Fathers. He was born probably about 330 at Arianzus, near Nazianzus in Cappadocia, and died at the end of 368 or the beginning of 369. His early years were shaped by the careful training he received from his saintly mother, Nonna, and from his father, Gregory, Bishop of Nazianzus, in whose devout household he was raised. Educated first, probably, at Caesarea in Cappadocia, and afterward at the celebrated schools of Alexandria, he devoted himself to geometry, astronomy, and above all to medicine, in which field he surpassed all his fellow students. His course of study carried him from his native region to some of the most renowned centers of learning in the ancient world.

About 355 he came to Constantinople, and there his medical skill soon won him a great reputation and high imperial favor. He was practicing in the capital when his brother Gregory, homeward bound from Athens, appeared there about 358, and Caesarius gave up a remunerative and honorable post in order to return to his parents with him. The capital, however, soon proved too great an attraction for him. He occupied an exalted position as a court physician under Constantius II and, much to the regret of his family, at that of Julian the Apostate. Julian failed in his efforts to win him over to paganism, and Caesarius, who prized his faith above imperial favor, ultimately left the court. He returned to Constantinople after Julian's death, and under the emperor Valens became quaestor of Bithynia, an administrative office, so that his career came to encompass both medicine and public service to the emperors.

Throughout these years of success, Caesarius was drawn toward the Christian faith by his brother's example, even as his profession placed him amid the wealth and honors of the court. The decisive turn came after the earthquake that shook Nicaea on 11 October 368. His remarkable escape from this disaster induced him at last to heed the insistent appeals of his brother and of St. Basil, who urged him to leave the world. Like many Christians of the period, Caesarius had deferred his baptism until late in life; he received it at last, and shortly afterward was suddenly seized with a fatal illness. Unmarried, he directed that all his goods should be distributed to the poor, an injunction which his servants abused in their own interests. His remains were interred at Nazianzus, where his brother pronounced the funeral oration in the presence of their parents, praising his integrity amid wealth and power.

Honored as a saint in both the Eastern Orthodox and the Roman Catholic Churches, Caesarius is commemorated with a feast on 9 March and is regarded as a patron of physicians and of scholars. His life is remembered as a model of faithfulness within secular professions, that of a gifted physician who served emperors without surrendering his faith and who placed his learning and his goods at the service of God and of the poor.

Two matters connected with his memory rest on less certain ground. The identification of this Caesarius with his namesake, the Prefect of Constantinople who in 365 was thrown into prison by Procopius, rests only on an assumption of James Godefroy, the editor of the Theodosian Code, and not on any solid historical ground. Similarly, the four Dialogues of one hundred and ninety-seven questions and answers that circulate under his name can hardly be from his pen, owing to their nature, contents, and anachronisms, and are today generally looked upon as spurious.

cedd.history:
Cedd, also recorded as Cedda, was a seventh-century monk and bishop of the East Saxons and the brother of St. Ceadda, known as Chad. He was born into an Angle family settled in Northumbria, and two of his brothers, Cynibill and Caelin, also became priests. With his younger brother Ceadda he was raised at the monastery of Lindisfarne under St. Aidan, receiving a formation in the Celtic tradition of that house.

In 653 he was one of four priests sent by Oswiu, King of Northumbria, to evangelize the Middle Angles at the request of their ealdorman, Peada. Shortly afterward he was recalled and sent on a similar mission to Essex, where he assisted Sigeberht, King of the East Saxons, in converting his people. There he was consecrated bishop and was very active in founding churches, establishing monasteries at Tilbury and Ithancester.

He occasionally returned to his native Northumbria, where at the request of Aethelwald he founded the monastery of Laestingaeu, now Lastingham in Yorkshire, and though retaining his episcopal responsibilities he became that house's first abbot. His brother Chad would succeed him there. In 664 he took part in the Synod of Whitby, which resolved the differences between the Roman and Celtic traditions within the Church in England; though formed in the Celtic observance, he, like St. Cuthbert, adopted the Roman Easter.

Immediately after the synod he visited Lastingham, where the plague then prevalent claimed his life; he died on October 26, 664. Tradition holds that he was weakened by illness while tending those stricken by the plague. Later chroniclers, Florence of Worcester and William of Malmesbury, counted him as the second Bishop of London, but St. Bede, almost a contemporary, never gives him that title. His festival was kept on January 7, and he is remembered as a patron of translators and linguists.

columba-of-terryglass.history:
Saint Columba of Terryglass was a son of Crinthainn and a disciple of Saint Finnian of Clonard. When Finnian lay dying of the plague, Columba administered Holy Viaticum to him. Having completed his studies, Columba in turn took charge of Caemban, Fintan, and Mocumin, three men who are themselves numbered among the saints of Ireland.

In 548 he founded the celebrated monastery of Tirdaglas, or Terryglass. It is said that he visited Tours and brought from there relics of Saint Martin. Columba died of the plague on 13 December 552 and was buried within the precincts of his own monastery at Terryglass.

His feast is kept on 12 December, and he is honored as a patron of monks and students. The Martyrology of Gorman also records some fifteen other Irish saints who bore the name Columba.

conan.history:
St. Conan, also known as Mochonna, was an Irish missionary who served as a bishop in the Isle of Man and died in January 684. He is remembered for carrying the Christian faith from Ireland across the Irish Sea to Manxland, where ancient sources record that he left a distinct impress of his zeal for souls.

Definite facts about his life are difficult to establish, as the history of the Isle of Man in the early centuries of Christianity is very obscure. The Bollandists place him among the early bishops of Man, and the hagiographer Colgan preserved an account of his life and labours. He is also described as Bishop of Inis-Patrick. As a bishop among the early Celtic saints, who traveled freely between Ireland, Scotland, and the islands, he would have ordained clergy, taught the faithful, and established churches. Tradition holds that he embodies the great missionary expansion of the Irish Church, which sent monks and bishops to preach Christ throughout the islands and beyond.

Some authorities give the date of his death as 26 January, but Colgan, citing the ancient Irish martyrologies, gives 13 January, and this is the day on which his feast is observed. St. Conan is not to be confounded with St. Conindrius, said to have been a disciple of St. Patrick who lived to a very advanced age. Several other Irish saints bear the same name, including St. Conan of Assaroe and St. Conan of Ballinamore. He is regarded as a patron of missionaries and bishops.

crescens.history:
Crescens was a companion of St. Paul during the Apostle's second Roman captivity, and he appears but once in the New Testament. Writing from Rome, the Apostle urges Timothy to make haste to come to him quickly, and records that Demas, loving this world, has gone to Thessalonica, while Crescens has gone into Galatia and Titus into Dalmatia. Commentators have always ranked Crescens with Titus rather than with Demas, and so read the passage not as a desertion but as a reference to a missionary journey into Galatia, undertaken in the service of the Gospel.

In New Testament times the term Galatia might denote either Gaul or the Roman province of Galatia in Asia Minor, where St. Paul had laboured so much, and the passage has been interpreted in both senses. In its other occurrences in the New Testament, however, the word denotes the province, and it was most probably so understood by Timothy, especially as the other regions mentioned lie likewise to the east of Rome. St. Paul might easily have had reason for sending a disciple to visit his old churches in Galatia, while there is no proof that he had an active interest in Gaul. Certain manuscripts, among them the Sinaiticus and the Ephraemi codex, read Gallia instead of Galatia, and this variant has been advanced in favour of a Gaulish mission; but the traditional reading is supported by the great mass of manuscript evidence.

The earliest tradition, preserved in the Apostolic Constitutions, represents Crescens as a bishop of the churches in Galatia. Later traditions, on the other hand, locate him as Bishop of Vienne in Gaul and also at Mainz on the Rhine. These claims appear to have arisen later from the desire of an apostolic origin, for the earliest traditions of Gaul itself know nothing of this disciple of the Apostle as a founder of their churches. The claims of Vienne have been most strongly urged, but they rest upon a mistaken identification of its first bishop, a Crescens of the third century, with the disciple of St. Paul; as little can be said for the tradition of Mainz.

Tradition holds that Crescens was one of the Seventy Disciples of Christ, though the list of the Pseudo-Dorotheus that records this has no authority. A martyrdom in Galatia under the emperor Trajan, commemorated on 27 June in the Roman Martyrology, likewise lacks the confirmation of the older martyrologies, and so the manner of his death must be left in some uncertainty. The Greek Church honours him on 30 July, the day on which his feast is kept.

His very name is drawn from the Latin crescere, to increase, and its meaning, increasing, was seen as a fitting emblem for one whose life was given to the growth of the Church. Venerated as a saint from the earliest Christian centuries, before the institution of the formal canonization process, he is remembered as one of that first generation of apostolic workers who served as companions and fellow-labourers of St. Paul in the great work of carrying the Gospel to the nations, their journeys knitting the young churches of the Mediterranean into a single body of faith. He is honoured today as a patron of missionaries and preachers.

cyprian-and-justina.history:
Saints Cyprian and Justina are commemorated as Christians of Antioch who suffered martyrdom during the persecution of Diocletian at Nicomedia on 26 September 304, the date afterwards kept as their feast, observed on September 26. Their recognition as saints belongs to the earliest centuries of the Church and predates the formal processes of canonization that later developed. They are honored in the Catholic Church, the Eastern Orthodox Church, and Oriental Orthodoxy, and they are regarded as patrons of converts and of those engaged in spiritual warfare.

Tradition holds that Cyprian, before his conversion, was a heathen magician of Antioch who had dealings with demons. By their aid he sought to bring Justina, a Christian virgin, to ruin, but she foiled the threefold attacks of the devils by the sign of the cross. Cyprian, brought to despair by his failure, made the sign of the cross himself and was freed from the toils of Satan. Thus the sorcerer who had served the powers of darkness was overcome by the steadfast faith of a virgin and became a Christian beside her. He was received into the Church, was made pre-eminent by miraculous gifts, and became in succession deacon, priest, and finally bishop, while Justina became the head of a convent.

The same account relates that, during the Diocletianic persecution, both were seized and taken to Damascus, where they were subjected to severe tortures. Their faith never wavered, and they were brought before Diocletian at Nicomedia, where at his command they were beheaded on the bank of the river Gallus. The same fate befell Theoctistus, a Christian who had come to Cyprian and had embraced him. After the bodies of the saints had lain unburied for six days, they were taken by Christian sailors to Rome, where they were interred on the estate of a noble lady named Rufina, and were later entombed in Constantine's basilica.

This is the outline of a legend, which some have read as an allegory, whose full literary form, adorned with diffuse descriptions and dialogues, is found in the writings of Symeon Metaphrastes, a source considered unreliable, and it was made the subject of a poem by the Empress Eudocia. The story, however, must have arisen as early as the fourth century, for it is mentioned both by Gregory of Nazianzus and by Prudentius; both writers confounded this Cyprian with Cyprian of Carthage, a mistake often repeated. It is certain that no Bishop of Antioch bore the name of Cyprian. The tale has been examined as a possible prototype of the Faust legend, and Calderon took it as the basis of his drama El magico prodigioso. The legend circulated in both Greek and Latin, and ancient Syriac and Ethiopic versions of it have also been published in modern times. Beyond these outlines, little can be established with certainty concerning the two martyrs themselves.

Revered in East and West alike, Cyprian and Justina are remembered on September 26 as witnesses to the triumph of grace over the powers of darkness and the victory of faith over fear. In Cyprian's passage from magic to the episcopate and in Justina's steadfastness under trial, the Church has long seen an image of the converting power of Christ and of the preservation of the faithful in temptation, and for this reason the two martyrs have been invoked especially by converts and in times of spiritual struggle.

cyril-of-alexandria.history:
Cyril of Alexandria, declared a Doctor of the Church, seems to have belonged to an Alexandrian family and was the nephew of Theophilus, Patriarch of Alexandria; he may also have spent some time as a monk. In 402 he accompanied Theophilus to Constantinople for the Synod of the Oak, by which St. John Chrysostom was deposed. Theophilus died on 15 October 412, and on the 18th of that month Cyril was consecrated his successor, after riots between his supporters and those of a rival, Timotheus. He governed the great see of Alexandria until his death in 444, at the height of its influence within the Roman Empire.

His early episcopate was turbulent. The historian Socrates complains that one of his first acts was to plunder and shut the churches of the Novatians; after tumults in which Christians were massacred, Cyril assembled a mob in their defense, and the Jews, whose community went back to Alexander the Great, were driven out of the city. The prefect Orestes, jealous of the patriarch's power, resisted him, and five hundred monks came down from Nitria to his defense; Orestes was wounded in the head by a stone thrown by a monk named Ammonius, whom the prefect had tortured to death, and Cyril honored the monk's remains for a time as those of a martyr. The Alexandrians were always riotous: in one outbreak, in 422, the prefect Callistus was killed, and in another a mob led by a lector named Peter killed the philosopher Hypatia, an aged teacher of Neo-Platonism and a friend of Orestes. Socrates records that this brought great disgrace on the church of Alexandria and its bishop, though he does not suggest that Cyril himself was to blame; the direct accusation against him comes from Damascius, a late and hostile writer.

Like Theophilus, who died out of communion with Rome over the Chrysostom affair, Cyril long refused to insert St. John Chrysostom's name in the diptychs of his church, despite the requests of Atticus, Chrysostom's supplanter in the see. He yielded in later years, apparently at the urging of Isidore of Pelusium, whom he called his spiritual father, and came to be fully trusted by Rome.

In the winter of 427-28 Nestorius became Patriarch of Constantinople, and his teaching soon became known to Cyril, who defended the title Theotokos for the Virgin Mary in his Paschal letter of 429 and in a letter to the monks of Egypt. He corresponded with Nestorius in a moderate tone, and when Nestorius sent his sermons to Pope Celestine, the pope asked Cyril for further information. Cyril declined to act in his own name and denounced Nestorius to Celestine, citing the ancient custom of bringing such matters before the pope. The pope's reply was severe: a Roman council was convoked, and Cyril was instructed to take to himself the authority of the Roman See, requiring Nestorius to recant within ten days of the ultimatum or be separated from the Church, after which Cyril was to provide for the church of Constantinople. Cyril then summoned a council of his suffragans and composed a letter to Nestorius, appended to which were twelve propositions for Nestorius to anathematize; the epistle was not conciliatory.

At the Council of Ephesus in 431, Cyril presided and was central to the deposition of Nestorius as Patriarch of Constantinople, affirming that Christ is one divine person in two natures. He was a principal figure in the Christological controversies of his time.

Cyril wrote extensively. Among his works, several of which survive in fragments, are a Thesaurus, commentaries and homilies on the Gospel of Luke preserved in Syriac, and books written against Julian. His feast is kept on different days in the Eastern and Western calendars. He is honored as one of the greatest theologians of the early Church and is venerated as a patron of theologians and of church unity.

drostan.history:
Saint Drostan, whose name appears in early sources as Drustan, Dustan, or Throstan, was a Scottish abbot who flourished about A.D. 600. He belonged to that wave of Celtic monks who carried the Gospel through Pictland in the early medieval period. Nearly all that is known of him comes from the Breviarium Aberdonense and the Book of Deir, a ninth-century manuscript now kept in the University Library of Cambridge, and these two accounts do not agree in every particular.

The sources describe him as a member of the royal family of the Scoti, his father's name being Cosgrach. Showing signs of a religious vocation at an early age, he was entrusted to the care of St. Columba, who trained him and gave him the monastic habit. He accompanied Columba on a visit to Aberdour in Buchan, where the Pictish ruler of the district granted them a site at Deir, fourteen miles farther inland. There they established a monastery, and when Columba returned to Iona he left Drostan as abbot of the new foundation, the community later known as Old Deer. Under his leadership it became a center of monastic life in Aberdeenshire, and his holiness drew disciples in that remote corner of the northeast.

Some years later, on the death of the Abbot of Dalquhongale, also known as Holywood, Drostan was chosen to succeed him. Feeling called afterward to a life of greater seclusion, he resigned his abbacy, went farther north, and became a hermit at Glenesk. There his sanctity attracted the poor and needy, and many miracles are ascribed to him, including the restoration of sight to a priest named Symon.

After his death his relics were translated to the church at New Aberdour and honorably preserved there, and a holy well near the church long drew pilgrims seeking healing. The monastery of Deir had fallen into decay, and in 1213 it was rebuilt for Cistercian monks and so continued until the Reformation. His feast is kept on July 11, though the Breviary of Aberdeen assigns it to December 15. He is honored as a patron of monks and of the sick, and is remembered as a patron of Aberdeenshire and of the monastic ideal lived out in simplicity and prayer.

d-chu.history:
Saint Díchu mac Trichim, the son of an Ulster chieftain, holds the singular honor of being counted the first convert of Saint Patrick in Ireland. Born in the last decade of the fourth century, he succeeded to the petty kingdom of Lecale, a territory which included Saul, in the present County Down. As a chieftain of the region, he ruled the very lands among which the apostle's mission would first take root.

On Saint Patrick's arrival at Tubber Slain, the estuary of the Slaney near Loch Cuan, or Strangford Lough, in the year 432, Díchu was still a pagan and strongly opposed the apostle's landing, and even attacked the saint. Tradition holds that, as he raised his sword against the stranger, his arm was miraculously stayed; touched with divine grace, he embraced the Faith of Christ and received baptism. What had begun in resistance ended in a welcome; his conversion opened a door for the mission that would transform Ireland.

Thereupon, after his baptism, Díchu presented Saint Patrick with Sabhall, or Saul, to serve as a church, and Saul thus became the first Irish foundation of the national apostle, being afterwards known as Sabhall-Padhraic. Tradition holds that the place given over was Díchu's own barn, made ready as a place of worship. Saul remained a particular favorite of Saint Patrick, who frequently sought a resting-place there during his arduous missionary labors, a preference that spoke of his affection for his first convert and for the ground where his work among the Irish had begun.

From the day of his conversion, Díchu is described as a model of sanctity, passing from a man of warlike proclivities to become a man of peace. He is remembered as the firstfruits of Patrick's preaching, the Gospel taking root through one man who welcomed the apostle. The details of his later career are obscure; of the incidents of those years, one of the few that has been preserved is the release of his two sons, who had been detained as hostages by Laoghaire, King of Ireland, and who were set free at the prayer of Saint Patrick.

It was at Saul that Saint Patrick died, and this monastery became in afterdays a famous abbey, under the rule of the Regular Canons of Saint Augustine. His feast is kept on 29 April and is noted in the Martyrology of Donegal as 'Diochu of Sabhall'. He is honored as a patron of converts and of homemakers.

earconwald.history:
Saint Earconwald, known also as Erkenwald, belonged to the princely family of Offa in East Anglia. He devoted a considerable portion of his patrimony to the founding of two monasteries, one for monks at Chertsey in Surrey, over which he himself discharged the duties of superior, and one for nuns at Barking in Essex, over which he placed his sister, Saint Ethelburga, as abbess. He continued this monastic life until the death of Bishop Wini of London in 675, when he was called to the vacant see at the instance of King Sebbi and Theodore, Archbishop of Canterbury.

His elevation made him the first post-Roman Bishop of London, in whose episcopate the unbroken succession of the restored Saxon see began. As monk and bishop he was renowned for his holiness of life and revered as a holy pastor, and miracles were wrought in attestation of his sanctity. The Venerable Bede testifies that the sick were cured by contact with the litter on which he had been carried. He was present in 686 at the reconciliation between Archbishop Theodore and Wilfrith, and King Ini, in the preface to his laws, addressed him as "my bishop." During his episcopate he enlarged his cathedral church, augmented its revenues, and obtained for it special privileges from the king. An ancient epitaph records that he ruled the Diocese of London for eleven years.

It is said that toward the end of his life he retired to his sister's convent at Barking, where he died on 30 April, about the year 693. He was buried in the church of St. Paul's, and his tomb became renowned for miracles. The citizens of London cherished a special devotion to him and regarded with pride the magnificence of his shrine, which remained for centuries a place of pilgrimage. When the cathedral burned in 1087, it is related that the shrine and its silken coverings remained intact. On 14 November 1148 his body was solemnly translated and raised above the high altar. In the sixteenth century the shrine was robbed of its jewels and ornaments, and the bones of the saint are said to have been buried at that time at the east end of the choir.

Before the Reformation, the anniversaries of the saint's death and of the translation of his relics were observed at St. Paul's as feasts of the first class, in accordance with an ordinance of Bishop Braybroke in 1386, a rank that attests to the antiquity of his cult. A feast in his honor is kept on 24 April, while English Catholics also observe 14 November, the anniversary of his translation. Popular tradition invoked him as a protection against gout and as a guardian of the city of London, and he is honored as a patron of bishops and of England. Medieval devotion to him found literary expression in the Middle English poem St. Erkenwald, which takes the saint as its subject and is counted among the important works in the foundations of English literature.

edmund-campion.history:
Edmund Campion, English Jesuit and martyr, was born in London on 25 January 1540, the son and namesake of a Catholic bookseller. Educated at Christ's Church Hospital, he was the schoolboy chosen to give the Latin salutatory to Queen Mary Tudor when she entered London in state. Sir Thomas White, founder of St John's College, Oxford, accepted him among the college's first scholars and made him a junior fellow at seventeen. Campion took both his degrees, became a celebrated tutor, and by 1568 was junior proctor, celebrated at Oxford for his eloquence. Queen Elizabeth, visiting the university, was won by his bearing and wit and bade him ask for whatever he would.

Outward success, however, sat uneasily on his conscience. He took the Oath of Supremacy and received deacon's orders according to the new rite, but scruples deepened into anguish, and when his proctorship ended he left for Ireland to await the revival of Dublin University, which fell through. Suspected there as too Catholic-minded an Anglican, he lived in hiding and composed his History of Ireland. His vocation declared itself, and after a course in the English seminary at Douai he walked as a barefoot pilgrim to Rome, entering the Society of Jesus in April 1573 as the first novice received by Mercurianus. Allotted to the Bohemian province, he made his noviceship at Prague and his probation year at Brunn in Moravia, taught in the Prague college, and was ordained in 1578. At Brunn he reported a vision in which Our Lady foretold his martyrdom, an omen his comrades at Prague marked with a scroll naming him martyr and a garland of painted roses.

Dr Allen, organizing the English mission, secured Fathers Robert Parsons and Edmund Campion as its first Jesuit helpers. Campion reached England in 1580 and moved about in disguise; his work was chiefly to reclaim Catholics wavering under government pressure, though his preaching made a profound impression widely felt. When an alarm was raised he fled north and composed his famous tract, the Decem Rationes; his pamphlet defending the faith, known as Campion's Brag, also circulated widely.

An informer, George Eliot, tracked him down at Lyford Grange near Wantage in Berkshire on 17 July 1581. Campion was paraded through London bound and riding backwards with a paper denoting the seditious Jesuit, and was thrown first into the Little Ease at the Tower. Taken privately to the house of his old patron, the Earl of Leicester, he met the queen and received earnest offers of liberty and preferment if he would forsake his faith; he would not. In the Tower he was examined under torture and was reported to have betrayed those who had harboured him, and several arrests were made on the strength of that report. He had asked for a public disputation; when four long conferences were held in the Norman chapel of the Tower, he had been denied preparation and severely racked, yet he stood through them without chair, table, or notes, undefeated. Philip Howard, Earl of Arundel, was thereby moved to return to God's service.

The privy council, at its wits' end over so purely spiritual a traitor, sought to impeach his loyalty through hired accusers; the trial followed, its charges a wholesale sham by the universal agreement of historians. He was executed at Tyburn on 1 December 1581, and a harvest of conversions followed. A young bystander, Henry Walpole, had his white doublet stained with Campion's blood; the incident made him in time, like Campion, a Jesuit and a martyr.

Admirers praise his high intelligence, his gaiety, his fiery energy, and his chivalrous gentleness, and see in him one of the great Elizabethans, holy as none other of them all. He was beatified by Pope Leo XIII on 9 December 1886 and, in 1970, canonized among the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales. His relics are preserved at Rome, Prague, Oxford, and Stonyhurst. His feast is kept on 1 December, and he is honored as a patron of martyrs and of writers.

ephraim-of-antioch.history:
Saint Ephraim of Antioch, also called Ephraim of Amida, was born at Amida in Mesopotamia and died in 545. Before his elevation to the episcopacy he served the Emperor Justinian I as Count of the East (Comes Orientis), a high imperial administrative office. In 527 he succeeded Euphrasius as Patriarch of Antioch, heading the Greek Orthodox Church of Antioch from that year until his death in 545, and he brought to the patriarchal throne both the gifts of an experienced administrator and firmness in matters of faith.

Ephraim stood among the defenders of the Definition of Chalcedon (451) against the Monophysites, and his patriarchate was marked by the doctrinal divisions of his age. He opposed the efforts of Emperor Justinian to enforce Monophysite doctrine and labored to uphold the orthodox teaching of the Council of Chalcedon within his troubled see. Venerated as a saint in both the Eastern Orthodox and Catholic Churches, he is remembered as a bishop who governed wisely in a time of division. He is honored as a patron of bishops and of church unity, and his feast is kept on 8 June.

Most of his many works have been lost, but the titles of several survive through later writers. Anastasius Sinaita (c. 700) quotes passages from a work of Ephraim against Severus, the Monophysite Patriarch of Antioch (512-519). The Sacra Parallela, attributed to St. John Damascene (d. about 754) or to another author, preserve a short passage cited from St. Ephraim, Archbishop of Antioch, taken from a work On John the Grammarian and the Synod. Photius (d. 891) describes four books by Ephraim: the first consisted of sermons and letters, while the second and third contained a treatise against Severus in three parts and an answer to five questions about Genesis addressed to Ephraim by a monk named Anatolius. The fragments quoted by Photius represent practically all that remains of his writings.

Cardinal Mai was able to add a few more fragments from a manuscript Catena in the Vatican library, and the scholar Krumbacher noted several others in the Paris library and elsewhere. Krumbacher judged that, had more of Ephraim's work been preserved, he would deserve the same reputation as Leontius Byzantinus. His surviving writings show an extensive knowledge of the Greek Fathers, and in his Christology he follows chiefly St. Cyril of Alexandria.

eugendus.history:
Saint Eugendus, known in French as Oyand or Oyan, was born around 450 at Izernore, in Ain, Franche-Comté. His first instruction in reading and writing came from his father, who had become a priest, and when the boy was seven years old his parents gave him to Saints Romanus and Lupicinus, the first abbots, to be educated at Condat, a monastery set in the remote Jura mountains at what is now Saint-Claude in eastern France. From that time he never left the monastery, and from his youth he was known for his love of prayer, his obedience, and his zeal for the discipline of the house.

As a monk he imitated the example of Romanus and Lupicinus with such zeal that it was difficult to tell which of the two he resembled more. Eugendus acquired much learning, read the Greek and Latin authors, and was well versed in the Scriptures, though he wrote little; his teaching was preserved in the lives of his disciples. He led a life of great austerity, but out of humility he did not want to be ordained a priest.

Abbot Minausius made him his coadjutor, and after Minausius' death, about 496, Eugendus became the fourth abbot of Condat. He always remained the humble religious he had been before, governing the community with wisdom and gentleness and leading the monks in the daily round of prayer and manual labour. His monks had in him a model of penitence and piety which God deigned to acknowledge by miracles. When the monastery, which Saint Romanus had built of wood, was destroyed by fire, Eugendus erected another of stone.

Eugendus also improved the common life of the community. Until his time the brethren had lived in separate cells after the fashion of the Eastern ascetics, and the observance of the house had been founded on the rules of the Oriental monasteries; under Eugendus it took on more of the active character of the Western brethren, the rule of Tarnate being thought to have served as a model. He built a beautiful church in honor of the holy Apostles Peter, Paul, and Andrew, and enriched it with precious relics. Condat began to flourish as a place of refuge for all who suffered from the misfortunes and afflictions of those eventful times, a school of virtue and knowledge amid the surrounding darkness, an oasis in the desert.

When Eugendus felt his end approaching, he had his breast anointed by a priest, took leave of his brethren, and died quietly after five days, on 1 January 510. A few years after his death his successor, Saint Viventiolus, erected a church over his tomb, to which numerous pilgrims travelled. A town was founded that bore the saint's name, Saint-Oyand de Joux, and it retained that name as late as the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, while the older name of Condat passed into oblivion.

When Saint Claudius resigned the Diocese of Besançon in 687 and died in 696 as the twelfth abbot, the pilgrims who came to visit his grave were so numerous that, since the thirteenth century, the name Saint-Claude came more and more into use and has today superseded the other. Eugendus is honored as one of the founding fathers of the great monastery of the Jura and is venerated as a patron of monks and of Europe. His feast is kept on 4 January, the date still observed in the dioceses of Besançon and Saint-Claude.

evodius.history:
Evodius is remembered as the first bishop of Antioch after St. Peter and is counted among the first identifiable post-apostolic bishops, the generation that received the faith from the apostles and handed it on to those who came after. Antioch in Syria was one of the great sees of the early Church, the city where the followers of Jesus were first called Christians, and its bishop would have shepherded a church already stretched across Syria and beyond. The earliest substantial witness to Evodius is Eusebius of Caesarea, who records that Evodius was established as the first bishop of the Antiochians while Ignatius flourished. Eusebius appears to have taken the episcopal lists of Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch from the Chronography published by Julius Africanus in 221, a list that gave no dates and which Eusebius synchronized only roughly with the bishops of Rome. In Jerome's Latin version of Eusebius's Chronicle, the ordination of Evodius as first bishop of Antioch appears alongside the entries that Peter founded the Church of Antioch before being sent to Rome and that Mark, the interpreter of Peter, preached Christ in Egypt and Alexandria. Most manuscripts assign the ordination to the fourth year of the emperor Claudius, that is A.D. 44, though others give the second or third year. No writer earlier than Africanus mentions Evodius, but Origen, Africanus's contemporary, confirms the sequence by calling Ignatius the second bishop after Peter.

The dates of Evodius's life remain quite uncertain. The year of his death, which would mark Ignatius's accession, was unknown to Eusebius, who places it in the Chronicle beside the death of Peter and the accession of Linus at Rome under Nero, while in the Ecclesiastical History he places that accession at the beginning of Trajan's reign. The fame of St. Ignatius later clouded the record of the succession: some writers spoke of Ignatius as the immediate successor of the apostles, Jerome and Socrates called him the third bishop after Peter only by counting Peter among his own successors, and Theodoret and the Pseudo-Ignatian writings described Ignatius as consecrated by Peter. Tradition holds, as preserved in the Apostolic Constitutions, that Evodius was ordained by Peter and Ignatius by Paul. The Byzantine chronicler John Malalas likewise relates that Evodius died as Peter passed through Antioch on his way to Rome, that Ignatius then succeeded him, and that Evodius was the first to devise the name Christian; such details belong to later tradition rather than to the earliest evidence. It is nonetheless held that Evodius was a genuine historical figure and truly the predecessor of St. Ignatius.

Eastern tradition honors Evodius as one of the seventy disciples and as a martyr, commemorating him together with Onesiphorus, mentioned in the second letter to Timothy, on 29 April and again on 7 September, although no early witness describes his martyrdom. His cult in the West came later still. He was unknown to the early Western martyrologies, and it was Ado who introduced his notice, on 6 May, drawing on the Pseudo-Ignatian writings; from Ado the notice passed to Usuard and into the Roman Martyrology, and his feast is kept on 6 May. As the first bishop of Antioch after St. Peter and the forerunner of St. Ignatius, Evodius is honored as a witness to the continuity of the apostolic ministry, a link between the age of the apostles and the age of the pastors, and he is venerated as a patron of priests and preachers.

exuperius.history:
St. Exuperius, also written Exsuperius, served as Bishop of Toulouse at the beginning of the fifth century. Neither the place nor the date of his birth is known; he died sometime after 410. Succeeding St. Silvius in the see, he completed the basilica of St. Saturninus, which his predecessor had begun.

He is remembered above all for his charity toward the poor. St. Jerome praised his munificence to the monks of Palestine, Egypt, and Libya, and his charity toward the people of his own diocese, who were then suffering from the depredations of the Vandals, Alans, and Suevi. A man of great austerity and simplicity of life, he sought not his own but gave what he had to the poor, even selling the altar vessels for their sake; he was thus compelled to carry the Sacred Host in an osier basket and the Precious Blood in a vessel of glass. In esteem for his virtues and in gratitude for his gifts, Jerome dedicated his Commentary on Zacharias to him.

Exuperius is best known in connection with the canon of the Sacred Scriptures. He had written to Pope Innocent I for instructions concerning the canon and several points of ecclesiastical discipline, and the pope replied with the letter Consulenti tibi, dated February 405, which contained a list of the canonical scriptures as the Catholic Church receives them today, including the deuterocanonical books. The assertion of non-Catholic writers that the canon of Innocent I excluded the Apocrypha is not true when the term Apocrypha is extended to the deuterocanonical books.

Little is certain of his early career. From Jerome's letter to Furia of Rome, written in 394, and from the epistle of St. Paulinus to Amandus of Bordeaux, written in 397, it seems probable that Exuperius was a priest at Rome and later at Bordeaux before he was raised to the episcopate, though both letters may refer to a different person of the same name. The opinion of Baronius that the bishop was identical with the rhetorician Exuperius, who taught Hannibalianus and Dalmatius, nephews of Constantine the Great, is quite generally rejected, since that rhetor lived over half a century before the bishop's period. Just when Exuperius became bishop is unknown, but that he occupied the See of Toulouse in February 405 is evident from the letter of Innocent I, and a statement of Jerome in a letter to Rusticus shows that he was still living in 411. It is sometimes said that Jerome reproved him, in a letter to Riparius, a priest of Spain, for tolerating the heretic Vigilantius; as Vigilantius, however, did not belong to the diocese of Toulouse, Jerome was probably speaking of another bishop.

Exuperius was venerated as a saint from an early period. Even in the time of St. Gregory of Tours he was held in veneration equal to that of St. Saturninus. His feast is kept on September 28; the first martyrologist to assign it to that date was Usuard, who wrote toward the end of the ninth century. Honored as a saint of the early Gallic Church, he is regarded as a patron of bishops and of the poor.

faustus-of-riez.history:
Faustus of Riez, Bishop of Riez (Rhegium) in Southern Gaul and the best known and most distinguished defender of Semipelagianism, was born between 405 and 410 and, according to his contemporaries Avitus of Vienne and Sidonius Apollinaris, was a native of the island of Britain; he died between 490 and 495. Nothing certain is known of his early life or education; he is thought by some to have been a lawyer, but, moved by the example of his mother, who was famed for her sanctity, he abandoned secular pursuits while still a young man and entered the monastery of Lérins.

At Lérins he was ordained to the priesthood, and in 432, because of his extraordinary piety, he was chosen head of the monastery in succession to Maximus, who had become Bishop of Riez. His abbacy lasted some twenty or twenty-five years and won him a high reputation for his gifts as an extempore preacher and for his stern asceticism. On the death of Maximus he was raised to the see of Riez. His elevation brought no change in his manner of life: he continued his ascetic practices and frequently returned to Lérins to renew his fervour. A zealous advocate of monasticism, he established many monasteries in his diocese.

Faustus took part in all the theological discussions of his time and became known as a stern opponent of Arianism in all its forms. For this, and also, it is said, for his teaching that the human soul is in a certain sense corporeal, God alone being a pure spirit, he incurred the enmity of Euric, King of the Visigoths, who had gained possession of a large portion of Southern Gaul, and was banished from his see. The exile lasted eight years, during which he was aided by loyal friends. On the death of Euric he resumed his labours at the head of his diocese and remained there until his death.

Throughout his life he was an uncompromising adversary of Pelagius, whom he styled Pestifer. He was equally decided in his opposition to the doctrine of predestination, which he called erroneous, blasphemous, heathen, fatalistic, and conducive to immorality. That doctrine, in its most repulsive form, had been expounded by a presbyter named Lucidus and was condemned by the synods of Arles and Lyons in 475. At the request of the bishops of these synods, and especially of Leontius of Arles, Faustus wrote his two books On the Grace of God and on the Free Will of the Human Mind, in which he refuted both the doctrines of the predestinarians and those of Pelagius.

The treatise was marred, however, by its decided Semipelagianism; for several years it was bitterly attacked, and it was condemned by the Synod of Orange in 529, after his death. The opposition to Faustus was not fully developed in his lifetime, and he died with a well-merited reputation for sanctity.

To the work on grace he added two books On the Holy Spirit, long and wrongly ascribed to the Roman deacon Paschasius, and a small treatise against the Arians and Macedonians, mentioned by Gennadius, which appears to have perished.

His own flock considered him a saint and erected a basilica in his honour. He is honoured as a patron of bishops and theologians, and his memory is kept on 28 September.

fergus.history:
Saint Fergus, known in the Irish martyrologies as Fergus Cruithneach, or "the Pict," died about the year 730. What is recorded of him comes chiefly from the Breviary of Aberdeen and from the Irish martyrologies. The Breviary relates that he had served as a bishop for many years in Ireland when he came on a mission to Alba, accompanied by a company of chosen priests and other clerics.
