He is remembered as one of the missionary bishops who carried the faith into the Pictish north, honoured as one of the apostles of the Pictish nation.

According to the same account, he settled first near Strageath, in what is now the parish of Upper Strathearn in Upper Perth, and in that district he erected three churches. The churches of Strageath, Blackford, and Dolpatrick are found there to this day dedicated to Saint Patrick, an enduring trace of the mission.

From Strathearn he moved north and evangelized Caithness, where he established the churches of Wick and Halkirk. Thence he crossed to Buchan in Aberdeenshire, the region with which his memory remains especially associated, and founded a church at Lungley, a village that bears his name to this day as Saint Fergus. He established, lastly, a church at Glammis in Forfarshire, so that his foundations reached from Strathearn through the far north to the eastern lowlands. In those lands, which remained in places only partly evangelized, he is said to have planted Christian communities.

His career brought him also beyond Britain. In 721 he went to Rome and, together with Sedulius and twenty other bishops, was present at a synod convened by Pope Gregory II in the basilica of Saint Peter. It stands as the one event of his life that can be dated to a precise year.

His remains were deposited in the church of Glammis, where they were an object of much veneration throughout the Middle Ages. The Abbot of Scone afterwards transferred his head to the church of Scone and encased it in a costly shrine; an entry in the accounts of the treasurer of James IV, dated October 1503, records "An offerand of 13 shillings to Sanct Fergus' heide in Scone," a sign that offerings were still being made at his shrine in the early sixteenth century.

The churches of Wick, Glammis, and Lungley held him as their patron. The Martyrology of Tallaght records his festival on the eighth of September, the day on which his feast is now kept, although in Scotland itself it appears once to have been observed on the eighteenth of November. As a bishop who spent his life in missionary labour he is honoured as a patron of bishops and of missionaries, and his memory endures in the place-names and church dedications of northeastern Scotland.

Several other early saints bore the same name. A bishop of Duleek died in 778, and a bishop of Downpatrick, probably the first bishop of that see, died in 583; the Martyrology of Donegal enumerates ten saints of this name in all.

fiacc.history:
Saint Fiacc, an early Irish bishop and poet, lived from about 415 to about 520. He is remembered as the chief bishop of Leinster and the founder of two churches. His father, MacDara, was prince of the Hy-Bairrche in the country around Carlow. His mother was the sister of Dubhtach, the chief bard and brehon of Erin, the first of Saint Patrick's converts at Tara and the apostle's lifelong friend. Trained under his uncle in the bardic profession, Fiacc soon embraced the Christian faith.

When Patrick came to Leinster, he stayed at Dubhtach's house in Hy-Kinsellagh and, on Dubhtach's recommendation, chose Fiacc to be consecrated bishop for the converts of that province. Fiacc was then a widower, his wife having recently died and left him one son, Fiacre. Patrick gave him an alphabet written with his own hand, and Fiacc acquired with remarkable rapidity the learning required for the episcopal order. Patrick consecrated him, and in later years appointed him chief bishop of the province.

Fiacc founded the church of Domnach-Fiech east of the Barrow, a site identified with Kylebeg. To this church Patrick presented sacred vestments, a bell, the Pauline Epistles, and a pastoral staff. After many years of austere life there, Fiacc was led, according to tradition, by an angelic command to remove to the west of the Barrow, to the place of his resurrection. Legend holds that he was directed to build his oratory where he should meet a hind and his refectory where he should find a boar. Consulting Patrick, he had the site of his new church fixed at Sletty, 'the highland', a mile and a half northwest of Carlow. There he built a large monastery, ruling it as abbot while at the same time governing the surrounding country as bishop.

The life of Fiacc by Jocelyn of Furness records his annual Lenten retreat to the cave of Drum-Coblai and the rigor of his Lenten fast, kept on five barley loaves mixed with ashes. In later years he suffered from a painful disease, and Patrick, commiserating his infirmity, sent him a chariot and a pair of horses to help him in the visitation of the diocese. He lived to a very old age, and sixty of his disciples were gathered to their rest before him. His festival has always been observed on October 12. He was buried in his own church at Sletty, where his son Fiacre, whom Patrick had ordained priest, occupied the same grave; several calendars mention the two as jointly revered in certain churches.

Fiacc is the reputed author of the metrical life of Saint Patrick in Irish, a document of undoubted antiquity and of prime importance as the earliest biography of Patrick that has come down to us. A hymn in honor of Saint Brigid, 'Audite virginis laudes', has sometimes been attributed to him, but on insufficient grounds. Honored for the union of the bard's gift with the bishop's office, he is remembered as a patron of writers and of bishops.

finnian-of-movilla.history:
Finnian of Movilla, born about 495 and died in 589, was an early Irish saint and monastic founder. Though not so celebrated as his namesake Finnian of Clonard, he belonged to the remarkable generation of holy men who labored to plant the Christian faith firmly in Irish soil, founding churches and monasteries that would endure for centuries. His memory is especially associated with Ulster, and he is honored as a patron of missionaries and monks. His festival is observed on 10 September.

He studied first under Saint Colman of Dromore and Saint Mochae of Noendrum, on Mahee Island, and subsequently at Candida Casa (Whithern). From there he proceeded to Rome, returning to Ireland in 540 with an integral copy of Saint Jerome's Vulgate.

About the year 540 he founded a famous school at Movilla, in County Down. His most distinguished pupil there was Saint Columba, whose surreptitious copying of the Psaltery led to a very remarkable sequel. What remains of the copy, together with the casket that contains it, is now in the National Museum, Dublin, where it is known as the Cathach, or Battler; it was wont to be carried by the O'Donnells in battle. The inner case was made by Cathbar O'Donnell in 1084, while the outer is fourteenth-century work. So prized was it that the family of MacGroarty served as hereditary custodians of the Cathach, which passed in 1802 to Sir Neal O'Donnell of County Mayo.

Finnian also wrote a rule for his monks and a penitential code, whose canons were published by Wasserschleben in 1851. Such documents attest the organized monastic life he fostered at Movilla, one of the many religious houses that sprang up across Ireland in the great age of the Irish saints. He is remembered as a faithful missionary who devoted himself to spreading the Gospel and establishing the faith among the people of Ulster.

firmilian.history:
Firmilian, Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, died about 269 after an episcopate of some forty years beginning around 232, and he stood among the most conspicuous figures of his age, his reputation comparable to that of Dionysius of Alexandria and Cyprian of Carthage. St. Gregory of Nyssa relates that Gregory the Wonder-Worker, then still a pagan, having completed his secular studies, fell in with Firmilian, a Cappadocian of noble family, like himself in character and talent. The two young men, agreeing in their desire to know more of God, became disciples of Origen, by whom Gregory, at least, was baptized; Firmilian was more probably brought up as a Christian.

Eusebius records that as bishop Firmilian had such love for Origen that he invited him to his own country for the benefit of the Churches, while Origen was staying in Caesarea of Palestine about 232 to 235, and that Firmilian afterwards went to him again and stayed some time that he might advance in theology. Dionysius of Alexandria counted him among the more eminent bishops, and the phrase "Firmilian and all Cappadocia" implies that Caesarea was already a metropolitan see. He opposed the antipope Novatian: about 252 to 253 he joined Helenus of Tarsus and Theoctistus of Caesarea in Palestine in calling Dionysius to a synod at Antioch, where some were trying to support the Novatian heresy.

Firmilian is remembered chiefly for his part in the baptismal controversy that followed the persecutions of Decius. When Cyprian of Carthage sought the support of the Eastern Churches against Pope Stephen I for his decision to rebaptize heretics who returned to the Church, he sent the deacon Rogatian to Firmilian at the end of the summer of 256 with his letter and the supporting documents. Firmilian's reply, received at Carthage about the middle of November, is the only writing of his that survives, preserved as the seventy-fifth letter in Cyprian's correspondence in a very literal Latin translation full of Graecisms. It upholds the African position that baptism conferred by heretics is invalid, since those outside the Church, not having the Holy Spirit, cannot admit others to the Church or give what they do not possess. Firmilian could oppose tradition to tradition, for in Cappadocia the custom was not new: he had formerly joined in a council at Iconium, with the bishops of Galatia and Cilicia and other provinces, which decided to rebaptize the Montanists. Against Stephen, who demanded nothing beyond the use of the Trinitarian formula, he wrote with great severity, observing that Rome itself had not preserved the apostolic traditions unchanged, since it differed from Jerusalem in the observance of Easter and in other mysteries, and telling Cyprian that Stephen, in thinking that all could be excommunicated by him, had cut off himself alone from the communion of all. Pope Stephen refused communion with Firmilian and the bishops of Cappadocia, Cilicia, and the neighboring lands, and Firmilian accordingly suffered excommunication for refusing Roman discipline.

Beyond this letter, one from Firmilian to Gregory the Wonder-Worker is extant, letters of his appear to have been included in Origen's published correspondence, and a fragment of Origen's reply to him survives. The Armenian historian Moses of Chorene attributed to him many books, among them a history of the persecutions under Decius and Diocletian, but this is regarded as a mistake. Doubts later cast on the genuineness of his letter to Cyprian were answered by its successful defense, and their most learned author afterwards accepted it.

The Church keeps his memory on October 28, and he is honored as a patron of bishops and theologians, esteemed as a bishop of formidable learning and conviction.

flavia-domitilla-wife-of-clemens.history:
St. Flavia Domitilla was a Christian Roman matron of the imperial family who lived towards the close of the first century. She was the third of three persons bearing the same name, the name passing from mother to daughter and granddaughter: the first was the wife of the Emperor Vespasian, and the second was his daughter, sister to the Emperors Titus and Domitian. Their daughter Domitilla, herself a granddaughter of Vespasian and niece of Titus and Domitian, was joined still more closely to the ruling house by her marriage to her kinsman Titus Flavius Clemens, a nephew of Vespasian and first cousin of Titus and Domitian, who held the consulship as the colleague of the emperor.

Two sons were born of this union. While they were still children, Domitian adopted them as his successors and commanded them to assume the names Vespasianus and Domitianus. It is quite probable that the boys were brought up as Christians by their pious mother, and thus the possibility presents itself that two Christian boys at the end of the first century had been designated for the imperial purple, an indication of how far the faith had reached within the emperor's own house. Their later fate is not known, for the Flavian line ended with Domitian.

Clemens had no sooner laid down his office than he was tried on charges of the most trivial character, resting on what Suetonius calls the slightest suspicion, 'ex tenuissima suspicione'. Dio Cassius records that husband and wife alike were accused of atheism and of the practice of Jewish rites and customs. Such accusations, as is clear from the works of the Christian apologists, could have meant nothing else than that both had become Christians. Doubts have been expressed, because of the silence of Christian tradition, as to whether Clemens himself was a Christian; yet the affirmative view is strengthened by Suetonius's further charge that he was a man of the most contemptible inactivity, 'contemptissimae inertiae', a reproach easily explained if he found most of the duties of his office incompatible with Christian faith and practice, so that total abstention from public life became almost an absolute necessity. As a result of the accusations made against them, Clemens was put to death, and Flavia Domitilla was banished to the island of Pandataria in the Tyrrhenian Sea.

Of Domitilla's own Christianity no doubt can remain. De Rossi showed that the cemetery known as the Coemeterium Domitillae stood on ground belonging to the Flavia Domitilla who was banished for her faith, and that it was used as a Christian burial place as early as the first century. In the Christian burial on ground that was her own, within so short a time of her own day, her faith possesses a material witness.

A difficulty surrounds her identity. Eusebius, the spurious acts of Nereus and Achilles, and St. Jerome represent Flavia Domitilla as the niece, not the wife, of Clemens, and say that her place of exile was Pontia, another island in the same sea. These statements gave rise to the opinion that there were two Christian Domitillas, aunt and niece, the latter generally known as Flavia Domitilla the Younger. Lightfoot, however, showed that this opinion, adopted by Tillemont and De Rossi and long maintained by many writers, is derived entirely from Eusebius, who was led into the error by mistakes in transcription, or by ambiguity of expression, in the sources which he used. The two Domitillas are therefore to be regarded as one, and the matron banished for her faith as the wife of Clemens.

Remembered among the early saints of Rome, she is venerated as a noblewoman who chose Christ above the favor of emperors, a convert through whom the Gospel touched the very household of the Caesars. Her feast is kept on May 7, and she is honored as patron of converts and of the oppressed.

francis-xavier.history:
Francis Xavier was born at the Castle of Xavier near Sanguesa, in the Kingdom of Navarre in present-day Spain, on 7 April 1506. In 1525 he went to Paris to study at the College of Sainte-Barbe, where he befriended Pierre Favre and met Ignatius of Loyola, then planning the Society of Jesus. With Favre and four others he joined in the vow of Montmartre on 15 August 1534 as one of the Society's seven founding companions.

He completed his studies and taught for a time in Paris, leaving on 15 November 1536 for Venice, where he served the sick in the hospitals. He was ordained with Ignatius on 24 June 1537, took part in the Roman conferences preparing the definitive foundation of the Society, and was then appointed, at the request of King John III of Portugal, to evangelize the East Indies. He left Rome on 16 March 1540, remained nine months in Lisbon, and embarked for India on 7 April 1541, landing at Goa on 6 May 1542.

In Goa he spent his first five months preaching and ministering to the sick, ringing a little bell to gather children for instruction in the catechism. About October 1542 he set out for the pearl fisheries of the far southern coast, seeking to restore a Christianity that had all but disappeared for lack of priests. He devoted nearly three years to Western India, converting many and reaching even the island of Ceylon, amid persecutions by local rulers and the bad example of Portuguese soldiers.

In the spring of 1545 he went to Malacca, and from there, early in 1546, to the Molucca Islands, preaching for a year and a half at Amboyna, Ternate, Baranura, and other settlements. Some seventeenth-century writers say that he also landed on Mindanao, and for this reason he has been called the first Apostle of the Philippines; the Bull of canonization states only that he preached the Gospel there, and his landing in the Philippines has never been absolutely proved.

Back in Malacca by July 1547, he met a Japanese called Anger (Han-Sir), whose accounts awakened his desire to carry Christianity to Japan. After strengthening the missions of India, establishing a novitiate and house of studies, he sailed for Japan at the end of June 1549 with Father Cosme de Torres and Brother Juan Fernandez. They landed at Kagoshima on 15 August 1549, and the first year was given to learning the language and translating the principal articles of faith, helped by Anger, baptized as Pablo de Santa Fe. Xavier's first converts aroused the hostility of the bonzes, who had him banished from the city. Leaving about August 1550, he preached in southern Japan and reached Meaco near the end of that year; unable to make headway there amid the civil dissensions rending the country, he continued preaching elsewhere during 1551.

China remained his ambition. With friends' help he arranged an embassy to the Sovereign of China and obtained from the Viceroy of India the appointment of ambassador, leaving Goa in April 1552. After overcoming opposition to the expedition at Malacca, he arrived in the autumn at the small island of Sancian (Shangchuan), near the coast of China. While planning to reach the mainland he fell ill, and the movement of the vessel aggravating his condition, he was taken to a rude hut ashore, where he died on 2 December 1552, aged forty-six, within sight of the mainland.

In ten years of missionary labor, from May 1542 to December 1552, he had visited many countries, crossed many seas, and preached the Gospel to many peoples. The Bull of canonization, published in 1623, records great miracles wrought through him, and he has long been honored as the greatest missionary since the Apostles. He was canonized with Ignatius of Loyola in 1622; his feast is kept on 3 December, and he is venerated as a patron of missions and of missionaries. His body remains enshrined at Goa in the church formerly belonging to the Society of Jesus, while his right arm, conveyed to Rome in 1614, is honored at an altar in the church of the Gesu.

gabriel-the-archangel.history:
Gabriel, whose name in Hebrew means “God is my strength” (Latin, Fortitudo Dei), is one of the three archangels named in Scripture, together with Michael and Raphael. His recorded appearances in the Bible are confined to the Book of Daniel and the Gospel of Luke, and throughout them he stands forth as the angel of the Incarnation and of consolation, the bearer of God’s message.

Three passages in Daniel concern him. Gabriel explains to the prophet the vision of the horned ram as portending the defeat of the Persian Empire by Alexander the Great, after whose death the kingdom would be divided among his generals, from one of whom Antiochus Epiphanes would arise. After Daniel had prayed for Israel, “the man Gabriel,” flying swiftly, touched him and communicated the mysterious prophecy of the “seventy weeks” of years that were to elapse before the coming of Christ. A further appearance is described in chapter 10, where the text does not make clear whether the angel is Gabriel, though the description of him in verses 5 and 6 may be applied to him as well.

In the Gospel, each appearance of Gabriel announces a birth: he foretells to Zechariah the birth of John the Baptist, the Precursor, and to Mary the birth of Jesus, the Saviour. Christian tradition has ever honored him as the angel of mercy, while Michael is rather the angel of judgment. In accordance with his name, the biblical passages concerning him speak often of greatness, might, power, and strength, so that he is called the angel of the Power of God.

Beyond what Scripture records, Christian tradition supposes that it was Gabriel who appeared to St. Joseph and to the shepherds, and that he was the angel who “strengthened” Our Lord in the garden. A further identification rests on later popular devotion rather than on the Bible: tradition holds that Gabriel is the angel who will sound the trumpet at the Last Judgment, and devotional art has often depicted him with a lily, the symbol of the Annunciation, or with a trumpet.

Jewish tradition dwells rather on the power suggested by his name and regards Gabriel as the angel of judgment, while Michael is called the angel of mercy. To Gabriel this tradition attributes the destruction of Sodom and of the host of Sennacherib, and it also regards him as the angel who buried Moses and as the one deputed to mark the figure Tau on the foreheads of the elect (Ezekiel 9:4). In later Jewish literature the names of angels were thought to have a peculiar efficacy. Magic bowls inscribed with Hebrew, Aramaic, and Syriac incantations bearing the names of Michael, Raphael, and Gabriel, found at Hillah, the site of Babylon, and now preserved in the British Museum, remain a relic of the Jewish captivity. The same names recur in apocryphal Christian writings, such as the Book of Enoch and the Apocalypse of the Blessed Virgin.

Gabriel is generally termed only an archangel. Raphael’s words, “I am the angel Raphael, one of the seven, who stand before the Lord” (Tobit 12:15), and Gabriel’s own, “I am Gabriel, who stand before God” (Luke 1:19), led some to think that these angels belong to the highest rank; the words are commonly explained, however, as referring to their standing as the highest of God’s messengers, not as placing them among the Seraphim and Cherubim, following the explanation of St. Thomas Aquinas.

As the bearer of the message of the Incarnation, Gabriel is honored as the messenger of God par excellence. He is the patron saint of postal workers and of television, and, more broadly, of messengers, of diplomats, of broadcasters, and of all who work in communications. His feast is kept on September 29, shared with the archangels Michael and Raphael.

gertrude-the-great.history:
Gertrude, later known as the Great, was born in Germany on 6 January 1256. Nothing is known of her family, not even the names of her parents; only that she was not born near Eisleben. At five years of age she entered the alumnate, or school, of the Benedictine monastery of Helfta in Saxony, then governed by the Abbess Gertrude of Hackeborn, a house renowned both for monastic observance and for learning. The child was entrusted to St. Mechtilde, the abbess's sister and mistress of the alumnate, and the intimacy between the two deepened over the years.

Gertrude devoted herself to study with great ardour and became skilled in Latin. In her twenty-sixth year, at the age of twenty-five, she received the first of the visions that continued to the end of her life. Newly conscious of an inner emptiness and of the vanity of all transitory things, she turned from profane letters to Scripture, the Fathers, and theology; her biographer describes her as passing from grammarian to theologian. There was no abrupt conversion from sin to holiness: outwardly her life remained that of a simple Benedictine nun, and her struggle lay in subduing a sensitive and impetuous nature.

Her charity embraced rich and poor, learned and simple alike, and showed itself tenderly toward the souls in purgatory and in a great yearning for the perfection of souls consecrated to God. Her humility was profound, and her frequent raptures so absorbed her faculties that she asked, for the sake of others, that no outward signs attend the favours she received. Tradition credits her also with gifts of prophecy and miracles.

Many of her writings have perished. Those extant, all in Latin, are the Legatus Divinae Pietatis, or Herald of Divine Love, in five books, recording her life and favours; her Exercises; and the Liber Specialis Gratiae of St. Mechtilde, which a comparison of the two works suggests is chiefly, if not entirely, Gertrude's own composition. The distinctive mark of her piety is devotion to the Sacred Heart, the symbol of Christ's immense charity shown in the Incarnation, the Eucharist, and the sacrifice of the Cross, a devotion she practised centuries before it became widespread.

She assisted at the deathbed and mourned Sister Mechtilde, who died in 1281; the Abbess Gertrude of Hackeborn, who died in 1291; and her chosen guide, St. Mechtilde, who died in 1298. Gertrude herself died at Helfta on 17 November, 1301 or 1302, in her forty-fifth or forty-sixth year. When the community moved in 1346 to New Helfta, now the Trud-Kloster within Eisleben, it kept the old home, but the place of her burial is unknown, for there is no record of any translation of her remains.

She was canonized in 1677, when her name was inscribed in the Roman Martyrology and her feast extended to the universal Church, with the note that she was illustrious for the gift of revelations. The feast is now kept on 16 November. At the petition of the King of Spain she was declared patroness of the West Indies; her cult was celebrated with solemnity in Peru, and a town in New Mexico built in her honour bears her name.

Her works won early approval, the superiors of Helfta having appointed Dominican and Franciscan theologians to examine them, and were propagated in the sixteenth century by Lanspergius and by Blosius. They were widely received, especially in Spain, and commended by many holy writers, among them St. Teresa, who took Gertrude as her model and guide, Francisco Suarez, and St. Francis de Sales. Her mysticism belongs to the ancient Benedictine tradition running from St. Gregory to Blosius and rests on the Rule of St. Benedict. She is the only woman saint honoured with the title the Great, and she is invoked as patroness of the souls in purgatory and of mystics.

ghislain.history:
St. Ghislain was a confessor and anchorite who lived in what is now Belgium. Born in the first half of the seventh century and probably of German origin, he died at Saint-Ghislain, then called Ursidongus, on October 9 of about 680. He lived in the province of Hainault in the time of St. Amand, Bishop of Tongres, who died in 679, and of Sts. Waudru, Aldegonde, and Madelberte. Dedicating his life to prayer and penance in the wilderness, he withdrew from the world to seek God in silence and solitude.

With two companions whose names are unknown, he made a clearing in the vicinity of Castrilocus, now Mons in Hainault. He later took up his abode at a place called Ursidongus, where he built an oratory, or chapel, dedicated to Saints Peter and Paul. Aubert, Bishop of Cambrai, summoned the then almost unknown hermit into his presence to sound his intentions, but afterwards accorded him effective protection. During his visit to Cambrai, Ghislain spent some time in the villa of Roisin and received as a gift the estates of Celles and Hornu.

He soon entered into relations with St. Waudru, whom he induced to build a monastery at Castrilocus, his former place of refuge. It is probable that Ghislain influenced the religious vocation of St. Aldegonde, Abbess of Maubeuge, as well as those of St. Madelberte and St. Aldetrude, the first being Waudru's sister and the last two her daughters. When Aldegonde, in her monastery of Maubeuge, had a vision in which, according to her biographer, the death of St. Amand, Bishop of Tongres, was revealed to her, Ghislain visited her in her villa of Mairieu, near Maubeuge, and explained to her that the vision was an announcement of her own approaching death. The intercourse between Ghislain and Aldegonde brought about a perfect understanding between Maubeuge and the monastery founded at Ursidongus under Ghislain's direction, and St. Waudru rewarded her counsellor with a portion of the villa of Frameries and of the oratory of St. Quentin, comprised within the boundaries of the villa of Quaregnon.

Ghislain died at Ursidongus, and the monastery which he had founded took his name. A settlement grew up around his hermitage, as his holiness drew others to the area, and the town that bears his name, Saint-Ghislain, testifies to the lasting memory of his presence among the people of Hainaut. His relics were first disinterred about 929, were transferred to Grandlieu, near Quaregnon, about the end of the tenth century or the beginning of the eleventh, and in 1025 Gerard I, Bishop of Cambrai, removed them to Cateau-Cambresis. They were visited several times in the course of the Middle Ages by the Bishops of Cambrai, and in 1647 they were removed to Saint-Ghislain, of which place the saint is patron.

His feast is celebrated on October 9. He is honored as a patron of hermits, recalling the solitary life he embraced, and his intercession has long been sought to ward off convulsions in children, so that parents through the centuries have implored him for their little ones, and he is likewise invoked as a patron of sick children. In iconography he is frequently represented with a bear, or a bear's cub, beside him, an allusion to the popular legend which relates that a bear, pursued in the chase by King Dagobert, sought refuge with Ghislain and later showed him the place where he should establish a monastery. Moreover, the site of the saint's cella was called Ursidongus, a name meaning bear's den.

pope-gregory-vii.history:
{"history": "Saint Gregory VII, born Hildebrand, was one of the greatest of the Roman pontiffs and one of the most remarkable men of his age. He was born between 1020 and 1025 at Soana, or Ravacum, in Tuscany, of humble origin; a contemporary abbot calls him a man of the people, and his father Bonizo is said by some chroniclers to have been a carpenter, by others a peasant. The name Hildebrand signified to those who loved him a bright flame and to those who hated him a brand of hell, suggesting some Lombard connection of his family. His early years are involved in obscurity. Sent to Rome at a tender age, he was educated in the monastery of Santa Maria on the Aventine Hill, presided over as abbot by his maternal uncle Laurentius; there, amid the austere spirit of Cluny that pervaded the cloister, he first imbibed the lofty principles of Church reform of which he was afterwards to become the most fearless exponent. Early in life he made his religious profession as a Benedictine monk at Rome, though the house of his profession and the year of his entrance remain undetermined.

Entering the service of John Gratian, Archpriest of San Giovanni, Hildebrand became his chaplain on Gratian's elevation to the papacy as Gregory VI, and followed him into exile at Cologne in 1046; on the deposed pontiff's death he withdrew to Cluny, where he remained more than a year. At Besançon, in January 1049, he met Bruno, Bishop of Toul, lately elected Pope Leo IX, and returned with him to Rome. Created a cardinal-subdeacon and appointed administrator of the Patrimony of St. Peter's, he gave early proof of the extraordinary administrative faculty that marked his later government of the Church: the property of the Holy See, diverted into the hands of the Roman nobility and the Normans, was largely recovered and its depleted revenues speedily augmented. Made propositus, not abbot, of the abbey of St. Paul outside the Walls, he restored its ancient rule and discipline by rigorous reform, and the house retained his lifelong attachment. In 1054 he went to France as papal legate to examine the cause of Berengarius.

While still in Tours he learned of the death of Leo IX; the Roman clergy and people were eager to elect Hildebrand himself, but he resisted and set out for Germany to implore a nomination from the emperor. After some eleven months of negotiation his candidate, Gebhard, Bishop of Eichstadt, was consecrated at Rome in 1055 as Victor II. Upon the death of Stephen X, when the Tusculan faction set up Benedict X, Hildebrand defeated their designs and secured the election of Nicholas II. The two chief acts of that pontificate, the celebrated decree vesting the choice of the pope in the college of cardinals and the alliance with the Normans confirmed by the Treaty of Melfi in 1059, were in large measure his achievement, and in the same year he was raised to the office of archdeacon. When Nicholas died in 1061, the issues raised by the decree of election brought conflict; after a schism enduring some years the imperial antipope Cadalous was discomfited and Hildebrand's candidate, Anselm of Baggio, was enthroned as Alexander II.

Raised to the papacy in 1073, Gregory VII made the reform of the Church the work of his pontificate, striving to free the clergy from simony, to enforce clerical celibacy, and to vindicate the spiritual authority of the See of Peter against the claims of emperors. His contest with the Emperor Henry IV over the investiture of bishops became the defining struggle of his age. Driven from Rome in his final years, he died in exile at Salerno on 25 May 1085; his last words are traditionally given as the verse of the Psalm, I have loved righteousness and hated iniquity. His feast is kept on May 25."}

gregory-the-illuminator.history:
Gregory the Illuminator (Lusavorich), the apostle, national saint, and patron of Armenia, is said to have been born about 257 and to have died about 337. He was not the first to bring Christianity to his country: the Armenians maintain that the faith was first preached there by the Apostles Bartholomew and Thaddaeus, and it is certain that Christians, even bishops, existed in Armenia before him; Dionysius of Alexandria wrote the Armenian Christians a letter on penitence. That earliest Church was destroyed after Ardashir I, founder of the Sassanid dynasty, overran Armenia and imposed the Mazdean religion on the subject kingdom.

Gregory's origins are told chiefly in a famous life attributed to Agathangelos, which embellishes the sober narrative with stories that need not be taken very seriously. According to this tradition, Gregory was the son of Anak, the Parthian who murdered King Khosrov I of Armenia at Persian instigation; Anak perished with nearly all his family, but two sons survived, and Gregory was carried by a Christian nurse to Caesarea in Cappadocia and baptized. Historically, he belonged to an illustrious Armenian family, was brought up as a Christian at Caesarea, was married, and had two sons, Aristakes and Bardanes.

Khosrov's son Trdat (Tiridates) escaped, was trained in the Roman army, and returned to drive out the Persians and restore the kingdom; in this restoration Gregory played an important part. The king at first defended the old Armenian religion and persecuted Gregory. Tradition relates that Gregory refused to take part in a great sacrifice, declared himself a Christian, and, when the king discovered he was his father's murderer's son, was tortured and thrown into a pit of dead bodies and serpents, where, tradition holds, he spent fifteen years fed by a widow's daily bread. The same tradition tells how the virgin Rhipsime won martyrdom resisting the king, and how Trdat, punished with possession and changed into a boar, could be saved only through Gregory's prayers; drawn from the pit, Gregory exorcized the evil spirit, restored the king, and began to preach.

Gregory had gone back to Caesarea to be ordained, and Leontius of Caesarea made him bishop of the Armenians; until the Monophysite schism the Armenian Church depended on Caesarea, its primates, the later Catholicoi, being ordained there. Trdat made Christianity the national faith; the nobility followed his example, and the people were baptized in thousands, under Diocletian (284-305), which supports Armenia's claim to be the first Christian state. Temples became churches, and the old religion was so effaced that little survives beyond the names of some gods; the great temple at Ashtishat, dedicated to Vahagn, Anahit, and Astlik, became the church called mother of all Armenian churches. Gregory set up bishops throughout the land, fixed his residence at Ashtishat in Taron, and preached and celebrated the liturgy in the national language, giving the Armenian Church the markedly national character it still has.

Toward the end of his life Gregory retired and was succeeded as Catholicos by his son Aristakes, present at the First General Council in 325. Gregory died about 337 and was buried at Thortan, where a monastery was built near his grave. His relics were taken to Constantinople, apparently brought back to Armenia, and part are said to have been carried to Naples during the Iconoclast troubles.

Venerated in the Armenian Apostolic Church and in the Catholic and Orthodox communions, the Armenian calendar keeps several commemorations of him, among them his deliverance from the pit. His feast is observed on 20 February; the Byzantine Church honors him on 30 September, and in 1837 Pope Gregory XVI admitted him to the Roman Calendar, with 1 October among feasts proper to particular places. He is patron of Armenia and of the Italian town of Nardo, where relics of his cult are preserved, and is invoked especially as patron of converts and missionaries.

helena.history:
Helena, the mother of Constantine the Great, was born about the middle of the third century, possibly at Drepanum, a town on the Nicomedian Gulf later renamed Helenopolis, and died about 330. Her parentage was humble; St. Ambrose calls her a stabularia, an inn-keeper. She nevertheless became the lawful wife of the Roman general Constantius Chlorus, and her only son Constantine was born at Naissus in Upper Moesia in 274. Medieval English chroniclers identified her as the daughter of a British prince, an account entirely without historical foundation.

In 292 Constantius, having become co-regent of the West, set Helena aside on political grounds in order to marry Theodora, the stepdaughter of the emperor Maximianus Herculius. Her son never lost his fidelity to her. On the death of Constantius he summoned his mother to the imperial court, conferred on her the title of Augusta, ordered that all honor be paid her as the mother of the sovereign, and had coins struck bearing her effigy. Under his influence she embraced Christianity after his victory over Maxentius; Eusebius testifies that she became such a devout servant of God that one might believe her a disciple of the Redeemer from childhood.

From her conversion Helena led an earnestly Christian life, and by her influence and liberality she furthered the spread of the faith. Tradition links her name with the building of churches in the western cities where the imperial court resided, notably Rome and Trier, and there is no good reason to reject it. Her charity, as Eusebius records it, reached not only individuals but entire communities; the poor and destitute were the special objects of her care, and she visited churches everywhere, enriching them with her donations.

After Constantine's victory over Licinius made him sole master of the Roman Empire, and therefore after 324, Helena, despite her advanced age, undertook a journey to Palestine. There she resolved to bring to God the homage and tribute of her devotion; she lavished bounties on the land and explored it with remarkable discernment. Having shown due veneration to the footsteps of the Saviour, she had two churches erected, one at Bethlehem near the Grotto of the Nativity, the other on the Mount of the Ascension near Jerusalem, and she adorned the sacred grotto with rich ornaments. Her sojourn in Jerusalem became the starting point of the story of the finding of the Holy Cross, first recorded by Rufinus; tradition holds that she discovered the True Cross there.

In Rome her memory is chiefly identified with the basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, raised where the Palatium Sessorianum formerly stood, near the Thermae Helenianae, baths that derived their name from the empress; two inscriptions in her honor were found on the site. The Sessorium, near the Lateran, probably served as her residence in the city, and it is quite possible that Constantine erected the basilica there at her suggestion and in honor of the true Cross.

Helena was still living in 326, when Constantine ordered the execution of his son Crispus. When the emperor later improved her native Drepanum and decreed that it be called Helenopolis, she probably returned from Palestine to her son, who was then residing in the East. Constantine was at her side when she died at about the age of eighty, around the year 330; the last coins struck with her name bear that date. Her body was laid to rest in the imperial vault of the church of the Apostles at Constantinople, and is presumed to have been transferred in 849 to the Abbey of Hautvillers, in the French archdiocese of Reims, as recorded by the monk Altmann.

She was revered as a saint from an early period, long before formal processes of canonization, and her veneration had spread, early in the ninth century, even to Western countries. Her feast falls on 18 August. She is honored as a patron of divorced people and of converts.

herbert-of-derwentwater.history:
Herbert, also recorded under the form Hereberht, was a seventh-century Anglo-Saxon priest and anchorite whose date of birth is unknown and who died on 20 March of the year 687. An anchorite was one who withdrew from ordinary society to pursue a life of prayer in a fixed, solitary dwelling. Herbert made his home for many years on the small island in the Lake of Derwentwater, in the lake country of Cumbria, which still bears the name of St. Herbert's Isle. The place is one of the loveliest and loneliest corners of England, and it was there that he passed his days in solitude and prayer.

He was for long the friend and disciple of St. Cuthbert of Lindisfarne. Little is known about him beyond what this friendship entailed: it was his custom every year to visit Cuthbert to receive his direction in spiritual matters. The earliest account of their last meeting was recorded by Bede, the historian of the early English Church.

In the year 686, hearing that his friend was visiting Carlisle for the purpose of giving the veil to Queen Eormenburg, Herbert went to see him there instead of at Lindisfarne as was usual. After they had spoken together, Cuthbert said: "Brother Herbert, tell to me now all that you have need to ask or speak, for never shall we see one another again in this world, for I know that the time of my decease is at hand." Herbert fell weeping at his feet and begged that Cuthbert would obtain for him the grace that they might both be admitted to praise God in heaven at the same time. And Cuthbert prayed and then made answer: "Rise, my brother, weep not, but rejoice that the mercy of God has granted our desire."

And so it came to pass. Herbert, returning to his hermitage, fell ill of a long sickness and, purified of his imperfections, passed to God on the very day on which St. Cuthbert died on Holy Island. Tradition holds that the two friends prayed to die together, and that their prayer was granted. This friendship of saints has moved believers and poets alike, and it was given lasting literary form in the verse of William Wordsworth.

It is said that the remains of his chapel and cell may still be traced at the northern end of the island on which he lived. Devotion to him continued for centuries: in 1374 Thomas Appleby, Bishop of Carlisle, granted an indulgence of forty days to all who, in honor of St. Herbert, visited the island in Derwentwater and were present at the Mass of St. Cuthbert to be sung there annually by the Vicar of Crosthwaite.

Almost nothing else is known of him, but what the sources preserve is characteristic: the annual journey for spiritual direction, the tears and petition laid at another man's feet, and the quiet readiness to await death in his cell. He remains a model for those who seek God in silence and in the companionship of kindred souls, and he is honored as a patron of hermits and contemplatives.

hereswith.history:
Saint Hereswith, also recorded under the forms Haeresvid, Hereswitha, or Hereswyde, was a seventh-century Northumbrian noblewoman, daughter of Hereric and Beorhtswith and sister of Saint Hilda, the great foundress of Whitby. Bede preserves her memory in his Ecclesiastical History, attesting her noble birth, her sisterhood with Hilda, and her religious vocation, and through this testimony she stands among that first generation of Anglo-Saxon women whose holiness helped plant the faith deep in the soil of a newly Christian people.

She was given in marriage to Aethelhere, King of East Anglia, a union that bound her to the royal dynasty of that kingdom, and to him she bore two sons, Aldwulf and Alfwold. The later Liber Eliensis states that she was instead the wife of King Anna, the elder brother of Aethelhere, but this is certainly a mistake, and the older testimony of her marriage to Aethelhere stands.

Her husband was killed in the battle of Winwaed in 655, after which Hereswith left her homeland and crossed the sea to Gaul. She became a nun at the Abbey of Chelles, then in the Diocese of Paris, and remained there in religious life until the end of her days, her choice of the cloister marking the passage of her life from the royal courts of early England to the religious houses of Gaul.

Her feast day is variously assigned rather than firmly established. It is given as 3 September by Stanton, as 20 September by the second edition of the English Martyrology, and as 23 September by the first edition and by Ferrari, while Bucelinus assigns it to 1 December, the date on which the Bollandists proposed to discuss her cultus. In her remembrance she is honored as a patroness of nuns and contemplatives, a witness to the holiness sought within monastic life by the noble women of the early Anglo-Saxon church.

hermenegild.history:
Saint Hermenegild, the eldest son of Leovigild, King of the Visigoths, died on 13 April 585; the date of his birth is unknown. Leovigild, who reigned from 569 to 586, was an adherent of Arianism and was fiercely defensive of it, while his first wife, the Catholic princess Theodosia, belonged to the Catholic confession. By her he had two sons, Hermenegild and Reccared, and the royal house into which Hermenegild was born thus joined political power to a divided faith.

In 576 Hermenegild married Ingundis, a Frankish Catholic princess, daughter of Sigebert and Brunhilde. Raised in his father's Arian confession, he was led by his own inclination, and influenced both by his devout wife and by the teaching of Saint Leander of Seville, to enter the Catholic fold around 579. Leovigild's second wife, Goswintha, a fanatical Arian, hated her daughter-in-law and sought by ill-treatment to force the young woman to abandon the Catholic faith. With his father's sanction, Hermenegild withdrew to Andalusia, taking his wife with him.

When Leovigild learned of his son's conversion, he summoned him back to Toledo, a command which Hermenegild did not obey. The king regarded his son's change of faith both as a religious betrayal and as a political threat. His stepmother's fanatical Arianism, together with his father's severe treatment of Catholics in Spain, stirred the young prince to take up arms in protection of his oppressed co-religionists and in defence of his own rights. His rising, undertaken in defence of persecuted Catholics, placed him at the same time in revolt against his father, and in the struggle he sought the aid of the Byzantines.

Leovigild took the field against his son in 582. The Byzantine alliance proved of no avail, for the king prevailed upon the Byzantines to betray Hermenegild for a sum of 30,000 gold solidi, then besieged him in Seville in 583 and captured the city after a siege of nearly two years. Hermenegild sought refuge in a church at Cordova, whence his father enticed him by false promises. Once in camp, he was stripped of his royal raiment and banished to Valencia in 584. He was thereafter held in prison, which tradition has placed at Tarragona, though the precise course of his subsequent fate is not fully recorded. Ingundis fled with her son to Africa, where she died; the boy was then given, by order of the Emperor Mauritius, into the hands of his grandmother Brunhilde.

The chief account of Hermenegild's last days comes from Pope Gregory the Great in the Dialogues. On Easter Eve of 585, Leovigild sent an Arian bishop to him in his prison, with a promise that he would forgive him all, provided Hermenegild consented to receive Holy Communion from the hands of this bishop. To accept such communion would have amounted to an abjuration of his Catholic belief, and the young prince firmly refused. In consequence, he was put to death on Easter Day of that same year, struck down by an axe at his father's command.

Gregory the Great presented Hermenegild as a Catholic martyr, one who chose death rather than receive the sacraments from schismatics. On this account the young prince came to be venerated as a martyr, and his cult spread quickly through Visigothic Spain. Acting at the suggestion of King Philip II, Pope Sixtus V extended in 1585 the celebration of his feast, kept on 13 April, throughout the whole of Spain. The memory of a prince who suffered death rather than abandon the faith has made him a patron of converts and of those who endure persecution for it.

hilarion.history:
Hilarion was born of pagan parents at Tabatha, south of Gaza in Palestine, around 291. The chief source for his life is the biography written by St. Jerome, which draws on a letter of St. Epiphanius, Archbishop of Salamis, who had known Hilarion personally in his later years, though the letter itself is not extant. The church historian Sozomen also preserves traditions handed down by the saint's disciples, among them that Sozomen's grandfather and another relative were converted to Christianity by Hilarion. Jerome states that Hilarion was sixty-five years old at the death of Anthony in 356, from which his birth date is reckoned.

As a boy he was sent to Alexandria to be educated, and there he became a Christian. At the age of fifteen, attracted by the renown of Anthony, the celebrated Father of Anchorites, he retired to the desert and spent two months in personal intercourse with him. Resolving to devote himself to the ascetic life of a hermit, he returned home, divided his fortune among the poor, and withdrew to a little hut in the desert of Majuma near Gaza, where he led a life modeled on that of Anthony.

His manner of life was rigorously ascetic. He wore a hair shirt, an upper garment of skins, and a short shepherd's cloak; he fasted strictly, taking his frugal meal only after sunset, and supported himself by weaving baskets, devoting the greater part of his time to prayer and religious exercises. Jerome records that miraculous cures and exorcisms spread his fame through the surrounding country, and by 329 numerous disciples had gathered around him. Many heathens were converted, and people came seeking his help and counsel in such numbers that he could scarcely find time for his own religious duties. From this solitary beginning he came to be honored as the founder of anchoritic life in Palestine, and his example shaped the monastic tradition of the Holy Land.

The crowds that sought him out at length induced him to bid farewell to his disciples, and about the year 360 he returned to Egypt, visiting the places where Anthony had lived and the spot where he had died. On the journey he met Dracontius and Philor, two bishops banished by the Emperor Constantius. Hilarion then dwelt at Bruchium near Alexandria, but on hearing that Julian the Apostate had ordered his arrest, he retired to an oasis in the Libyan desert. Later he journeyed to Sicily and for a long time lived as a hermit near the promontory of Pachinum. His disciple Hesychius, who had long sought him, discovered him there, and Hilarion soon found himself again surrounded by disciples desirous of following his example.

Leaving Sicily, he went to Epidaurus in Dalmatia, where, on the occasion of a great earthquake in 366, he rendered valuable assistance to the inhabitants. Finally he passed to Cyprus and spent his last years in a lonely cave in the interior of the island; it was there that he became acquainted with St. Epiphanius, Archbishop of Salamis. He died about 371 at the age of eighty, bequeathing to his faithful disciple Hesychius his only possession, his poor and scanty clothing. His body was buried near the town of Paphos, but Hesychius secretly removed it and carried it to Majuma, where the saint had lived so long.

Hilarion was greatly honored as the founder of anchoritic life in Palestine. Venerated by the Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox, and Roman Catholic Churches, he is remembered as a pioneer of monastic life beyond Egypt, a model of the hermit's single-hearted devotion to God, and a patron of hermits and monks. Early attempts to relegate him to the realm of imagination did not prevail; the chief features of his life are held to rest on solid historical testimony. His feast is kept on 21 October.

hugh-of-lincoln.history:
Hugh of Lincoln, also known as Hugh of Avalon, was born about 1135 at the castle of Avalon near Pontcharra in Burgundy. After his wife's death, his father, William, Lord of Avalon, retired to the Augustinian monastery of Villard-Benoît near Grenoble, taking Hugh with him. Hugh became a religious and was ordained deacon at nineteen, and about 1159 he was sent as prior to the nearby cell of St-Maximin. Longing for the contemplative life, he sought entry to the Grande Chartreuse; first discouraged and bound by a hasty promise to give up the design, he later judged that promise not binding and entered as a novice. Ordained priest at about thirty, he was entrusted with the important office of procurator, which he retained until he was called to England.

Witham in Somerset, the first Carthusian house in England, had been founded by Henry II in compensation for failing to undertake the crusade imposed as penance for the murder of St. Thomas of Canterbury; its first two priors had succumbed to the hardships of the new foundation, where the monks lacked even a roof, and Hugh was appointed prior at the king's special request. He planned the charterhouse, an exact copy of the Grande Chartreuse, secured compensation for any royal tenants evicted, and carried the work through despite the king's parsimony. The king placed great confidence in him, yet Hugh was fearless in reproving him for keeping sees vacant to appropriate their revenues and for interfering in ecclesiastical elections.

When the king's council resolved to fill the see of Lincoln, vacant for about sixteen years, the canons chose Hugh. He refused the first election because it was not free; chosen unanimously in a second, canonically held election, he still declined until the prior of the Grande Chartreuse consented. He was consecrated Bishop of Lincoln by Archbishop Baldwin of Canterbury in Westminster Abbey on 21 September 1186 and enthroned at Lincoln eight days later. He attacked the iniquitous forest laws and excommunicated the king's chief forester, and refused to install a courtier Henry had recommended to a prebend; when the enraged king summoned him to Woodstock, his ready wit won royal approval for both actions. He tended lepers with his own hands, held regular canonical visitations, and chose worthy men for the care of souls.

In 1188 he went on an embassy to the French king, was in France when Henry II died, and was present at the coronation of Richard I. A mighty builder, he rebuilt Lincoln cathedral, ruined by the earthquake of 1185, raising the four bays of the choir in the Early English pointed style, and began the great hall of the bishop's palace. He died at London on 16 November 1200, and King John assisted in carrying his coffin to its resting-place in the north-east transept of Lincoln cathedral.

Canonized by Pope Honorius III in 1220, Hugh was translated in 1280 to a conspicuous place in the great south transept, where a golden shrine made Lincoln the most celebrated centre of pilgrimage in northern England; the shrine was stripped by Henry VIII at the Reformation, and what became of his relics is unknown. Tradition holds that a white swan at Stowe formed a deep and lasting friendship with the saint, guarding him while he slept, and the swan became his emblem. In the Carthusian Order he is second only to St. Bruno, and the great modern Charterhouse at Parkminster in Sussex is dedicated to him. Remembered as one of the best-loved saints of medieval England, he is invoked as a patron of sick children and of cobblers.

ignatios-of-constantinople.history:
St. Ignatios of Constantinople was born about 799, the son of Emperor Michael I and Procopia, and bore the name Nicetas until his fourteenth year. When Leo the Armenian deposed Michael I in 813, the boy was made a eunuch and confined to a monastery so that he could not reclaim his father's throne. There he freely embraced the religious life, became in time an abbot, and was ordained by Basil, Bishop of Paros, on the Hellespont.

On the death of Theophilus in 841, Theodora governed as regent for her son Michael III. In 847, with the empress's goodwill, Ignatius succeeded Methodius as Patriarch of Constantinople. He stood firmly against iconoclasm and in defense of the veneration of sacred images. His tenure soon collided with the court: he indignantly refused to help the young emperor and his uncle Bardas force Theodora into a convent, and he rebuked Bardas for repudiating his wife and living in incestuous union with his daughter-in-law. When a minor revolt broke out, Bardas laid the blame on the patriarch, who was banished to the island of Terebinthus; when emissaries failed to obtain his resignation, they heaped indignities upon him. A synod under the direction of Gregory of Syracuse, an excommunicated bishop, declared him deposed, and Photius, a layman of brilliant parts who served the emperor as first secretary of state, passed through every ecclesiastical order in six days to occupy the see. A further synod in 859 reaffirmed the deposition, though some bishops denounced Photius as a usurper.

Photius appealed to Pope Nicholas I, representing that Ignatius, worn out with age and disease, had retired voluntarily. Nicholas sent legates instructed to investigate and to treat Photius as a layman, but the legates, yielding to intimidation, decided for Photius at a synod in 861. There Ignatius, denied leave to speak, refused to acknowledge the synod's authority and appealed to the pope; he was condemned and degraded, and an order for his death was issued, from which he escaped by flight. Informed through the archimandrite Theognostus of the unlawful proceedings, Nicholas refused to confirm the acts, recognized Ignatius as the legitimate patriarch, and forbade the eastern patriarchs to acknowledge the usurper, who answered with a declaration of excommunication against the pope.

In 867 Michael III was assassinated by Basil the Macedonian, who among his first official acts deposed Photius and recalled Ignatius to the patriarchate on 23 November 867, after nine years of exile and persecution. Pope Adrian II confirmed both measures and, at Ignatius' recommendation, convoked the Eighth Ecumenical Council on 5 October 869, whose participants were obliged to approve the papal action in the dispute.

Ignatius lived a decade after his restoration in the peaceful exercise of his duties. Tension with Rome nonetheless arose over Bulgaria: Boris I had embraced Christianity in 864, and Ignatius promoted Constantinople's jurisdiction over the Bulgarian Church; in the controversy that followed, the Latin hierarchy was expelled from that land, deepening the estrangement between the eastern and western sees.

He died on 23 October 877 and was buried in St. Sophia, his remains later translated to the church of St. Michael near the Bosphorus. The Roman Martyrology commemorates him on that date, recording how he reproved Bardas the Caesar, endured many injuries and exile, and was restored by Pope Nicholas before going to his rest in peace. Honored for his steadfastness through deposition and exile, he is invoked as a patron of church unity and church reform.

pope-innocent-i.history:
Very little is known of Innocent I before his elevation to the See of Rome. According to the Liber Pontificalis he was a native of Albano, the son of a man named Innocentius, and he grew up among the Roman clergy in the service of the Roman Church. After the death of Pope Anastasius in December 401 he was unanimously chosen Bishop of Rome. From the beginning of his pontificate he acted as head of the whole Church, both East and West, and was recognized as a general arbitrator in ecclesiastical disputes.

In Rome he showed zeal for the purity of the faith and for church discipline, taking several churches from the Novatians and banishing the Photinian Marcus. An edict of the Emperor Honorius issued from Rome on 22 February 407 against the Manicheans, Montanists, and Priscillianists was very probably granted with his concurrence. Through the munificence of Vestina, a wealthy Roman matron, he built and richly endowed a church dedicated to Saints Gervasius and Protasius, the Titulus Vestinae that still stands as San Vitale.

His government of the Church was exercised largely by correspondence. In a letter to Archbishop Anysius of Thessalonica announcing his election, he confirmed the privileges earlier popes had granted that see, and in 412 he entrusted the administration of Eastern Illyria to the Archbishop of Thessalonica as vicar of the Holy See. On 15 February 404 he sent an important decretal to Bishop Victricius of Rouen on the consecration of bishops, clerical ordination and celibacy, the reception of converted Novatians and Donatists, and monks and nuns, presenting the discipline of the Roman Church as the norm for other bishops. Similar letters went to the Spanish bishops, to Exuperius of Toulouse, to Decentius of Gubbio, and to two British bishops, Maximus and Severus. At the request of envoys from the Synod of Carthage of 404 he also obtained from Honorius an edict against the Montanists, by which many of their adherents were reconciled with the Church.

The Christian East also claimed his energy. St. John Chrysostom, Bishop of Constantinople, persecuted by the Empress Eudoxia and the Patriarch Theophilus of Alexandria, appealed to Innocent, who refused to recognize the deposition pronounced by the illegal Synod of the Oak. He summoned Theophilus to a new synod at Rome, consoled the exiled patriarch, and announced his intention of convoking a general synod to decide the case. He informed Honorius, who wrote to his brother Arcadius, the Eastern Emperor, on John's behalf, but the messengers were ill received, for Arcadius favored Theophilus, and the appeal for the patriarch's restoration proved unavailing.

In his pontificate the Goths under Alaric besieged Rome. At the first siege in 408, Alaric declared that he would withdraw only if the Romans arranged a peace favorable to him, and an embassy sent to Honorius at Ravenna to seek peace included Innocent himself. His efforts failed, the siege was renewed, and the pope was absent from the city when it was taken and sacked in 410, a catastrophe he labored to relieve.

In the Pelagian controversy he acted with the bishops of Africa. After the Synod of Diospolis in December 415, deceived by Pelagius as to his real teaching, had acquitted him, the bishops assembled at Carthage in 416 confirmed the earlier condemnation of Celestius, as did the bishops of Numidia at Mileve. Both synods asked Innocent to confirm their acts, and five African bishops, among them St. Augustine, wrote to him personally. He praised them for appealing to the Chair of Peter, rejected the teaching of Pelagius, confirmed their judgments, and rejected those of Diospolis. A confession of faith that Pelagius sent him arrived only after his death.

Innocent died on 12 March 417 and was buried in a basilica above the catacomb of Pontianus, where he was venerated as a saint. He is honored in East and West as an energetic and gifted ruler of the Church, devoted to her discipline and unity.

jacob-baradaeus.history:
Jacob Baradaeus was born at Tella toward the end of the fifth or the beginning of the sixth century. His father, Theophilus bar Manu, was a priest of Tella, and his proper name was accordingly Jacob bar Theophilus, that is, Jacob, son of Theophilus; he is sometimes also called Jacob bar Addai. The surname by which he is known was drawn from his clothing: Burde'ana in Syriac, afterward corrupted into Baradaeus, it derives from the coarse horse-cloth called barda'than which he usually wore. He died in 578.

After receiving a good education he embraced the monastic state in the monastery of Pesilta and became a disciple of Severus, the head of the Monophysites, the non-Chalcedonian party of the Christian East. The work of his life would lie within this communion.

In the first half of the sixth century the Monophysite cause stood upon the verge of disappearing. It had been weakened by internal dissensions and by the opposition of the Emperor Justinian, and the death of Severus in 538 appeared to deprive it of its leader.

Probably through the influence of the Empress Theodora, Jacob was made Bishop of Edessa in 543, and from that time forward he devoted all his energies to the defense of Monophysitism. Through untiring activity he breathed new life into what had seemed a mere expiring faction. Traversing the eastern Roman provinces in disguise and at the cost of great hardship, he went about ordaining priests and deacons and strengthening his coreligionists, who suffered for their confession of faith.

His preeminence is documented in a profession of faith addressed to him by the abbots of the province of Arabia, bearing 137 signatures, which shows that he was the undisputed leader in Monophysite circles. From this prominence the Monophysites were, and still are, known as Jacobites after his name; the Syriac Orthodox Church likewise came to bear the name of Jacobite from him.

He has left very little in writing: a liturgy and a few letters. The chief source for his life is the Ecclesiastical History of John of Ephesus.

He died in 578, bringing to a close an episcopate of some thirty-five years. By his labors a communion that had seemed near extinction received shepherds, order, and continuity, and a flock pressed by persecution was preserved and handed on as a living church. He is venerated as a saint in the Oriental Orthodox Churches; his feast is kept on July 31, and he is honored as a patron of those who suffer persecution and of missionaries.

jane-frances-de-chantal.history:
Jane Frances Frémyot was born at Dijon, France, on 28 January 1572, daughter of the president of the Parliament of Burgundy, a leader of the royalist party during the League. In 1592 she married Baron de Chantal and went to live in the feudal castle of Bourbilly, where she restored order to a household on the brink of ruin and brought back its prosperity. During her husband's absences at court or with the army, she answered those who reproached her sober manner of dressing: "The eyes which I must please are a hundred miles from here."

The baron was accidentally killed by a harquebus while out shooting in 1601. Left a widow at twenty-eight with four children, she forgave the man who shot him and even became godmother to his child, took a vow of chastity, and prayed continually for a guide; a vision showed her the spiritual director God held in reserve. Until her children's property could be secured she lived at Monthelon, in the home of a father-in-law ruled by an arrogant servant, and bore that servitude patiently for seven years until her virtue prevailed.

During Lent of 1604 she visited her father at Dijon, where St. Francis de Sales was preaching at the Sainte Chapelle. She recognized in him the director of the vision and placed herself under his guidance, beginning an admirable correspondence, the greater part of which she destroyed after his death. Having secured her children's future and provided for the education of her fourteen-year-old son Celse-Bénigne, she set out for Annecy with her two remaining daughters, the elder lately married to the Baron of Thorens, a brother of St. Francis de Sales. When Celse-Bénigne barred her way by lying across the threshold, a holy priest asked whether the tears of a child could shake her resolution. "Oh! no", she replied, "but after all I am a mother!"—and she stepped over him.

The Congregation of the Visitation was canonically established at Annecy on Trinity Sunday, 6 June 1610. It was founded to receive young girls and even widows who had not the desire or strength for the austere ascetical practices then in force in religious orders, and it embodied St. Francis de Sales's cherished method of perfection: the continual union of one's will with the Divine will. The undertaking prospered—the order numbered thirteen houses at his death in 1622, eighty-six at hers, and one hundred sixty-four at her canonization.

The remainder of her life was spent under the protection of the cloister. Where gentle kindness predominated in St. Francis de Sales, firmness and vigour prevailed in St. Jane Frances, who did not like to see her daughters yield to human weakness. Her trials were continuous; Celse-Bénigne, an incorrigible duellist, was granted a Christian death on the battlefield during the campaign against the Isle of Ré in 1627, and from family troubles there were added interior crosses that, particularly during the last nine years of her life, kept her in agony of soul from which she was not freed until three months before her death.

Her reputation for sanctity was widespread. Queens, princes, and princesses came to her reception room, and people gave her ovations wherever she went to establish foundations; "these people", she would say, "do not know me; they are mistaken." She died at the Visitation convent of Moulins on 13 December 1641, and her body is venerated with that of St. Francis de Sales at Annecy. Beatified in 1751 and canonized in 1767, she is honored as a patron of widows and of forgiveness; her feast is kept on 12 August.

Her extant writings include instructions on the religious life, many letters, a "Deposition for the Process of Beatification of St. Francis de Sales," and the practical code of religious life "Réponses sur les Règles, Constitutions et Coutumes."

john-berchmans.history:
John Berchmans was born at Diest in Brabant on 13 March 1599. His parents watched with great care over the formation of his character; he was naturally kind, gentle, and affectionate, of a bright, joyful disposition, though by temperament impetuous and fickle. At the age of seven his parish priest, M. Emmerick, remarked that the Lord would work wonders in the soul of the child. Even then the boy rose early to serve two or three Masses, attended sermons and religious instructions with deep recollection, and made pilgrimages to the sanctuary of Montaigu near Diest, reciting the rosary as he went.

When he was nine, his mother was stricken with a long and serious illness, and John passed several hours each day at her bedside, consoling her with affectionate yet serious words. Later, while living with other boys at his parish priest's house, he undertook more than his share of the domestic work and chose the harder tasks by preference. Loved by his playmates, he repaid their affection with kindness, yet discreetly used his influence to correct their negligences and restrain frivolous conversation. Eager to learn and endowed with a bright intellect and a retentive memory, he devoted to study whatever time he could take from his recreation.

As soon as he entered the Jesuit college at Mechlin he was enrolled in the Society of the Blessed Virgin, resolved to recite her Office daily, and each month asked the sodality's director to prescribe special acts of devotion to Mary. On Friday nights he went out barefooted to make the Stations of the Cross in the town. Toward the end of his rhetoric course he felt a distinct call to the Society of Jesus; his family was decidedly opposed, but on 24 September 1616 he was received into the novitiate at Mechlin. After two years he made his simple vows and was sent to Antwerp to begin the study of philosophy; a few weeks later he set out for Rome, walking three hundred leagues with a wallet on his back, and entered the Roman College, where he studied for two years and passed to the third-year class in philosophy in 1621.

Early in August 1621 the prefect of studies selected him to take part in a philosophical disputation at the Greek College, then in the charge of the Dominicans. He opened the discussion with great perspicuity and erudition, but on returning to his own college was seized with a violent fever, of which he died on 13 August, at the age of twenty-two years and five months.

Berchmans offered the type of the saint who performs ordinary actions with extraordinary perfection. In purity, obedience, and charity he resembled many religious, but he surpassed them all by his intense love for the rules of his order. The Constitutions of the Society of Jesus, as Pope Julius III and his successors declared, lead those who observe them exactly to the highest degree of sanctity, and the attainment of that ideal was what he proposed to himself. "If I do not become a saint when I am young," he used to say, "I shall never become one." He would have preferred death to the violation of the least rule; his penance, he said, was to live the common life, and he resolved to pay the greatest attention to the least inspiration of God. His fidelity in all his duties until his last day was attested by his spiritual directors, Fathers Bauters, Cepari, Ceccoti, Massucci, and Piccolomini.

After his death a large multitude crowded for several days to see him and to invoke his intercession, and that same year Phillip, Duke of Aerschot, petitioned Pope Gregory XV for information with a view to his beatification. Berchmans was declared Blessed in 1865 and canonized in 1888. He is venerated as a patron of students and altar servers, and his feast is kept on 26 November. His statues represent him with hands clasped, holding his crucifix, his book of rules, and his rosary.

john-iv-bishop-of-naples.history:
St. John IV, called the Peacemaker and known also as John the Serene, was an Italian Catholic prelate who served as Bishop of Naples from 26 February 842 until his death. His feast day is unknown.

The material preserved about him is sparse, and the account below rests on the saint record rather than on the encyclopedia article cited for this entry, which, as explained at the end, concerns another man. According to that record, his episcopate fell in a turbulent age of Italian history. The Church of Naples was beset by the shifting politics of the Lombards, by Saracen incursions along the Campanian coast, and by the disputes that lingered after the Iconoclast controversy. Though his tenure is poorly documented, he is remembered by the Neapolitan Church as a man of serene judgment and of a reconciling spirit, a pastor who worked to hold his clergy and people together amid external threats and internal divisions, and who preferred peace to strife.

His cult is ancient and local. The record presents him as a saintly bishop whose labors steadied a see beset by the storms of the ninth century, and in keeping with that memory he is honored as a patron of bishops and of peace.

A note on the sources is necessary. The encyclopedia article associated with this entry does not treat the Bishop of Naples; it concerns a homonymous but distinct figure, Pope John IV, who reigned from 640 to 642, was a native of Dalmatia and the son of the advocate Venantius, died on 12 October 642, and was buried in St. Peter's. That article therefore offers no corroboration for the Neapolitan biography given above, and every detail recorded here of the saint's life derives from the saint record. Readers consulting the article should bear in mind that its subject is the seventh-century pontiff and not the ninth-century Bishop of Naples commemorated in this entry.

john-scholasticus.history:
John Scholasticus (in Greek, ho Scholastikos; also called John of Antioch) was patriarch of Constantinople from 565 until his death in 577, occupying the patriarchal list as John III. Born at Sirimis near Antioch, he is remembered above all as the author of an important collection of ecclesiastical laws. His epithet points to his learning and to the profession he followed before ordination, for he was a lawyer before he became a cleric. He is honored as a saint of the Eastern Orthodox Church, and he is regarded as a patron of bishops and of canon lawyers, a patronage that reflects the two strands of his life: the pastoral office of a hierarch and the legal learning that shaped his principal work.

Of his career the sources preserve only an outline. Ordained a priest within the Antiochene patriarchate, he was sent by his patriarch to Constantinople as legate (apocrisarius) during the reign of Justinian I (527-65). The appointment placed this Antiochene priest in the imperial capital, where he represented the patriarch of Antioch at court. In 565, when Eutychius I of Constantinople was deposed, John succeeded him in the patriarchate. He thus governed the church of the capital during the reign of Justin II, in an age when empire and Church were closely intertwined. He died on August 31, 577, and upon his death Eutychius was restored to the see.

John's lasting significance rests less on the events of his patriarchate than on a labor completed before his elevation, for he had already made a collection of canons. Such collections were in use before his time: at first the decrees of the more important synods were gathered in loose, roughly chronological compilations, of which the "Codex canonum" used by the Council of Chalcedon (451) is an example. Since the fifth century these collections had multiplied, and attempts were made to replace the merely chronological order with a systematic one. Of such systematic arrangements, John's was, if not absolutely the first, at any rate the first of any importance. Between 540 and 560 he compiled the work he called Synagogy kanonon, and Pope Nicholas I (858-67), writing to Photius, alludes to it under the title "Concordia canonum."

The collection was arranged under fifty titles, each followed by the canons concerning the subject of the title. The first title, "Of the honour towards patriarchs ordained by the Canons," is established by canons vii and vi of Nicaea, canon ii of Constantinople I, and canon viii of Ephesus. Altogether the compiler quotes the Apostolic canons, the canons of ten synods, and sixty-eight canons drawn from St. Basil's second and third letters to Amphilochius.
