It is the first attempt to collect canons from the letters of the Fathers. The first edition contained 377 canons arranged under the fifty titles.

The work continued to grow under his own hand. After John became patriarch, he enlarged his collection to sixty titles and added to it eighty-seven chapters taken from the "Novellae" of Justinian. Toward the end of the sixth century, another author added twenty-five more chapters, drawn from both the "Codex" and the "Novellae," concerning civil laws that affected the affairs of the Church. In this way the collection expanded, little by little, until it was finally enlarged into the "Nomocanon" of Photius.

Through this compilation John Scholasticus helped to order the discipline of the Eastern churches for generations, a service that joined his episcopal office to the legal learning of his earlier years, and his memory is preserved among the sainted hierarchs of Constantinople. The date of his feast day is not recorded.

julian-and-basilissa.history:
Julian and Basilissa were a husband and wife venerated as saints by both the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Churches. No historically certain data about them survives; nearly everything reported comes from their Acts, which belong to the class of pious romances appreciated in early times, whose authors, concerned only for the edification of their readers, drowned the few known facts in a mass of imaginary details, miracles, prodigies, and improbable utterances lacking historical value. Any account of the two therefore rests chiefly on tradition rather than verified record, yet their veneration was ancient and well established before the eighth century.

Tradition holds that Julian, forced by his family to marry, agreed with his spouse Basilissa that both would preserve their virginity. Basilissa was encouraged to found a convent for women and became its superior, while Julian gathered a large number of monks and undertook their direction. The marriage thus became the origin of two communities devoted to prayer and the service of others, and their household is remembered as a refuge for the sick and the stranger. For this reason the couple has been honored as models for married life, and they are invoked today for difficult marriages and by engaged couples.

Basilissa is said to have died a very holy death, and martyrdom was reserved for Julian. In the persecution of Diocletian, early in the fourth century, he was arrested, tortured, and put to death. Latin sources place his execution at Antioch in Syria, by order of the governor Martian; Greek sources place it at Antinoe in Egypt, a setting judged the more probable. Summary notices state simply that the two died at Antioch or, more probably, at Antinoe, in the reign of Diocletian.

Their commemoration spread early but varied widely in date. The Roman Martyrology records them on 9 January, while the Greek Menaia keep the feast on 8 January. The Martyrologium Hieronymianum mentions them under 6 January; Usuard, Ado, and Notker place them under the ninth, Rabanus Maurus under the thirteenth of the same month, Vandelbert under 13 February, and the Menology of Canisius under 21 June, the day to which the Greek Menaia assign St. Julian of Caesarea. A church under the invocation of these saints once existed at Constantinople, and its dedication is inscribed in the Greek Calendar under 5 July.

Distinguishing this couple from other early saints of the same name is itself part of the difficulty of their history. The Roman Martyrology mentions thirty-nine saints named Julian, eight of whom are commemorated within January alone, and this Julian of Antinoe has been confounded more than once with Julian of Cilicia. Such confusion, together with the legendary character of the Acts, explains why so little can be affirmed with certainty about either saint.

Julian and Basilissa are commemorated on 9 January. They stand as patrons of married couples who seek to sanctify their union through mutual devotion and self-giving, particularly those enduring difficulty in marriage and those preparing for it. Tradition holds that the faithful have invoked Basilissa against chilblains, the painful inflammation of the skin caused by cold, and that the pair have been honored by all who suffer the hardships of winter for love of Christ. Whatever can no longer be verified of their lives, the witness of a marriage ordered wholly to God, and of Julian's death in time of persecution, gave them a lasting place in the memory of both East and West.

justinian-i.history:
Flavius Anicius Julianus Justinianus was born about 483 at Tauresium in Illyricum, near Uskup, the nephew of the emperor Justin I and the son of Justin's sister Vigilantia and a certain Sabatius. During his uncle's reign he was already the chief power in the state: proclaimed consul in 521 and general-in-chief, he was made Augustus in April 527, and when Justin died in August of that year he became sole ruler. His thirty-eight years on the throne are counted among the most brilliant periods of the later empire, a sustained endeavor to restore the Roman world to greatness, power, and unity.

Much of that endeavor was military. The long war against Persia brought mixed success: Belisarius routed the Persians at Daras in 530, but the Romans were defeated near Callinicum in 531, and a peace followed on fairly equal terms. In 533 a fleet of five hundred ships sailed for Africa under Belisarius; two battles annihilated the Vandal kingdom, and its king, Gelimer, was led captive to Constantinople. In 535 Belisarius took Sicily, and in 536 he took Rhegium and Naples and entered Rome in triumph, sustaining a siege there until the Goths retired in 538. With reinforcements under Narses, Milan and Liguria fell in 539, and by 540 all Italy up to the Frankish frontier was reunited to the empire. The Gothic revolt under Totila, begun in 542, was crushed by 553; Narses became the first Exarch of Italy, and Verona and Brescia, the last Gothic strongholds, fell in 562. The south-eastern provinces of Spain were likewise won, the Crimean Goths, the Bosporus, and even the southern Arabs acknowledged Roman rule, and a second Persian war (540-545) and the Lazic War (549-556) left the empire without a rival on the Black Sea. At home the dangerous Nika revolt of 532, born of the factions of the Circus, was put down severely and confirmed the absolutist character of his rule.

The most enduring of his works was the codification of the laws, for he held that a state rests on arms and law. Ten lawyers under the famous Tribonian reduced the scattered decrees of his predecessors to order: the Codex of 529, the Digest or Pandects of 530, the Institutes drawn from the commentaries of Gaius in the same year, and, after a revision in 534, the Novels containing his own later decisions. These four parts form the Corpus Juris Civilis, which became the foundation alike of canon law, for the Church lived by Roman law, and of the civil law of many later nations.

In ecclesiastical polity Justinian sought peace and union within the empire, though Catholic judgment has viewed the policy with reserve while honoring its intent. For the faith he convoked the Fifth Ecumenical Council and lavished his treasure on the churches, above all in the rebuilding of Hagia Sophia, one of the great churches of Christendom. Theodora, whose courage and presence of mind saved the throne in the crisis of the Nika revolt, shared his counsels for twenty-one years, and historians ascribe to her influence his leaning toward semi-Monophysitism.

Justinian died in November 565 and was succeeded by his nephew Justin II. He has been judged the greatest emperor after Constantine, perhaps the greatest of the long line of Roman Caesars: Dante acclaimed him in the Divine Comedy, and his portrait gleams still from the mosaic in S. Vitale at Ravenna, where he stands diademed amid his court with a bishop at his side. Though a sovereign and not a monk, he is honored as a saint in the Eastern tradition for his zeal for the faith and the churches he raised to the glory of God. His feast is kept on November 14, and he is remembered as a patron of church reform and of the laity.

kateri-tekakwitha.history:
Tekakwitha, who took the name Catherine at her baptism and is remembered as Kateri Tekakwitha, was a Mohawk woman born in 1656 in what is now New York. Celebrated as the "Lily of the Mohawks" and the "Genevieve of New France," she has also been recorded under the spellings Tegakwitha and Takwita. Accounts of her birthplace differ: some authorities place it at the Turtle Castle of Ossernenon, others at the village of Gandaouge.

Her mother was a Christian Algonquin who had been captured by the Iroquois and saved from a captive's fate by Tekakwitha's father; the couple also had a son. When Tekakwitha was about four years old, her parents and brother died of smallpox, and the child was adopted by her aunts and by an uncle who had become chief of the Turtle clan. The disease had left her face scarred and seriously impaired her eyesight, and her manner was reserved and shrinking. Her aunts nonetheless began when she was very young to arrange marriages for her, from which she shrank with growing aversion as she grew older.

In 1667 the Jesuit missionaries Fremin, Bruyas, and Pierron, accompanying Mohawk deputies who had been to Quebec to conclude peace with the French, spent three days in her uncle's lodge. From them Tekakwitha received her first knowledge of Christianity; she eagerly accepted it in her heart, but she did not at that time ask to be baptized. Some time later the Turtle clan moved to the north bank of the Mohawk River, its castle standing above what is now the town of Fonda. There, amid scenes of violence and idolatry, she lived a life of remarkable virtue, firmly and often at great risk to herself resisting all efforts to induce her to marry.

When she was eighteen, Father Jacques de Lamberville arrived to take charge of the mission that included the Turtle clan, and at her earnest request she received baptism from him. Thereafter she practiced her religion unflinchingly in the face of almost unbearable opposition, until her uncle's lodge ceased to be a place of protection for her. Assisted by some Christian Indians, she escaped to Caughnawaga on the St. Lawrence near Montreal.

At Caughnawaga she lived in the cabin of Anastasia Tegonhatsihonga, a Christian Indian woman. Her extraordinary sanctity impressed not only her own people but also the French and the missionaries, and she gave herself to prayer, penance, and care for the sick and the elderly. Her mortifications were extreme, and the chronicler Chauchtiere says that she had attained the most perfect union with God in prayer.

She died at Caughnawaga, Canada, on 17 April 1680, at the age of twenty-four. Tradition holds, as witnesses of the time reported, that the scars on her face vanished at her death. Devotion to her began immediately to be manifested among her people. Many pilgrims visit her grave at Caughnawaga, where a monument to her memory was erected by the Reverend Clarence Walworth in 1884, and the Councils of Baltimore and Quebec have petitioned for her canonization.

She was beatified by Pope John Paul II on 22 June 1980 and canonized in 2012, becoming the first Native American saint from North America. Her feast day is celebrated on 14 July, and she is honored as a patron of ecology, the environment, and Native peoples.

leander-of-seville.history:
Leander of Seville was born at Carthage about 534, of a Roman family established in that city. His father, Severian, was a citizen of Carthage, though some historians have described him as duke or governor of the city. About 554 the family emigrated to Seville. The children of Severian became figures of great eminence in the Spanish Church: Leander and his brother Isidore both served as bishops of Seville, his brother Fulgentius became Bishop of Carthagena, and his sister Florentina was a nun who directed forty convents and one thousand nuns. A later belief that another daughter, Theodosia, became the wife of the Visigothic king Leovigild has been judged unfounded.

Leander first became a Benedictine monk, and in 579 he was made Bishop of Seville. In the meantime he had founded a celebrated school, which soon became a center of learning and orthodoxy. As bishop he confronted the Arianism then dominant among the Visigoths. He assisted the princess Ingunthis in converting her husband Hermenegild, the eldest son of King Leovigild, and defended the convert against his father's cruel reprisals. In endeavoring to save his country from Arianism he acted both as an orthodox Christian and as a patriot concerned for his nation's welfare. Exiled by Leovigild, he withdrew to Byzantium from 579 to 582.

The exile proved consequential. It is possible, though not proved, that Leander sought to rouse the Emperor Tiberius to take up arms against the Arian king; in any case the attempt was without result. He profited by his stay at Byzantium to compose important works against Arianism, and there formed a close friendship with the future Pope Gregory the Great, then legate of Pelagius II at the Byzantine court. The correspondence between the two men remains one of Leander's greatest titles to honor. The exact date of his return from exile is unknown. Leovigild put his son Hermenegild to death in 585 and died himself in 589.

In that decisive hour for the future of Spain, Leander did much to secure the religious unity, fervent faith, and broad culture on which the country's later greatness was to rest. He had a share in the conversion of Reccared and never ceased to exercise over the king a deep and beneficial influence. At the Third Council of Toledo, where Visigothic Spain abjured Arianism, Leander delivered the closing sermon. On his return from the council he convened an important synod in his metropolitan city of Seville, and he never afterward ceased his efforts to consolidate the work, in which his brother and successor Isidore was to follow him. Leander received the pallium in August 599.

Leander died at Seville on 13 March, in 600 or 601. Of his writings, which were judged superior to those of his brother, only two works survive: De institutione virginum et contemptu mundi, a monastic rule composed for his sister, and the Homilia de triumpho ecclesiae ob conversionem Gothorum, on the triumph of the Church in the conversion of the Goths. Isidore wrote of his brother that he was a man of suave eloquence and eminent talent who shone as brightly by his virtues as by his doctrine, and that by his faith and zeal the Gothic people were converted from Arianism to the Catholic faith. Venerated as a saint, Leander is honored as a doctor of the Spanish Church and is remembered as a patron of bishops and converts.

pope-leo-iii.history:
Leo III, a Roman and the son of Atyuppius and Elizabeth, was elected pope on 26 December 795, the very day his predecessor Adrian I was buried, and consecrated the next day, perhaps to forestall any Frankish interference with the freedom of Roman elections. At that time he was Cardinal-Priest of St. Susanna and seemingly also vestiarius, chief of the pontifical treasury. With the letter announcing his unanimous election to Charlemagne he sent the keys of the confession of St. Peter and the standard of the city, showing that he regarded the Frankish king as protector of the Holy See; in return he received a great part of the treasure captured from the Avars, wealth that enabled him to become a great benefactor to the churches and charitable institutions of Rome.

On 25 April 799, during the procession of the Greater Litanies, Leo was attacked near the Flaminian Gate by armed men, relatives of Adrian I, who sought to render him unfit for his sacred office. Dashed to the ground, he was left bleeding in the street after an attempt to root out his tongue and tear out his eyes, and was then hurried by night to the monastery of St. Erasmus on the Coelian, where he recovered, in what seemed a miraculous manner, the full use of his eyes and tongue. Escaping, he betook himself to Charlemagne, who received him with honour at Paderborn and had him escorted back to Rome, where the populace received him with joy. Tried by Charlemagne's envoys, his enemies could establish neither Leo's guilt nor their own innocence, and were sent as prisoners to France.

In 800 Charlemagne came to Rome. The assembled bishops declared that they had no right to judge the pope, but Leo, of his own free will, declared on oath that he was wholly guiltless of the charges, and at his request the death sentence passed upon his principal enemies was commuted into exile. A few days later, on Christmas Day in St. Peter's, after the Gospel had been sung, the pope approached Charlemagne, who was kneeling before the Confession of St. Peter, and placed a crown upon his head while the multitude acclaimed him. By this act the Empire was revived in the West, and, in theory at least, the world was declared by the Church subject to one temporal head as Christ had made it subject to one spiritual head, the first duty of the new emperor being the protection of the Roman Church and of Christendom.

Pope and emperor acted together in combating the Adoptionist heresy that had arisen in Spain, and their joint action was felt even in England, where Eardulf of Northumbria recovered his kingdom. Leo likewise intervened in English affairs on his own account: by his command the synod of Clovesho in 803 condemned the appointing of laymen as superiors of monasteries, and he excommunicated Eadbert Praen for seizing the throne of Kent and restored the ecclesiastical jurisdiction of the See of Canterbury.

After Charlemagne died on 28 January 814, evil times broke anew upon Leo. A fresh conspiracy, of which the pope was warned before it came to a head, ended in the seizure and execution of its chief authors, and nobles of the Campagna who rose in arms and plundered the country were overpowered by the Duke of Spoleto. The treasure Charlemagne had given enabled Leo to be an efficient helper of the poor, a patron of art, and a renovator of churches of Rome and even of Ravenna, adorned with mosaic, especially his titular church of St. Susanna.

Leo died on 12 June 816 and was buried in St. Peter's, where his relics rest with those of Sts. Leo I, Leo II, and Leo IV. Venerated from antiquity as a saint, he was canonized in 1673; his feast is kept on 12 June, and he is honored as a patron of bishops and of church unity.

pope-linus.history:
Pope Linus is honored as the second bishop of Rome and the immediate successor of the Apostle Peter. The ancient records of the Roman bishops preserved by Irenaeus, Julius Africanus, Hippolytus, and Eusebius, together with the Liberian catalogue of 354, all place his name directly after that of Peter. These records go back to a list of Roman bishops existing in the time of Pope Eleutherus, about 174 to 189, when Irenaeus wrote his book Against Heresies. A few later Latin writers, following Tertullian, placed St. Clement immediately after Peter instead, but the Roman list standing behind Irenaeus holds the stronger claim to historical authority. According to Irenaeus, the apostles Peter and Paul, having founded the church at Rome, handed over the episcopal office to Linus, whose successor was Anacletus. He governed the Christian community at Rome after the Apostle's death; the opinion of some fourth-century writers that he led the Roman church during Peter's lifetime has no historical foundation.

Little is recorded of his pontificate, which is generally placed from about the year 68 until his death around 80. The papal lists credit him with a term of twelve years, reckoned in the Liberian Catalogue as twelve years, four months, and twelve days, although the exact dates given there are regarded as incorrect. His reign was counted from the death of the apostles Peter and Paul, the year of which is not known for certain. Irenaeus identifies him with the Linus whom St. Paul greets in his second letter to Timothy, though it cannot be determined whether this identification rests on an ancient and reliable source or arose later from the similarity of the name.

Later tradition, recorded in the Liber Pontificalis, gives Tuscany as his homeland and names his father as Herculanus, though the origin of these assertions cannot be discovered. The same work attributes to him a decree, in accordance with the ordinance of St. Peter, that women should have their heads covered in church; this decree is considered apocryphal, drawn from St. Paul's first letter to the Corinthians and arbitrarily attributed to the first successor of the Apostle in Rome. An epistle on the martyrdom of the apostles Peter and Paul, later ascribed to Linus and supposedly sent by him to the Eastern Churches, is likewise apocryphal. The Liber Pontificalis further states that he suffered martyrdom, an assertion that cannot be proved, since no persecution of the church of Rome is recorded between Nero and Domitian, and Irenaeus names only Telesphorus among the early Roman bishops as a glorious martyr.

Tradition holds that Linus was buried in the Vatican beside St. Peter. Peter was certainly buried at the foot of the Vatican Hill, and the earliest bishops of the Roman church may have been interred there as well. When the present confession of St. Peter's Basilica was constructed in 1615, sarcophagi were uncovered, among them one bearing the name Linus; yet other letters on the stone suggest that this formed part of some other name, such as Aquilinus or Anullinus, and the place of the discovery shows that it cannot have been the tomb of Linus.

The feast of St. Linus is now celebrated on 23 September, the date given in the Liber Pontificalis. He appears in none of the fourth-century lists of the feasts of the Roman saints, since special feasts of martyrs were first instituted at the end of the second century. Though little is known of his life, his office placed him at the head of the church that claimed the memory of Peter, and he held the community together in the years after the apostles, through times of suspicion and persecution under the emperors. He is venerated as one of the first to sit in the chair of Peter and to guard the faith of the apostles, and he is honored in particular as a patron of priests and of church unity.

lucifer-of-cagliari.history:
Lucifer of Cagliari was bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia in the fourth century; he was probably born in the early years of that century and died in 371, though his birthplace and the circumstances of his youth are unknown. His name, in late antiquity a Latin word meaning light-bearer, was borne by Christians of devotion, though its later associations have startled many readers. He is remembered as a strenuous and unyielding defender of the Nicene faith against Arianism, which denied the full divinity of Christ, and in Sardinia he is honoured as a confessor who suffered for that divinity.

He first appears in ecclesiastical history in 354, when Pope Liberius deputed him, together with the priest Pancratius and the deacon Hilary, to ask the Emperor Constantius to convene a council to deal with the accusations directed against St. Athanasius. The council met at Milan in 355, and there Lucifer defended the Bishop of Alexandria with passion, though in language so violent that it gave the saint's adversaries a pretext for resentment and contributed to a new condemnation of Athanasius. Constantius, unaccustomed to independence on the part of bishops, grievously maltreated Lucifer and his colleague Eusebius of Vercelli and exiled them both. Lucifer was sent first to Germanica in Syria, then to Eleutheropolis in Palestine, and at last relegated to the Thebaid.

In the course of this exile he wrote two books addressed to Constantius in defence of St. Athanasius. The work was an eloquent vindication of Catholic orthodoxy, but its exaggerated language overshot its mark and injured the cause it was meant to serve; its author spoke of it with pride, while the emperor, for his part, refrained from further revenge. After the death of Constantius the Emperor Julian allowed the exiles to return to their cities. Lucifer went to Antioch and at once entered the dissensions dividing the Catholic party, consecrating a bishop whom he judged capable of continuing opposition to the party he considered the weaker, and so prolonging and embittering the conflict. Incapable of tact, he aggravated the dissenters instead of dealing cautiously with them, and showed special severity toward Catholics who had wavered in their adherence to the Nicene Creed. About this time a Council of Alexandria, presided over by St. Athanasius, decreed that Arians renouncing their heresy should be pardoned and that bishops who had temporized under compulsion should not be disturbed. Against this indulgence Lucifer protested, going so far as to anathematize his former friend Eusebius of Vercelli, who carried out the council's decrees.

Seeing that his extreme opinions won partisans neither in East nor West, Lucifer withdrew to Sardinia, resumed his see, and formed a small sect called the Luciferians. These maintained that all priests who had participated in Arianism should be deprived of their dignity and that bishops who recognized the rights of even repentant heretics should be excommunicated. The sectaries commissioned two priests, Marcellinus and Faustinus, to present to the Emperor Theodosius the petition known as the Libellus precum; the emperor forbade further pursuit of them, and the schism seems not to have lasted beyond its first generation.

Lucifer died in 371. Whatever judgment later ages have passed on his harshness toward the fallen, his fidelity did not waver: he refused at Milan to condemn St. Athanasius and bore banishment rather than betray the divinity of Christ. He is commemorated on 20 May and honoured as a patron of bishops and of those engaged in spiritual warfare.

pope-marcellinus.history:
According to the Liber Pontificalis, Marcellinus was a Roman, the son of a certain Projectus. He was elected bishop of Rome on 30 June 296 and died in 304, after a pontificate of some eight years, of which almost no record survives. It is known, however, that before the outbreak of the Diocletian persecution new burial chambers were laid out in the Catacomb of Callistus, the chief cemetery of the Roman Church, at the order of Marcellinus himself, as the epitaph there of the Roman deacon Severus records.

The persecution begun under Diocletian in 303, whose severe edicts against the Christians were executed in the West by Maximianus Herculeus, brought great confusion upon the Roman Church. The Catacomb of Callistus was confiscated together with the other public meeting places of the Roman community, and it has been inferred that the Christians blocked its principal galleries to protect from desecration the tombs of the numerous martyrs buried there. Marcellinus died in the second year of the persecution, in all probability a natural death. No trustworthy source of the fourth or fifth century calls him a martyr: his name appears neither in the Roman Chronograph of 354 nor in the Martyrologium Hieronymianum, and Eusebius says only that the persecution affected him as well, an expression which suggests that he did not suffer a martyr's death.

Rumours nevertheless circulated that the pope had surrendered the sacred books or offered incense to the gods to save himself. In letters of 400 and 410 the Donatist bishop Petilianus of Constantine asserted that Marcellinus, together with the Roman priests Melchiades, Marcellus and Sylvester, had given up the sacred books and offered incense, but he could produce no proof, and at the great Carthaginian conference between Catholics and Donatists only the two Roman deacons Straton and Cassius were named as traitors. Augustine decisively rejected the charge, answering that the accused were innocent. Tradition holds, in the account preserved in the Liber Pontificalis, which appears to draw on a lost passion of the pope, that Marcellinus was led to the sacrifice and scattered incense, that a few days later he was seized with remorse, and that Diocletian condemned him to be beheaded with three other Christians. A sixth-century collection of forged documents, made during the dispute between Pope Symmachus and Laurentius, added an apocryphal tale of a synod of three hundred bishops held at Sinuessa in 303, in which the pope was said to have confessed his lapse and done penance; these acts are almost certainly spurious. The silence of contemporary writers is decisive, and it is accepted as certain that Marcellinus did not comply with the imperial edict by any overt act, such as surrendering the sacred writings or offering incense, since an apostasy of a Roman bishop would surely have received the greatest prominence from the authors of the age.

The tomb of Marcellinus in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria was venerated by the Christians of Rome from a very early date. This burial ground, which belonged to the Acilii Glabriones, remained at the disposal of the Roman Christians while their chief cemetery at Callistus lay confiscated, and a seventh-century itinerary of the graves of the Roman martyrs expressly records his grave among the sacred graves of Priscilla. Excavation has identified the crypt of St. Crescentius, beside which was his burial chamber, but no monument referring to the pope has been found, and its precise position remains uncertain. He was honoured as a martyr by the end of the fifth century, when the lost passion utilized by the Liber Pontificalis was written, though his name appears first in the Martyrology of Bede, drawn from that same source. His feast is kept on 26 April; the earlier breviaries, which repeated the story of his lapse and repentance, were altered in 1883.

margaret-clitherow.history:
Margaret Clitherow, known as the Pearl of York, was born in York around 1556, a daughter of Thomas Middleton, who served as Sheriff of York and worked as a wax-chandler. On 8 July 1571 she married John Clitherow, a wealthy butcher and chamberlain of the city, in the church of St Martin on Coney Street, and the couple lived in the Shambles, a street that remains much altered little since her day. In 1574, about three years after her marriage, she converted to the Catholic faith at a time when it was outlawed in England, and she became fervent in its practice.

Her husband remained a member of the Established Church, although a brother of his was a priest. Margaret maintained two hiding places for clergy, one adjoining her house and a second in another part of the city, where priests were sheltered and Mass continually celebrated through the thick of the persecution. She was frequently imprisoned for harbouring and maintaining priests, on occasion for two years at a time, yet she remained undaunted. Some of the priests she sheltered were themselves martyred, and she desired the same grace above all things, making secret pilgrimages by night to York Tyburn to pray beneath the gibbet.

She was arrested on 10 March 1586 and committed to the castle. On 14 March she was arraigned at the York assizes before Judges Clinch and Rhodes and members of the Council of the North, on the charge of having harboured priests and heard Mass. She refused to plead, because the only witnesses against her would have been her own young children and servants, whom she could not bear to involve in the guilt of her death. For this refusal she was condemned to the peine forte et dure, death by pressing. "God be thanked, I am not worthy of so good a death as this", she said.

The sentence was carried out on Lady Day, 25 March 1586, which fell on Good Friday according to the New Style reckoning, and she was probably with child at the time. After an agony of fear the previous night, she faced the ordeal calm, joyous, and smiling. She walked barefoot to the tollbooth on Ousebridge, having sent her hose and shoes to her daughter Anne, in token that she should follow in her steps. Urged even then to confess, she answered, "No, no, Mr. Sheriff, I die for the love of my Lord Jesu." She was laid on the ground with a sharp stone beneath her back, her hands stretched in the form of a cross and bound to two posts, and a door was placed upon her and weighted until she was crushed to death. During an agony of some fifteen minutes, her last words were, "Jesu! Jesu! Jesu! have mercy on me!"

Her right hand is preserved at St Mary's Convent in York, but the resting place of her body is not known. Her sons Henry and William became priests, and her daughter Anne became a nun at St Ursula's in Louvain. An early account of her life was written by her confessor, John Mush. She was canonized by Pope Paul VI in 1970 as one of the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales, and her feast is kept on 26 March; she is honoured as a patroness of mothers and of martyrs.

pope-martin-i.history:
Martin I was born at Todi on the Tiber, a son of Fabricius. His biographer Theodore describes him as of noble birth, of commanding intelligence and profound learning, and of great charity to the poor. He had earlier served Pope Theodore I as apocrysiary, or ambassador, to Constantinople, arranging for the canonical deposition of the heretical patriarch Pyrrhus. Chosen to succeed Theodore at Rome, probably on 21 July 649, he had himself consecrated without awaiting the imperial confirmation, the only pope of the period of Byzantine control whose election did not wait for the imperial mandate.

He governed the Church while the leaders of the Monothelite heresy, upheld by Emperor Constans II, labored to spread their tenets in East and West. Soon after his election Martin summoned the Lateran council, at which one hundred five bishops met in five sessions in October 649. It rejected the Ecthesis of Heraclius and the Typus of Constans II, excommunicated Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul of Constantinople, Cyrus of Alexandria, and Theodore of Phran, and enacted twenty canons defining Catholic doctrine on the two wills of Christ. The decrees, signed by pope and bishops, were sent throughout the world and to the emperor.

Martin appointed John, Bishop of Philadelphia, as his vicar in the East, and excommunicated and deposed Paul of Thessalonica for refusing to recall his heretical letters. Paul, Patriarch of Constantinople, urged the emperor to force the pope and the Western bishops at least to subscribe to the Typus. The exarch Olympius tried in vain to form a faction among the council fathers and is said then to have plotted to slay Martin while pretending to receive Holy Communion from his hands; Providence protected the pope, and Olympius left for Sicily, dying in the war against the Saracens. Constans next sent Theodore Calliopas, who reached Rome on 15 June 653 and announced in the Lateran two days later that Martin, an unworthy intruder, was deposed and must be taken to Constantinople. Wishing to avoid the shedding of human blood, the pope forbade resistance.

Ill and suffering, the prisoner reached Constantinople on 17 September 653 or 654, having touched nowhere but Naxos, where he perhaps remained a year. From Abydos messengers announced the coming of a captive branded heretic, rebel, and enemy of God and the State; exposed for hours on deck to the mockery of onlookers, Martin was shut for ninety-three days in the prison Prandearia, enduring hunger, cold, and thirst. On 19 December he was brought before the senate, with the imperial treasurer acting as judge; the charges were political, but the true one was his refusal to sign the Typus. Carried to an open space before the emperor and the crowd, few of whom would pronounce anathema upon him, he was stripped of nearly all his clothing, loaded with chains, dragged through the streets, and held again for eighty-five days in the prison of Diomede. Perhaps because of the death of the patriarch Paul, Constans sent him not to death but to exile.

He was put aboard ship on 26 March 654, or perhaps 655, and reached Cherson in the Crimea on 15 May, amid a great famine. There he passed the remaining days of his life, dying of privation on 16 September 655, after a reign of six years, one month, and twenty-six days, in the course of which he ordained eleven priests, five deacons, and thirty-three bishops. He was buried in the church of Our Lady, called Blachernae, near Cherson, and many miracles are related as wrought by him in life and after death; most of his relics are said to be in the Roman church of San Martino ai Monti. Seventeen of his letters are extant.

For his resolute confession of the two wills of Christ, Martin is honored as a martyr and venerated as a confessor of the faith, the last pope to be recognized as a martyr. In the hymns of their liturgy the Greeks style him the infallible teacher of the faith, as successor of St. Peter in the See of Rome.

nicholas-of-myra.history:
Nicholas of Myra, also venerated as Nicholas of Bari, was Bishop of Myra in Lycia, in Asia Minor. Though he is one of the most popular saints in both the Greek and the Latin Churches, there is scarcely anything historically certain about him except that he was Bishop of Myra in the fourth century and that he died on 6 December; the year of his death is given as 345 or 352.

Tradition holds that he was born at Patara, a city of Lycia in Asia Minor, and that in his youth he made a pilgrimage to Egypt and Palestine; shortly after his return he is said to have become Bishop of Myra.

According to the same tradition, he was cast into prison during the persecution of Diocletian and was released after the accession of Constantine. He is said to have been present at the Council of Nicaea in 325, where later legend tells that he struck the heretic Arius in his zeal for the faith; but his name appears in none of the old lists of the bishops who attended that council, and his presence there is therefore doubted.

The numerous miracles attributed to him, both before and after his death, are outgrowths of a long tradition, first collected and written in Greek by Metaphrastes in the tenth century. Later accounts credit him with calming storms at sea and saving sailors in peril, and with rescuing three innocent men from execution; stories such as these rest on legend rather than on contemporary historical record.

His veneration is ancient. As early as the sixth century the Emperor Justinian I built a church in his honour at Constantinople, and his name occurs in the liturgy ascribed to St. Chrysostom; his cult in the Greek Church is old, and it has long been especially popular in Russia. In Italy his veneration appears to have begun with the translation of his relics, when in 1087 Italian merchants carried his body from Myra and brought it to Bari, where it is still preserved in the church of San Nicola. Tradition says that an oily substance, known as the Manna di S. Nicola, has flowed from these relics up to the present day and is highly valued for its medicinal powers. In Germany his cult began already under Otto II, probably because his wife Theophano was a Grecian; Bishop Reginald of Eichstaedt (d. 991) is known to have written a metrical Vita S. Nicholai.

The course of centuries has not lessened his popularity. Nicholas is honoured as patron by many places and peoples: Greece, Russia, the Kingdom of Naples, Sicily, Lorraine, the Diocese of Liège; many cities in Italy, Germany, Austria, and Belgium; Campen in the Netherlands; Corfu in Greece; Freiburg in Switzerland; and Moscow in Russia. He is invoked as patron of children and sailors, and likewise of merchants, bakers, and travellers. His representations in art are as various as his alleged miracles. In Germany, Switzerland, and the Netherlands arose the custom of making him the secret purveyor of gifts to children on 6 December, the day on which the Church celebrates his feast; in the United States and some other countries St. Nicholas has become identified with Santa Claus, who distributes gifts to children on Christmas eve.

ninian.history:
{"history": "Saint Ninian, whose name is recorded by ancient writers under the forms Ninias, Ninus, Dinan, Ringan, and Ringen, is honored as the first Apostle of Christianity in Scotland and as the Apostle to the Southern Picts. The earliest account of him appears in Bede's Ecclesiastical History, written in the eighth century, which records that the southern Picts received the true faith through the preaching of Bishop Ninias, a most reverend and holy man of the British nation who had been regularly instructed at Rome in the faith and mysteries of the truth. Bede further relates that Ninian's episcopal see was named after St. Martin and was famous for a church dedicated to that saint, in which Bede says Ninian himself and many other saints rest in body, and that the place, belonging to the province of the Bernicians and by Bede's time in the possession of the English nation, was commonly called Candida Casa, the White House, because Ninian built there a church of stone, which was not usual among the Britons. These facts form practically all that is known of his life and work.

The fullest later life was compiled in the twelfth century by St. Ælred, who professes to draw upon Bede and upon an older book concerning Ninian's life and miracles, written in a rough and unpolished style, but the legendary element in that life is largely evident. Tradition holds, on Ælred's authority, that while engaged in building his church at Candida Casa, Ninian learned of the death of St. Martin and resolved to dedicate the church to him. Because St. Martin died about 397, Ninian's mission to the southern Picts is reckoned to have begun toward the end of the fourth century. He died about 432; the date of his birth is unknown.

At Whithorn Ninian founded a monastery that became famous as a school of monasticism within a century of his death. His work among the southern Picts seems to have had only short-lived success: St. Patrick, in his epistle to Coroticus, terms the Picts apostates, and references to Ninian's converts having abandoned Christianity appear also in the writings of Sts. Columba and Kentigern.

Whithorn remained the center of his cult, and Whithorn Priory later ranked among the great medieval pilgrimage sites of Scotland. His body was buried in the church at Whithorn in Wigtownshire, although no relics are now known to exist. Numerous dedications to him survive across Scotland and northern England, where he is known as Ringan in Scotland and Trynnian in northern England, names that testify to the devotion he inspired. The Clogrinny, or bell of St. Ringan, a work of very rough craftsmanship, is preserved in the Antiquarian Museum at Edinburgh.

The Church keeps his feast on September 16, honoring him as bishop and confessor, and venerates him as a patron of missionaries and pilgrims. Candida Casa stands in Christian memory as the cradle of Scottish Christianity, and Ninian is remembered as the missionary bishop who carried the Gospel to the southern Picts and established the Church among peoples who had never before heard the name of Christ."}

norbert.history:
Norbert was born around 1080 at Xanten on the left bank of the Rhine, near Wesel, into a noble family; his father, Heribert, Count of Gennep, was related to the imperial house of Germany and to the house of Lorraine. Ordained a subdeacon, he received a canonry at Xanten and was soon summoned to the court of Frederick, Prince-Bishop of Cologne, and later became almoner to the Emperor Henry V, though he declined the offered bishopric of Cambrai. He lived a worldly life until 1115, when, while riding near Xanten, a thunderbolt fell at his horse's feet and the frightened animal threw him, leaving him for nearly an hour as if dead. Taking the event as a summons to conversion, he renounced his appointments at court and retired to Xanten to lead a life of penance.

Placing himself under the guidance of Cono, Abbot of Siegburg, Norbert founded and endowed the Abbey of Fürstenberg. Feeling called to the priesthood, he received Holy Orders from the Bishop of Cologne, and after a forty days' retreat he celebrated his first Mass at Xanten, where he bore with patience the insults of certain clerics, one of whom spat in his face. Accused as an innovator at the Council of Fritzlar, he resigned his ecclesiastical preferments, gave his estate to the poor, and set out barefoot as a begging preacher. Pope Gelasius, unable to keep him at his court, granted him faculties to preach wherever he judged proper, and at Valenciennes in 1119 he met Burchard, Bishop of Cambrai, whose chaplain joined him in his apostolic journeys through France and Belgium.

That same year, at the request of Pope Calixtus II and Bartholomew, Bishop of Laon, Norbert agreed to found a religious order in the Diocese of Laon so that his work might be perpetuated. He chose a lonely, marshy valley in the Forest of Coucy, about ten miles from Laon, named Prémontré, where his first disciples, among them Hugh of Fosses, Evermode of Cambray, and Antony of Nivelles, lived at first in huts of wood and clay around a chapel of St. John the Baptist. The community, known as the Order of Canons Regular of Prémontré or the Norbertines, combined the contemplative life with pastoral ministry, and bishops soon entreated Norbert to found houses in their dioceses, including Floreffe, Viviers, Antwerp, and Kappenberg. When Norbert went to Cologne to obtain relics for the new church, a vision is said to have shown him where those of St. Ursula and her companions and of other martyrs lay hidden. He journeyed to Rome in 1125, and the new pope, Honorius II, confirmed the order by bull dated 27 February 1126.

In 1122, having persuaded Theobald, Count of Champagne, that God wished him to marry and do good in the world, Norbert prescribed a rule of life and invested him with the white scapular, thus instituting the Third Order of St. Norbert; Blessed Ricwera, widow of Count Raymond of Clastres, was his first spiritual daughter. Sent by the Bishop of Cambrai to combat the heresies Tanchelin had promulgated, which had their center at Antwerp, Norbert preached with such effect that the people abjured their errors, and he came to be honored as the Apostle of Antwerp. Returning from Rome, he was reported to have restored sight to a blind woman at Würzburg; the inhabitants were so impressed that they considered electing him their bishop, and he quietly withdrew.

Norbert later became Archbishop of Magdeburg, where he worked to reform the clergy. He died at Magdeburg on 6 June 1134 and was canonized in 1582, his feast being kept on 6 June. He is venerated as a patron of peace and of expectant mothers, and he was also proclaimed Patron and Protector of Bohemia. The order he founded carried on his ideal of joining contemplation with pastoral care in the years after his death.

novatus.history:
Novatus is venerated as a saint of the first Christian centuries, and his canonization belongs to the pre-Congregation era, resting upon the ancient and unbroken cult of the Roman Church. He is commemorated on June 20 together with his brother, the martyr Timotheus. He is honored as a patron of theologians and of conversion.

He belonged to a family closely bound to the apostolic age. His father was St. Pudens and his mother Claudia Rufina, and he was brother to Sts. Pudentiana and Praxedes. His paternal grandfather was Quintus Cornelius Pudens, a Roman senator who, with his wife Priscilla, was among St. Peter's earliest converts in Rome; in the senator's house the Apostle dwelt while he was in that city.

A portion of the superstructure of the modern church of St. Pudentiana on the Via Urbana is thought to be part either of the senatorial palace or of the baths built by Novatus, a trace of the family's standing in early Christian Rome.

Beyond these records, the particulars of his life and ministry have been obscured by the centuries. He is nonetheless numbered among the holy ones of the early Church who witnessed to the faith in the generations following the apostles, and the continued keeping of his feast on June 20 testifies to the devotion he inspired among the early Christians.

othmar.history:
Saint Othmar was a medieval monk, priest, and abbot, remembered as the first abbot of the Abbey of Saint Gall in what is now Switzerland. He was of Alemannic descent and received his education in Rhaetia, where he was ordained a priest. For a time he presided over a church dedicated to Saint Florinus in Rhaetia, which was probably identical with the church of Saint Peter at Remus, where Saint Florinus had labored as a priest and been buried.

In 720, Waltram of Thurgau appointed Othmar superior over the cell of Saint Gall. Othmar united the monks who lived about the cell into a monastery, organized according to the rule of Saint Columban, and became their first abbot. He added a hospital and a school to the community, and during the course of his abbacy the Rule of Saint Columban was replaced by the Rule of Saint Benedict.

His abbacy also brought him into contact with the rulers of his day. When Karlmann renounced his throne in 747, he visited Othmar at Saint Gall and entrusted him with a letter to his brother Pepin, recommending Othmar and his monastery to the king's liberality. Othmar personally brought the letter to Pepin and was kindly received.

The closing years of his life were marked by an unjust conflict. When the Counts Warin and Ruodhart unjustly sought to gain possession of property belonging to Saint Gall, Othmar fearlessly resisted their demands. In consequence, they captured him while he was on a journey to Constance and held him prisoner, first at the castle of Bodmann and then on the island of Werd in the Rhine. After six months of imprisonment he died there on 16 November 759, and he was buried on the island, bearing this final trial with patience and faith.

Veneration of Othmar began to spread soon after his death. His body was transferred to the monastery of Saint Gall in 769, and in 867 it was solemnly entombed in the new church of Saint Othmar at Saint Gall. He ranks, after Saint Maurice and Saint Gall, among the most popular saints in Switzerland. He is honored as the founder and first abbot of the abbey he established, and, as recorded in the register of his cult, is venerated as a patron of monks and builders.

Tradition holds that a barrel belonging to the saint never became empty, no matter how much was taken from it to give to the poor. This miracle is reflected in his customary depiction in art, where he is represented as a Benedictine abbot generally holding a little barrel in his hand.

pope-paul-i.history:
Paul I, pope from 757 until his death at Rome on 28 June 767, was a brother of his predecessor, Stephen II. The two had been educated for the priesthood at the Lateran palace, and before his election Paul served as a Roman deacon. Stephen entrusted him with important ecclesiastical affairs, among them the effort to recover for the Roman States cities seized by the Lombard kings Aistulf and Desiderius.

While Paul remained with the dying Stephen, a party of Romans gathered at the house of Archdeacon Theophylact to further that cleric's claim to the see. Stephen died on 26 April 757, but Paul was elected by a large majority and consecrated bishop on 29 May. He continued his predecessor's policy toward the Frankish king Pepin, upholding papal authority over Rome and central Italy against the Lombards and the Eastern Empire. In 758 Pepin sent the cloth used at the baptism of a newborn daughter, renewing the papal sponsorship.

Relations with Desiderius proved difficult. The Lombard king failed to deliver Imola, Osimo, Ancona, and Bologna to Rome, devastated the Pentapolis, and annexed the duchies of Spoleto and Benevento in 758, and at Benevento he concluded with the Greek ambassador Georgios an alliance of Byzantines and Lombards in central Italy. On a visit to Rome he refused the pope's demand for the cities, offering Imola only if Pepin returned the Lombard hostages, and threatened war otherwise. Pressed even to inform the Frankish court, Paul sent envoys with two letters: one, meant to secure safe passage through Lombard territory, appeared to accept Desiderius' terms, while a secret letter disclosed the Lombard-Byzantine agreement concerning Ravenna and implored Pepin's aid. Frankish envoys obtained fresh promises from Desiderius in 760, but he again refused to honor them, forcing his way into Roman territory.

Byzantine action heightened the danger as reports spread in 760 of a large fleet bound for Rome and an army intended for Rome and Ravenna, while the emperor sought the voluntary submission of Ravenna and Venice. Archbishop Sergius of Ravenna forwarded the imperial letter to the pope, who notified Pepin; the ambassador Georgios even won over a papal envoy at the Frankish court, yet could not move Pepin himself. Paul also opposed the Emperor Constantine Copronymus, defending orthodoxy regarding the Trinity and the veneration of images through legates and letters to Byzantium; and the returning legates reassured the pope on the Frankish ruler's views.

As Lombard support might prove necessary in a war with the East, Pepin desired an agreement with Desiderius, who then showed greater complaisance over the Roman patrimony in Lombard territory; when Desiderius himself visited Rome in 765, the boundary disputes between him and the pope were arranged. The Frankish king then directed Desiderius to aid the pope in recovering the Roman patrimony in Byzantine-ruled southern Italy and to uphold the pope's ecclesiastical rights against the bishops of those districts. At Rome Paul held a synod in 761 in connection with a church he had founded, and transferred the bones of numerous martyrs from catacomb sanctuaries devastated by the Lombards in 756. He moved the relics of St. Petronilla, then regarded as a daughter of St. Peter and the special Roman patroness of the Frankish rulers, from the catacomb of St. Domitilla to a chapel in St. Peter's, built an oratory of the Blessed Virgin in that basilica, and erected a church in honor of the Apostles on the Via Sacra beyond the Roman Forum.

He died near San Paolo fuori le mura, where he had gone during the heat of summer, and was buried there; after three months his body was transferred to St. Peter's. The Liber Pontificalis praises the Christian charity and benevolence that he united with firmness. Paul is venerated as a saint and is honored as a patron of bishops and deacons, remembered among the early medieval popes who labored to secure the Church's freedom in turbulent times.

peter-canisius.history:
Peter Canisius was born at Nijmegen in the Netherlands on 8 May 1521, the son of Jacob Canisius, the city's wealthy burgomaster; his mother, Ægidia van Houweningen, died shortly after his birth. His name appears in records also as Kannees, Kanys, or De Hondt.

In 1536 he was sent to Cologne, where he studied arts, civil law, and theology at the university, received the degree of Master of Arts in 1540, and formed friendships with steadfast Catholics such as the cathedral canon Johann Gropper and the Carmelite Eberhard Billick. Although his father wished him to marry a wealthy young woman, he pledged himself to celibacy in February 1540.

While visiting Peter Faber in 1543 he made the Spiritual Exercises under Faber's direction and was admitted into the Society of Jesus at Mainz. With Leonhard Kessel and other helpers, laboring under great difficulties, he founded at Cologne the first German house of the order, preaching in the city and vicinity and teaching and debating at the university. Ordained a priest in 1546, he was sent by the clergy and university of Cologne to seek aid from Emperor Charles V, the papal nuncio, and the clergy of Liège against the apostate archbishop Hermann von Wied.

In 1547, as theologian to Cardinal Otto Truchsess von Waldburg, he took part in the general ecclesiastical council held at Trent and Bologna, speaking twice before the theologians, and afterward spent several months in Rome under Ignatius of Loyola. He taught rhetoric at Messina, and in 1549 he made his solemn profession at Rome in the founder's presence, received the doctorate in theology at Bologna on his journey north, and reached Ingolstadt as one of the Jesuits requested for the university by Duke William IV of Bavaria. He was elected rector there in 1550.

Ignatius sent him to Vienna in 1552, where he taught theology, preached at the cathedral of St. Stephen and at the court of Ferdinand I, and visited many abandoned parishes in Lower Austria. He opposed the court preacher Phauser, a married priest who preached Lutheran doctrine, and so incurred the lasting resentment of the king's son, the future Maximilian II. Three times Ferdinand offered him the bishopric of Vienna, and three times he refused.

One of the first Jesuits to labor in Germany during the Reformation, he spent more than fifty years traveling through Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. He attended the Diet of Augsburg with Ferdinand in 1555, preached at Prague, opened Jesuit colleges at Ingolstadt and Prague, and was appointed by Ignatius first provincial of Upper Germany. During the winter of 1556-57 he advised the king at the Diet of Ratisbon, and in the religious discussions at Worms he spoke repeatedly against Melanchthon as champion of the Catholics. He preached at Strasburg and strengthened the Catholics of Alsace and Freiburg, and at Straubing, whose pastors had fled, he preached three or four times a day for six weeks, undoing much harm by his gentleness. Summoned to Rome for the First General Congregation of his order, he was sent on with a papal nuncio to the imperial Diet of Pieterkow in Poland and addressed the clergy and university at Cracow. From 1559 to 1566 he was the cathedral preacher at Augsburg.

Above all he was a teacher. He composed three catechisms, written in clear and simple language, which went through hundreds of editions and shaped Catholic instruction for generations. He is commonly represented in art with his catechism and other books, or surrounded by children whom he is instructing.

He died at Fribourg in Switzerland on 21 November 1597. He was canonized and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1925, and his feast is kept on 21 December. He is venerated as a patron of catechists and of Germany.

martyrdom-of-pionius.history:
Pionius was a Christian presbyter of Smyrna who was martyred at Smyrna on 12 March 250, most likely during the persecution ordered by the emperor Decius. He is known to us through an ancient account, The Martyrdom of Pionius, also called the Acts of Pionius and known in Latin as the Martyrium Pionii or Passio Pionii, composed between roughly 250 and 300. Through this narrative he appears as a pastor who defended the Christian faith with learning and eloquence, refusing to offer sacrifice to the gods or to deny Christ.

Pionius was arrested on 23 February, the anniversary of St. Polycarp's martyrdom, together with Sabina and Asclepiades, as they prepared to commemorate the saint's death. The three had passed the previous night in prayer and fasting. Expecting arrest, Pionius had already fastened fetters around his own neck and those of his companions, to signify that they were already condemned; were Christians seen led away unbound, onlookers might otherwise have supposed—as they did of so many other Christians in Smyrna, the bishop included—that they were prepared to sacrifice. In the morning, after partaking of the Holy Bread and of water, they were conducted to the forum.

The forum was thronged with Greeks and Jews, for the day was a great Sabbath and therefore a general holiday in the city, an indication of the importance of the Jewish community in Smyrna. There Pionius addressed the multitude. He begged the Greeks to refrain from mocking the Christians who had apostatized, reminding them of what Homer had said against mocking the corpse of an enemy; to the Jews he offered the same plea in words drawn from Moses and Solomon. The address closed with a vehement refusal to offer sacrifice.

After the customary interrogatories and threats, Pionius and his companions were relegated to prison to await the arrival of the proconsul. There they found other confessors, among them a Montanist. Many pagans visited the prisoners, as did Christians who had sacrificed and lamented their fall; these last Pionius exhorted to repentance. Before the proconsul came, a further attempt was made to force the party into apostasy: they were carried off to a temple, where every effort was made to compel their participation in a sacrifice.

On 12 March Pionius was brought before the proconsul, who tried persuasion first and torture afterward; both having failed, he condemned Pionius to be burnt alive. He suffered in company with Metrodorus, a Marcionite priest, sealing his confession with his blood.

Eusebius dated the martyrdom to the reign of Antoninus, a mistake probably arising because he found the account of Pionius in a volume containing martyr-acts of an earlier date, possibly a manuscript lacking the chronological note found in present copies. The feast of St. Pionius is kept by Roman Catholics on 1 February and in the Eastern Orthodox churches on 11 March.

Pionius is remembered as a learned pastor who loved his flock unto death and as a faithful heir of the martyrs of Smyrna; he is honored as a patron of preachers and of the oppressed.

The narrative's mention that the martyrs partook of the Holy Bread and water is read, more probably, as an account of a private Communion rather than of a celebration, since only the bread is spoken of as holy and the small number present would make a celebration improbable; celebrations with bread and water are otherwise attested in the letters of St. Cyprian. A life of St. Polycarp is also attributed to Pionius.

pius-x.history:
Giuseppe Melchiorre Sarto was born on 2 June 1835 at Riese in the province of Treviso, in Venetia. His parents were Giovanni Battista Sarto, a postman who died in 1852, and Margarita Sanson, who lived to see her son made a cardinal. After early Latin lessons from the arch-priest of his town and studies at the gymnasium of Castelfranco Veneto, he received the tonsure in 1850 and a scholarship to the seminary of Padua, where he completed his classical, philosophical, and theological studies with distinction and was ordained a priest in 1858.

For nine years he was chaplain at Tombolo, assuming parish duties while the pastor was old and an invalid; he studied Saint Thomas and canon law, opened a night school for adults, and preached in neighboring towns. Named arch-priest of Salzano in 1867, he restored the church, maintained and enlarged the hospital at his own expense, labored among the sick during a cholera outbreak, and showed great care for the religious instruction of adults. In 1875 he became a canon of Treviso cathedral, serving as seminary rector and spiritual director, examiner of the clergy, and vicar-general, and arranging religious instruction for public school students; in 1878 he was elected vicar-capitular.

Created Bishop of Mantua in November 1884, he found a troubled see. His chief care was the formation of the clergy: he taught dogmatic theology at the seminary for several years and moral theology for one, followed the doctrine and method of Saint Thomas, gave copies of the Summa theologica to poorer students, and cultivated Gregorian chant with the seminarians. He held a diocesan synod in 1887, gave an example of pastoral zeal at the confessional, and supported the Opera dei Congressi.

In June 1893 Leo XIII made him a cardinal, with the title of San Bernardo alle Terme, and three days later named him Patriarch of Venice; a dispute with the Italian government over the exequatur delayed his taking possession for eighteen months. At Venice he attended to the seminary, where a faculty of canon law was established, promoted Gregorian chant, patronized Lorenzo Perosi, encouraged social works such as rural parochial banks, and opposed the dangers of certain doctrines and the conduct of certain Christian-Democrats. After Leo XIII's death he was elected pope on 4 August 1903 by fifty-five of sixty votes and was crowned on 9 August.

His first encyclical set the motto of his pontificate: instaurare omnia in Christo, to restore all things in Christ. He urged frequent and, if possible, daily reception of Holy Communion, relaxed the law of fasting so that the sick might receive Communion more often, and by the decree Quam Singulari in 1910 provided that children should make their first Communion soon after reaching the age of discretion. He promoted the reform of church music and began the codification of canon law, and combated the errors of Modernism. His charity extended to calamities: for the earthquakes in Calabria, Catholics worldwide contributed nearly seven million francs at his appeal, and he likewise aided victims of the eruption of Vesuvius and of disasters in Portugal and Ireland.

Honored as patron of first communicants and catechists, he died in 1914, heartbroken at the outbreak of the First World War. He was canonized in 1954, the first pope to be canonized since Saint Pius V. His feast day is 21 August.

placidus-abbot.history:
Saint Placidus, a monk of the sixth century, is remembered as one of the first disciples of Saint Benedict of Nursia. He was the son of the Roman patrician Tertullus, and while still a child he was brought to Saint Benedict's monastery at Subiaco and dedicated to God in the manner provided for in chapter 69 of Saint Benedict's Rule. In this he belongs to the first generation of Benedict's followers. His feast is kept on 5 October, and he is venerated as a patron of monks and of youth and as co-patron of Messina.

The Dialogues of Saint Gregory the Great preserve the best-known incident of his boyhood. Sent to draw water from the lake below the monastery, Placidus fell in and was carried off by the current. At Saint Benedict's order his fellow monk Maurus ran across the surface of the lake and drew the boy safely to shore, the rescue having come at Benedict's prayer. Gregory's account has given the episode its lasting meaning as an image of the bond between master and disciple.

It appears certain that Placidus accompanied Saint Benedict when, about 529, Benedict removed his community to Monte Cassino. Tradition holds that the mountain had been made over to Benedict by Placidus's father, so that the senator's family is remembered in connection with the founding of that abbey.

Of his later life nothing is known. The oldest witness to his veneration is liturgical: his name appears in the Litany of the Saints in an ancient psalter at Vallombrosa, placed among the confessors immediately after those of Saint Benedict and Saint Maurus, and the same order is found in a codex at Subiaco attributed to the ninth century. In these early lists he is honored as a confessor rather than as a martyr, a detail that bears on the later accounts of his death.

The tradition that he died a martyr rests on a later and disputed source, an account known as the Passio Sancti Placidi, which purports to have been written by Gordianus, a servant of the saint; on its authority he has often been described as abbot and martyr. By this account he is said to have met death in Sicily at the hands of Saracen invaders from Spain, a dating that is plainly anachronistic for the sixth century, though intelligible if the work was composed after the Muslim invasions of Sicily. It is now generally agreed that the narrative is in fact the work of Peter the Deacon, a monk of Monte Cassino of the twelfth century, and that the writer began by confusing Saint Placidus with an earlier Placitus, who with Euticius and thirty companions was martyred in Sicily under Diocletian, whose feast falls on 5 October in the earlier martyrologies. Having thus made Saint Placidus a martyr, the author accounted for his death by the Saracen invasion. The whole question has been discussed by the Bollandists.

Such, in substance, is what may be affirmed of him. He was a Christian boy entrusted by a noble Roman father to Saint Benedict at Subiaco; he was a disciple preserved from the lake in Gregory's narrative, and a companion of Benedict in the removal to Monte Cassino. On the testimony of a later and disputed tradition he journeyed to Sicily and met martyrdom, and at Messina he is honored as co-patron. The incident of the lake and the austere schooling of the cloister have made his name a lasting image of the monastic life: obedience, humility, and readiness to suffer for Christ.

pontius-pilate.history:
Pontius Pilate, the fifth Roman procurator of Judaea, took office in A.D. 26, succeeding Valerius Gratus after the deposition of Archelaus, the son of Herod. He held greater authority than most procurators of the empire, combining financial administration with supreme judicial power, and his unusually long term, ending in A.D. 36, spanned the whole of the active ministry of Saint John the Baptist and of Jesus Christ.

Pilate was necessarily of equestrian rank, but little is known of his family or origin; the Pontii were a Samnite gens, and the conjecture that he had been a freedman rests on no adequate evidence. He owed his appointment to the influence of Sejanus. His official residence was the palace of Herod at Caesarea, garrisoned by some three thousand soldiers, who came up to Jerusalem at the feasts; it was thus that Pilate was in the city at the time of the Crucifixion.

Contemporaries spoke harshly of his government. Philo called him inflexible, merciless, and obstinate, and the Jews hated an administration that was severe and heedless of their religious susceptibilities. Standards bearing the image of Tiberius, which he had set up in Jerusalem, provoked an outbreak that nearly ended in massacre, and Tiberius afterward ordered him to remove certain gilt shields erected against popular remonstrance. The Gospel of Luke likewise records the Galilaeans whose blood he mingled with their sacrifices, an incident in keeping with the rest of his rule, and Pilate grew anxious lest further hostile reports reach the emperor.

It is for his part in the trial of Jesus that his name, recited in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds, is forever covered with infamy, though the matter appeared to him at the time of small importance. He stands as a type of the worldly man, knowing the right and wishing to do it so far as it involves no personal sacrifice: he would gladly have acquitted Christ and made serious efforts in that direction, but gave way at once when his own position was threatened, and ordered the crucifixion.

His rule ended through trouble in Samaria. An impostor claimed that he could discover the sacred vessels said to have been hidden by Moses on Mount Gerizim, and armed Samaritans gathered there in great numbers. Suspecting some deeper design, Pilate hurried forces against them, and many were slain; the Samaritans appealed to Vitellius, legate of Syria, and Pilate was summoned to Rome to answer charges against his whole administration. Before he could reach the city, Tiberius had died. There the authentic sources fall silent, though tradition, reported by Eusebius on the authority of earlier unnamed writers, holds that he fell into great misfortunes under Caligula and eventually took his own life. The Mors Pilati describes his body as carried from river to river until it was sunk, according to later tradition, in a tarn on the mountain called Pilatus near Lucerne, whose name more probably derives from the cap of cloud that often covers it.

The canonical Gospels already lay stress on Pilate's efforts to acquit Christ, and this tendency advanced in the apocryphal Gospels until later ages claimed that he actually became a Christian. On this tradition the Abyssinian Church reckons him among the saints, assigning 25 June to him and to his wife Claudia Procula, whose conversion was believed as early as the second century. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church venerates him as a martyr and saint, holding that he came to faith in Christ, while Coptic tradition relates that he confessed Christ and suffered for his confession after returning to Rome.

Thus the Ethiopian synaxarium keeps the memory of the procurator who washed his hands before the crowd, holding that the judge who washed his hands at Gabbatha was in the end washed in the blood of the Lamb he condemned. For this reason he is honored as a patron of converts and of martyrs.

prisca.history:
Prisca, whose name also appears in the form Priscilla, was a martyr of the Roman Church whose dates are unknown. Her name occurs frequently in the early authorities on the history of the Church of Rome, but several early Christians bore it: the wife of Aquila, a pupil of St. Paul, was so called, and the epitaph of a Roman Christian named Priscilla has also been found in the larger catacomb on the Via Nomentana. Which of these persons, if any, can be identified with the martyr cannot be established with certainty.

A martyr named Prisca was buried in the Catacomb of Priscilla on the Via Salaria, where her grave was venerated. The place of her interment is explicitly mentioned in all the seventh-century itineraries to the graves of the Roman martyrs. The Martyrologium Hieronymianum likewise records under 18 January a martyr Priscilla on the Via Salaria, evidently identical with the Prisca whose grave was honored there. Her feast is observed on 18 January.

On the Aventine Hill there still stands a church of St. Prisca, built on the site of the Titulus Priscoe, a title church mentioned in the fifth century and probably erected in the fourth. Near the church there was found in the eighteenth century a bronze tablet of the year 224 by which the senator Caius Marius Pudens Cornelianus was granted citizenship in a Spanish city; since such tablets were generally put up in the house of the person honored, it is possible that the senator's palace occupied the spot. It is probable that the Prisca who founded the title church — or who, perhaps as early as the third century, gave the use of part of the house standing there for Christian services — belonged to his family. Whether she was herself the martyr cannot be proved, though some family relationship is likely, for the name Priscilla appears also in the senatorial family of the Acilii Glabriones, whose burial place was the Catacomb of Priscilla.

Later tradition attached a fuller story to her name. One legend identified the founder of the Aventine title with St. Paul's friend Priscilla, whose home would have stood on the spot, and from which St. Paul was said to have sent a greeting in his Epistle to the Romans. Tradition likewise holds that a Prisca of noble birth was singled out for her refusal to renounce Christ, that she was scourged, burned, and exposed to wild beasts in the arena, and that she remained unharmed through each ordeal before at last winning the crown of martyrdom. Another legend relates that she was beheaded at the tenth milestone on the Via Ostiensis and that Pope Eutychianus translated her body to the church of St. Prisca on the Aventine; this whole narrative is judged unhistorical and its details impossible. Because 18 January is assigned as the day of this execution, the Prisca of these legends is probably the same as the Roman martyr buried in the Catacomb of Priscilla.

Prisca is revered as a martyr in the Catholic Church, in Eastern Orthodoxy, and in the Anglican Communion. Her feast is kept on 18 January, and she is honored as a patron of single women, invoked for protection amid trials for the faith.

raymond-nonnatus.history:
St. Raymond Nonnatus was born around 1204 at Portell, in the diocese of Urgel in Catalonia, though some accounts place his birth in 1200; he died at Cardona on 31 August 1240, and his feast is celebrated on 31 August. According to a long tradition, his mother died in bearing him and the child was delivered from her womb, whence his surname, Nonnatus, meaning 'not born.' He was of a noble but poor family and early showed traits of piety and great talent. His father first ordered him to tend a farm, but later gave him permission to take the habit of the Mercedarians at Barcelona, which he received at the hands of the founder of the order, St. Peter Nolasco. That order had been established for the ransom of Christians held captive by Muslim rulers.

Raymond made such progress in the religious life that he was soon considered worthy to succeed his master in the office of ransomer, and he succeeded St. Peter Nolasco as head of the order. He was sent to Algiers in North Africa, where he liberated many captives. When the money for ransom failed, he gave himself as a hostage in exchange for the freedom of others. He was zealous in teaching the Christian religion and made many converts, and this success embittered the Muslim authorities.

He was then subjected to all kinds of indignities and cruelty, was made to run the gauntlet, and was at last sentenced to impalement. The hope of a greater sum of ransom money caused the governor to commute this sentence into imprisonment. Tradition holds that, to prevent him from preaching for Christ, his lips were pierced with a red-hot iron and closed with a padlock, an emblem that has remained associated with his image. In time he was ransomed, and he returned to Spain.

After his arrival in Spain in 1239, Pope Gregory IX made him a cardinal. In the following year he was called to Rome by the pope, but came only as far as Cardona, where he died on 31 August 1240. His body was brought to the chapel of St. Nicholas near his old farm.

Pope Alexander VII placed Raymond's name in the Roman Martyrology in 1657, the year given for his canonization. Because of the manner of his birth, he is invoked by expectant mothers, by women in labor, and by midwives, and he is honored as a patron of childbirth; he is also invoked by persons falsely accused. The appendix to the Roman Ritual provides a formula for the blessing of water in his honor, to be used by the sick, and another for the blessing of candles. In art he is pictured in the habit of his order, surrounded by ransomed captives, with a padlock on his lips.

rita-of-cascia.history:
St. Rita of Cascia was born at Rocca Porena in the Diocese of Spoleto in 1386 and died at the Augustinian convent of Cascia in 1456. Her feast is kept on 22 May. In sacred art she is represented holding roses, or roses and figs, and sometimes bearing a wound in her forehead, which tradition holds to have come from a thorn of Christ's crown.

According to the Life written at the time of her beatification by the Augustinian Jacob Carelicci, compiled from two older biographies, she was the daughter of parents advanced in years, distinguished for a charity that merited them the surname of "Peacemakers of Jesus Christ". Rita's great desire was to become a nun, but in obedience to the will of her parents she was married at the age of twelve to a man extremely cruel and ill-tempered. For eighteen years she lived as a model wife and mother.

When her husband was murdered, she tried in vain to dissuade her twin sons from attempting to take revenge. Appealing to Heaven to prevent such a crime on their part, she saw them taken away by death, reconciled to God.
