Widowed, she applied for admission to the Augustinian convent at Cascia, but, being a widow, she was refused. By continued entreaties, and, as is related, by Divine intervention, she gained admission, received the habit of the order, and in due time made her profession. As a religious she was an example to all, she excelled in mortifications, and she became widely known for the efficacy of her prayers.

In 1637 Urban VIII permitted her Mass and Office. On account of the many miracles reported to have been wrought at her intercession, she received in Spain the title of La Santa de los impossibiles, the saint of the impossible. She was solemnly canonized on 24 May 1900. In popular devotion she is honored as a patroness of impossible causes and of difficult marriages, a standing that reflects both the Spanish title given her and the patience with which she bore her own marriage.

robert-bellarmine.history:
{"history": "Robert Bellarmine was born at Montepulciano in Italy on 4 October 1542. His father was Vincenzo Bellarmino, and his mother, Cinthia Cervini, was the sister of Cardinal Marcello Cervini, afterwards Pope Marcellus II, which made him nephew to that pope. Brought up at the newly founded Jesuit college in his native town, he entered the Society of Jesus on 20 September 1560 and made his first vows the next day. After three years of philosophy at the Roman College, he taught the humanities at Florence and then at Mondovì, and began his theology at Padua in 1567.

In 1569 he was sent to finish his studies at Louvain, where he could gain a fuller acquaintance with the prevailing heresies. Ordained there, he quickly won a reputation both as professor and as preacher, drawing to his pulpit Catholics and Protestants alike.

In 1576 he was recalled to Italy and entrusted with the newly founded chair of Controversies at the Roman College. The lectures he delivered there grew into De Controversiis, the Disputationes that form the chief title to his greatness. The earliest attempt to systematize the controversies of the age, the work made an immense impression throughout Europe, and its blow to Protestantism was so keenly felt in Germany and England that special chairs were founded to provide replies to it. Later criticism has impaired the value of some of its historical arguments, but it long remained the classical book on its subject.

In 1588 he was made Spiritual Father to the Roman College, and in 1590 he went with Cardinal Gaetano as theologian on the embassy Pope Sixtus V was sending to France amid the troubles of the civil wars. He learned there that Sixtus, who had warmly accepted the dedication of his great work, now proposed to put its first volume on the Index, because it assigned to the Holy See not a direct but only an indirect power over temporals. Bellarmine, whose loyalty to the Holy See was intense, took this greatly to heart; the matter was averted by Sixtus's death, and the new pope, Gregory XIV, granted the work a special approbation. Bellarmine likewise sat on the final commission for the revision of the Vulgate desired by the Council of Trent. When a defective edition printed under Sixtus V had to be replaced without affixing a stigma to his name, Bellarmine proposed that the corrected edition continue in Sixtus's name with a prefatory explanation, and he himself wrote the preface still prefixed to the Clementine edition.

Resuming his work as Spiritual Father, he guided the last years of the young St. Aloysius Gonzaga, who died in his arms at the Roman College in 1591; many years later he successfully promoted the youth's beatification. He was made Rector of the Roman College in 1592 and Provincial of Naples in 1595. In 1597 Pope Clement VIII recalled him to Rome, made him his own theologian, Examiner of Bishops, and Consultor of the Holy Office, and in 1599 created him Cardinal-Priest of the title of Santa Maria in via, alleging as his reason that the Church of God had not his equal in learning. He then served as an assessor in the Congregation de Auxiliis, instituted to settle the recent controversy between the Thomists and the Molinists.

In later years, as Archbishop of Capua, he was known for his pastoral care of the poor. Alongside his two famous catechisms, he wrote a series of spiritual works during his annual retreats, including De Ascensione mentis in Deum (1615), De Aeterna felicitate sanctorum (1616), De gemitu columbae (1617), and De arte bene moriendi (1620), as well as a lucid exposition of all the psalms (1611). In 1613, at the request of two Jesuit fathers, he also wrote a brief account of his own life.

Bellarmine died on 17 September 1621, the date on which his feast is now observed. He was canonized in 1930 and declared a Doctor of the Church the following year, and he is venerated as a patron of catechists and canon lawyers."}

romuald.history:
Romuald was born at Ravenna, probably about 950, into the noble class of tenth-century Italy. As a young man he lived the careless, even dissipated life usual in his rank, yet felt drawn to the eremitical ideal. At the age of twenty, stricken with horror because his father had killed an enemy in a duel, he fled to the Abbey of San Apollinare-in-Classe and, after some hesitation, entered religion. The abbey had recently been reformed by St. Maieul of Cluny, but its observance still seemed too lenient to him; his blunt efforts to correct the less zealous monks stirred up such enmity that he obtained leave to retire to Venice, where he placed himself under the direction of a hermit named Marinus and led a life of extraordinary severity.

About 978 his counsel figured in a notable conversion. Pietro Orseolo I, Doge of Venice, who had obtained his office through acquiescence in the murder of his predecessor, began to suffer remorse for the crime. On the advice of Guarinus, Abbot of San Miguel-de-Cuxa in Catalonia, and of Marinus and Romuald, the doge abandoned his office and relations and fled to Cuxa, where he received the Benedictine habit, while Romuald and Marinus built a hermitage beside the monastery. Romuald lived there five years in great austerity, gathering a band of disciples. Hearing that his father Sergius, who had become a monk, was tormented with doubts about his vocation, he returned in haste to Italy and, by subjecting Sergius to severe discipline, resolved them.

For about thirty years he then wandered through Italy founding monasteries and hermitages, with Pereum as a favorite resting place. In 1005 he went to Val-di-Castro for about two years and, on leaving it, foretold that he would return to die there alone and unaided. A projected journey to Hungary was prevented by persistent illness. He appeared at Vallombrosa in 1012 and then moved into the Diocese of Arezzo, where, tradition holds, a certain Maldolus, who had seen a vision of monks in white garments ascending into heaven, gave him land afterward known as the Campus Maldoli, or Camaldoli. Romuald built five cells for hermits on this land, and together with the nearby monastery of Fontebuono, built two years later, these formed the mother-house of the Camaldolese Order, a branch of the Benedictine family that joined the solitary life of hermits to community life.

He retired to Monte-Sitria in 1013 and to Bifolco in 1021, and five years later returned to Val-di-Castro, where he died alone in his cell on 19 June 1027, as he had foretold. St. Peter Damian, his first biographer, and nearly all Camaldolese writers asserted that he died at the age of one hundred and twenty, which would place his birth about 907; most modern writers dispute this, regarding it as irreconcilable with the known dates of his life. He is remembered for his strict asceticism and for a counsel attributed to him, that one should sit in one's cell as in paradise.

Veneration of Romuald gathered around his tomb. Many miracles were reported there, over which an altar was permitted at his grave in 1032; in 1466 his body was found incorrupt, and in 1481 it was translated to Fabriano. He was canonized in 1582, and in 1595 Clement VIII extended the celebration of his feast to the whole Church. The liturgical reform of 1969 assigned his memorial to 19 June, the day of his death, and his feast is kept on that date. In art he is shown pointing to a ladder on which monks ascend to heaven. He is honored as a patron of hermits and monks.

sebastian.history:
St. Sebastian is venerated as a Roman martyr of the late third century, although little more than the fact of his martyrdom can be established with certainty. The Depositio martyrum of the chronologer of 354 records that Sebastian was buried on the Via Appia, and St. Ambrose attests that he came from Milan and was venerated there even in Ambrose's own time. Beyond these facts, the story of his life and death rests chiefly on a later account.

That account, the Acts of Sebastian's martyrdom, probably written early in the fifth century and formerly ascribed erroneously to Ambrose, presents him as an officer in the imperial bodyguard. According to this tradition, Sebastian had secretly performed many acts of love and charity for his brethren in the faith. When he was discovered to be a Christian, in 286, he was handed over to the Mauretanian archers and pierced with arrows. Left for dead, he is said to have been found alive and healed by the widowed St. Irene. He was finally killed by the blows of a club. These narratives, however, are regarded as unhistorical and not worthy of belief. The earliest mosaic of St. Sebastian, probably belonging to the year 682, shows a grown, bearded man in court dress, with no trace of an arrow; it was the art of the Renaissance that first portrayed him as a youth transfixed by arrows.

A basilica, numbered among the seven chief churches of Rome, was built over his grave in 367, and the present church on the site was completed in 1611 by Scipio Cardinal Borghese. Part of his relics were taken in 826 to St. Medard at Soissons.

Sebastian is honored as a patron of soldiers and as a protector against the plague. Celebrated answers to prayer for his protection against the plague are related of Rome in 680, Milan in 1575, and Lisbon in 1599. His feast day is 20 January.

pope-sergius-i.history:
Sergius I was bishop of Rome from 687 until his death on 8 September 701, having been consecrated, probably on 15 December 687, amid a bitter rivalry between Paschal and Theodore. While Pope Conon lay dying, the archdeacon Paschal offered the exarch of Ravenna a large sum of money to bring about his own election as successor, and through the exarch's influence the archdeacon was elected by a number of people. At about the same time, another faction elected the archpriest Theodore. The mass of the clergy and people, however, set the two rivals aside and chose Sergius, who was then duly consecrated. Sergius, the son of Tiberius, was a native of Antioch, born to an Antiochene family in Syria; he had been educated in Sicily and ordained by Pope Leo II.

The new pope had numerous relations with England and the English. He received Caedwalla, king of the West Saxons, and baptized him in 689; when Caedwalla died in Rome, Sergius caused him to be buried in St. Peter's. He ordered that St. Wilfrid be restored to his see, and he greatly favoured St. Aldhelm, Abbot of Malmesbury. He is also credited with endeavouring to secure the Venerable Bede as his adviser. Finally, he consecrated the Englishman St. Willibrord bishop and sent him to preach Christianity to the Frisians.

The major conflict of his reign concerned the so-called Quinisext, or Trullan, Council of 692. The emperor Justinian II wanted Sergius to sign the council's decrees, in which the Greeks allowed priests and deacons to keep the wives they had married before their ordination, and which aimed at placing the Patriarch of Constantinople on a level with the Pope of Rome. Sergius refused to acknowledge the synod; his refusal, grounded in his judgment that its canons were contrary to Roman tradition, was resolute. The emperor thereupon sent an officer to bring the pope to Constantinople, but the Roman people protected their pope, and Justinian himself was soon afterwards deposed, in 695.

Sergius also succeeded in extinguishing the last remnants of the Schism of the Three Chapters in Aquileia. Within Rome itself he repaired and adorned many basilicas, added the Agnus Dei, the invocation of the Lamb of God, to the Mass, and instituted processions to various churches.

He died on 8 September 701, after a pontificate of nearly fourteen years. His reign thus joined a resolute defence of Roman practice, the settlement of the schism at Aquileia, and sustained engagement with the English Church, and he is honoured as a patron of church unity and of bishops.

simeon-stylites-the-younger.history:
Simeon Stylites the Younger was born at Antioch in 521 and died there on 24 May 597. His father was a native of Edessa, and his mother, Martha, afterwards came to be revered as a saint; a life of her preserves a letter that Simeon sent from his pillar to Thomas, the guardian of the true cross at Jerusalem. Like his earlier namesake, the first of the pillar saints, he appears to have been drawn to a life of austerity from an early age.

He attached himself to a community of ascetics living within the mandra, or enclosure, of another pillar-hermit named John, who acted as their spiritual director. While still only a boy, Simeon had a pillar erected for himself close to that of John, and in the letter to Thomas he states that he was living on a pillar when he lost his first teeth. For eight years, until John died, he remained near his master's column, close enough for the two to converse, and during this period the older hermit kept his austerities in a measure of restraint.

In all, Simeon maintained the life of a stylite for 68 years, moving on several occasions to a new pillar. On the occasion of the first of these changes, during the short time he spent upon the ground, the Patriarch of Antioch and the Bishop of Seleucia ordained him deacon. After John's death he gave fuller rein to his ascetical practices; the historian Evagrius reports that he lived on nothing but the branches of a shrub growing near Theopolis. In time he was ordained priest and was thus able to offer the Holy Sacrifice in memory of his mother, his disciples climbing the ladder one after another to receive Communion at his hands.

As with most of the pillar saints, a large number of miracles came to be attributed to him, and in several reported instances cures were believed to have been effected through pictures representing him. Toward the close of his life he occupied a column on a mountainside near Antioch, called from his miracles the 'Hill of Wonders', and it was here that he died. He is also remembered by the title Simeon of the Admirable Mountain.

Several writings are attributed to the younger Simeon: short spiritual tractates, an 'Apocalypse', and letters to the Emperors Justinian and Justin II, as well as liturgical hymns known as troparia. The principal sources for his life are a long work by Nicephorus of Antioch, the life of his mother Martha, and the Ecclesiastical History of Evagrius.

Later tradition holds that pilgrims came from far and wide to seek his counsel, drawn by the endurance of a man who spent nearly seven decades living upon the pillar. Venerated in both the Catholic and the Eastern Orthodox Churches, he is honored as a patron of hermits and contemplatives, though his feast day is not fixed in the universal calendar.

pope-simplicius.history:
Simplicius, according to the Liber Pontificalis the son of Castinus, a citizen of Tivoli, was elected Bishop of Rome without difficulty upon the death of Pope Hilarius in 468. The date of his birth is unknown; he governed the Roman Church until his death on 10 March 483.

His pontificate witnessed the end of the Western Roman Empire. In 476 the Herulian ruler Odoacer deposed the last emperor, Romulus Augustulus, and assumed the title of King of Italy. Though an Arian, Odoacer treated the Catholic Church with much respect and retained the greater part of the former administration, so that Rome changed little. Simplicius thus guided the See of Peter across the collapse of the imperial order in the West.

In the East the Monophysite controversy still carried on. Simplicius defended the independence of the Church against the Caesaropapism of the Byzantine rulers and the authority of the Apostolic See in questions of faith. When the emperor pressed him to confirm the twenty-eighth canon of Chalcedon, which granted the See of Constantinople the same privileges of honor as the Bishop of Old Rome, he rejected the request and opposed its enforcement.

The usurpation of Basiliscus, who in 476 drove Emperor Zeno into exile, intensified the dispute. Basiliscus sought the support of the Monophysites, allowing the deposed patriarchs Timotheus Ailurus of Alexandria and Peter Fullo of Antioch to return, and issued an edict commanding that only the first three ecumenical synods be accepted, rejecting Chalcedon and the Letter of Pope Leo. Acacius of Constantinople wavered, but the firm stand of the populace and of monks zealous for the Catholic faith moved him to oppose the emperor. Simplicius wrote to Acacius and to Basiliscus himself, declaring of the See of Peter in a letter of 10 January 476: “This same norm of Apostolic doctrine is firmly maintained by his successors.” For the displaced Catholic Patriarch of Alexandria, Timotheus Salophakiolus, he labored untiringly, and when Zeno recovered the throne in 477 and sent the pope a thoroughly Catholic confession of faith, Simplicius congratulated him and bade him ascribe the victory to God.

Zeno recalled the edicts of Basiliscus, banished Peter Fullo, and reinstated Salophakiolus, yet strife continued at Alexandria. When Salophakiolus allowed the name of the Monophysite Dioscurus to be read in the diptychs, Simplicius wrote to Acacius on 13 March 478 urging that the disgrace be wiped away. At Acacius's request the pope condemned by name Mongus, Fullo, Paul of Ephesus, and John of Apamea. After Salophakiolus died, the Monophysites again chose Peter Mongus, while the Catholics elected John Talaia; Acacius and the emperor sided with Mongus and agreed with him upon a formula of union, a course that led to the lasting rupture with Constantinople known as the Acacian schism.

In Rome he built a fourth church, honoring St. Balbina near the Licinian palace at the place of her grave, which still remains. He likewise secured regular services, baptism, and the discipline of penance at the great catacomb churches outside the walls—St. Peter's in the Vatican, St. Paul's on the Via Ostiensis, and St. Lawrence's on the Via Tiburtina—by assigning the clergy of three sections of the city to serve them in an established order.

Simplicius was buried in St. Peter's in the Vatican. After his death Odoacer sought to influence the filling of the papal see, and the prefect Basilius asserted that the dying pope had begged that no one be consecrated Roman bishop without his consent; the Roman clergy opposed the edict as limiting their right of election, maintaining that only canonical election with universal consent made a rightful bishop. Venerated as a saint from early times, with his feast kept on 10 March, Simplicius is honored as a patron of bishops and of church reform.

pope-sixtus-iii.history:
Sixtus III, also written Xystus III, was consecrated bishop of Rome on July 31, 432, and served until his death on August 18, 440. Before his elevation he had been prominent among the Roman clergy and carried on correspondence with St. Augustine. His pontificate unfolded amid the Nestorian and Pelagian controversies, and it was probably on account of his conciliatory disposition that he was falsely accused of leaning toward these heresies.

As pope, Sixtus approved the Acts of the Council of Ephesus and endeavored to restore peace between Cyril of Alexandria and John of Antioch. In the Pelagian controversy he frustrated the attempt of Julian of Eclanum to be readmitted to communion with the Catholic Church. He likewise defended the pope's right of supremacy over Illyricum against the local bishops and the ambitious designs of Proclus of Constantinople.

At Rome he left his mark on the city's sacred buildings. He restored the Basilica of Liberius, now known as St. Mary Major; later tradition holds that he dedicated it to the Mother of God and adorned it with mosaics. He also enlarged the Basilica of St. Lawrence-Without-the-Walls and obtained precious gifts from the Emperor Valentinian III for St. Peter's and the Lateran Basilica.

Eight letters of his survive. The works On Riches, On False Teachers, and On Chastity that bear his name were not written by him, and an account asserting that the consul Bassus accused him of a crime is a forgery.

His feast is kept on March 28. In later devotional tradition he is honored as a patron of bishops and of Marian devotion.

stephen-of-muret.history:
Stephen of Muret, who died at Muret on 8 February 1124, is honored as the founder of the Abbey and Order of Grandmont. Born in 1045, he was drawn from his youth toward the eremitical life. The traditional account of his early life runs as follows: in his twelfth year he accompanied his father, the Viscount of Thiers, to Italy, and was left there to be educated by Milo, Archbishop of Benevento. After twelve years in the archbishop's household he lived as an inmate of a Benedictine monastery in Calabria, though he never received the habit. He returned to France to bid farewell to his parents, having resolved to enter religion, but finding them dead he went back to Italy. When his patron Milo had also died, Stephen established himself at Rome, where he studied the rules of the city's religious houses. After four years there he obtained from Gregory VII a Bull authorizing him to found an institute resembling the solitaries he had frequented in Calabria, and then returned to France, settling, according to tradition, at Muret in 1076, a retreat in the forests of the Limousin.

This narrative presents serious chronological difficulties and cannot be accepted as it stands. According to the same tradition, Stephen's father visited Italy on pilgrimage to St. Nicholas at Bari, yet that saint's relics were not placed there until some years later; and Milo was not Archbishop of Benevento for twelve years. The exact truth of the saint's life accordingly cannot now be established. It remains that Stephen went to Italy and there saw certain religious whose holy life inspired him to imitate them, though who these were—Carthusians or Benedictines—is no longer known. The long quarrel over which great order could claim Grandmont as its offspring, together with the forgeries occasioned by that dispute, has done much to involve the founder's life in obscurity.

What is certain is that Stephen founded the Order of Grandmont, although he did little for his disciples except to offer them the example of his holy life; it was not until after his death that the order was firmly established. Grandmont thereafter took its place among the austere reformed monastic congregations of the Middle Ages.

Drawn in his own day to the eremitical life, Stephen is venerated today as a patron of hermits and of monks. Though the details of his career remain clouded, the memory of his sanctity endured. He was canonized in 1189, and his feast occurs on 8 February. His head is preserved in the parish church of St. Sylvestre, in the canton of Laurière (Haute-Vienne). Writings attributed to him are not considered authentic.

pope-sylvester-i.history:
{"history": "Pope Sylvester I governed the Church of Rome for twenty-one years during one of the most decisive turning points in Christian history, serving as bishop of Rome from 31 January 314 until his death on 31 December 335. The date of his birth is unknown. According to the Liber Pontificalis, the ancient chronicle of the Roman pontiffs, he was the son of a Roman named Rufinus, while the legendary Vita beati Sylvestri calls his mother Justa. He was raised to the See of Rome after the death of his predecessor Miltiades, and his pontificate coincided with the reign of Constantine the Great, when the public position of the Church improved so greatly that the change must have been very noticeable at Rome. It is consequently to be regretted that so little authoritative information concerning his pontificate survives.

From an early date, legend brought Sylvester into close relationship with the first Christian emperor, but in ways contrary to historical fact. The legendary Vita beati Sylvestri, which appeared in the East, has been preserved in Greek, Syriac, and Latin in the Constitutum Sylvestri, an apocryphal account of an alleged Roman council belonging to the Symmachian forgeries and appearing between 501 and 508, and also in the Donatio Constantini. The accounts these writings give of a persecution of Sylvester, of the healing and baptism of Constantine, of the emperor's gift to the pope, of the rights granted to him, and of a council of 275 bishops at Rome are entirely legendary. Tradition thus associates him with the baptism of Constantine, but this detail rests on later legend rather than on history.

What can be affirmed with confidence concerns the Arian controversy. Sylvester took part in the negotiations concerning Arianism and the Council of Nicaea, and the expression homoousion was probably agreed upon with him before the council met. He also sent legates to this first ecumenical council. It remains uncertain, however, whether Constantine had arranged beforehand with Sylvester concerning the actual convening of the council, nor whether there was an express papal confirmation of its decrees beyond the signatures of the papal legates.

The great churches of his era form the most visible monument of his pontificate. During his years as bishop there rose at Rome the basilica and baptistery of the Lateran near the former imperial palace where the pope lived, the basilica of the Sessorian palace known as Santa Croce, the church of St. Peter in the Vatican, and several cemeterial churches over the graves of martyrs, all founded by Constantine; the pope no doubt helped toward their construction. His memory is especially connected with the titular Church of Equitius, named for a Roman presbyter said to have erected it on his property near the baths of Diocletian; the church still exists, and parts of the present building may date from the fourth century. On the Via Salaria he built a cemeterial church over the Catacomb of Priscilla, and in this church he was buried.

Sylvester is also remembered for the inner development of the Roman Church. He doubtless contributed to the development of its liturgy, the first martyrology of the Roman martyrs was probably drawn up during his reign, and he is connected with the establishment of the Roman school of singing.

His feast is kept on 31 December, the date given in the Depositio episcoporum, the list of the burial days of the Roman bishops compiled barely a year after his death, and the same date appears in the Calendar of Philocalus; this day is therefore doubtless the day of his burial. His possible relations with Armenia, treated in connection with St. Gregory the Illuminator, remain obscure. Honored as a steadfast pastor who guided the Church from the age of suffering into the age of peace, he is invoked as a patron of bishops and of church unity."}

pope-symmachus.history:
St. Symmachus, a native of Sardinia whose father, according to the Liber Pontificalis, was named Fortunatus, was baptized at Rome and ordained deacon. Upon the death of Pope Anastasius II he was elected pope by a majority of the Roman clergy at the Lateran Basilica on 22 November 498 and consecrated Bishop of Rome the same day, with the approval of part of the Roman senate. A minority of the clergy, friendly to the Byzantines, met that same day at the Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore and chose the archpresbyter Laurentius as antipope. According to the chronicler Theodorus Lector, this faction was aided with money from the senator Festus, who hoped Laurentius would favor the Henotikon of Emperor Zeno.

Both parties agreed to submit the dispute to Theodoric, the Gothic king who ruled Italy, and he decided for Symmachus as the candidate elected first and by the majority. Laurentius submitted, and at a Roman synod on 1 March 499 the pope conferred on him the Diocese of Nocera in Campania. The same synod decreed deposition for any Roman cleric who sought votes for a papal successor during a pope's lifetime.

The peace did not hold. In 501 the Laurentian party appealed anew to Theodoric, citing the pope's celebration of Easter on 25 March according to the old Roman reckoning while they observed 22 April, and made further accusations, among them the squandering of the Church's property. Summoned to the king, Symmachus learned the terms of the indictment at Rimini and, refusing to acknowledge the king as his judge, returned home; his opponents occupied the Lateran palace, so that he resided near the Basilica of St. Peter outside the walls. He consented to a synod of investigation but protested against the visitor, Bishop Peter of Altinum, whom Theodoric sent to administer the Roman See; contrary to the king's command, Peter went over to the pope's opponents and was later dismissed.

The synod met at the Basilica of Julius between May and July 502, and the pope declared himself ready to answer the accusations if the visitor were removed and he restored as administrator of the Church; Theodoric refused these conditions. At a second session on 1 September 502 in the Sessorian Basilica, Symmachus set out from St. Peter's to defend himself but was attacked and maltreated on the way, escaping with difficulty while several priests with him were killed or wounded. He then refused to appear, though summoned three times, and the assembled bishops, finding no precedent by which an occupant of the Roman See could be judged by other bishops, declared that they could not pass sentence.

At a fourth session on 23 October 502, the Synodus Palmaris, the matter was commended to the judgment of God, and Symmachus was declared free of all the crimes alleged against him and restored to the full exercise of his office. The schism gradually subsided, and he governed the Church until his death on 19 July 514.

The Liber Pontificalis credits him with severe measures against the Manichaeans, including the burning of their books and their expulsion from the city. He built or adorned the Church of St. Andrew near St. Peter's and a Basilica of St. Agnes on the Via Aurelia, adorned St. Peter's itself, rebuilt the Basilica of Sts. Sylvester and Martinus, and improved the Catacomb of the Jordani on the Via Salaria, while episcopal houses beside St. Peter's recall his long residence there during the disorders of the schism. He erected asylums for the poor near the three basilicas of Sts. Peter, Paul, and Laurence outside the walls, and sent large sums to the Catholic bishops of Africa persecuted by the Arian Vandals and to the suffering provinces of upper Italy.

He was buried at St. Peter's and is venerated in the Roman Church as a saint, honored as a patron of bishops and the poor, and remembered as a defender of the authority of the Apostolic See, which he maintained could not be tried by any earthly tribunal, and as a charitable shepherd amid turbulent times.

pope-telesphorus.history:
St. Telesphorus was the seventh Bishop of Rome in succession from the Apostles. His pontificate fell within the reigns of the emperors Hadrian and Antoninus Pius, extending from about 126 to 137. Eusebius dates the beginning of his pontificate to the twelfth year of Hadrian's reign (128-129) and his death to the first year of Antoninus Pius (138-139), though the precise chronology has been debated by later scholars.

The chief early testimony to his life comes from St. Irenaeus of Lyons, who attests that Telesphorus suffered a glorious martyrdom. A fragment of Irenaeus's letter to Pope Victor concerning the celebration of Easter, preserved by Eusebius, names Telesphorus among the Roman bishops who always celebrated Easter on a Sunday, while never abandoning church fellowship with communities that followed a different custom, an early witness to Roman observance coexisting with differing practice elsewhere.

Later tradition holds that he introduced several liturgical developments, including the singing of the Gloria at Mass and the establishment of a special Christmas liturgy. The earliest sources, however, lend these attributions no support: the statements of the Liber pontificalis and other late authorities concerning the liturgical and other decisions of this pope are not regarded as genuine.

He is honored as a martyr, with the Roman Martyrology assigning his feast to 5 January and the Greek Church commemorating him on 22 February. He is venerated as a patron of contemplatives and of nuns, and the Carmelite Order honors him among its spiritual ancestors. Though the details of his life are sparse, his pontificate spans a formative period in which the Roman Church was shaping its public worship, and he is remembered as a faithful shepherd who nurtured the prayer life of the early Church.

ternan.history:
Saint Ternan is venerated as a Bishop of the Picts and one of the earliest heralds of the Christian faith among the peoples of ancient Scotland. Much obscurity attaches to his history, and it is difficult to reconcile his chronology as given by the various writers who record it. Some accounts say he was consecrated by Saint Palladius in 440, which would place him in the mid-fifth century; others identify him as a monk of Culross in Fife, one of the monasteries founded by Saint Serf, also called Servan, the tutor of Saint Kentigern. Since the conversion of the Picts is generally dated to about 570, under the zeal of Saint Columba, and since Saint Serf of Culross died in 583, it is considered safe to assert only that Saint Ternan was a contemporary of Saint Serf. Tradition holds that he labored among the Picts of the Mearns, planting the Gospel in soil long given to paganism, and that his see and shrine were associated with the region of Aberdeenshire, where his memory was kept for centuries.

The Aberdeen Martyrology makes mention of the Gospel of Matthew belonging to Saint Ternan, which was enshrined in a metal case, or cumdach, covered with silver and gold after the Irish fashion. He is commemorated on June 12 and must not be confounded with Saint Trumwine. Honored as one of the apostles of Scottish Christianity, he carried the cross into the north while the faith was still young, and he is venerated as a patron of bishops and missionaries.

tewdrig.history:
Tewdrig ap Teithfallt was a king of the post-Roman Welsh kingdom of Morganwg (Southern Wales) and the son of King Teithfallt. He flourished probably in the sixth century. He is recorded as a liberal benefactor of the church of Llandaff, and his reign was marked by Christian devotion. In time he resigned the government to his son Meurig and withdrew to Tintern in Monmouthshire, where he devoted himself to religion and contemplation, living as a hermit.

His solitude was interrupted when the Saxons under Ceolwulf crossed the River Severn and pressed hard upon Meurig. Leaving his retreat, Tewdrig put himself at the head of his old troops and gained a brilliant victory, but he was killed in the main battle. Because he fell in defense of his kingdom, he was honored as a royal martyr, and he is venerated as a patron of hermits and of soldiers.

A church was erected over his grave, called Marthyr Tewdrig and now known as Mathern, near the junction of the Rivers Wye and Severn in Monmouthshire; his shrine there was for centuries a place of pilgrimage. His feast day is kept on 1 April, although some sources give the day of his death as 3 January; the year of his death is uncertain, dates as widely separated as 470 and 610 having been proposed.

tha-s-saint.history:
Thaïs (in some sources Thaisis or Thaisia) is venerated as a penitent of fourth-century Egypt. Her commemoration on 8 October appears in the Greek menology, and her name is found also in the martyrologies of Maurolychus and Greven, though she is not entered in the Roman Martyrology. Two lives of the saint are extant: one composed originally in Greek, perhaps in the fifth century, and another in verse by Marbod, Bishop of Rennes, who died in 1123.

According to her legend, Thaïs was a public sinner in Egypt, remembered as a courtesan who lived in wealth and pleasure. Her conversion is attributed to a holy monk whom the sources most often name as Paphnutius; tradition holds that, with patience and the power of the Gospel, he turned her heart to repentance. Renouncing her former life, she is said to have burned her treasures and ornaments, after which she was brought to a convent and enclosed in a cell. There she spent three years in penance and prayer, imploring the mercy of God. At the end of that time she was released from her enclosure and placed among the nuns, but survived only fourteen days, dying a short time later in peace.

The identity of the converting monk is not settled in the sources; his name is given also as Bessarion and as Serapion the Sidonite. Delahaye judged that, if the legend is historical, the hermit must have been Paphnutius.

In Christian art Thaïs is represented burning her treasures and ornaments, or praying in a cell and displaying a scroll inscribed with the words, 'Thou who didst create me have mercy on me.' Her story was cherished in East and West as a testimony to the depth of divine forgiveness. Her feast is kept on 8 October, and she is honored as a patroness of converts, invoked by all who seek conversion and a new beginning.

theodard.history:
Saint Theodard was Archbishop of Narbonne, a see in the south of Gaul in present-day France. The account of his life gives his birth at Montauban about the year 840 and his death at the same place on 1 May 893. He appears to have belonged to a noble and wealthy family, and in his youth he applied himself with great zeal to both ecclesiastical and secular learning.

While still a subdeacon, he gave proof of his education and ability at a synod held at Toulouse, which had been called upon to settle a dispute between the Jews of the city and Bishop Bernhard. The presiding officer of the synod, Archbishop Sigebod of Narbonne, formed so high an opinion of Theodard that he made him his archdeacon. In that office Theodard was distinguished by faultless morals, modesty, piety, and charitableness, and was described as "eyes to the blind, feet to the lame, a father to the poor, and the consoler of all the oppressed".

Upon Sigebod's death in 885, Theodard was elected to succeed him and was consecrated on 15 August of that year. In 886 he went to Rome and received the pallium from Pope Stephen VI, the emblem of an archbishop's metropolitan authority. As archbishop he maintained with energy the rights of his see and of its suffragan dioceses, and repaired the injuries that these churches had suffered from the incursions of the Saracens. He restored the cathedral and gave up his own revenues and the treasures of his church to secure the release of captive Christians; at a later date he was able to replace the treasures he had thus expended.

He lived at the Benedictine Abbey of Saint Martin at Montauban, and there he died and was buried. In time the abbey is said to have borne his name. It was afterward plundered by the Huguenots, and since then all the relics of Saint Theodard, apart from a small remnant, have disappeared.

Though the surviving account of his life is brief, it presents a bishop who defended the rights and unity of the Church, rebuilt what invaders had destroyed, and spent his possessions for the relief of captives and the poor. For this reason he came to be venerated as a saint, and he is invoked as a patron of bishops and of church unity.

thomas-aquinas.history:
Thomas Aquinas was born at Roccasecca in the Kingdom of Naples. The end of 1225 is usually assigned as the time of his birth, though even at his death there was doubt about his exact age; Prümmer, on the authority of the biographer Calo, thinks 1227 the more probable date. His father, Landulph, was Count of Aquino, his mother, Theodora, Countess of Teano, and the family was related to the emperors Henry VI and Frederick II and to the kings of Aragon, Castile, and France. Calo relates that a holy hermit foretold before his birth that he would enter the Order of Friars Preachers and that no one of his day would equal his learning and sanctity. At the age of five, according to the custom of the times, he was sent to the Benedictine monks of Monte Cassino, where he was early noted as meditative and devoted to prayer, and where his preceptor was surprised to hear the child ask frequently, "What is God?" About 1236 he was sent to the University of Naples, where he soon surpassed his master Martini at grammar and was then trained by Peter of Ireland in logic and the natural sciences. His heart remained pure amid the corruption around him, and he resolved to embrace the religious life.

Some time between 1240 and August 1243 he received the habit of the Order of St. Dominic, drawn by John of St. Julian, a noted preacher of the convent of Naples. The Dominicans, fearing his mother would take him away, sent him to Rome, but his brothers, soldiers under the Emperor Frederick, captured him near Aquapendente and held him nearly two years in the fortress of San Giovanni at Roccasecca, his family trying by every means to destroy his vocation. Tradition holds that he drove a temptress from his room with a brand snatched from the fire, and that he later confided to his companion Reginald of Piperno that two angels girded him with the girdle of perpetual virginity. The captivity was not idle time: through his sister he obtained the Holy Scriptures, Aristotle's Metaphysics, and the Sentences of Peter Lombard, and made as much progress as if he had been in a general school. When at length he was set free, lowered in a basket into the arms of the Dominicans, he pronounced his vows; Pope Innocent IV examined his motives closely, dismissed him with a blessing, and forbade any further interference with his vocation.

John the Teutonic, fourth master general of the order, took him to Paris and, according to most of his biographers, to Cologne, where he arrived in 1244 or 1245 and studied under Albertus Magnus, the order's most renowned professor. In the schools Thomas's humility and taciturnity were mistaken for dullness, but after hearing his defense of a difficult thesis Albert declared that this dumb ox would one day make his bellowing in doctrine resound throughout the world. Thomas taught in Paris and in Italy and came to be regarded as the greatest theologian of the Middle Ages. His Summa Theologiae and Summa contra Gentiles brought Christian faith together with the philosophy of Aristotle, and he wrote hymns for the feast of Corpus Christi, among them the Tantum Ergo; the clarity of his thought earned him the title of Angelic Doctor.

In 1274 he set out for the Council of Lyon but died at Fossanova on 7 March of that year. He was canonized in 1323 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1567.

His writings remained a touchstone long after his death: Leo XIII, in the encyclical Providentissimus Deus of 1893, drew from them principles for the scientific criticism of the Sacred Books, and Pius X, in prescribing remedies against Modernism, gave the first place to scholastic philosophy as taught by Thomas Aquinas. He is honored as the patron of Catholic universities, colleges, and schools, and of students and scholars; his feast is kept on 28 January, and he is still remembered as the Angel of the Schools.

pope-urban-i.history:
Urban I was bishop of Rome from 222 until his death on 23 May 230. According to the Liber Pontificalis he was a Roman, the son of a man named Pontianus, and his date of birth is unknown. He was elected to the see after the death of Pope Callixtus I on 14 October 222. Eusebius gives him eight years at the head of the Roman Church, while the Liberian catalogue of popes places the beginning of his pontificate in 223 and its close in 230.

His pontificate coincided with a period of unusual external peace. Alexander Severus became emperor in 222 and, without changing Christianity's legal status, protected its adherents, so that the Roman Church went unmolested throughout his reign. In one dispute heard before the imperial court, Christians who wished to build a church on land also claimed by tavern-keepers prevailed, the emperor ruling that it was better that God be worshipped on that spot. Within the Church, the dissension led by Hippolytus carried over from the previous pontificate; Hippolytus and his adherents persisted in schism, and it was probably during Urban's reign that he composed the Philosophumena, a severe attack on Pope Callixtus. Urban maintained his predecessor's firm attitude toward the schismatic party and its leader, and contemporary authorities record no other factional troubles in the Roman Church of this era.

Nothing is known of Urban's personal labors, but the increase in extent of various Roman catacombs in the first half of the third century proves that Christians grew greatly in numbers during this period. Later tradition, preserved in the legendary Acts of St. Cecilia, connects Urban with that saint and holds that he baptized her husband and her brother-in-law; the narrative is purely legendary and has no historical value. The statement in the Liber Pontificalis that he converted many by his sermons rests on that legend, and the same source's claim that he ordered the making of silver liturgical vessels is judged an invention of an early sixth-century editor, who assigned to Urban the making of certain vessels for the titular churches of his own day. He is remembered as a patron of physicians and of families.

The particulars of Urban's death are unknown, but the peace of his era supports the conclusion that he died a natural death on 23 May 230. For centuries he was nonetheless honored as a martyr, and medieval accounts told of his suffering; later historical study corrected this tradition, and the liturgical commemoration has been adjusted accordingly. The Liber Pontificalis further describes him as a confessor of the Diocletianic persecution, though the date it supplies has no authority, and his name does not appear in the fourth-century Depositio Episcoporum.

Two early traditions concern his grave, and only one refers to the pope. The Acts of St. Cecilia and the Liber Pontificalis place his burial in the Catacomb of Praetextatus on the Via Appia, where the seventh-century itineraries to the Roman martyrs' graves likewise locate an Urban honored as bishop and confessor; from the fourth century onward, Roman tradition venerated the pope in this saint. Excavations in the Catacomb of Callistus later brought to light a sarcophagus fragment bearing the name of an Urban, and the archaeologist De Rossi concluded that the pope lay there; but the lettering of that inscription is later than that of the papal epitaphs in the papal crypt, and a list of those buried in Callistus drawn up under Pope Sixtus III records this Urban not in the succession of popes but among foreign bishops who died at Rome. The older testimony is therefore retained: Pope Urban was buried in Praetextatus, while the Urban honored in Callistus seems to have been a bishop of another see. The Martyrologium Hieronymianum records under 25 May the burial of a bishop Urban in the cemetery of Praetextatus, a date that remains his feast day.

pope-victor-i.history:
Victor I served as Bishop of Rome from about 189 to 198 or 199, at the close of the second century, in the final years of the Emperor Commodus and the early reign of Septimius Severus. The Liber Pontificalis records him as a native of the Roman province of Africa and names his father as Felix. He was the first pope to come from that region, a Roman African of Berber origin who brought to the see of Peter the theological vigor of the North African Church.

The Roman church enjoyed general external peace in his time. Christians served even at the imperial court, and Commodus looked on them with favor through the influence of Marcia, a courtier favorably inclined toward the faith. Marcia asked Pope Victor for a list of Christians condemned to forced labor in the mines of Sardinia; the pope supplied the names, Marcia obtained the required pardon from the emperor, and the presbyter Hyacinthus carried the order of release to the confessors. Callistus, later himself bishop of Rome, was among those set free, though he remained at Antium, supported by a monthly pension from the Roman Christians. Under the early years of Septimius Severus they were still treated kindly, and the church advanced in the capital.

Internal discord, however, attended the date of Easter. Christians who had come to Rome from the province of Asia observed the feast on the fourteenth day of Nisan, whatever day of the week it fell, as they had done at home. Victor sought to unify the observance. He wrote to Bishop Polycrates of Ephesus, who gathered the bishops of Asia at his request but declared in reply that he stood firm in the Quartodeciman custom of so many holy bishops of his land. Victor then assembled the Italian bishops at Rome, the earliest Roman synod known, and urged the leading bishops elsewhere to take counsel in like manner. Synods in Palestine, with Theophilus of Caesarea and Narcissus of Jerusalem presiding, and in Pontus under the aged Palmas, together with the churches of Gaul under Irenaeus of Lyons, the bishops of Osrhoene, and individual bishops such as Bakchylus of Corinth, unanimously reported that Easter was kept on Sunday. Victor accordingly called upon the bishops of Asia to accept the prevailing Sunday practice, declaring that refusal would exclude them from the fellowship of the Church.

This severity did not please all. Irenaeus of Lyons and others wrote to him, blaming his harshness and urging him to keep peace and charity with the bishops of Asia; they recalled that his predecessors had indeed always kept Easter on Sunday, as was right, yet had never broken communion with those of another custom. No record tells how the matter ended under Victor; it is known only that in the third century the Roman practice became gradually universal. At Rome itself, where Victor enforced the Sunday observance, an Oriental named Blastus, with a few followers, opposed him and brought about a schism that never grew in importance. Victor also had difficulties with Florinus, a Roman priest probably come from Asia Minor.

Jerome calls him the first Latin writer in the Church and mentions small treatises of his on the paschal question; apart from the letters of the Easter controversy none of his works survives. It was perhaps in his administration that the canon of Scripture used at Rome, preserved in part in the Muratorian Fragment, was drawn up. Later Roman tradition attributes to him the introduction of the sequentes among the clergy and an ordinance on baptism in cases of necessity, though such entries are judged to have little historical value. His pontificate is chiefly remembered for its labor to unify the Church's celebration of Easter; he is honored as a patron of church unity and of theologians, and his feast is kept on January 11.

vincent-ferrer.history:
Vincent Ferrer was born at Valencia on 23 January 1350 into a noble line; his parents, William Ferrer and Constantia Miguel, were descended from families ennobled in the conquest of Valencia in 1238, and his brother Boniface Ferrer later served as General of the Carthusians. Educated at Valencia, he completed his study of philosophy at fourteen, entered the Dominican Order in 1367, and continued his formation at Barcelona, where during a famine he foretold the near approach of ships bearing wheat, which arrived as he had said.

In 1379 he was retained by Cardinal Pedro de Luna, the papal legate to Aragon, and became a steadfast champion of the Avignon pontiffs, convinced of the legitimacy of their claims. He taught theology in the cathedral at Valencia from 1385 to 1390. At Valladolid he converted a rabbi later known as Bishop Paul of Burgos, and Queen Yolanda of Aragon chose him as her confessor from 1391 to 1395. When cited before the Inquisition for preaching that Judas had done penance, he was protected by Pedro de Luna, recently become Pope Benedict XIII, who brought the case to his own tribunal and burned the papers. Benedict then summoned him to Avignon as confessor and Apostolic penitentiary; Vincent steadfastly refused every honor offered to him, including the cardinalate.

In 1398, after France withdrew from the Avignon obedience and troops besieged the city, Vincent fell gravely ill of fever. He was miraculously cured during an apparition of Christ accompanied by St. Dominic and St. Francis, and sent to preach penance and prepare people for the coming judgment. In November 1399 Benedict XIII granted him full legatine powers, and for twenty years he traversed western Europe preaching penance for sin and preparation for judgment. Provence was his first field, where the crowds were so numerous that he preached in squares and open places; in 1401 he evangelized Dauphiny, Savoy, and the Alpine regions, converting many Cathari and Waldensians, and afterward passed through Lombardy, Switzerland, Genoa, Flanders, and northern France. Penitents from every rank of society, at times ten thousand, followed him. Though he spoke only Limousin, the language of Valencia, he made himself understood across Europe; many biographers hold that he was endowed with the gift of tongues, a view supported by Nicholas Clemangis, a doctor of the University of Paris who had heard him preach. In Italy he singled out the young Bernardine of Siena, destined to evangelize that land.

In 1408 he was at Genoa consoling the plague-stricken; there he again urged Benedict XIII to seek an end to the schism with Gregory XII, but in vain. Disappointed, he returned to Spain and worked almost continuously south of the Pyrenees from 1408 to 1416, visiting Castile, Aragon, Granada, and Andalusia. Christians, Jews, and Muslims alike were moved by his preaching; Ranzano, his first biographer, estimated the number of Jewish converts at 25,000, and in the Kingdom of Granada he converted thousands of Moors. As counselor of kings he took the leading part in the Compromise of Caspe, which elected Ferdinand of Castile to the throne of Aragon.

His manner of life was austere. The floor was his usual bed; fasting perpetually, he rose at two in the morning to chant the Office, celebrated Mass daily, and then preached, sometimes for three hours. After his midday meal he tended sick children, and at eight o'clock he prepared the following day's sermon; he usually traveled on foot, poorly clad. His writings include De suppositionibus dialecticis, De natura universalis, De moderno ecclesiae schismate, a defense of the Avignon pontiffs, and De vita spirituali.

Vincent died at Vannes, Brittany, on 5 April 1419, the day on which his feast is kept, and was canonized by Pope Calixtus III at the Dominican church of Santa Maria Sopra Minerva in Rome on 3 June 1455. He is venerated as a patron of preachers and builders.

vincent-of-l-rins.history:
St. Vincent of Lérins was an ecclesiastical writer of Southern Gaul in the fifth century whose work is far better known than his life. Almost all that is known of him comes from Gennadius' De viris illustribus. He entered the monastery of Lérins, today the Isle of St. Honorat off the coast of Provence, and there, under the pseudonym Peregrinus, wrote the Commonitorium in 434. He died before 450, probably shortly after 434. St. Eucherius of Lyons called him a holy man, conspicuous for eloquence and knowledge. It is likely, if not certain, that he was the writer against whom Prosper, St. Augustine's friend, directed the Responsiones ad capitula objectionum Vincentianarum.

Vincent was a Semi-Pelagian, opposed to St. Augustine's doctrine of grace. He lived in a center deeply imbued with Semi-Pelagianism, and his writings show affinities with Cassian and with Faustus of Riez, who became Abbot of Lérins as he wrote, and employ technical expressions like those of the Semi-Pelagians against Augustine. As Benedict XIV observed, this was before the controversy had been decided by the Church.

The Commonitorium, his only certainly authentic extant work, was a memorial meant to guide the author's belief according to the traditions of the Fathers. It was planned in two parts; the second survives only in the résumé Vincent himself appended to the first, which he complains had been stolen from him, and neither Gennadius nor any known manuscript preserves a trace of it. A projected work against Photinus, Apollinaris, and Nestorius has not been discovered, if it was ever written. The Objectiones Vincentianae are known only through Prosper's refutation, and Vincent probably collaborated in, or at least inspired, the Objectiones Gallorum, which Prosper likewise answered.

The preserved text proposes a practical rule for distinguishing heresy from true doctrine: first Holy Scripture, and, where that does not suffice, the tradition of the Catholic Church. From this comes the famous canon, much discussed at the time of the Vatican Council, that what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all must be held. Vincent applies it in stages: a novelty in one part of the Church, as Donatism was, is met by adherence to the belief of the universal Church; an error of almost universal extent, as Arianism was, by clinging to antiquity; beyond this, one stands by the general councils or, in their default, by the consent of those who in diverse times and places remained steadfast in the unanimity of the Catholic faith. He points to St. Ambrose, the martyrs, St. Stephen against rebaptism, and St. Paul as witnesses to this method, and holds that God allows distinguished men, such as Tertullian, Origen, Nestorius, and Apollinaris, to teach novelties as a test of the faithful.

So that the faith might not stagnate, Vincent taught that it progresses after the manner of grain and acorn, provided it grows in the same doctrine, sense, and judgment (eodem sensu ac sententia), the well-known passage on dogmatic development. The canon has been variously interpreted; de San and Franzelin, generally in agreement in their views, were at variance in explaining it. Vincent took the three criteria in a relative and disjunctive sense, and by antiquity he meant a relative consensus of antiquity. Newman judged the canon more fit to determine what is not Catholic doctrine than what is.

Written in a literary style full of classical expression, though familiar and easy in its course, the Commonitorium draws attention chiefly to its two ideas of fidelity to Tradition and the progress of Catholic doctrine. It has been frequently printed and translated, from Sichardus' first edition of 1528 through Baluze's Paris edition of 1663 to Rauschen's collated edition of 1906. Vincent's feast is kept on May 24, and he is honored as a patron of monks and theologians whose writing helped the Church articulate how it preserves the apostolic faith.

pope-vitalian.history:
Vitalian was elected pope after the death of Eugene I and consecrated and enthroned on 30 July 657; he died on 27 January 672, the day on which he is commemorated. Nothing is known of his life before his elevation to the Holy See. According to the Liber Pontificalis, he was a native of Segni in Campagna, and his father's name was Anastasius.

Like his predecessor, he sought to restore relations with Constantinople and to prepare the way for a settlement of the Monothelite controversy, the teaching that Christ possessed only a single will. He announced his elevation by letters to Emperor Constans II and to Patriarch Peter of Constantinople, who inclined toward Monothelitism. The emperor confirmed the privileges of the Roman Church and sent a richly ornamented Gospel codex to St. Peter's, while the patriarch answered evasively. Ecclesiastical intercourse between the two sees was thus restored on a basis of mutual reserve over the dogmatic question, and Vitalian's name was entered on the diptychs of the Byzantine Church, the only pope so honored between Honorius I and the Sixth Ecumenical Council.

In 663 Constans II came to Rome during his campaign against the Lombards; Vitalian met him outside the walls and accompanied him to St. Peter's, where the emperor offered gifts, attended Mass, and dined with the pope. Before departing, however, Constans carried off many bronze works of art, including the bronze tiles from the roof of the Pantheon. He was assassinated at Syracuse in 668, and Vitalian supported his son Constantine IV against a usurper, thereby aiding him to the throne. The new emperor declined to enforce his father's Monothelite decree by force, and Vitalian probably used this opening to take a more decided stand against the error and to win the emperor to orthodoxy, though in this he did not succeed. The Monothelite patriarch Theodore later removed Vitalian's name from the diptychs; it was restored only after Monothelitism was suppressed at the Sixth Ecumenical Council of 681.

The pontificate was significant for the English Church. After the Synod of Whitby, King Oswy of Northumbria accepted Roman practice regarding Easter and the tonsure, and together with King Egbert of Kent sent the priest Wighard to Rome for consecration as archbishop after the death of Deusdedit of Canterbury; Wighard died there of pestilence. The pope wrote to Oswy promising to send a suitable bishop, and Theodore of Tarsus, a monk learned in Latin and Greek, was chosen and consecrated Archbishop of Canterbury on 26 March 668. Accompanied by Abbot Hadrian, he was recognized by all the Saxon and British clergy, and Vitalian confirmed to him the privileges Gregory the Great had granted to Augustine.

The See of Ravenna, immediately subject to Rome, became a lasting sorrow of his reign. Archbishop Maurus refused to justify his views when summoned, declared himself independent, and exchanged excommunications with the pope. Constans II sided with Maurus, removed Ravenna from Roman jurisdiction by edict, and ordained that its archbishop receive the pallium from the emperor; Maurus's successor Reparatus was so consecrated in 671. The rupture endured until the reign of Pope Leo II, when Constantine IV repealed the edict and confirmed the ancient rights of the Roman See.

Vitalian also exercised his office as supreme judge in the Eastern Church. Bishop John of Lappa in Crete, deposed by a synod of Metropolitan Paulus and imprisoned for appealing to Rome, escaped to the city, where the pope held a synod in December 667, pronounced him guiltless, and demanded his restoration and the return of unjustly taken monasteries. Some letters attributed to Vitalian are spurious. He was buried at St. Peter's. Remembered as a pope who held fast to the faith while laboring for peace among divided churches, he is invoked as a patron of church unity and of priests.

wendelin-of-trier.history:
Saint Wendelin of Trier is remembered as a hermit and abbot whose cult spread widely across the German-speaking lands, and who became one of the best-loved rural saints of the Rhineland and the German countryside. The details of his life rest on biographies written long after his death: the earliest accounts, two in Latin and two in German, did not appear until after 1417, and it is difficult to say how far the later biographers are to be trusted. According to their narrative, Wendelin was born about 554, the son of a Scottish king; after a piously spent youth he secretly left his home on a pilgrimage to Rome, and on his way back he settled as a hermit at Westricht in the Diocese of Trier.

When a great landowner blamed him for what seemed an idle life, Wendelin entered the lord's service as a herdsman; a miracle later obliged the lord to allow him to return to his solitude. His holiness drew disciples, and he established a company of hermits from which sprang the Benedictine Abbey of Tholey. According to the later legends, Wendelin was consecrated abbot of that community about 597; Tholey itself appears to have been founded as a collegiate body about 630. The saint died, probably in 617, and was buried in his cell; a chapel was built over his grave, and the small town of St. Wendel grew up nearby.

Separating history from legend is therefore not possible in every particular: the dates preserved for his birth, his consecration as abbot, and his death rest on these later accounts rather than on contemporary record, and the founding of Tholey as a collegiate body about 630 belongs to the abbey's own history more certainly than to a fixed chronology of Wendelin's life.

His hagiography gives particular weight to his care for animals and fields, and for centuries his intercession has been sought in the farms and villages of central Europe for the flocks and the harvest, and especially in times of pestilence and contagious disease among cattle. When a pestilence was checked through his intercession in 1320, Archbishop Baldwin of Trier had the chapel rebuilt; Baldwin's successor, Boemund II, built the present Gothic church, dedicated in 1360, to which the saint's relics were transferred. Since 1506 those relics have rested in a stone sarcophagus.

Wendelin is the patron of country people and herdsmen, honored in particular as a patron of shepherds and farmers, and he is still venerated in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. He is not mentioned in the Roman Martyrology, but his feast is observed in the Diocese of Trier on 22 October. In art he is represented as a youth or as a bearded man, with a shepherd's bag and a book in one hand and a shepherd's crook in the other, while lambs, cattle, and swine feed about him and a crown and a shield lie at his feet.

werburgh.history:
Werburgh was a Benedictine abbess and the patroness of Chester; born in Staffordshire early in the seventh century, she died at Trentham on 3 February, 699 or 700. Daughter of Wulfhere, king of Mercia and son of Penda, and of St. Ermenilda, daughter of Ercombert, king of Kent, she united two very different royal lines, one fierce and pagan, the other marked by gentle Christian sanctity. Whether Wulfhere was an unbaptized pagan or a relapsed Christian was controverted; earlier chroniclers dismiss the graver crime later writers imputed to him. Ermenilda's zeal won many subjects to the faith and is said to have made her passionate husband a model Christian king.

Sought in marriage for her beauty and grace, Werburgh remained constant until her father consented to her entry into the Abbey of Ely, founded by her great-aunt, St. Etheldra. Wulfhere did not long survive her consecration; Ermenilda took the veil at Ely and in time succeeded her mother, St. Sexburga, as abbess, while their uncle Ethelred took the throne, Kenred being still a child.

Ethelred invited Werburgh to direct all the nunneries of his dominion, wishing to bring them to the discipline he had admired at Ely. With some difficulty she sacrificed the seclusion she prized, reformed the Mercian houses and founded Trentham, Hanbury and Weedon, which the king endowed; she is reckoned abbess also of Minster in Sheppy and of Ely. Trained at home by St. Chad, afterwards Bishop of Lichfield, and in the cloister by her mother, aunt and grandmother, she ruled in marked humility, seeming the servant rather than the mistress of those committed to her care.

Tradition holds that her childlike trust was rewarded by many miracles, which made her one of the best known and loved of the Saxon saints. The story most appealing to popular imagination, immortalized in her iconography, tells how by a simple command she banished the wild geese working havoc in the cornfields at Weedon, after which none of those birds was seen there; she was also credited with prophecy and with reading the secrets of hearts.

Knowing that her communities would each strive to secure her body after death, she chose Hanbury for her burial. Tradition relates that the nuns of Trentham locked the coffin in a crypt and set a guard, but that the men of Hanbury, arriving at midnight, found the bolts yielding at their touch and the guards overpowered by sleep, and bore the coffin away. So numerous were the cures worked at the tomb that in 708 the body was translated to a more conspicuous place in the church, before her brother Kenred, now king. Though nine years in the tomb, the body was found intact, and Kenred resolved to resign his crown and follow his sister's path.

In 875, fearing the Danes and to honour the saint, the body was removed to Chester. The church of St. Peter and St. Paul, on the site of the present cathedral, was rededicated to St. Werburgh and St. Oswald, most probably in the reign of Athelstan. Leofric, Earl of Mercia, and his wife, Lady Godiva, repaired and enlarged the church, and in 1093 Hugh Lupus, Earl of Chester, richly endowed the abbey, through which Chester, formerly served by secular canons, became a great Benedictine abbey, the name of St. Anselm, then a monk at Bec, being associated with the change.

At the suppression under Henry VIII the cathedral was sacked and the saint's relics scattered; fragments of the ten-foot-high shrine served as the base of an episcopal throne, and thirty of the original figures survive, four having been lost. The restored fragments were later placed at the west end of the south choir aisle, near the shrine's original position. Her feast is kept on 3 February. Remembered as a model of royal virginity and a wise ruler of religious women, she has been honoured for centuries as the heavenly protector of Chester, and is invoked for conversion and protection.

willigis.history:
St. Willigis was born at Schladen, in Saxony, in the tenth century and rose to become one of the most influential churchmen of his age. Through the influence of Bishop Volkold of Meissen he entered the service of Emperor Otto I, and after 971 served as chancellor of Germany. In 975 Emperor Otto II appointed him Archbishop of Mainz, the primatial see of Germany, and Archchancellor of the Empire. In March of that year he received the pallium from Pope Benedict VII and was named Primate of Germany, serving until his death on 23 February 1011.

A trusted counselor to Otto II and Otto III, he was known as a good and fluent speaker, well educated himself, and demanded solid learning in his clergy. On Christmas Day 983 he crowned Otto III at Aachen, and in June 1002 he performed the coronation of Henry II at Mainz. He presided over the Synod of Frankfort in 1007, at which thirty-five bishops signed the bull of Pope John XVIII erecting the Diocese of Bamberg. In his capacity as archchancellor he rendered valued service to the state.

Willigis always stood in friendly relations with Rome. In 996 he accompanied Otto III on his journey to Italy, assisted at the consecration of Pope Gregory V, and took part in the synod convened a few days later, in which he strongly urged the return of St. Adalbert to his see of Prague, a diocese suffragan to Mainz. Willigis had probably consecrated the first bishop of Prague, Thietmar, and had consecrated Adalbert himself; when Adalbert left his see, unable to bear the opposition to his labors, much correspondence between the Holy See and Willigis ended in his being forced to return. In 997 Gregory V sent the decrees of a synod of Pavia to Willigis, his vicar, for publication.

His relations with Rome were briefly disturbed by a dispute with the Bishop of Hildesheim over jurisdiction of the convent at Gundersheim, originally situated at Brunshausen in the Diocese of Hildesheim but transferred to Gundersheim within the bounds of Mainz. Both bishops claimed jurisdiction, and Pope Silvester declared in favor of Hildesheim. When the sentence was about to be published at the Synod of Pohlde on 22 June 1001, Willigis withdrew in great excitement despite the remonstrances of the papal delegate, who thereupon placed the sentence of suspension on the archbishop. No formal opposition to Rome was intended; Willigis publicly rectified the matter by a declaration at Gundersheim on 5 January 1007, when he resigned all his claims to the Bishop of Hildesheim.

In his diocese he labored as a builder and pastor, erecting bridges and roads and fostering the arts. He built the great cathedral of Mainz and consecrated it on 29 August 1009 in honor of St. Martin, only to see it destroyed by fire on the same day. He greatly helped the restoration of the old Church of St. Victor, built the church of St. Stephen in Mainz, and raised another church at Brunnen in Nassau. He showed great solicitude for the religious and substantially aided the monasteries of Bleidenstadt, St. Disibod, and Jechaburg in Thuringia. Tradition holds that he also labored to bring the Gospel to the Slavic peoples at the empire's edges.

Willigis died on 23 February 1011 and was buried in the Church of St. Stephen at Mainz. His feast is kept on 23 February. He is venerated as a patron of workers and of Germany, and tradition honors him in particular as a patron of wheelwrights.

cyril-and-methodius.history:
Cyril and Methodius, brothers known as the Apostles of the Slavs, were born in Thessalonica in 827 and 826 respectively. Members of a senatorial family, they renounced secular honors and became priests and monks. Cyril was originally named Constantine and was known as Constantine the Philosopher before taking the name Cyril late in life. While they were living in a monastery on the Bosphorus, the Khazars sent to Constantinople for a Christian teacher; Cyril was selected for the mission, with Methodius accompanying him, and the two learned the Khazar language and converted many of the people.

Soon afterward a request came from the Moravians for a preacher of the Gospel. German missionaries had already labored among them without success, and the Moravians wished for a teacher who could instruct them and conduct divine service in the Slavonic tongue. On account of their acquaintance with that language the brothers were chosen for the work. Sent in 862 by the Byzantine emperor at the request of Prince Rastislav, they reached Moravia in 863 and labored there for four and a half years. In preparation Cyril had devised an alphabet, known as Glagolitic and the ancestor of the later Cyrillic, and with the help of Methodius had translated the Gospels and the necessary liturgical books into Slavonic.

Their success nonetheless drew the distrust of the German clergy, first because the brothers had come from Constantinople, where schism was then rife, and again because they held the Church services in the Slavonic language. Summoned to Rome by Pope Nicholas I, who died before their arrival, they were received kindly by his successor, Adrian II; convinced of their orthodoxy, he commended their missionary activity, sanctioned the Slavonic liturgy, and ordained both brothers bishops. Cyril did not return to Moravia, but died in Rome on 4 February 869.

At the request of the Moravian princes Rastislav and Svatopluk and of the Slav Prince Kocel of Pannonia, Adrian II erected the Archdiocese of Moravia and Pannonia, made it independent of the German Church, and appointed Methodius archbishop. In 870 King Louis and the German bishops summoned him to a synod at Ratisbon, where he was deposed and condemned to prison; after three years he was set free at the command of Pope John VIII and reinstated as Archbishop of Moravia. He then worked to spread the faith among the Bohemians and among the Poles of northern Moravia.

Opposition continued through the German priest Wiching, whose allegations against Methodius on the score of orthodoxy and the use of Slavonic in the liturgy led to another summons to Rome. After an inquiry John VIII again sanctioned the Slavonic liturgy, decreeing that in the Mass the Gospel be read first in Latin and then in Slavonic. Wiching, in the meantime, had been made one of the suffragan bishops under Methodius and continued to oppose his metropolitan, going so far as to produce spurious papal letters, which the pope assured Methodius were false. About this time Methodius also visited Constantinople and, with the assistance of several priests, completed the translation of the Holy Scriptures, all but the Books of Machabees; he also translated the Nomocanon, the Greek ecclesiastico-civil law.

His health worn out by the long struggle, Methodius died on 6 April 885, recommending as his successor Gorazd, a Moravian Slav who had been his disciple. The brothers are honored as patrons of missionaries and of Europe.

Their feast, extended to the universal Church by Pope Leo XIII in 1880 through the encyclical Grande Munus, is celebrated on 14 February in the Latin Church.

abundius.history:
St. Abundius, venerated as a saint in the Catholic Church, was an Italian bishop, though he was born at Thessalonica early in the fifth century. He died in 469, having served as the fourth Bishop of Como in northern Italy.

His episcopate fell within the period of the great christological controversies of the fifth century. He was present at the Council of Constantinople in 450, and at the Council of Chalcedon in 451 he took an active part against the Eutychian heresy, serving there as the representative of Pope Leo the Great. In 452 he took part in the Council of Milan, which had been convened to refute the same heresy. In these assemblies he acted in support of the orthodox teaching whose defense had brought the councils together.

Tradition also connects him, without certainty, with one of the Church's most familiar hymns: he is one of the figures to whom the authorship of the Te Deum is occasionally attributed, though this attribution is not established.

His feast is kept on April 2. He is honored as a patron of bishops, and his memory remains especially associated with the city and diocese of Como, whose fourth bishop he was. His career linked that Lombard see with the decisive councils of the fifth century, and he stands as an example of the steadfast episcopal service of late antiquity.

agatha.history:
Agatha is honored among the most highly venerated virgin martyrs of Christian antiquity. She was put to death for her steadfast profession of the Christian faith at Catania, Sicily, and historical certitude attaches only to the fact of her martyrdom and to the public veneration paid her in the Church since primitive times. The persecution in which she died cannot be certainly identified, although a legendary life composed at a later date, thought to rest on ancient tradition, places her death under the emperor Decius (250-253); she is commonly said to have died around 251. Like the saints of the early centuries, she was revered as a martyr from antiquity rather than formally canonized.

Her cult is ancient and widely attested. Her name is recorded on 5 February in the Martyrologium Hieronymianum and in the ancient Carthaginian martyrology of the fifth or sixth century, and in the sixth century the poet Venantius Fortunatus celebrated her among the Christian virgins and martyrs.
