A hymn long attributed to Pope Damasus but actually the work of a later unknown author was evidently meant for the liturgical celebration of her feast. Two early churches also witness to her veneration: a basilica dedicated to her on the estate of Caclano, known from a letter of Pope Gelasius (492-496), and a church of St. Agatha in the Subura at Rome, already standing in the latter half of the fifth century, enriched with a mosaic by Ricimer, later given to the Arian Goths, and restored to Catholic worship by Pope Gregory I (590-604).

No reliable account of the details of her death has survived. The Acts of her martyrdom exist in Latin and Greek recensions, but neither can lay claim to historical credibility, and the Latin Acts in their present form are not older than the sixth century. According to these later accounts, Agatha, a daughter of a distinguished family and remarkable for her beauty, was pursued by the Senator Quintianus, whose advances she resolutely spurned as a pious Christian virgin. Tradition holds that he then entrusted her to an evil woman whose seductive arts her unswerving faith defeated, and that he next had her subjected to cruel tortures, including the order that her breasts be cut off, a detail that gave medieval Christian iconography its peculiar characteristic of Agatha and because of which she is invoked against breast disease and other illnesses of women. The Acts further relate that she was consoled by a vision of St. Peter, who miraculously healed her, and that she at length died of the repeated cruelties she endured. Writers such as Allard have judged these Acts the work of a later author concerned with an edifying narrative abounding in miracles rather than with history, so these particulars rest on pious tradition rather than verified record.

Both Catania and Palermo claim the honor of being her birthplace. Her feast is kept on 5 February, and her office in the Roman Breviary is drawn in part from the Latin Acts. Catania honors her as its patron saint; from early times her intercession was credited with staying the eruptions of Mount Etna that threatened the city, and throughout the region of Etna she is invoked against the eruptions of the volcano, as elsewhere against fire and lightning. In some places bread and water are blessed during Mass on her feast after the Consecration, the bread being known as Agatha bread. She is also named among the virgin martyrs commemorated in the Roman Canon of the Mass.

albert-the-great.history:
Albert the Great was born at Lauingen in Swabia, in present-day Bavaria, around 1206, though many historians give the year as 1193. The eldest son of the Count of Bollstädt, he was sent as a youth to study at the University of Padua, chosen either because an uncle resided there or because of the city's famous cultivation of the liberal arts. In 1223 he joined the Order of St. Dominic, attracted by the preaching of Blessed Jordan of Saxony, the order's second Master General.

After completing his studies he taught theology at Hildesheim, Freiburg, Ratisbon, Strasburg, and Cologne. Ordered to Paris in 1245, he received his Doctor's degree at the university then most celebrated as a school of theology. It was during his teaching at Cologne and Paris that St. Thomas Aquinas, then a silent, thoughtful youth, was among his hearers; Albert recognized the young man's genius and foretold his future greatness. Thomas accompanied his master to Paris in 1245 and returned with him in 1248 to the new Studium Generale at Cologne, where Albert served as Regent and Thomas as second professor and Master of Students.

Albert was elected Provincial of his Order in Germany in 1254 and journeyed to Rome in 1256 to defend the Mendicant Orders against the attacks of William of St. Amour, filling during that stay the office of Master of the Sacred Palace. He resigned the office of Provincial in 1257 to devote himself to study and teaching. At the Dominican General Chapter of Valenciennes, working alongside St. Thomas and Peter of Tarentasia, afterward Pope Innocent V, he drew up rules for the direction of studies and the system of graduation in the order. Appointed Bishop of Ratisbon, or Regensburg, in 1260, he governed the diocese until 1262 and then, his resignation accepted, voluntarily resumed teaching at the Studium at Cologne.

His later career included a sustained struggle against the Averroists: his treatise De Unitate Intellectus Contra Averroem appeared in 1256, and in 1270 he sent a memoir to Paris to aid St. Thomas in combating Siger de Brabant. Summoned by Pope Gregory X to the Council of Lyons in 1274, he took an active part in its deliberations. The announcement of St. Thomas's death on his way to that council was a heavy blow; Albert declared that the "Light of the Church" had been extinguished, and tradition holds that ever afterward he could not restrain his tears at the mention of his pupil's name. In 1277, when Stephen Tempier and others sought to condemn the writings of St. Thomas, he journeyed to Paris to defend his disciple's memory. After drawing up his testament in 1278 he suffered a gradual lapse of memory, and he died at Cologne on November 15, 1280.

Known as "Doctor Universalis," the universal doctor, Albert was proficient in every branch of learning cultivated in his day and surpassed all his contemporaries, except perhaps Roger Bacon, in the knowledge of nature; a contemporary, Ulrich Engelbert, called him the wonder and the miracle of his age. He wrote on logic, theology, philosophy, astronomy, chemistry, botany, zoology, geography, and the physical sciences, including works on minerals and the heavens, and he insisted that the study of nature is a path to God. In theology he stands between Peter Lombard and his illustrious pupil: his Summa Theologiae marked an advance in the scientific order of his time, yet it was Albert who trained the disciple through whom, under God, the Christian world received the Summa Theologica.

Albert was beatified by Pope Gregory XV in 1622, and his feast is kept on November 15. The bishops of Germany, assembled at Fulda in 1872, petitioned the Holy See for his canonization, and he was canonized in 1931. In 1941 Pope Pius XII declared him the patron saint of natural scientists.

aloysius-gonzaga.history:
Aloysius Gonzaga was born in the castle of Castiglione on 9 March 1568, a son of the noble Gonzaga family of northern Italy. His childhood was spent amid the great courts of Europe: at the age of eight he was placed in the court of Francesco de' Medici in Florence, where he remained for two years before going on to Mantua. At Brescia, when he was twelve, he came under the spiritual guidance of St. Charles Borromeo and received his First Communion from him. Though raised amid courtly splendor, he resolved early in life to give himself to God.

In 1581 he accompanied his father to Spain, where he and his brother were made pages of James, the son of Philip II. There he had distinguished himself by a public examination not only in philosophy but also in theology at the University of Alcalá. During this period he formed the resolution of becoming a Jesuit, though he first thought of joining the Discalced Carmelites. He returned to Italy in 1584 after the death of the Infanta, and after much difficulty in securing his father's consent he renounced his heritage in favor of his brother on 2 November 1585. Because Castiglione was a fief of the empire, the renunciation required the approval of the emperor. On 25 November 1585 he presented himself to Father Claudius Acquaviva, then General of the Society of Jesus.

Aloysius had already completed his philosophical and mathematical studies before his entrance into the Society, and before the end of his novitiate he passed a brilliant public act in philosophy. He made his vows on 25 November 1587 and immediately thereafter began his theological studies, in which Fathers Vasquez and Azor were among his professors.

In 1591, while he was in his fourth year of theology, famine and pestilence broke out in Italy. Though himself of delicate health, Aloysius devoted himself to the care of the sick, serving in the Jesuit hospital in Rome. He fell ill on 3 March and died on 21 June 1591, at the age of twenty-three. He was remembered for intense prayer and penance and for his devotion to the poor and the sick.

He was beatified by Gregory XV in 1621 and canonized by Benedict XIII in 1726, and his feast is kept on 21 June. He is honored as a patron of students and of young people. His remains rest in the church of St. Ignazio in Rome, in a magnificent urn of lapis lazuli wreathed with festoons of silver, and the altar bears for its centerpiece a large marble relief of the saint by Le Gros.

ambrose.history:
Ambrose was born probably in 340, with Trier, Arles, and Lyons each contending for the honor of his birth. He came of an ancient Roman family, Christian from an early period, which counted martyrs and high officials among its members. His father, likewise named Ambrosius, was Prefect of Gallia, one of the four great prefectures of the Empire, ruling territories that included present-day France, Britain, and Spain. After the father's death about 354 the family removed to Rome, where the future saint's religious formation was guided especially by his sister Marcellina, about ten years his senior, who had received the virginal veil from Pope Liberius and lived as a consecrated virgin in their mother's house. From her he drew the love of virginity that marked him thereafter, and his mastery of Greek, rare among Western churchmen of his age, kept pace with his growth in piety. His brother Satyrus later resigned a prefecture to live with him and relieve him of temporal cares.

Trained in law, he distinguished himself by the eloquence of his pleadings at the court of the praetorian prefect Anicius Probus, who took him into his council and obtained for him from Emperor Valentinian the office of consular governor of Liguria and Aemilia, with residence in Milan. The prefect dismissed him with the words, 'Conduct thyself not as a judge, but as bishop.' His upright and gentle administration won him the universal esteem of his subjects, no small matter in a province shaken by religious discord: since the orthodox Bishop Dionysius had been carried into exile in 355, the church of Milan had been governed by the intruded Arian Auxentius, and the death of that persecutor in 374 ended a bondage of nearly twenty years, leaving the city amid religious chaos.

The bishops of the province, dreading the tumults of a popular election, begged Valentinian to appoint a successor, but the emperor insisted the election proceed in the usual way. Keeping order fell to Ambrose as consular governor. Proceeding to the basilica where the disunited clergy and people were assembled, he began a conciliatory discourse in the interest of peace, but was interrupted by a voice - according to Paulinus, the secretary who later wrote his life, the voice of an infant - crying 'Ambrose, Bishop.' The cry was repeated by the entire assembly, and he was unanimously elected. Quite apart from any supernatural intervention, he was the only logical candidate, known to the Catholics as a firm believer in the Nicene Creed yet acceptable to the Arians, since he had kept aloof from theological controversy. The sole obstacle was that he was still only a catechumen, and so ineligible by the canons; his repugnance and his attempts to decline the office proved unavailing, and he was baptized, ordained, and consecrated bishop within a week, giving his wealth to the poor.

As bishop of Milan from 374 to 397 he defended the Catholic faith against Arianism and asserted the Church's independence before imperial power, famously barring Emperor Theodosius from the cathedral until the emperor repented of a massacre. A gifted preacher, he helped bring Augustine to the faith, and his hymns and liturgical texts shaped the worship of the West. With Augustine, John Chrysostom, and Athanasius he is honored as one of the four great Doctors of the Western Church.

Tradition holds that as an infant a swarm of bees settled on his face and left a drop of honey, foreshadowing his eloquence, and for this reason he is venerated as the patron saint of beekeepers, candle makers, and students. He died on April 4, 397, and has been honored as a saint since antiquity, before the formal canonization process existed; his feast is kept on December 7.

angela-merici.history:
Angela Merici was born on 21 March 1474 at Desenzano, a small town on the southwestern shore of Lake Garda in Lombardy, and died at Brescia on 27 January 1540. Left an orphan at the age of ten, she went with her elder sister to live in the home of an uncle at the neighboring town of Salò, where the two girls were known for the innocence of their lives. When her sister died suddenly without receiving the last sacraments, Angela was much distressed. She became a tertiary of St. Francis and greatly increased her prayers and mortifications for the repose of her sister's soul; in her anguish she prayed to know her sister's condition, and tradition holds that a vision assured her that her sister was in the company of the saints in heaven.

When Angela was twenty years old her uncle died, and she returned to her paternal home at Desenzano. Convinced that the great need of her times was a better instruction of young girls in the rudiments of the Christian religion, she converted her home into a school, where she daily gathered the little girls of the town, at stated intervals, to teach them the elements of Christianity. It is related that while in an ecstasy she received a vision revealing that she was to found an association of virgins who would devote their lives to the religious training of young girls. The school at Desenzano soon bore abundant fruit, and she gladly accepted an invitation from the neighboring city of Brescia to establish a similar school there.

In 1524, while making a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, Angela was suddenly stricken blind on the island of Crete. She nevertheless continued her journey to the holy places, and on her return she was cured while praying before a crucifix at the same place where she had lost her sight a few weeks before. In the jubilee year 1525 she went to Rome to gain the indulgences. Pope Clement VII, who had heard of her holiness and of her extraordinary success as a religious teacher of young girls, invited her to remain in the city; but Angela, who shunned publicity, returned to Brescia.

On 25 November 1535, in a small house near the Church of St. Afra in Brescia, Angela chose twelve virgins and laid the foundation of the Company of St. Ursula, the community afterwards known as the Ursulines. Its members were dedicated to the religious education of girls, and the foundation is regarded as the first teaching order of women in the Church. Having served as superior of the new community for five years, Angela died on 27 January 1540. Her body lies buried in the Church of St. Afra at Brescia.

She was beatified in 1768 by Pope Clement XIII and canonized in 1807 by Pope Pius VII. Her feast is celebrated on 27 January, having formerly been observed on 31 May. She is venerated as the patroness of teachers.

anne.history:
Anne, from the Hebrew Hannah, meaning grace, is honored as the mother of the Blessed Virgin Mary and the grandmother of Jesus. She is not named in Scripture; what is told of her and of Saint Joachim, the husband traditionally given to her, comes from apocryphal literature, chiefly the Protoevangelium of James, whose earliest form reaches back to about A.D. 150, together with the Gospel of the Nativity of Mary and the Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew.

The Protoevangelium relates that a rich and pious couple in Nazareth, Joachim and Hannah, lived long without children. When Joachim came to offer sacrifice in the temple, he was driven away by Ruben, who deemed men without offspring unworthy of admission, and he withdrew to the mountains to lament before God. Hannah prayed that the Lord would take from her the curse of sterility, promising to dedicate her child to God; an angel announced to both that she would conceive, and she bore a daughter whom she named Miriam, that is, Mary. Because the story closely parallels the biblical account of the conception of Samuel, whose mother was also named Hannah, even the traditional name of Mary's mother rests on uncertain ground.

Devotion to Anne is ancient in the East, where the Protoevangelium enjoyed great authority and portions of it were read on the feasts of Mary by the Greeks, Syrians, Copts, and Arabians. Her cult there can be traced to the fourth century: Justinian I had a church dedicated to her, the oldest parts of the Greek Office in her honor are ascribed to Anatolius of Byzantium, and her feast appears in the Calendar of Constantinople, the oldest liturgical document of the Greek Church.

In the Latin Church she was not widely venerated before the thirteenth century, except perhaps in the south of France, though an eighth-century picture of her found at Santa Maria Antiqua in Rome reflects Byzantine influence. When Jacobus de Voragine incorporated the old narrative into his Golden Legend, the story of Saint Anne spread through the West and she became one of the most popular saints of the Latin Church. Her feast is kept on 26 July; first attested at Douai in 1291, it was introduced into England by Urban VI in 1378 and extended to the universal Latin Church in 1584. As with many early saints, she is recognized through long and continuous devotion rather than by a formal act of canonization.

Medieval and later writers added freely to this sparse material. John of Eck gave the names of Anne's parents and made her, after Joachim's death, the wife successively of Cleophas and Salomas and the mother of two other Marys. A sixteenth-century controversy over her supposed marriages ended with Baronius and Bellarmine defending her union with Joachim alone, and in 1677 the Holy See condemned Imperiali's teaching that Anne remained a virgin in the conception and birth of Mary.

Relics honored as hers were brought from the Holy Land to Constantinople in 710 and were still kept in the church of Saint Sophia there in 1333. Tradition at Apt in southern France holds that her body was brought there by Saint Lazarus, hidden by Saint Auspicius, and rediscovered in the reign of Charlemagne; her head was kept at Mainz until it was stolen in 1510 and carried to Düren.

Anne is venerated as the patroness of mothers, and popular devotion extends her patronage to grandmothers, to women hoping to conceive, and to women in childbirth; miners likewise invoke her, Mary being compared to silver and Christ to gold. She is the patroness of Brittany, where her shrine at Sainte-Anne-d'Auray has long drawn pilgrims, and in Canada she is the principal patroness of the province of Quebec, honored at the shrine of Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré. She is customarily depicted holding the child Mary in her lap, while Mary in turn carries the infant Jesus.

apollonia.history:
Apollonia suffered martyrdom at Alexandria during a local uprising against the Christians that took place shortly before the persecution of Decius, at the end of 248 or the beginning of 249. The violence arose amid festivities commemorating the first millenary of the Roman Empire, when agitation among the pagan populace rose to a great height; after one of their poets prophesied a calamity, the crowd committed bloody outrages against Christians whom the authorities made no effort to protect. Dionysius, Bishop of Alexandria from 247 to 265, described the sufferings of his people in a letter to Fabius, Bishop of Antioch, long extracts of which Eusebius preserved in his Church History.

After recounting how a Christian man and woman named Metras and Quinta were seized by the seditious mob and put to death with cruel tortures, and how the houses of other Christians were pillaged, Dionysius wrote that Apollonia, whom he calls parthénos presbûtis (virgo presbytera), a phrase probably meant to designate a deaconess rather than a virgin advanced in years, was held in high esteem. The mob seized her as well and, by repeated blows, broke all her teeth. Outside the city gates her captors erected a pile of fagots and threatened to burn her alive unless she repeated after them impious words, either a blasphemy against Christ or an invocation of the heathen gods. Given, at her own request, a little freedom, she sprang quickly into the fire and was burned to death.

Apollonia thus belongs to the class of early Christian martyrs who did not await the death with which they were threatened but, when confronted with the alternative of renouncing their faith or suffering death, voluntarily embraced the latter in the form prepared for them. In the honor paid to the martyrs, the Church made no distinction between these and others. Augustine considered the question in the first book of the City of God: noting that certain holy women in time of persecution had quitted life to preserve their threatened chastity and were nonetheless honored as martyrs, he wrote that he dared not pass judgment lightly, for the Church may have been divinely authorized, through trustworthy revelations, to honor their memory, and they may have acted not through human caprice but in obedience to a command of God. The narrative of Dionysius suggests no reproach of Apollonia's act; in his eyes she was as much a martyr as the others, and as such she was revered in the Alexandrian Church.

In time her feast became popular in the West as well. A later legend assigned a similar martyrdom to another Apollonia, a Christian virgin of Rome in the reign of Julian the Apostate, but there was in fact only one martyr of this name, the saint of Alexandria. The Roman Church celebrates her memory on 9 February. Because of the torments she endured, she is popularly invoked against toothache, and she is honored as the patron of dentistry. In art she is represented with pincers in which a tooth is held. A church dedicated to her at Rome no longer exists, but the little square in which it stood is still called the Piazza Sant'Apollonia.

asaph.history:
Saint Asaph, also called Asa, is honoured as the first bishop of the Welsh see that bears his name, and he served in the second half of the sixth century. No Welsh life of the saint has come down to us, a silence that leaves much of his story in obscurity. Local tradition, however, has long preserved his memory in the country near Holywell, where sites are pointed out as his ash tree, his church, his well, and his valley, known by the names Onen Asa, Fynnon Asa, Llanasa, and Pantasa. The gathering of these places in the district of Tengenel suggests that the saint probably once kept a hermitage in that neighbourhood, a quiet beginning from which a cathedral city and an ancient diocese would one day take his name.

The chief source for his life is the account of Saint Kentigern, or Mungo, the founder of the Diocese of Glasgow, written by Jocelyn of Furness. According to this narrative, Kentigern during his exile, about the year 545, withdrew to Wales and there founded the Celtic monastery of Llanelwy, the church on the river Elwy, a name by which the Welsh still call the town of Saint Asaph. Of the many disciples who gathered in that community, Asaph was one.

Few Celtic monasteries are so well described in the sources as Llanelwy. Jocelyn records that the church was built of smoothed wood, after the manner of the Britons, who could not yet build of stone. The community numbered 965 disciples, divided into three groups: three hundred, who were unlettered, farmed the outlying lands; three hundred worked in the offices around the monastery; and 365, a number corresponding to the days of the year, attended to the divine services. The oldest among these assisted Kentigern in the government of the diocese, while the rest were formed into three choirs, so ordered that as soon as one choir ended its service in the church, another entered and began it, and the praise of God continued without pause.

Tradition holds that Kentigern came to know the sanctity of his young disciple through a wonder. The founder, after the manner of other Celtic saints, was accustomed to pray standing in the icy cold river, and once, having suffered severely from the cold, he sent the boy Asaph, who was then attending upon him, to bring a fagot with which to warm himself. The disciple brought back live coals in his apron, and the miracle revealed to Kentigern the holiness of the one who served him. After the battle of Ardderyd in the year 573, the only definite date preserved in the account, Kentigern was recalled to Strathclyde, and Asaph was consecrated bishop to succeed him, thus becoming the first Welsh bishop of the see.

Of Asaph's own episcopate no further details are recorded, and the year of his death is unknown. The feast of his deposition is kept on the first of May, the day on which his memory is observed. The see that traces its succession back to him numbers among the oldest in Wales. He is venerated as a saint in the Catholic Church and in the Eastern Orthodox Church, and is honoured as a patron of bishops, remembered among the founding fathers of Welsh Christianity, the bishop who planted the faith in the river valleys of the north and whose name endures in his cathedral, his city, and his see.

augustine-of-hippo.history:
Few ancient figures are as well documented as Augustine. His own Confessions tell the story of his soul, his Retractations give the history of his mind, and the Life written by his friend Possidius recounts his apostolate. He was born at Tagaste, now Souk-Ahras in proconsular Numidia, on 13 November 354, a small city some sixty miles from Hippo. His father, Patricius, remained a pagan until his baptism shortly before a holy death around 371; his mother, Monica, a model of Christian motherhood, prayed unceasingly for her son. Augustine received a Christian education and was enrolled among the catechumens; gravely ill as a boy, he asked for baptism, but, the danger soon passing, he deferred the sacrament after the custom of the times.

Sent to Carthage towards the end of 370 to prepare for a career in rhetoric, he fell into a sinful liaison; a son was born to him in 372, and the entanglement held him for some fifteen years, although from his nineteenth year he genuinely wished to break free. In 373 the reading of Cicero's Hortensius turned his heart to philosophy, and in the same year he and his friend Honoratus fell into the snares of the Manichaeans. Their promised 'free philosophy unbridled by faith', their boasted refutation of Scripture, and their claims about the secrets of nature captivated an ardent, inquiring mind; he defended the sect with ardour and drew his friend Alypius and his father's friend Romanianus into error.

Years of interior struggle ended at Milan, where the preaching of Bishop Ambrose and the example of Christian ascetics broke through his resistance. As he tells it in the Confessions, in a garden in 386 he heard a child's voice saying 'Take up and read', opened the letters of St. Paul, and was converted. Ambrose baptized him at Easter 387, and after Monica's death he returned to Africa.

He became bishop of Hippo in 395 and gave the rest of his life to pastoral care and immense literary labour: the Confessions, the first great spiritual autobiography, and The City of God shaped Western Christianity for centuries. When some, informed by Prosper of Aquitaine, sought a middle course between his teaching and that of Pelagius, maintaining that grace must be given to those who merit it, he answered in his De Praedestinatione Sanctorum that even the first desires for salvation are due to the grace of God. He is honoured as the patron of those seeking conversion and of theologians.

In 426, at seventy-two, wishing to spare his city the turmoil of an election after his death, he had clergy and people acclaim the deacon Heraclius as his auxiliary and successor and transferred to him the administration of externals. The revolt of Count Boniface (427) convulsed Africa: the Goths sent by the Empress Placidia and the Vandals summoned by Boniface were all Arians, and the Arian bishop Maximinus entered Hippo with the imperial troops. Augustine defended the Faith at a public conference in 428 and in various writings, and laboured to reconcile Boniface and Placidia. Peace was restored, but not with Genseric, the Vandal king; Boniface, vanquished, took refuge in Hippo with the bishops who had fled there, and the city endured an eighteen months' siege. Early in it Augustine fell gravely ill, knowing the sickness to be fatal, and after three months of patience and fervent prayer he died on 28 August 430, in the seventy-sixth year of his age, the day kept as his feast.

barbara.history:
Barbara is honored as a virgin and martyr, though no reference to her appears in the authentic early historical authorities for Christian antiquity, and her name is absent from the original recension of St. Jerome's martyrology. Veneration of the saint was common, however, from the seventh century, by which date legendary Acts of her martyrdom existed; these were inserted in the collection of Symeon Metaphrastes and were used by compilers of the enlarged martyrologies of ninth-century Western Europe, such as Ado and Usuard.

These narratives, essentially the same, make Barbara the daughter of a rich heathen named Dioscorus, who kept her shut up in a tower to preserve her from the outside world and who communicated to her an offer of marriage that she rejected. Before departing on a journey, her father had a bath-house erected for her use near her dwelling, and during his absence Barbara had three windows put into it, as a symbol of the Holy Trinity, instead of the two originally intended. On his return she acknowledged herself a Christian, was ill-treated by him, and dragged before Martinianus, prefect of the province, who cruelly tortured her and condemned her to death by beheading. Her father carried out the sentence himself, but in punishment he was struck by lightning on the way home and his body consumed. A Christian named Juliana suffered martyrdom along with Barbara, and a pious man called Valentinus buried the saints, at whose grave the sick were healed and pilgrims who came to pray received aid and consolation. The emperor in whose reign the martyrdom is placed is sometimes called Maximinus and sometimes Maximianus, but, owing to the purely legendary character of the accounts, there is no good basis for earlier investigations to decide whether Maximinus Thrax or Maximinus Daza is meant.

The place of martyrdom also varies: Symeon Metaphrastes and the Latin legend given by Mombritius make Heliopolis in Egypt the site, while other accounts, to which Baronius ascribes more weight, give Nicomedia. The Martyrologium Romanum parvum of about 700, the oldest martyrology of the Latin Church in which her name occurs, states, 'In Tuscia Barbarae virginis et martyris,' a statement repeated by Ado and others, while later additions to the martyrologies of St. Jerome and Bede read 'Romae Barbarae virginis' or place her passion at Antioch. These varied statements prove only the local adaptation of the veneration of a martyr concerning whom there is no genuine historical tradition. It is certain, however, that before the ninth century she was publicly venerated in both East and West, and that she was very popular with the Christian populace.

The legend that her father was struck by lightning probably caused her to be regarded by the common people as patron in time of danger from thunderstorms and fire, and later, by analogy, as protectress of artillerymen and miners; she is also honored as patron of architects. She was called upon as intercessor to assure the reception of the Sacraments of Penance and Holy Eucharist at the hour of death, and is invoked against sudden death. An occurrence of 1448 did much to further her veneration: Henry Kock, nearly burnt to death in a fire at Gorkum, called on St. Barbara, to whom he had shown great devotion; she aided him to escape the burning house and kept him alive until he could receive the last sacraments. A similar circumstance is related in an addition to the Legenda aurea.

Her feast falls on 4 December in the Greek and present Roman calendars, while the martyrologies of the ninth century, with the exception of that of Rabanus Maurus, place it on 16 December. St. Barbara has often been depicted in art: she is represented standing in a tower with three windows, carrying the palm of a martyr, and often holds a chalice and sacramental wafer, with cannon sometimes displayed near her.

basil-of-amasea.history:
Basil of Amasea, called Basileus or Basilius in the ancient sources, was a bishop and martyr of the early fourth century. He governed the church of Amasea, a city in Pontus, in what is now northern Turkey, and died a martyr in the reign of the emperor Licinius. Jerome's Latin version of the Chronicle of Eusebius records, under the 275th Olympiad (A.D. 321-324), that Basileus, Bishop of Amasea, suffered martyrdom at this time, and there is no reason for doubting the trustworthiness of this information.

His name appears among the signatures of the bishops who attended the Councils of Ancyra and Neo-Caesarea in the year 314, where Basileus of Amasea stands listed among the participants. Attendance at these councils marks him as a bishop active in the ecclesiastical life of the early fourth-century Church, taking part in its efforts to define and defend orthodox doctrine. Apart from this signature, the early sources preserve no account of his origins or of his tenure as bishop.

The historical setting of his death is given by Eusebius, who relates in his Church History that in the time of Licinius Christians were treated with great cruelty, especially in Amasea and the other cities of Pontus, and that the governor inflicted upon several bishops the ordinary punishments of evildoers. Basil's martyrdom is understood against this background: his own see was among the places where the persecution fell most heavily, and he gave his life for the faith he had labored to defend.

St. Athanasius likewise mentions the great Basileus of Pontus among the bishops of the early part of the fourth century who held firmly to the like substance of the Son with the Father. The reference is evidently to the martyr-bishop of Amasea, and it presents him as a defender of the Church's teaching on the substance of the Son with the Father. The testimony places Basil in that company of bishops who suffered in the persecution under Licinius.

A statement of Philostorgius, that Basileus attended the Council of Nicaea, cannot be quoted against the proof of his martyrdom under Licinius, since it evidently contains a mistake: among the signatures at the Council of Nicaea appears that of Eutychianus as Bishop of Amasea. The Acts of Basil's martyrdom, which purport to have been written by an eyewitness, a presbyter named Johannes, are not authentic, and their narrative is entirely legendary. Little can therefore be known of the circumstances of his death beyond the general account of the persecution.

His feast is kept on 26 April, the date on which it occurs both in the Greek synaxaria and menaea and in the Roman martyrology. He is remembered as a bishop and martyr of the early fourth century, a pastor of the church of Amasea whose witness to the faith ended in death under Licinius.

benedict-of-nursia.history:
St. Benedict of Nursia, the founder of Western monasticism, was born at Nursia, a small town near Spoleto, around the year 480, the son of a Roman noble. Tradition, accepted by the historian Bede, holds that he was the twin brother of St. Scholastica. The only authentic account of his life is found in the second book of St. Gregory the Great's Dialogues, which rests on the testimony of the saint's own disciples, Constantinus and Honoratus, who afterward served as abbots of Monte Cassino and Subiaco. Gregory's work is less a chronological biography than a character sketch, drawn from miraculous incidents that illustrate Benedict's holiness.

Benedict passed his boyhood in Rome, attending the schools into his higher studies. Around the year 500 he left the city, giving over his books and forsaking the wealth of his father's house to serve God. Gregory's narrative suggests he was older than the fourteen years often assigned; he was more likely nineteen or twenty, old enough to recognize the corruption of his companions, to have felt deeply the love of a woman, and to weigh the life taught in the Gospel against his prospects as a Roman noble. He did not at first intend to become a hermit. Accompanied by his old nurse as a servant, he settled at Enfide, some forty miles from Rome, near a church dedicated to St. Peter, in association with a company of virtuous men. There he is said to have worked his first miracle, restoring a broken wheat-sifter to perfect condition, and the attention this drew made him flee secretly to the more retired district of Subiaco, resolved to live poorly and to labor for his bread.

At Subiaco a monk named Romanus clothed him in the monastic habit and counseled him to withdraw into a cave high above the lake, beside the ruins of Nero's villa and the distant falls that once fed the valley below. Tradition holds that Benedict lived there as a hermit for three years, unknown to men, while Romanus brought him food on fixed days. According to Gregory, Benedict ceased to be a youth and became a man of God, and his holiness attracted disciples, whom he organized into small monasteries.

Around 529 Benedict moved to Monte Cassino, where he founded the monastery that became the cradle of Western monasticism. There, tradition holds, he composed the Rule that bears his name: a balanced guide to community life built on prayer, work, and obedience, long summarized in the motto Ora et labora, pray and work. Gregory preserves from the Rule Benedict's ideal of the abbot, learned in the law of God, who must prefer mercy to justice, study rather to be loved than feared, correct with prudence, and temper all things so that the strong have something to strive after and the weak nothing at which to take alarm. The Rule shaped monastic life across Europe and, through the centuries, helped preserve learning within the Church.

Gregory also sketches Benedict's private life at Monte Cassino. Disciples found him weeping silently in prayer in his cell, or standing at its window in the night hours offering his prayers to God, and he was often seen reading before the monastery gate, as Totila, the Gothic king, is said to have found him.

Benedict died at Monte Cassino about 543, though tradition often gives the year as 547. He is honored as a patron of students and of those seeking protection from evil, and in 1964 Pope Paul VI declared him patron of Europe. His feast is kept on July 11.

bernardino-of-siena.history:
Bernardino of Siena was born on 8 September 1380 at Massa, a Sienese town of which his father was then governor, into the noble Albizeschi family. Orphaned at six, he was raised by pious aunts and, after studying civil and canon law, joined in 1397 the confraternity serving the hospital of Santa Maria della Scala in Siena. When plague revisited the city in 1400, he left the secluded life of prayer he had embraced and, with ten companions, took entire charge of the hospital for four months, labor that permanently damaged his health. He gave his patrimony to charity, received the Franciscan habit at San Francesco in Siena on 8 September 1402, retired to the Observantine convent of Columbaio, and was professed in 1403 and ordained in 1404.

About 1406 the preacher Vincent Ferrer is said to have foretold that his mantle would descend upon Bernardino, leaving him the task of evangelizing Italy. After nearly twelve years of obscurity, much of them spent in retirement at Capriola, his preaching career began at Milan at the close of 1417. Cities then contended for the honor of hearing him; often forced into the marketplaces, he drew audiences of up to thirty thousand and gained immense influence over the turbulent, luxurious cities of Italy. Pius II, who as a young man had listened to him spellbound, recorded that Bernardino was heard as another Paul; the Florentine writer Vespasiano da Bisticci credited his sermons with cleansing Italy from every kind of sin.

Penitents, it is recorded, flocked to confession "like ants", and several cities enacted his moral program into law, the Riformazioni di frate Bernardino. He preached with apostolic freedom, censuring the Visconti, Duke of Milan, and rebuking the vice in high places; his hearers cast "vanities" onto bonfires by the cartload. Usury was a principal target, and his preaching helped prepare the way for the Monti di Pietà, charitable loan societies. His watchword, like that of St. Francis, was "Peace": on foot he crossed Italy reconciling Guelphs and Ghibellines, and at Crema his preaching brought about the recall and reinstatement of political exiles.

At the heart of his preaching was devotion to the Holy Name of Jesus. He persuaded cities to replace the arms of their warring factions on church and palace walls with the initials IHS, and while preaching he held up a tablet bearing the monogram painted amid rays, afterward exposing it for veneration, a custom he appears to have introduced at Volterra in 1424. In Bologna a card-painter ruined by his sermons against gambling earned a living, and soon a small fortune, painting such tablets.

Success brought persecution. In 1427, at the instance of adherents of the Dominican Manfred of Vercelli, whose preaching about Antichrist Bernardino had combated, he was charged with heresy for introducing a profane, new devotion through his tablets that exposed the people to the danger of idolatry. Martin V at first forbade him to preach or exhibit the tablets, but at a hearing at St. Peter's on 8 June 1427, with St. John Capistran directing his defense, the charges collapsed; the pope not only justified his teaching but urged him to preach in Rome. When his enemies renewed their accusations under Eugene IV, a papal bull of 7 January 1432 annulled their secret proceedings.

Bernardino declined the bishopric of Siena and the sees of Ferrara and Urbino, offered in 1431 and 1435, saying that all Italy was already his diocese. He died at Aquila in the Abruzzi on 20 May 1444, the date kept as his feast, and was canonized in 1450, only six years after his death. In memory of an eloquence that filled the market squares of Italy and of the emblem through which he shaped public devotion, he is honored as the patron of advertisers and remembered as the "Apostle of Italy".

blane.history:
Saint Blane, whose name is also written Blaan, was a bishop and confessor of sixth-century Scotland, belonging to the early generations of the Church in northern Britain. He was born on the island of Bute, the date of his birth being unknown, and he was a nephew of St. Cathan. Educated in Ireland under Sts. Comgall and Kenneth, he became a monk, went to Scotland, and eventually was a bishop among the Picts.

Several miracles are related of him in later tradition, among them the restoration of a dead boy to life. The Aberdeen Breviary gives these and other details of the saint's life, which are rejected, however, by the Bollandists; such traditions are best regarded as devotional legend rather than established history.

The chronology of his life is not easy to fix. The year of his death is variously given as 446, 590, and 1000. The first, found in Butler's Lives of the Saints, is evidently incorrect. The date 1000, which appears in Adam King's Kalendar of Scottish Saints (Paris, 1588), in Dempster's Menologium Scotorum (Bonn, 1622), and in the Acta Sanctorum, seems to have crept in through a confusion between St. Kenneth, whose disciple Blane was, and a Kenneth who was King of Scotland about the year 1000. The highest authorities assign his death to the year 590.

From early times, devotion to St. Blane was popular in Scotland. His monastery became the site of the Cathedral of Dunblane, and the bell of his monastery is preserved there; later devotion at Dunblane kept his memory alive across the centuries. There was also a church of St. Blane in Dumfries and another at Kilblane. The ruins of his church at Kingarth on Bute, where his remains were buried, are still standing and form an object of great interest to antiquarians.

His feast has been kept on 10 August from ancient times, and he is honored as a patron of bishops. He is remembered as one of the apostolic figures of Scottish Christianity, a patient builder of the Church in a hard and beautiful land.

blathmac.history:
Saint Blathmac, a distinguished Irish monk, was born in Ireland about the year 750. A scion of a noble family, he showed a religious turn of mind from his early years, and longed to be enrolled in the noble army of martyrs, a wish that was afterwards fulfilled. His name, formed from the Irish word blath, meaning a flower, was latinized as Florentius.

As a religious he was most exemplary, and in time he became an abbot. In 824 he joined the community of Columban monks on the island of Iona, where the shrine of St. Columba was kept.

Not long afterwards the island was ravaged by Danish raiders. One morning, as Blathmac was celebrating Mass, Scandinavian rovers entered the monastic church and put the monks to death. The shrine of St. Columba was the object of their plunder, but Blathmac refused to point it out, and for this he was hacked to pieces on the altar step. Thus he received the martyrdom he had desired from his youth.

His body was afterwards reverently interred on the spot where the martyrdom took place, and numerous miracles are claimed to have been wrought through his intercession.

He is fortunate in having had his biography written by Strabo, Benedictine Abbot of Reichenau from 824 to 849, and thus the story of his martyrdom has been handed down through the ages. Strabo's life of the saint is composed in Latin hexameters and was printed in Messingham's Florilegium Insulæ Sanctorum at Paris in 1624. The year of Blathmac's death is given variously: the common account places it about 835, the Annals of Ulster record 825, and Mabillon places it thirty-six years earlier.

A distinguished monk of the early Irish church, he is honored as a patron of monks.

bonaventure.history:
St. Bonaventure was born at Bagnorea, near Viterbo in Italy, in 1221, and died at Lyons on 15 July 1274, the day kept as his feast. Nothing is known of his parents, Giovanni di Fidanza and Maria Ritella, beyond their names. His baptismal name was John; how it came to be changed to Bonaventure is not clear. Tradition holds that he was preserved from death in childhood through the intercession of St. Francis, but the story that the name came from an exclamation of St. Francis over the infant rests on a late fifteenth-century legend and is considered improbable.

He entered the Order of Friars Minor, in 1238 or 1243, the exact year being uncertain, and was sent from the Roman Province to complete his studies at the University of Paris under Alexander of Hales, founder of the Franciscan school. He received the licentiate in 1248, with the right to teach publicly, and lectured at the university with great success until 1256, when he had to cease amid a violent dispute: the secular professors, apparently jealous of the academic successes of the Dominicans and Franciscans, sought to exclude the Mendicant orders from teaching. The discord flared in 1256, when Guillaume de Saint-Amour published The Perils of the Last Times, attacking the Friars with great bitterness; in connection with it Bonaventure wrote his treatise De paupertate Christi. After the Holy See restored the Mendicants to all their privileges and Saint-Amour's book was formally condemned, the degree of Doctor was solemnly conferred on Bonaventure and on St. Thomas Aquinas at the university on 23 October 1257, and he became a master of the university alongside his friend Aquinas.

Before that, although not yet thirty-six, he had been elected Minister General of the Friars Minor on 2 February 1257. The order was then divided between two factions: the Spirituales, who insisted on the literal observance of the original Rule, especially on poverty, and the Relaxati, who favored mitigations and innovations. The controversy was aggravated when many of the Spiritual Friars embraced doctrines connected with the name of Abbot Joachim of Floris as set forth in the so-called Evangelium aeternum. Bonaventure struck vigorously at both extremes: he proceeded against several of the Joachimite Spirituals as heretics before an ecclesiastical tribunal at Città della Pieve, where two of their leaders were condemned to perpetual imprisonment, while an encyclical letter issued soon after his election outlined a program for the reform of the Relaxati. This he enforced at the General Chapter of Narbonne, where the constitutions he had revised, the Constitutiones Narbonenses, were promulgated; they form an exposition of the Rule of capital importance in Franciscan legislation.

In 1260 the chapter asked him to write a life of St. Francis to supersede those then in circulation, and at a general chapter convoked at Pisa in 1263 this life was officially approved as the standard biography of the saint, to the exclusion of all others. At the same chapter he fixed the limits of the order's provinces and prescribed that at nightfall a bell be rung in honor of the Annunciation, a pious practice from which the Angelus seems to have originated.

Amid these labors he wrote many works of theology and mysticism, including The Journey of the Mind to God and the Breviloquium, together with commentaries on the Book of Sentences and on Scripture, a corpus preserved in the critical Quaracchi edition of 1882-1902.

He was later made a cardinal and Cardinal-Bishop of Albano and took a leading part in the Second Council of Lyons, at which he died. Canonized in 1482 and declared a Doctor of the Church, he is known as the Seraphic Doctor and is honored as a patron of scholars. No formal contemporary biography of him survives.

brendan.history:
Brendan of Ardfert and Clonfert, known also as Brendan the Voyager or Brendan the Navigator, was born in 484 in Ciarraighe Luachra, near the present city of Tralee in County Kerry, Ireland, and died in 577 at Annaghdown. He was baptized at Tubrid, near Ardfert, by Bishop Erc, spent five years of his education under St. Ita, remembered as the Brigid of Munster, and completed his studies under St. Erc, who ordained him a priest in 512.

Between 512 and 530 Brendan built monastic cells at Ardfert and at Shanakeel, at the foot of Brandon Hill; from this place he is said to have set out on his famous voyage. Crowds of pilgrims and students soon gathered, and additional religious houses were formed at Gallerus, Kilmalchedor, Brandon Hill, and the Blasquet Islands to receive them. About the year 550 he founded a monastery at Inis-da-druim, now Coney Island in County Clare, and then journeyed to Wales and Iona, leaving traces of his work at Kilbrandon, near Oban, and in Kilbrennan Sound. After a three-year mission in Britain he returned to Ireland and worked in various parts of Leinster, especially at Dysart in County Kilkenny and at Killiney. He established the Sees of Ardfert and Annaghdown, founded churches at Inchiquin in County Galway and at Inishglora in County Mayo, and in 557 made his most celebrated foundation, the monastery of Clonfert, over which he appointed St. Moinenn as prior and head master. He was interred at Clonfert.

Brendan's lasting fame rests chiefly on the story of his Atlantic voyage. The old Irish calendars assigned a special feast to the departure of the family of St. Brendan, and St. Aengus the Culdee, at the close of the eighth century, invokes the sixty who accompanied Brendan in his quest of the Land of Promise. According to the Navigatio Sancti Brendani, a Latin narrative of the tenth or eleventh century built upon traditions current from the ninth, Brendan sailed in search of the Promised Land with a company of monks whose number is variously given as from eighteen to one hundred and fifty, and after a voyage of seven years they reached the Terra Repromissionis, a most beautiful land with luxuriant vegetation. No historical proof of the journey exists. Doubt was expressed very early: Honorius of Augsburg declared that the island had vanished, Vincent of Beauvais denied the authenticity of the pilgrimage, and the Bollandists do not recognize it, while geographers have ranked the story among geographical legends. Some scholars have nevertheless proposed that the narrative preserves the memory of actual Atlantic voyages that may have reached the American continent, though this remains conjecture.

The legend long shaped ideas of the western ocean. The land visited by Brendan was placed not far west of Ireland on the Catalonian chart of 1375, identified with the Fortunate Isles of the ancients, set among the Canary Islands or substituted for Madeira on charts of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, and pushed far out into the ocean on Martin Behaim's globe. The inhabitants of Ferro, Gomera, Madeira, and the Azores told Columbus that they had often seen the island, and belief in its existence was finally abandoned in the early nineteenth century. Recognized as a saint in the era before formal canonization processes were established, Brendan is venerated as the patron of sailors, and his feast is kept on 16 May.

camillus-de-lellis.history:
Camillus de Lellis was born at Bucchianico in Abruzzo in 1550, the son of an officer who had served in both the Neapolitan and French armies. His mother died when he was a child, and he grew up neglected. While still a youth he became a soldier, serving first Venice and then Naples until his regiment was disbanded in 1574. Military life made him a confirmed gambler, and his losses at play at times reduced him to destitution. Encouraged by the kindness of a Franciscan friar, he sought admission to that order but was refused. He then went to Rome, where he found employment in the Hospital for Incurables, drawn chiefly by the hope of a cure for the abscesses in both feet from which he had long suffered, but he was dismissed on account of his quarrelsome disposition and his passion for gambling. He took up soldiering again and took part in the campaign against the Turks, and was afterwards employed by the Capuchins at Manfredonia on a building they were erecting. His gambling still pursued him until a discourse of the convent's guardian so startled him that he determined to reform. Admitted to the Capuchins as a lay brother, he was soon dismissed on account of his infirmity.

Camillus then returned to Rome and entered the hospital in which he had previously been. After a temporary cure of his ailment he became a nurse, and his piety and prudence won such admiration that he was appointed director of the institution. While in this office he attempted to found an order of lay infirmarians, but the scheme was opposed, and on the advice of his friends, among them his spiritual guide, St. Philip Neri, he resolved to become a priest. At the age of thirty-two he began the study of Latin at the Jesuit College in Rome. In 1584 he established his order, the Fathers of a Good Death, later known as the Camillians, binding its members by vow to devote themselves to the plague-stricken. Its members wore a red cross on their habit, and their care extended from the hospitals to the sick in their own homes. Camillus insisted that the sick be cared for as if they were Christ himself, and his work reformed hospital care in Rome and beyond.

Pope Sixtus V confirmed the congregation in 1586 and ordained that a general superior should be elected every three years; Camillus was its first superior, and was succeeded by an Englishman named Roger. Two years afterwards a house was established at Naples, where two members of the community, nursing the sick aboard a fleet quarantined off the harbour, became the first martyrs of charity of the congregation. In 1591 Gregory XIV erected the congregation into a religious order with the privileges of the mendicants, a status confirmed again by Clement VIII in 1592.

The infirmity which had prevented his entrance among the Capuchins afflicted Camillus for forty-six years, and other ailments made his life one of uninterrupted suffering; he would permit no one to wait on him, and when scarcely able to stand he crawled from his bed to visit the sick. He resigned the generalship of the order in 1607 so as to have more leisure for the sick and the poor, and had by then established houses in many cities of Italy. He was said to have had the gifts of miracles and prophecy. He died at Rome on 14 July 1614, at the age of sixty-four, while pronouncing a moving appeal to his brethren. He was buried near the high altar of the church of St. Mary Magdalen, and when the miracles attributed to him had been officially approved, his body was placed beneath the altar itself.

Camillus was beatified in 1742 and canonized in 1746 by Pope Benedict XIV. His feast day is kept on 14 July. In 1930 Pope Pius XI named him, together with St. John of God, principal co-patron of nurses and nursing associations, and he is honored as a patron of the sick and of hospitals.

casimir.history:
St. Casimir, prince of Poland, was born in the royal palace at Cracow on 3 October 1458, the second son of King Casimir IV and Queen Elizabeth, an Austrian princess and daughter of the Emperor Albert II. His family stood at the center of European affairs: his grandfather Wladislaus II Jagiello had introduced Christianity into Lithuania, his uncle Wladislaus III died at Varna in 1444 defending Christendom against the Turks, and his brothers occupied in turn the thrones of Bohemia, Hungary, and Poland.

The prince's early training was entrusted to Father Dlugosz, the Polish historian and later Archbishop of Lwow, and to the humanist Filippo Buonaccorsi, called Callimachus. Placed in the care of these tutors at the age of nine, Casimir was already remarkable for ardent piety.

At thirteen he was offered the throne of Hungary by a faction discontented under King Matthias Corvinus. Eager to defend the Cross against the Turks, he accepted the call and went to Hungary to receive the crown; the enterprise failed, however, and he returned to Poland as a fugitive. Tradition holds that he could not bring himself to wage an unjust war to secure it. He resumed his studies under Dlugosz until 1475 and was then associated with his father in public affairs, becoming heir-apparent to the Polish throne after his elder brother Wladislaus took the Bohemian crown.

When the king went to Lithuania in 1479, Casimir governed Poland in his absence and from 1481 to 1483 administered the state with notable prudence and justice. His father sought to arrange his marriage to a daughter of the Emperor Frederick III, but the prince declined and preferred to remain single. He was distinguished by justice and chastity, knelt for hours at night before the locked doors of churches regardless of the weather, and had a special devotion to the Blessed Virgin. The hymn Omni die dic Mariae, written by St. Bernard of Clairvaux, was long attributed to him, and tradition holds that he recited it daily.

His fastings and mortifications had weakened him when, on a journey to Lithuania, he contracted tuberculosis, a severe illness of the lungs that he could not withstand. He died at the court of Grodno on 4 March 1484, at the age of twenty-five, and was buried in the chapel of the Blessed Virgin in the cathedral of Vilna.

Veneration of Casimir as a saint followed soon after his death on account of the miracles attributed to him. King Sigismund I of Poland petitioned for his canonization, and Pope Leo X appointed the papal legate Zaccaria Ferreri, Bishop of Guardalfiera, together with the Archbishop of Gnesen and the Bishop of Przemysl, to investigate the prince's life and miracles. The inquiry was completed at Turn in 1520, and in 1522 Casimir was canonized by Pope Adrian VI. Pope Clement VIII afterwards fixed his feast on 4 March.

He is honored as the patron of youth, and as patron of Poland and Lithuania, with veneration reaching as far as Belgium and Naples. Churches and chapels were dedicated to him in both lands, and tradition holds that he contributed miraculously to a Polish victory over the Russians near the River Dzwina. Early in the seventeenth century King Sigismund III began a chapel in his honor at Vilna, completed under King Wladislaus IV and adorned by Peter Danckerts of the Netherlands with paintings of the saint's life; there an old picture, renovated in 1594, represents him with a lily in his hand.

catherine-of-alexandria.history:
St. Catherine of Alexandria is honored as a virgin and martyr, and her feast is celebrated on 25 November in the Latin Church and in the various Oriental churches. For almost six centuries she was the object of widely popular devotion, although the story of her life has come down only in later, heavily embellished texts, and no longer in their original form. According to the traditional Acts, Catherine was of noble birth and learned in the sciences, and when only eighteen years old she presented herself to the reigning emperor, who was violently persecuting the Christians. She upbraided him for his cruelty and endeavored to show how iniquitous was the worship of false gods.

Astounded at her audacity but unable to match her learning, the emperor detained her in his palace and summoned numerous scholars, commanding them to use all their skill in specious reasoning so that she might be led to apostatize. The Acts recount that Catherine emerged from the debate victorious, and that several of her adversaries, conquered by her eloquence, declared themselves Christians and were at once put to death. Furious at being baffled, the emperor had her scourged and then imprisoned. The empress, eager to see so extraordinary a young woman, went with Porphyry, the head of the troops, to visit her in her dungeon, and both in turn yielded to Catherine's exhortations, believed, were baptized, and soon received the martyr's crown. Catherine herself was condemned to die on the wheel; at her touch this instrument of torture is said to have been miraculously destroyed, and she was beheaded instead. Tradition holds that angels carried her body to Mount Sinai, where a church and monastery were later built in her honor.

The legend acquired immense authority in the Middle Ages, when such extraordinary narratives were read without question of their historical value. Ranked with St. Margaret and St. Barbara among the fourteen most helpful saints in heaven, Catherine was praised by preachers and sung by poets: Bossuet dedicated one of his most beautiful panegyrics to her, and Adam of Saint-Victor wrote a poem in her honor. Her feast was kept with the utmost solemnity, in several dioceses of France as a holy day of obligation up to the beginning of the seventeenth century, and numberless chapels were placed under her patronage. In medieval iconography she is depicted with the wheel, her instrument of torture, and with the sword of her martyrdom. Because she had triumphed in science by closing the mouths of the sophists, her intercession was implored by theologians, apologists, pulpit orators, and philosophers before they studied, wrote, or preached, and she came to be honored as a patroness of students; wheelwrights and mechanics likewise placed themselves under her protection. In France this devotion gained further renown at the beginning of the fifteenth century, when it was rumored that she had appeared to Joan of Arc and, with St. Margaret, been divinely appointed Joan's adviser.

Modern criticism has weighed this legend with care. Contemporary hagiographers look upon the authenticity of the texts containing it as more than doubtful, although this is not meant to cast any doubt on the saint's existence. The conclusion reached by careful study is that the principal facts forming the outline may be accepted as true, while the mass of details, the marvelous narratives, and the long discourses put into Catherine's mouth are to be rejected as inventions pure and simple. Although all the texts mention the miraculous translation of her body to Mount Sinai, the itineraries of the ancient pilgrims who visited Sinai contain no allusion to it. In the eighteenth century Dom Deforis, the Benedictine who prepared an edition of Bossuet's works, declared that tradition largely false, and about that time the feast of St. Catherine disappeared from the Breviary of Paris. Since then devotion to the virgin of Alexandria has lost all its former popularity.

catherine-of-bologna.history:
Catherine of Bologna was born at Bologna on 8 September 1413 into a noble family. She is remembered as a Poor Clare, a mystical writer, and an artist. When she was ten years old, her father sent her to the court of the Marquis of Ferrara, Nicolò d'Este, to serve as a companion to the Princess Margarita. In this setting she pursued the study of literature and the fine arts, and she received the education in letters, music, and art for which she was afterwards noted. She became a gifted painter and illuminator, and a manuscript illuminated by her, which once belonged to Pope Pius IX, is today reckoned among the treasures of Oxford.

After the marriage of the Princess Margarita to Roberto Malatesta, Prince of Rimini, Catherine returned home. She resolved to join the little company of devout maidens who were living in community in the neighboring town of Ferrara and following the rule of the Third Order of Saint Augustine, and in 1426 she became one of them. Later, yielding to her entreaties, the community adopted the Rule of Saint Clare, and in 1432 its members were clothed with the habit of the Second Order of Saint Francis by the provincial of the Friars Minor. From that time the community belonged to the Poor Clares.

The increasing number of vocations made further foundations necessary, and monasteries of the Poor Clares were established in Italy. In pursuance of the Brief of Callistus III, convents were founded at Bologna and at Cremona. The monastery in her native city was founded in 1456, and Catherine was chosen abbess of that community, an office she held until her death. As abbess she guided the sisters, and a large part of her counsels and instructions on the spiritual life has come down through her writings.

The grievous and persistent temptations of the early days of her religious life tried her patience, her humility, and above all her faith. In the years that followed, these trials gave place to the most abundant spiritual consolation and to the enjoyment of the heights of contemplation.

Her principal work is the Treatise on the Seven Spiritual Weapons. It gathers a large part of her counsels and instructions on the spiritual life, and it contains, besides, an account of the saint's own struggles in the path of perfection. The title alludes to the spiritual weapons by which the soul is armed against temptation, and the union of practical counsel with the record of her own experience is the treatise's particular character. She composed it with the aid of her confessor shortly before her death.

Catherine died at Bologna on 9 March 1463. Her body remains incorrupt and is preserved in the chapel of the Poor Clares at Bologna. She was canonized by Pope Benedict XIII in 1712. Her feast is kept on 9 March throughout the Order of Friars Minor, the order from whose provincial she had received the habit. She is venerated as the patron saint of artists, an honor that corresponds to her accomplishments in painting and illumination, and the survival of her illuminated manuscript, her writings, and her incorrupt remains has kept her memory alive as a religious, a writer, and an artist.

catherine-of-siena.history:
St. Catherine of Siena was born at Siena on March 25, 1347, the twenty-fourth of twenty-five children. Her father, Giacomo di Benincasa, was a dyer, and her mother, Lapa, was the daughter of a local poet. From early childhood she saw visions and practiced severe austerities, and at the age of seven she consecrated her virginity to Christ. In her sixteenth year she received the habit of the Dominican Tertiaries and lived as a recluse in a little room in her father's house. Tradition dates her mystical 'spiritual espousals' to about the carnival of 1366, after which she rejoined her family and began to tend the sick, especially those with the most repulsive diseases, to serve the poor, and to work for the conversion of sinners.

Though she suffered constant physical pain and lived for long intervals on almost nothing but the Blessed Sacrament, she was radiantly happy and full of practical wisdom, and disciples of both sexes gathered around her in a spiritual fellowship. During the summer of 1370, after a prolonged trance in which she had visions of Hell, Purgatory, and Heaven, she came to believe she was commanded to leave her cell and enter public life. Her letters went to men and women of every condition and to the princes and republics of Italy, she was consulted by papal legates, and she worked to stay the fury of civil war. She urged Gregory XI to leave Avignon and to reform the clergy and the administration of the Papal States, and backed his plan for a crusade in the hope of restoring peace to Italy.

At Pisa, on the fourth Sunday of Lent in 1375, she received the stigmata, which, at her own prayer, remained invisible in her body during her life. In June 1376 she went to Avignon as ambassador of the Florentines; the embassy failed, but she made so profound an impression on the pope that, despite the opposition of the French king and most of the Sacred College, he returned to Rome on January 17, 1377. Much of 1377 she spent in a spiritual revival of the country districts under Siena, and tradition holds that she then miraculously learned to write, though she still chiefly relied on secretaries.

Early in 1378 Gregory sent her again to Florence to seek peace. Drawn into the city's internal politics, she lived through a popular tumult in which an attempt was made on her life on June 22, a deliverance she bitterly regretted as the loss of the martyrdom she craved. She remained in or near Florence through the revolution of the Ciompi until word of peace came in early August, then returned to Siena and dictated her Dialogue, the book of her meditations and revelations, cast as a series of colloquies between the Eternal Father and the human soul.

When the Great Schism broke out, she adhered to the Roman claimant, Urban VI, who summoned her to Rome in November 1378. There she spent her remaining years laboring for the reform of the Church, serving the destitute and afflicted, and writing letters in Urban's behalf. As her strength failed she offered her sufferings for the unity and renovation of the Church, and after a mysterious agony of some three months, from Sexagesima Sunday until the Sunday before the Ascension, she died at Rome on April 29, 1380, the date kept as her feast. Her last political work, carried out almost from her deathbed, was the reconciliation of Urban VI with the Roman Republic.

Her confessor and biographer, Fra Raimondo delle Vigne of Capua, afterwards became General of the Dominicans. The Dialogue ranks among the classics of spiritual literature, and the Letters, addressed to popes, sovereigns, and private persons alike, are prized both as documents of history and as spiritual counsel, their keynote the call to abide in the cell of self-knowledge. She was canonized in 1461, declared a Doctor of the Church in 1970, and is honored as a patron of single women.

cecilia.history:
Cecilia was a Roman virgin and martyr who died at Rome, and she ranks among the most venerated martyrs of Christian antiquity. The Church honors her as patroness of church music and of musicians. Tradition places her life in the second or third century and remembers her as a young noblewoman who consecrated her virginity to God.

The earliest historical notice of Cecilia appears in the Martyrologium Hieronymianum, which shows that her memory was kept in the Roman Church by the fourth century. That martyrology enters her name under September 16, evidently the day of her burial in the Catacomb of Callistus on the Appian Way and not her feast; her feast day is November 22, on which day it is still celebrated in her church in Rome's Trastevere quarter. Early guides to the Roman martyrs' burial places point to her tomb on the Via Appia beside the crypt of the third-century bishops of Rome; her grave has been located in the Catacomb of Callistus, in a crypt adjoining the popes' chapel, where an empty niche probably once held her sarcophagus. A titular church in Trastevere, built as early as the fourth century and certainly dedicated to her by the fifth, appears in the acts of the Roman Council of 499 as the titulus sanctae Caeciliae. The ground beneath the oldest part of the Callistus catacomb probably belonged to her family, and the church may have been her gift to the Roman Church. Her name is absent from the earliest fourth-century list of Roman feasts, but five masses in her honor in the Sacramentarium Leonianum, completed near the end of the fifth century, testify to her great veneration.

About the middle of the fifth century arose the Acts of her martyrdom, preserved in numerous manuscripts, translated into Greek, and used in the prefaces of the Leonine masses. These Acts relate that Cecilia, a virgin of senatorial family and a Christian from infancy, was given in marriage by her parents to a noble pagan named Valerian. When they retired to the wedding chamber, she told him that an angel jealously guarded her and that he must not violate her virginity. Valerian asked to see the angel, and Cecilia sent him to the third milestone of the Via Appia, where he met Bishop Urban, received baptism, and returned a Christian; an angel then appeared to the two and crowned them with roses and lilies. Valerian's brother Tiburtius was likewise won to the faith, and the brothers distributed alms and buried the bodies of confessors who had died for Christ. The prefect Turcius Almachius condemned them to death, and Maximus, the officer appointed to execute the sentence, was converted and suffered martyrdom with them. Cecilia buried their remains in one tomb; when she in turn was sought, she arranged for her house to be kept as a place of worship for the Roman Church. After a profession of faith she was condemned to suffocation in the bath of her own house; remaining unhurt in the overheated room, she was sentenced to beheading. The executioner struck three times without severing her head and fled; bathed in her own blood, the virgin lived three days, made provision for the poor, and asked that her house be dedicated as a church. Urban buried her among the bishops and confessors in the Catacomb of Callistus.

In this form the account has no historical value; it is a pious romance like others compiled in the fifth and sixth centuries. The existence of the martyrs, however, is a historical fact, and the bond between Cecilia, Valerian, Tiburtius, and Maximus may have some historical foundation. She is venerated as a genuine martyr; tradition places her death around the year 230, and her body, later recovered from the Catacombs of St. Callixtus, is enshrined in the Roman church that bears her name.

Tradition holds that she sang to God in her heart while the wedding music played, which is why she is honored as patroness of musicians. Her feast on November 22 has inspired centuries of music, art, and poetry.

clare-of-assisi.history:
Clare was born at Assisi on 16 July 1194, the eldest daughter of Favorino Scifi, Count of Sasso-Rosso, the wealthy representative of an ancient Roman family; her mother, Blessed Ortolana, of the noble family of Fiumi, was conspicuous for her zeal and piety. From her earliest years Clare was devoted to prayer and to practices of mortification, and as she passed into girlhood her distaste for the world deepened into a yearning for a more spiritual life.

At eighteen she heard Saint Francis preach the Lenten course in the church of San Giorgio at Assisi. Moved by his words, she sought him out secretly and begged him to help her live after the manner of the holy Gospel. On Palm Sunday she received the palm from the bishop while the rest of the congregation pressed forward to the altar-rail, and that same night she secretly left her father's house, accompanied by her aunt Bianca and another companion, and went to the Porziuncula, where Francis and his brethren met her with lights. There she laid aside her rich dress, her hair was cut, and she was clothed in a rough tunic and thick veil, thereby vowing herself to the service of Jesus Christ. The date was 20 March 1212.

Francis first placed her with the Benedictine nuns of San Paolo near Bastia; her father, who had expected a splendid marriage, tried in vain to force her return. Transferred for greater solitude to Sant' Angelo in Panzo, she was joined about sixteen days after her flight by her younger sister Agnes. Soon afterward Francis settled Clare and the other women who had followed her at San Damiano, a poor chapel outside Assisi which he had to a great extent rebuilt with his own hands. There the first community of the Order of Poor Ladies, later called the Poor Clares, was founded, and Clare led it as its first abbess for more than forty years.

At first the sisters had no written rule beyond the short formula of life Francis had given them. Some years later, apparently in 1219, Cardinal Ugolino, then protector of the order and afterwards Pope Gregory IX, drew up a written rule based on the Rule of Saint Benedict, approved by Honorius III, which allowed the community to hold property in common. Clare courageously resisted this departure from the absolute poverty Francis had intended. When Gregory came to Assisi in 1228 for the canonization of Saint Francis, he visited San Damiano and pressed her to accept some provision for the community, even offering to absolve her from her vow; she replied, "Holy Father, I crave for absolution from my sins, but I desire not to be absolved from the obligation of following Jesus Christ." His admiration for her is preserved in letters still extant, and Clare ultimately secured the Privilege of Poverty, the right of her community to own nothing.

Tradition holds that in 1240, when soldiers threatened Assisi, Clare faced them bearing the Blessed Sacrament and the attackers fled, and that while confined to bed she had a vision of the Christmas Mass at the Basilica of Saint Francis, for which she was later named patroness of television. She is invoked especially for diseases of the eyes.

Clare died at Assisi on 11 August 1253. On 26 September 1255 she was solemnly canonized by Alexander IV, and the church of Santa Chiara was soon begun in honor of Assisi's second great saint. Her remains were transferred there on 3 October 1260 and buried beneath the high altar.
