After remaining hidden for six centuries, her tomb was rediscovered in 1850, and on 29 September 1872 her bones were translated by Archbishop Pecci, afterwards Pope Leo XIII, to a shrine in the crypt at Santa Chiara, where they may now be seen. Her feast is celebrated on 11 August.

clare-of-montefalco.history:
Clare was born at Montefalco about the year 1268, and the town remained the setting of her whole religious life. From her very childhood she gave evidence of the exalted sanctity she was one day to attain, and she became the recipient of many signal favours from God. While still a very young girl, she embraced the rule of the Third Order of St. Francis in its secular form, together with her older sister and a number of other pious young maidens. They wore the habit of the Third Order of St. Francis and followed in community a mode of life suggested by their own piety and fervour, though as yet they were not bound by religious vows.

Much dispute has existed as to whether Clare ought to be counted a Franciscan or an Augustinian. The Franciscan historian Wadding, together with the Franciscan biographers of the saint, contended that she belonged to the Third Order of St. Francis, while Augustinian writers, whom the Bollandists seemed to favour, held that she belonged to their order. It appears more probable, however, that her earliest formation was Franciscan, while her formal profession as a religious was later made under an Augustinian rule.

In 1290, desiring to enter the religious state in its strict sense and to profess the three vows of religion, the young women petitioned the Bishop of Spoleto for an approved rule of life. Since the Third Order of St. Francis did not then exist as an approved religious institute in its regular form, the bishop imposed upon them the rule of the Third Order Regular of St. Augustine.

Upon the death of her older sister in 1295, Clare was chosen to succeed her as abbess of the community at Santa Croce, and it was only in obedience to the command of the Bishop of Spoleto that she could be prevailed upon to accept the dignity. In that office she guided the community with wisdom and charity. Kind and indulgent towards others, she treated herself with the most unrelenting severity, multiplying her fasts, vigils, and other austerities to such an extent that at one time her life was even feared for.

To these acts of penance she joined the practice of profound humility and of perfect charity, while the sufferings of her Redeemer formed the continual subject of her meditation. She was especially known for her deep devotion to the Passion of Christ, and she was likewise remembered for her care of the poor. This union of penance towards herself and charity towards others, joined to her constant contemplation of the Passion, was the distinguishing mark of her sanctity.

Clare died in her native town of Montefalco on 18 August 1308. Tradition holds that after her death symbols of the Passion were found impressed upon her heart. Shortly after her death, an inquiry into her virtues and into the miracles wrought through her intercession was instituted in preparation for her canonization.

The process moved slowly, and it was not until several centuries later that Clare was canonized by Pope Leo XIII in 1881, more than five centuries after her death. Her feast is kept on 17 August, and she is venerated as a patron of the poor.

colman-of-templeshambo.history:
Saint Colman of Templeshambo was a saint of Connacht in the west of Ireland, though the sphere of his ministry lay in what is now County Wexford. He has often been confounded with Saint Colman, the patron of Kilmacduagh, to whom later generations assigned his memory, but he lived somewhat earlier and the two are distinct figures.

Colman was a contemporary of Saint Aidan, who appointed him Abbot of Templeshambo, the mother church of Enniscorthy. His monastery there was known as Temple Sean Bothe, and it stood at the foot of Mount Leinster, where he laboured zealously as a monk and pastor. The place name Templeshambo itself preserves the memory of his church and his prayer.

Tradition holds that many legends gathered around his name, including stories of a holy well with its sacred ducks associated with his monastery. Such accounts belong to the devotional folklore that grew up around the early Irish monastic saints rather than to documented history.

He died around 595 on 27 October, on which day his feast is recorded in the Martyrology of Donegal, and his commemoration is still kept on that date. Few details of his life survive, but the devotion of the people kept his name alive through the centuries, a quiet witness to the early flowering of Irish monastic sanctity. In keeping with his life as abbot and monk, he is venerated as a patron of monks.

colm-n-elo.history:
Colmán Elo, known in some sources as Elo Colman and also styled St. Colman Macusailni, was an Irish abbot and bishop of the early medieval period. He was born around 555 at Glenelly, in what is now County Tyrone, Ireland. Because the Irish Church honored many saints of the same name, the epithet Elo serves to identify him among them, and it derives from Lann Elo, the Irish name of Lynally, the monastery with which he is chiefly associated.

Tradition holds that he studied under his maternal uncle, St. Columcille, and that it was Columcille who procured for him the site of a monastery now known as Lynally. From this place he took the designation Colman Elo, rendered in Latin sources as Colmanellus. He is famed in Irish hagiography as a holy monk and abbot, a representative of the flowering of Irish monasticism, when monks and hermits sanctified the land through lives of prayer, penance, and learning.

Tradition further records that he founded and served as first Abbot of the Abbey of Muckamore, though the precise details of his foundation remain uncertain. He was also appointed Bishop of Connor, a dignity suggested by the style 'Coarb of MacNisse', through which he is regarded as occupying the episcopal succession associated with that see.

He died at Lynally on 26 September 611, and his feast is celebrated on that date. He is remembered among the many illustrious Colmans of early Ireland for his sanctity and a life given wholly to God, and in later Christian tradition he has come to be honored as a patron of monks.

cyprian-of-toulon.history:
Saint Cyprian was bishop of Toulon in Provence during the sixth century, serving in the turbulent decades that followed the collapse of Roman authority in Gaul. Born at Marseilles in 476, he died on 3 October 546. He is numbered among the pre-congregational saints of southern France, bishops whose sanctity was acknowledged through the veneration of the faithful rather than by formal canonization, and he is honored as a patron of bishops.

He owed his formation to St. Caesarius of Arles, of whom he was the favorite pupil and by whom he was trained for the service of the Church. Caesarius ordained him to the diaconate in 506 and consecrated him as Bishop of Toulon in 516. He governed the see of Toulon for thirty years, until his death, guiding its church through an age when bishops bore much of the burden of sustaining Christian life amid the migrations and conflicts of the early medieval period.

The record of his public activity lies chiefly in the councils of his age. He appears to have been present at the synod of Arles in 524, and in the following years to have attended a number of councils. At all these assemblies he showed himself a vigorous opponent of Semipelagianism, the doctrine concerning grace then at issue among the churches of southern Gaul.

Of his episcopate itself little is recorded beyond his office and his veneration, yet one literary undertaking secured his name for later centuries. Soon after the death of Caesarius in 543, Cyprian wrote a life of his great teacher in two books, moved to the undertaking by the entreaty of the Abbess Caesaria the Younger, who had been head of the convent at Arles since 529. He was aided in the task by the two bishops Firminus and Viventius, friends of Caesarius, as well as by the priest Messianus and the deacon Stephen. The main part of the work, up to the fortieth chapter of the first book, was most probably written by Cyprian himself. The life is accounted one of the most valuable biographical remains of the sixth century.

A further writing of his became known in modern times: a letter to Bishop Maximus of Geneva which discusses some of the disputed theological questions of that age. The letter shows him engaged with the doctrinal debates of his day, beyond the immediate affairs of his own diocese.

His memory endured among the people of Toulon, and his feast is kept on 3 October, the anniversary of his death. He stands with that generation of southern French bishops who preserved the faith and maintained ecclesiastical order in uncertain times; the quiet fidelity of such shepherds, though little chronicled in detail, was essential to the continuity of the Church in the region.

dominic.history:
Dominic was born about 1170 at Caleruega in Old Castile, son of the noble couple Felix Guzman and Joanna of Aza. His mother's sanctity drew such popular veneration that she was beatified by Leo XII in 1828, and his brothers Antonio and Manes were likewise noted for holiness, Manes becoming a Friar Preacher. From his seventh to his fourteenth year Dominic studied under his uncle, the archpriest of Gumiel d'Izan, and in 1184 he entered the University of Palencia, where for ten years he was held up as a model student. Amid the frivolities of a university city he stood apart by seriousness and austerity, yet carried a heart of rare tenderness, selling his annotated books to relieve the starving poor of Palencia. His contemporary Bartholomew of Trent records that he twice tried to sell himself into slavery to ransom captives held by the Moors.

Called while still a student by Martin de Bazan, Bishop of Osma, to join the cathedral chapter and assist its reform, Dominic became a canon regular and sub-prior, and was raised to the office of prior in 1201 under Bishop Diego d'Azevedo. For nine years he led a hidden life of contemplation, seldom passing beyond the chapter house.

In 1203 the bishop was sent by King Alfonso IX of Castile on an embassy to obtain a bride for Prince Ferdinand, and Dominic accompanied him. Passing through Toulouse, they beheld with sorrow the spiritual ruin wrought by the Albigensian heresy, and there Dominic first conceived the idea of an order devoted to combating heresy and spreading the Gospel by preaching. A second journey ended with the death of the princess, leaving the two free to go to Rome, where Diego sought to resign his see for the conversion of unbelievers. Innocent III refused the project and instead dispatched them to Languedoc, where the Cistercians, whose worldly display contrasted with the austerity of the heretics, had made little headway. Diego and Dominic prevailed upon them to adopt a stricter manner of life, after which converts increased, and Dominic engaged his opponents in the theological disputations that were their chosen weapon. From these labors arose the Order of Preachers, which Dominic founded in 1216, an order devoted alike to study and to the proclamation of the Gospel, with friars and contemplative nuns; later tradition associates him with the spread of the rosary.

On 30 May 1221 he presided over the second general chapter of the order at Bologna, and at its close set out to visit Cardinal Ugolino in Venice before returning to Bologna, where fatal illness overtook him. He bore three weeks of sickness with heroic patience and died on 6 August 1221. Gregory IX canonized him in 1234, and in a Bull of 13 July of that year made his cult obligatory throughout the Church, declaring that he no more doubted the saintliness of Dominic than that of Peter and Paul. His feast is kept on 8 August.

His biographers record wonders said to attest his holiness, among them the failure of the fire at Fanjeaux to consume the dissertation thrice cast into the flames, the raising of Napoleone Orsini, and the occurrence in the refectory of Saint Sixtus in answer to his prayers. He prayed and preached almost uninterruptedly as he journeyed from place to place; his penances caused fear among the brethren who discovered them; his boundless charity never displaced his stern sense of duty; and his hatred of heresy flowed from love of truth and of souls, for he never failed to distinguish between sin and the sinner. The order he founded later gave the Church saints and scholars such as Thomas Aquinas and Catherine of Siena, and he is honored as the patron of preachers.

dunstan.history:
Dunstan was born in the earliest years of the tenth century near Glastonbury, on the estate of his father Heorstan, a West Saxon noble. Committed as a boy to the Irish scholars who then frequented the desolate sanctuary of Glastonbury, he showed an extraordinary appetite for human knowledge and unusual manual skill, and was noted through life for his devotion to learning and mastery of many kinds of craftsmanship. With his parents' consent he was tonsured, received minor orders, and served in the church of St. Mary.

His fame for learning is said to have brought him to court under King Aethelstan, but jealous courtiers accused him of studying heathen literature and magic and procured his dismissal. Beaten, bound, and thrown into a filthy pit as he left, he made his way to Winchester and entered the service of his kinsman, Bishop Aelfheah the Bald. Urged to become a monk, he at first doubted his vocation to a celibate life, until a severe illness, a covering of swelling tumours that he feared was leprosy, changed his mind, and he made his profession at Aelfheah's hands. He then returned to Glastonbury as a hermit, living in a little cell built against the church of St. Mary, where he studied, worked at his handicrafts, and played the harp. A late eleventh-century legend tells that there the devil tempted him and was seized by the face with the saint's tongs.

While at Glastonbury he became the trusted adviser of Lady Aethelflaed, the king's niece, and on her death found himself master of her great wealth, which he devoted to fostering the monastic revival, as he did his own inheritance at his father's death. Named a councillor by the new king Eadmund in 940, he was soon driven from court again by jealous courtiers. As the story relates, however, the king, following a stag at speed toward the Cheddar cliffs, found death imminent and remembered his harsh treatment of Dunstan, promising amendment; his horse was stopped at the very edge of the precipice. In thanksgiving Eadmund rode to Glastonbury, led Dunstan to the abbot's throne, and promised him assistance in restoring Divine worship and regular observance. As abbot, Dunstan restored the abbey and made it a centre of learning.

Subsequently bishop of Worcester and then of London, Dunstan was raised to the see of Canterbury in 960. From there he directed the reform of the English Church and of its monasteries and crowned several kings, while maintaining his lifelong pursuits as metalworker, musician, and scribe.

On the vigil of Ascension Day, 988, a vision of angels warned him that he had but three days to live. On the feast itself he pontificated at Mass and preached three times, announcing his approaching death in the last address and bidding the people farewell. That afternoon he chose the spot for his tomb, then took to his bed, and on the Saturday morning, 19 May, after Mass had been celebrated in his presence, he received Extreme Unction and the Holy Viaticum, expiring as he recited the words of thanksgiving: 'He hath made a remembrance of his wonderful works, being a merciful and gracious Lord.' He was buried in his cathedral.

At the Synod of Winchester in 1029 his feast was ordered to be kept solemnly throughout England on 19 May. When the cathedral was burnt down in 1074, his relics were translated with great honour by Archbishop Lanfranc to a tomb on the south side of the high altar in the new church; the monks of Glastonbury claimed that his body had been carried to their abbey during the Danish sack of Canterbury in 1012, but this was disproved when Archbishop Warham opened the Canterbury tomb in 1508 and found the relics. Until his fame was overshadowed by that of St. Thomas the Martyr, Dunstan was the favourite saint of the English people, and his shrine was destroyed at the Reformation. Throughout the Middle Ages he was the patron of the goldsmiths' guild, and in art he is most often depicted holding a pair of smith's tongs.

eligius.history:
Eligius (French, Eloi) was born around 588 or 590 at Chaptelat near Limoges in Gaul, of Roman parents, Eucherius and Terrigia, and died at Noyon on 1 December 660, the date kept as his feast. Recognizing unusual talent in his son, his father placed him with the noted goldsmith Abbo, master of the mint at Limoges. Eligius later went to Neustria, where he worked under the royal treasurer Babo, on whose recommendation King Clotaire II commissioned him to make a throne of gold adorned with precious stones. The honesty with which he carried out the commission so pleased the king that Eligius was appointed master of the mint at Marseilles and taken into the royal household.

After the death of Clotaire in 629, Dagobert I made his father's friend his chief councillor. The fame of Eligius spread so widely that ambassadors paid their respects to him before approaching the king, and in 636-37 his mediation induced the Breton King Judicail to submit to Frankish authority, a success that further increased his influence. He used it to obtain alms for the poor and to ransom Roman, Gallic, Breton, Saxon, and Moorish captives arriving daily at Marseilles. With the king's consent he sent his servants through towns and villages to take down the bodies of executed criminals and give them decent burial.

He devoted his means to monasteries and churches. He founded Solignac in 632, where he introduced the Irish monastic rule brought into Gaul by St. Columbanus, and extended that rule, wholly or in part, to a Paris convent of three hundred virgins under the Abbess Aurea; at court he and his friend Dado (Audoenus) lived under the same rule. He built the basilica of St. Paul in Paris, restored that of St. Martial, and erected churches in honor of the relics of St. Martin of Tours, the national saint of the Franks, and of St. Denis, whom the king chose as patron saint.

On the death of Dagobert in 639, Queen Nanthilde took charge of the government, and Eligius and Dado left the court to enter the priesthood. When Acarius, Bishop of Noyon-Tournai, died on 13 May 640, Eligius succeeded him with the unanimous approbation of clergy and people. The inhabitants of the diocese were for the most part pagan, and he undertook the conversion of the Flemings, Antwerpians, Frisians, Suevi, and the barbarian tribes along the coast. In his episcopal city of Noyon he built and endowed a monastery for virgins. In 654 he approved the celebrated privilege exempting the Abbey of Saint-Denis at Paris from the jurisdiction of the ordinary. After the finding of the body of St. Quentin he erected a church in his honor, joined to a monastery under the Irish rule; he also discovered the bodies of St. Piatus and his companions, and in 654 removed the remains of St. Fursey, the celebrated Irish missionary.

Eligius was buried at Noyon. A sermon in which he combats the pagan practices of his time, a homily on the last judgment, and a letter of 645 begging the prayers of Bishop Desiderius of Cahors survive from his pen, though fourteen other homilies attributed to him are of doubtful authenticity.

He is particularly honored in Flanders, in the province of Antwerp, and at Tournai, Courtrai, Ghent, Bruges, and Douai, and in the Middle Ages his relics were the object of special veneration, being several times transferred, in 881, 1066, 1137, 1255, and 1306. He is honored as patron of goldsmiths, blacksmiths, and all workers in metal; cabmen, too, have put themselves under his protection. In Christian art he is generally represented in the garb of a bishop, with a crosier in his right hand and a miniature church of chased gold upon the open palm of his left.

elizabeth-ann-seton.history:
{"history": "Elizabeth Ann Bayley was born in New York City on August 28, 1774, into a prominent Episcopalian family. Her father, Dr. Richard Bayley, was the first professor of anatomy at Columbia College and served as health officer of the Port of New York; her mother, Catherine Charlton, died when Elizabeth was three years old. Educated chiefly by her father, she was devout from youth, wearing a small crucifix and reading the Scriptures, especially the Psalms, a practice she retained until her death. On January 25, 1794, she married William Magee Seton, a merchant of New York, and the couple had five children. With her sister-in-law Rebecca Seton, whom she called the "friend of her soul," she went about missions of mercy in New York, and the two were called the "Protestant Sisters of Charity."

Business troubles beset the Seton firm in the late 1790s, and family trials deepened with the death of her father-in-law in 1798 and of her own father in 1801; she shared her husband's financial anxieties, aiding him with sound judgment. In 1803, hoping to restore his failing health, William sailed with Elizabeth and their eldest daughter for Italy, where business friends, the Filicchi brothers, lived. After a long detention in quarantine, he died at Pisa on December 27, 1803, leaving Elizabeth a widow at twenty-nine.

While staying with the Catholic Filicchi families and praying in the churches of Italy, Mrs. Seton first came to see the beauty of the Catholic faith. She returned to New York in June 1804 and passed through a season of spiritual searching, praying for light while clergy and friends on both sides sought to influence her. On Ash Wednesday, March 14, 1805, she was received into the Catholic Church by Father Matthew O'Brien in St. Peter's Church, New York.

Her conversion cost her the support of relatives who would otherwise have provided amply for her and her children. A boys' school she helped open near New York was forced to close amid circulated reports that it was a proselytizing scheme, and her later boarding-house for boys had to be given up. Her sister-in-law Cecilia Seton's decision to become a Catholic drew threats that Elizabeth would be expelled from the state. At the suggestion of Father Dubourg of St. Mary's Seminary in Baltimore, she undertook to open a school for girls, and in 1808 she and her daughters reached Baltimore, where she opened a school beside the chapel of St. Mary's Seminary.

In 1809 she moved to Emmitsburg, Maryland, where she founded the Sisters of Charity of St. Joseph's, the first religious community for women established in the United States, and served as its first superior. She also opened St. Joseph's Academy and Free School there, laying the foundation of the American Catholic parochial school system. She died at Emmitsburg on January 4, 1821.

Her community grew and gave rise to other foundations; by 1911 the sisters originating from her foundation numbered about six thousand. In 1880 Cardinal Gibbons urged that steps be taken toward her canonization, and the official inquiries held in Baltimore over several years were conveyed to Rome in 1911. She was beatified in 1963 and canonized on September 14, 1975, becoming the first native-born citizen of the United States to be declared a saint. Her feast is kept on January 4, the anniversary of her death, and she is honored as a patron of widows."}

elizabeth-of-hungary.history:
Elizabeth of Hungary, also called Elizabeth of Thuringia, was born in 1207, probably at Pressburg, to King Andrew II of Hungary and Gertrude of the counts of Andechs-Meran. Her brother later reigned as Bela IV, her aunt was St. Hedwig of Silesia, and her great-niece was St. Elizabeth of Portugal.

In 1211, when Elizabeth was four years old, an embassy from Landgrave Hermann I of Thuringia arranged a marriage alliance intended, in the politics of the day, against Emperor Otto IV. The child was taken to the Thuringian court, centered on the Wartburg castle near Eisenach, to be raised with her future husband. Her mother was murdered by Hungarian nobles in 1213, and in 1216 the death of the eldest son Hermann left her betrothed instead to Ludwig, the second son. Though courtiers of a more frivolous sort treated the pious child with hostility, her mother-in-law, the Landgravine Sophia, contrary to later legend, was a religious and kindly guardian.

Elizabeth and Ludwig IV were married in 1221, the groom aged twenty-one and the bride fourteen. The union was happy and exemplary: Ludwig shielded her charity and penances, and the Germans came to call him St. Ludwig. They had three children: Hermann, who died young; Sophia, ancestress of the landgraves of Hesse; and Gertrude, born after her father's death and later abbess of Altenberg near Wetzlar.

In the spring of 1226, while floods, famine, and pestilence ravaged Thuringia and Ludwig was away in Italy attending the Diet of Cremona for Emperor Frederick II, Elizabeth took charge of affairs. She distributed alms throughout the territory, gave even state robes and ornaments to the poor, built a hospital of twenty-eight beds below the Wartburg, visited its inmates daily, and aided nine hundred poor each day. Ludwig, on his return, confirmed all she had done.

In 1227 Ludwig departed on crusade with Frederick II and died at Otranto on 11 September. The news reached Elizabeth that October, just after the birth of her third child. Twenty years old, she cried out: "The world with all its joys is now dead to me." The Franciscans, who had first settled in Germany in 1221, shaped her later path; Brother Rodeger had instructed her at the Wartburg in the ideals of St. Francis. She joined the Third Order of St. Francis and spent her remaining years serving the sick at Marburg, where she died on 17 November 1231, aged twenty-four.

Her canonization followed in 1235, resting on such testimony as the letters of Conrad of Marburg to Pope Gregory IX and the evidence of her four female attendants. Her shrine at Marburg drew pilgrimages compared to those of Santiago de Compostela until 1539, when Landgrave Philip the Magnanimous, then a Protestant, removed the relics and ended the pilgrimages. German veneration endured, renewed by the celebration of the seven hundredth anniversary of her birth in 1907.

Tradition holds that bread she was secretly carrying to the poor was turned into roses when Ludwig met her unexpectedly on an errand of mercy, a legend also told of other saints. In art she appears as a princess graciously giving alms or holding roses in her lap. She is honored as patron of bakers, hospitals, and charitable societies, and her feast is kept on 17 November.

elizabeth-of-portugal.history:
Saint Elizabeth of Portugal, sometimes known as the Peacemaker, was born in 1271, the daughter of Pedro III, King of Aragon, and Constantia, granddaughter of Emperor Frederick II. She was named after her great-aunt, Saint Elizabeth of Hungary, and is known in Portuguese history by the Spanish form of her name, Isabel. Her upbringing was deeply religious, and from childhood she led a life of strict regularity and self-denial: she recited the full Divine Office daily, observed fasts and other penances, and gave up amusement.

While still very young she was married to Diniz, King of Portugal, a poet known as the Rei Lavrador, or working king, from his hard labor in his country's service. His morals, however, were extremely bad, and the court to which the young queen was brought was consequently most corrupt. Elizabeth quietly pursued the religious practices of her maidenhood, while doing her best to win her husband's affections by gentleness and extraordinary forbearance. She was devoted to the poor and the sick, giving every moment she could spare to helping them and even pressing her court ladies into their service. Such a life was a reproach to many around her and caused ill will in some quarters.

A popular tradition tells how the king's jealousy was roused by an evil-speaking page, how he condemned the queen's supposed guilty accomplice to a cruel death, and how he was finally convinced of her innocence by the strange accidental substitution of her accuser for the intended victim. Tradition further holds that Diniz did not reform in morals until late in life, when the saint won him to repentance by her prayers and unfailing sweetness. The marriage brought two children, a daughter, Constantia, and a son, Affonso.

Affonso so greatly resented the favors shown to the king's illegitimate sons that he rebelled, and in 1323 war was declared between him and his father. Elizabeth rode in person between the opposing armies and so reconciled her husband and son. Diniz died in 1325, and his son succeeded him as Affonso IV. The widowed queen then retired to a convent of Poor Clares that she had founded at Coimbra, where she took the habit of a Franciscan tertiary, wishing to devote the rest of her life to the poor and sick in obscurity.

But she was called forth once more to act as peacemaker. In 1336 Affonso IV marched his troops against the King of Castile, to whom he had married his daughter Maria and who had neglected and ill-treated her. In spite of age and weakness, the queen dowager insisted on hurrying to Estremoz, where the two armies were drawn up. She again stopped the fighting and caused terms of peace to be arranged. The exertion brought on her final illness, and as soon as her mission was fulfilled she died of a fever, full of heavenly joy and exhorting her son to the love of holiness and peace.

Elizabeth died on 4 July 1336 and was buried at Coimbra, where miracles were reported after her death. She was canonized by Pope Urban VIII in 1625, and her feast is kept on 4 July. She is venerated as the patron saint of peace.

eosterwine.history:
Saint Eosterwine, also recorded under the form Eosterwini, was Abbot of Wearmouth, the Northumbrian monastery founded by Saint Benedict Biscop, and served as the house's second abbot. Born in 650, he was descended from the noblest stock of Northumbria and was the nephew of Benedict Biscop himself. He died on 7 March 686, when only thirty-six years of age.

As a young man he led the life of a soldier in the army of King Egfrid, the son of Oswy. When twenty-four years old he gave up the soldier's profession to become a monk at Wearmouth, then ruled over by his uncle. He is described as a noble youth, conspicuous for his humility and bodily activity, but withal infinitely gentle; a most exact observer of the rule and one who loved to perform the lowliest work.

He was ordained priest in 679, and in 682 Benedict Biscop appointed him abbot of Wearmouth as coadjutor. As superior, when he was compelled to reprove a fault, it is related, it was done with such tender sadness that the culprit felt himself incapable of any new offence which should bring a cloud over the benign brightness of that beloved face.

Tradition remembers him as prizing humility above the rank of his birth, sharing the toil and the meals of his brethren with equal devotion, and caring tenderly for the sick and the poor who came to the abbey gates.

In 686 a deadly pestilence overspread the country and reached the community at Wearmouth, and the youthful abbot was among its victims. He bade farewell to all the day before he died and passed away on 7 March. Saint Benedict was absent in Rome at the time of his death, and the monks chose Sigfried as his successor. His abbacy lasted about four years, and he is not known to have been the author of any works. He is commemorated as a patron of monks, and his feast is kept on 7 March.

eskil.history:
Saint Eskil was an Anglo-Saxon monk who carried the Christian faith to Sweden in the closing years of the eleventh century. The early sources for his life are sparse, and much that is told of him rests on the tradition of the Swedish church rather than on contemporary documentation, so that accounts of his origin and his death belong largely to later legend. What the record preserves is nevertheless clear: a monk from England who went as a missionary to the Norse.

Tradition holds that he settled in the province of Södermanland, on the shores of Lake Mälaren, and founded there the first Christian community of the region. From this settlement grew in time the church that became the Diocese of Strängnäs, and Eskil has been honored as its founder and as the patron saint of Södermanland and of that diocese. His preaching met the hostility of pagan holdouts, and he is remembered as one of the patient planters of the faith in the rocky soil of the North. He is likewise invoked as a patron of monks, in keeping with the monastic life from which his apostolate began.

His veneration in the region is ancient, and no date of formal canonization is recorded for him; his cult belongs to the earliest local tradition of the Swedish church, which took shape long before the modern canonization process was established. His feast is kept on June 12.

Eskil was a common name among Norse and Danish churchmen, and the apostle of Södermanland is to be distinguished from Eskil, Archbishop of Lund, the most prominent churchman of that name, whose career is far more fully documented. Born about 1100 into a noble family of Jutland, the archbishop was educated at the cathedral school of Hildesheim, served as provost of Lund from 1131, became Bishop of Roskilde in 1134, and succeeded his uncle Asser as Archbishop of Lund in 1137. He received the pallium from Innocent II, consecrated the completed cathedral of Lund in 1145, and was afterwards named Primate of Sweden and papal legate for the North. In these offices he defended the rights of the church against the civil power and raised the standard of religious life throughout his province.

The monastic orders were especially indebted to the archbishop of Lund. He called the Benedictines to Næstved and founded the first Cistercian monastery at Herivadum in 1144 (in Skåne), which was soon followed by one at Esrom in Nordseeland in 1154, and from these two houses various branches were established. He maintained a close association with St. Bernard of Clairvaux, whose order he asked to enter in 1152 and was declined, Bernard judging that his episcopal service was of greater benefit to the Church. He preached a crusade against the pagan Wends, was at one point imprisoned for the Church's rights, and remained faithful to Pope Alexander III against the antipope Victor. In 1164 he consecrated Stephen of Alvastra, the first Archbishop of Upsala. He resigned his see in 1177 in favor of Absalon of Roskilde and withdrew to Clairvaux, where he died in 1181 as a simple monk, honored by the Cistercians as venerable. The feast of June 12 belongs to the missionary of Lake Mälaren, not to this great prelate of Denmark.

pope-eugene-i.history:
Eugene I was elected Bishop of Rome on August 10, 654, and died in that city on June 2, 657. His pontificate began amid grave trouble. His predecessor, Pope Martin I, had been carried off from Rome by force on June 18, 653, because he would not submit to Byzantine dictation in the matter of Monothelitism, the dispute concerning the wills and operations in Christ, and he remained in exile until his death in September 655. For about a year and two months the Church of Rome was governed, as custom then prescribed during a vacancy or the absence of the pope, by the archpriest, the archdeacon, and the primicerius of the notaries, until a successor was given to Martin in the person of Eugene.

Eugene was a Roman of the first ecclesiastical region of the city and the son of Rufinianus. A cleric from his earliest years, he is set down by his biographer as distinguished for gentleness, sanctity, and generosity. The circumstances of his election cannot be certainly known. If, under imperial power, he was placed on the Chair of Peter in the hope that he would follow the emperor's will, those calculations miscarried; and if he was in the first instance elevated against the will of the reigning pope, Martin himself subsequently acquiesced in his election.

One of the new pope's first acts was to send legates to Constantinople with letters to Emperor Constans II, informing him of the election and presenting a profession of faith. The legates allowed themselves to be deceived or won over, and brought back a synodical letter from Peter, who had newly become Patriarch of Constantinople, while the envoy sent by the emperor brought offerings for St. Peter and a request that the pope enter into communion with the patriarch. Peter's letter proved to be written in the most obscure style and avoided making any specific declaration as to the number of wills or operations in Christ. When its contents were communicated in 656 to the clergy and people assembled in the church of St. Mary Major, they rejected the letter with indignation and would not allow the pope to leave the basilica until he had promised that he would never accept it on any account.

Byzantine officials were so furious at this rejection of the wishes of their emperor and patriarch that they threatened, when the state of politics might allow it, to deal with Eugene as they had dealt with Pope Martin. Eugene was spared the fate of his predecessor by the advance of the Muslims, who took Rhodes in 654 and defeated Constans himself in the naval battle of Phoenix in 655.

It was almost certainly this pope who received the youthful St. Wilfrid on the occasion of his first visit to Rome around 654, a journey the young Englishman undertook because he was anxious to learn the ecclesiastical and monastic rites in use there. At Rome Wilfrid gained the affection of the archdeacon Boniface, a counsellor of the pope, who presented him to his master. According to the account preserved by Bede and by Eddius, Wilfrid's biographer, Eugene placed his hand upon the head of the youthful servant of God, prayed for him, and blessed him.

Little more is recorded of him except that he consecrated twenty-one bishops for different parts of the world and that he was buried in St. Peter's. The Roman Martyrology reckons him among the saints on the day of his death, June 2, and he is venerated as a saint in both the Roman and the Eastern churches. Remembered for governing the Church with quiet fidelity through one of its most troubled seasons, seeking peace without surrendering the truth received, he is honored as a patron of church unity.

eulogius-of-alexandria.history:
St. Eulogius served as Greek Patriarch of Alexandria from 580 to 607, guiding the ancient see founded by Saint Mark through a turbulent era. He is remembered as a learned theologian and a successful combatant of the heretical errors then current in Egypt, notably the various phases of Monophysitism, and as a steadfast upholder of the orthodox faith amid the Christological controversies that still divided the Christian East.

He was a warm friend of Pope St. Gregory the Great and corresponded with him, receiving from that pope many expressions of esteem and admiration. Gregory made special mention of his defense of the primacy of the Roman See. Baronius records that Gregory wished Eulogius to survive him, recognizing in him the voice of truth.

Within his own diocese Eulogius refuted the Novatians, some communities of which ancient sect still existed there, and he vindicated the hypostatic union of the two natures in Christ against both Nestorius and Eutyches. It has rightly been said that he restored, for a brief period, to the church of Alexandria that life and youthful vigor which are characteristic of churches closely united to Rome.

He was also a diligent writer for the faith. Besides a commentary against the several sects of the Monophysites (the Severians, Theodosians, Cainites, and Acephali), he composed eleven discourses in defense of Pope Leo I and the Council of Chalcedon, and a work against the Agnoetae, which he submitted to Gregory before publication and which the pope, after some observations, authorized unchanged. With the exception of a single sermon and a few fragments, however, all of his writings have perished.

He cared for his flock with wisdom and charity amid the political upheaval and rivalries that troubled Alexandria, a city renowned for both sanctity and strife. His episcopate is recalled as an example of doctrinal steadfastness joined to pastoral care. Honored as a saint, with a feast kept on June 13, he is remembered as a faithful pastor of one of the great patriarchal sees and is invoked as a patron of bishops.

fiacre.history:
St. Fiacre was an Irish abbot born about the end of the sixth century. After his ordination as a priest he withdrew to a hermitage on the banks of the River Nore in County Kilkenny, where the townland of Kilfiachra, or Kilfera, still preserves the memory of his presence. Disciples gathered around him, but desiring greater solitude he left Ireland and in 628 arrived at Meaux in France, where St. Faro then held episcopal sway. Faro received him generously, mindful of the blessings that he and his father's house had received from the Irish missionary Columbanus.

From his own patrimony Faro granted Fiacre a wooded site at Brogillum, known as Breuil, near what is now Saint-Fiacre in Seine-et-Marne. There Fiacre built an oratory in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary, a hospice in which he received strangers, and a cell in which he lived apart. His life was one of great mortification, given to prayer, fasting, vigil, and the manual labour of the garden, and disciples soon gathered around him so that a monastery was formed. Tradition holds that Faro allowed him as much land as he might surround in one day with a furrow, and that Fiacre turned up the earth with the point of his crosier; when a woman hastened to tell the bishop that he was being beguiled, Faro came to the wood, recognized Fiacre as a man of God, and sought his blessing. The same tradition says that Fiacre thereafter excluded women from the precincts of his monastery on pain of severe bodily infirmity, though the exclusion of women was in fact a common rule in Irish foundations.

His fame for miracles was widespread. He was credited with curing all manner of diseases by the laying on of his hands; blindness, polypus, and fevers are mentioned, and especially a tumour or fistula that came to be called le fic de S. Fiacre. He died on 18 August 670 and was buried in the church at Breuil, where his sanctity was soon attested by the numerous cures wrought at his tomb. His shrine there remains a resort for pilgrims with bodily ailments, and many churches and oratories throughout France have been dedicated to him.

His remains were honoured with increasing ceremony in later centuries. In 1234 Pierre, Bishop of Meaux, placed them in a shrine, his arm being encased in a separate reliquary. In 1479 the relics of Saints Fiacre and Kilian were set in a silver shrine, which was removed in 1568 to the cathedral church at Meaux for safety from the Calvinists. In 1617 the Bishop of Meaux gave part of the saint's body to the Grand Duke of Tuscany, and in 1637 the shrine was opened again and part of the vertebrae given to Cardinal Richelieu. A mystery play of the fifteenth century celebrated his life and miracles, and among his most famous clients were St. John of Matha, Louis XIII, and Anne of Austria.

Fiacre is honoured as the patron of gardeners, a patronage reflecting the manual labour of cultivation that marked his life. His name attached itself also to the French cab: the Hôtel de St-Fiacre in the Rue St-Martin in Paris first let such coaches on hire in the middle of the seventeenth century, and because the sign of the inn bore an image of the saint, the coaches came in time to be called fiacres. His feast is kept on 30 August.

francis-de-sales.history:
Francis de Sales was born at Thorens in the Duchy of Savoy on 21 August 1567, eldest of six brothers in an old Savoyard aristocratic family. His father, François de Sales de Boisy, intended him for the magistracy; after studies at La Roche and Annecy, he went from 1583 to 1588 to the Jesuit college of Clermont in Paris, where he studied rhetoric and began theology. There, after a prolonged temptation to despair arising from the predestination disputes of the day, he was, as tradition holds, delivered while praying before an image of Our Lady, and then made a vow of chastity and consecrated himself to the Blessed Virgin. He studied law at Padua from 1588, receiving his doctorate in 1592.

Admitted as a lawyer before the senate of Chambéry, he renounced that career for the ecclesiastical state. Claude de Granier, Bishop of Geneva, obtained for him the provostship of the chapter, the highest office in the diocese, and in 1593 Francis was ordained. The see of Geneva had its seat at Annecy, where he gave himself to preaching and the confessional. In 1594 he volunteered to evangelize Le Chablais, where the Reformed religion had been imposed under Geneva's rule. From his headquarters at the fortress of Allinges, he risked his life journeying and preaching through the district, settling at Thonon, where he confuted the ministers sent from Geneva and converted the syndic and other prominent Calvinists. By 1597 and 1598 a large part of the inhabitants had returned to the Catholic faith.

Chosen as coadjutor by Claude de Granier despite his own refusal, he went to Rome in 1599, where Pope Clement VIII ratified the appointment after an improvised examination before the Sacred College that proved a triumph; the Pope likened his learning to a wellspring whose waters were to become public fountains. Sent to Paris in connection with the district of Gex, he formed a close friendship with Cardinal de Bérulle and with Henry IV, who had him preach the Lent at Court and urged him to keep teaching souls in the world how to trust in God and be truly pious.

On the death of Claude de Granier, Francis was consecrated Bishop of Geneva in 1602. He instituted catechetical instruction for young and old, made prudent regulations for his clergy, visited the mountain parishes of his diocese, and reformed the religious communities. His goodness, patience, and mildness became proverbial, and he lived with such economy in food, dress, and household that he could give more abundantly to the poor, whom he loved intensely. He heard confessions, preached incessantly, and wrote innumerable letters of spiritual direction. With St. Jane Frances de Chantal, whom he first met at Dijon in 1604, he founded in 1607 the Order of the Visitation, an institute for girls and widows called to the religious life who lacked the strength or inclination for the austerities of the great orders.

He preached celebrated Lenten and Advent courses at Dijon, Chambéry, and Grenoble, where he converted the Maréchal de Lesdiguières. During his long stay in Paris from November 1618 to September 1619 he preached daily for the throngs that came to hear him, and there he came into contact with St. Vincent de Paul. His Introduction to the Devout Life, published in 1609, taught that holiness is possible in every state of life: a life of loving, simple, and constant fidelity to the will of God, with Christ as the model, through remembrance of the presence of God, filial prayer, right intention, and frequent recourse to God.

Francis died at Lyons on 28 December 1622 and was canonized in 1665. Honored as a Doctor of the Universal Church, he was named patron of writers and journalists by Pope Pius XI in 1923, and his feast is celebrated on 24 January. Congregations later formed under his patronage include the Missionaries of St. Francis de Sales of Annecy, the Salesians founded at Turin by Don Bosco, and the Oblates of St. Francis de Sales established at Troyes.

francis-of-paola.history:
Francis of Paola was born in 1416 at Paola in Calabria, southern Italy. His parents, notable for holiness of life, remained childless for some years and especially commended themselves in prayer to the intercession of St. Francis of Assisi, in whose honor they named their eldest son. While Francis was still in the cradle, a swelling endangered the sight of one eye; his parents had recourse again to St. Francis of Assisi and vowed that their son would spend a year in the little habit of St. Francis in a Franciscan convent, and the child was immediately cured.

At thirteen, admonished by a vision of a Franciscan friar, he entered a convent of the Franciscan Order to fulfill his parents' vow, giving great edification by his love of prayer and mortification, humility, and obedience. At the year's end he accompanied his parents on a pilgrimage to Assisi, Rome, and other places of devotion. Returning to Paola, he lived in solitude on his father's estate and later withdrew to a cave on the sea coast, where he remained alone for about six years in prayer and mortification.

In 1435 two companions joined him, for whom Francis built three cells and a chapel, and in this way the new order was begun. As disciples increased he raised, about 1454 and with the permission of Pyrrhus, Archbishop of Cosenza, a large monastery and church; the people, even nobles, carried stones in the work, and their devotion grew through the many miracles wrought at his prayers. The rule of life was one of extraordinary severity, with perpetual abstinence and great poverty, but its distinguishing mark was humility: the brothers were to seek to live unknown and hidden from the world. To express this character Francis obtained from the Holy See that they be styled Minims, the least of all religious. In 1474 Sixtus IV permitted him to write a rule and to assume the title of Hermits of St. Francis; the rule was formally approved by Alexander VI, who changed their title to that of Minims.

After the approbation of the order, Francis founded several new monasteries in Calabria and Sicily, and established convents of nuns and a third order for people living in the world. He was credited with a gift of prophecy and with discernment of consciences, and foretold the capture of Otranto by the Turks in 1480 and its subsequent recovery by the King of Naples. No respecter of persons, he rebuked the King of Naples for his ill-doing and suffered much persecution in consequence.

When Louis XI of France lay gravely ill in 1483, he sent an embassy to Calabria to beg the saint to come; Francis refused until the pope ordered him to go. He then attended the king at Plessis-les-Tours and was with him at his death, remaining near the French court as a counselor. Charles VIII kept him by the court, frequently consulted him, and built monasteries for the Minims at Plessis and at Rome on the Pincian Hill. Louis XII, succeeding in 1498, held him in like esteem and would not permit his return to Italy. The last three months of his life Francis spent in entire solitude, preparing for death. On Maundy Thursday he gathered his community and exhorted them to mutual charity and to the rigor of their life, especially perpetual abstinence; on Good Friday he gave his last instructions, appointed a vicar-general, and received the last sacraments. While the Passion according to St. John was read to him, his soul passed away on April 2, 1507, at the age of ninety-one.

Leo X canonized him in 1519. When the Huguenots broke open his tomb at Plessis in 1562, his body was found incorrupt; it was dragged forth and burned, but some of the bones were preserved by the faithful and enshrined in various churches of his order. Though never extensive, the Order of Minims had houses in many countries; its definitive rule was approved by Julius II in 1506, who also approved a rule for the nuns. Honored as the patron of sailors, Francis is kept by the universal Church on April 2, the anniversary of his death.

fulcran.history:
Fulcran served as Bishop of Lodève, in the Languedoc region of southern France, until his death on 13 February 1006. The principal source for his life is a biography written by Bernard Guidonis, another Bishop of Lodève who died in 1331; because this account was composed roughly three centuries after Fulcran's death, the details of his life rest largely on that later testimony. According to it, Fulcran came from a distinguished family and consecrated himself to the service of the Church at an early age. He became a priest and was remembered for leading a pure and holy life from his youth.

In 949, Theoderich, Bishop of Lodève, died, and Fulcran, notwithstanding his own unwillingness, was chosen as his successor. He was consecrated by the Archbishop of Narbonne on 4 February of the same year. As bishop he labored untiringly for the moral life of his diocese, attending with particular care to the clergy and the religious orders, and he governed the Church of Lodève as a successor of the apostles, proclaiming the Gospel and ministering to the souls entrusted to him.

His episcopate was also marked by extensive building and works of charity. He rebuilt many churches and convents, most notably the cathedral dedicated to St. Genesius and the church of the Holy Redeemer with its attached Benedictine monastery. The poor and the sick were the special objects of his care; for their support he founded hospitals and endowed others that already existed.

The biography records an episode concerning a bishop of Gaul who had fallen away from the Faith and had accepted Jewish teachings. When news of this reached Fulcran, he exclaimed in an excess of zeal, "This bishop should be burned!" Shortly afterward the renegade prelate was seized by his incensed flock and delivered up to death by fire. Fulcran was then filled with remorse that his utterance had been the occasion of the apostate's death, and after performing severe penance he undertook a pilgrimage to Rome, there to receive absolution for what he regarded as his guilt.

Fulcran died on 13 February 1006 and was buried in the cathedral of Lodève, where he was honored as a saint. His body, said to have been preserved intact, was burned by the Huguenots in 1572, and only a few particles of his remains were saved. He is venerated as the second patron of the Diocese of Lodève and is honored as a patron of bishops. His memory endured for centuries among the faithful of the diocese, who regarded him as a holy pastor and intercessor before God, and his feast is kept on 13 February.

george.history:
St. George was an early Christian martyr whose feast is kept on 23 April. Tradition holds that he was a Christian soldier of Greek origin, born in Cappadocia, who served in the Roman army in the late third century and rose to the rank of tribune. He suffered death at or near Lydda, also known as Diospolis, in Palestine, probably before the time of Constantine, and a traditional date is about 303. He is honored as patron of England and is invoked by soldiers. Despite his ancient cultus and pre-eminent renown in both East and West, these few facts sum up nearly all that can safely be affirmed about his life.

The apocryphal Acts of St. George, ancient and preserved in many languages with endless variations, fill out this outline with marvels that modern scholarship has rejected. The earliest narrative, fragments of which survive in a fifth-century palimpsest, has him put to death three times — chopped into small pieces, buried deep in the earth, and consumed by fire — resuscitated each time by the power of God, along with the dead raised for baptism, wholesale conversions, armies and idols destroyed instantaneously, and milk flowing from his severed head instead of blood. The Bollandist Father Delehaye, in his careful investigation of the whole question, concluded that these Acts afford absolutely no indication of the saint's authentic history. Even a mitigated version of the story, once favored by older scholars, is now agreed to have been derived from the more extravagant account by a process of rationalization.

This verdict does not imply that the martyr never existed. An ancient cultus connected with a definite locality is in itself a strong historical argument, and St. George possesses one. Pilgrim narratives from the sixth to the eighth century, those of Theodosius, Antoninus, and Arculphus, speak of Lydda or Diospolis as the seat of his veneration and the resting place of his remains. Inscriptions from ruined churches attest early dedications to him in Syria, Mesopotamia, and Egypt, and the church of St. George at Thessalonica is considered by some authorities to belong to the fourth century. A decree attributed to Pope Gelasius in 495 acknowledged that apocryphal Acts of St. George were already in circulation, yet ranked him among the saints whose names are justly reverenced among men but whose actions are only known to God.

Later attempts to complete his biography have found no firm footing. It is now generally admitted that he cannot be identified with the nameless martyr described by Eusebius, who tore down Diocletian's edict of persecution at Nicomedia: the version of the legend featuring Diocletian is not primitive, the emperor's name being a rationalized form of the legendary Dadianus, and the connection with Nicomedia is inconsistent with the early cultus at Diospolis. Nor is he, as Gibbon suggested, a legendary double of George of Cappadocia, the disreputable Arian bishop who opposed St. Athanasius; Bury judged that theory to have nothing to be said for it, though it is possible the apocryphal Acts borrowed some incidents from the bishop's story.

The celebrated legend in which George slays a dragon to rescue a princess, which made him an ideal of Christian chivalry, is a very late development, traceable no further back than the twelfth or thirteenth century, and probably owes its wide diffusion to the Golden Legend of James de Voragine. It may have arisen from an allegorization of the persecuting tyrant, who is called a dragon in some older texts, though its origin remains obscure. The motif does not relegate the saint to the realm of myth, for other martyrs celebrated as dragon slayers were historical persons. Beyond the legends, then, stands a martyr of the early Church whose cultus, rooted at Lydda from an early epoch, spread through both East and West.

giles.history:
St. Giles (Latin, Ægidius) is said to have been born of illustrious Athenian parentage about the middle of the seventh century. Tradition holds that, having devoted himself early to a life of prayer, he regarded his noble birth and the repute of his sanctity in his native land as obstacles to his spiritual perfection, and accordingly passed over to Gaul. He is said to have settled first in a wilderness near the mouth of the Rhône and afterward by the River Gard, but in both places the fame of his holiness drew multitudes to him. He therefore withdrew to a dense forest near Nîmes, where he spent many years in the greatest solitude, his sole companion being a hind, which, tradition relates, sustained him with her milk.

The saint's final retreat was discovered when the king's hunters, pursuing the hind, traced it to its place of refuge; tradition further holds that one of the hunters wounded Giles with an arrow in the encounter. The king, whom the legend identifies as Wamba, King of the Visigoths, conceived a high esteem for the solitary, although the identification is doubtful, since the Franks had expelled the Visigoths from the neighborhood of Nîmes almost a century and a half earlier. He would have heaped every honor upon the hermit, but the humility of the saint was proof against all temptation. He consented, however, to receive disciples, and built a monastery in his valley under the Rule of St. Benedict. Here he died in the early part of the eighth century, with the highest repute for sanctity and miracles.

His cult spread rapidly and widely throughout Europe in the Middle Ages, as is witnessed by the numberless churches and monasteries dedicated to him in France, Germany, Poland, Hungary, and the British Isles, by numerous manuscripts in prose and verse commemorating his virtues and miracles, and above all by the vast concourse of pilgrims who flocked to his shrine from every part of Europe. In the devotion that grew up around his name, Giles has been invoked by the sick, the poor, and the disabled, and he is honored as a patron of those suffering from leprosy. In medieval art he is a frequent subject, invariably depicted with his symbol, the hind.

In 1562 his relics were secretly transferred to Toulouse to preserve them from the violence of the Huguenots then ravaging France, and the pilgrimage in consequence declined. With the restoration of a great part of the relics to the church of St. Giles in 1862 and the discovery of his former tomb there in 1865, the pilgrimages were resumed. Besides the city of St-Gilles, which sprang up around the abbey, nineteen other cities bear his name; celebrated relics of the saint are venerated at St-Gilles and Toulouse and in a multitude of French cities, at Antwerp, Bruges, and Tournai in Belgium, at Cologne and Bamberg in Germany, at Prague and Gran in Austria-Hungary, and at Rome and Bologna in Italy.

His feast is kept on September 1, the day on which the Church also commemorates another St. Giles, an Italian hermit of the tenth century, and a Blessed Giles, a Cistercian abbot of Castaneda in the diocese of Astorga in Spain, who died about 1203.

hubert.history:
St. Hubert was born about 656, the eldest son of Bertrand, Duke of Aquitaine, and grandson of Charibert, King of Toulouse. As a youth he went to the court of Neustria, where his agreeable manners won him high esteem among the courtiers and the dignity of count of the palace. A man of the world whose chief passion was the chase, he later followed the emigrating nobles to the court of Austrasia, where Pepin Heristal made him grand-master of the household. About 682 he married Floribanne, daughter of Dagobert, Count of Louvain.

His conversion came on a Good Friday morning. While the faithful crowded the churches, Hubert went out hunting, and as he pursued a magnificent stag the animal turned toward him. According to the pious legend, a crucifix shone between its antlers, and he heard a voice warning him that unless he turned to the Lord and led a holy life he would quickly go down into hell. On his submission he was directed to seek St. Lambert, Bishop of Maastricht, who received him kindly and became his spiritual director. After the death of his wife shortly afterward, Hubert renounced his honors and military rank, gave up his birthright to the Duchy of Aquitaine to his younger brother Eudon, entrusted his infant son Floribert to Eudon's care, distributed his wealth among the poor, and, after studying for the priesthood, was ordained and became one of Lambert's chief associates in the administration of the diocese.

Sent on a pilgrimage to Rome at Lambert's advice, Hubert learned during his absence that the saint had been assassinated by the followers of Pepin; a vision is said to have revealed this to the pope at the same hour, with an injunction to appoint Hubert bishop as a worthy successor to the see. He is counted the thirty-first Bishop of Maastricht and the first of Liège. Though he sought the martyr's crown on many occasions without success, he distributed his episcopal revenues among the poor, was diligent in fasting and prayer, and became famous for his eloquence in the pulpit. In 720 he translated St. Lambert's remains from Maastricht to Liège with great ceremony; the church built for the relics on the site of the martyrdom was made a cathedral the following year, when the see was removed from Maastricht to Liège, then only a small village. This laid the foundation of the future greatness of Liège, of which Lambert is honored as patron and Hubert as founder and first bishop.

Idolatry still lingered in the fastnesses of the Ardennes, in Toxandria and in Brabant, and Hubert penetrated these remote regions at the risk of his life in pursuit of souls, finally bringing about the abolition of idol worship in his neighborhood and earning the title Apostle of the Ardennes. While at Fura, the modern Tervueren in Brabant, for the dedication of a new church, he was apprised of his impending death by a vision, preached his valedictory sermon, fell sick almost immediately, and died six days later, on 30 May 727 or 728, with the Our Father on his lips. His body was laid in the collegiate church of St. Peter at Liège and solemnly translated in 825 to the Abbey of Amdain, thereafter called St. Hubert's, near the present Luxemburg frontier; the coffin disappeared in the sixteenth century.

Many miracles are recorded of him in the Acta Sanctorum. In the Middle Ages he was honored as the patron of huntsmen and invoked as a healer of hydrophobia, or rabies, and many military orders were named after him. His feast is kept on 3 November, probably the date of the translation of his relics. Tradition holds that his conversion is commemorated in the Hubertus Mass and in the blessing of hunting dogs, and he remains venerated as the patron saint of hunters.

ignatius-of-loyola.history:
Ignatius of Loyola was born in 1491 at the castle of Loyola above Azpeitia in Guipuscoa, the youngest son of Don Beltrán Yañez de Oñez y Loyola and Marina Saenz de Lieona y Balda. Baptized Iñigo, after St. Enecus, Abbot of Oña, he assumed the name Ignatius only years later while residing in Rome. Brought up in the household of Juan Velásquez de Cuellar, comptroller-general to Ferdinand and Isabella, he frequented the court and was affected and extravagant about his hair and dress, consumed with the desire of winning glory; in later life he confessed himself to have been a great sinner. When Velásquez died in 1517, Ignatius took service in the army.

The turning point came in 1521, while the French were besieging the citadel of Pampeluna. On Whit-Tuesday, 20 May, a cannonball passed between his legs, tearing open the left calf and breaking the right shin. Carried on a litter to Loyola, he submitted to the rebreaking and resetting of the limb, to the sawing away of a protruding bone, and to the stretching of the shortened leg by weights, enduring all without a cry or restraint. During the weary hours of convalescence he asked for the romances of chivalry, but none were in the castle, and the lives of Christ and the saints were brought to him instead. Reading them with his former competitive spirit, he noticed that dreams of worldly glory left him dry and dissatisfied, while thoughts of imitating the saints braced him with joy and peace; he came to see one set of thoughts as of the world and the other as God-sent. One night, pondering these lights, 'he saw clearly', as his autobiography records, 'the image of Our Lady with the Holy Child Jesus'. His conversion was now complete.

In 1522 he went to the sanctuary of Montserrat, where after three days of self-examination he made a general confession, gave his rich clothes to the poor, hung his sword and dagger before the altar of Our Lady, and kept a night's vigil before them in a garment of sackcloth. On the feast of the Annunciation, after Communion, he set out with no settled plan, and a kind woman, Iñes Pascual, showed him a cavern near Manresa where he might live on alms in prayer and austerity. The months there brought severe scruples and great desolation; at one time he was violently tempted to end his miseries, and he vowed to take neither food nor drink, unless his life were in danger, until God granted him the peace he sought, until his confessor stopped him at the week's end. When at last he triumphed over these trials he abounded in graces and visions. It was here that he began to set down notes of his spiritual experience, from which the Spiritual Exercises in time took shape, a method of prayer and discernment that has guided countless souls.

Ignatius afterwards studied at Paris, where he gathered companions, among them Francis Xavier, and in 1540 he founded the Society of Jesus, the order dedicated to the service of the Church and of education, whose members are known as Jesuits. He governed the young order from Rome with firm discipline, while despising every motive for action except the love of God and man. At his death, sixteen years after the foundation, the Society numbered about 1000 religious, of whom only 35 were yet professed, in about 100 religious houses arranged in 10 provinces.

In the summer of 1556 he was attacked by Roman fever. His doctors foresaw no serious consequences, but the saint did. On 30 July he asked for the last sacraments and the papal blessing, and was told that no immediate danger threatened; next morning at daybreak the infirmarian found him lying in peaceful prayer, and the end came before the holy oils could be fetched. He died on 31 July 1556, the day now kept as his feast. He was beatified by Paul V on 27 July 1609, and canonized by Gregory XV on 22 May 1622. His body lies under the altar designed by Pozzi in the Gesù in Rome. He is honored as a patron of retreats.

isidore-of-seville.history:
St. Isidore of Seville was born at Cartagena, Spain, around 560, the son of Severianus and Theodora. Holiness marked his family: his elder brother Leander was his immediate predecessor in the metropolitan see of Seville, his younger brother Fulgentius presided over the bishopric of Astigi, and his sister Florentina, a nun, is said to have ruled over forty convents and a thousand religious.

He was educated at the cathedral school of Seville, the first of its kind in Spain, where the trivium and quadrivium were taught by learned men, among them Leander. He studied so diligently that he soon mastered Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. Whether he ever embraced monastic life is an open question, but he esteemed the religious orders highly; as bishop he constituted himself protector of the monks, and in 619 he pronounced anathema against any ecclesiastic who should molest the monasteries.

On Leander's death, around 600, Isidore succeeded to the see of Seville in an age of transition: the classic learning of the Roman Empire was fast disappearing, and the Goths, who had ruled Spain for nearly two centuries, threatened her progress with contempt of learning. Isidore set himself to weld the various peoples of the Hispano-Gothic kingdom into a homogeneous nation through the resources of religion and education. Arianism, long rooted among the Visigoths, was eradicated, the heresy of the Acephales was stifled at the outset, and religious discipline was strengthened. With Leander he shaped the councils of Toledo and Seville, whose legislation modern historians credit with influencing the beginnings of representative government.

He presided over the Second Council of Seville, begun 13 November 619 in the reign of Sisebut, but his greatest service came at the Fourth National Council of Toledo, begun 5 December 633, where all the bishops of Spain attended and he originated most of its enactments. Through his influence a decree commanded all bishops to establish seminaries in their cathedral cities on the model of the Seville school, where Greek and Hebrew and the liberal arts were prescribed and law and medicine were encouraged.

Long before the Arabs had awakened to an appreciation of Greek philosophy, he had introduced Aristotle to his countrymen. He was the first Christian writer to essay a summa of universal knowledge: the Etymologiae, sometimes called the Origines, which epitomized all learning, ancient and modern, preserved fragments of classical learning that would otherwise have been lost, and imparted a new impetus to encyclopedic writing throughout the Middle Ages.

Isidore was the last of the ancient Christian philosophers and the last of the great Latin Fathers, and undoubtedly the most learned man of his age, exercising a far-reaching influence on medieval education. His contemporary and friend Braulio, Bishop of Saragossa, regarded him as a man raised up by God to save the Spanish people from the tidal wave of barbarism. The Eighth Council of Toledo (653) acclaimed him as 'the extraordinary doctor, the latest ornament of the Catholic Church', a tribute endorsed by the Fifteenth Council of Toledo in 688.

As a writer he was prolific and versatile, and his works constitute the first chapter of Spanish literature. De ecclesiasticis officiis treats of divine worship and the old Spanish liturgy and contains a lucid explanation of the Eucharist, while his Regula monachorum provides for the admission of men of every rank, even slaves, insisting that in the monastery all are equal in the sight of God and of the Church. A three-book work treating of ecclesiastical orders and the judgment and chastisement of God is believed to have influenced Peter Lombard's Book of Sentences.

He died at Seville on 4 April 636, and his feast is kept on the same date. He was canonized in 1598, and in 1997, for his work as a compiler of knowledge, he was proposed as patron saint of the internet and of computer users.

jerome.history:
Jerome was born at Stridon, a town on the confines of Dalmatia and Pannonia, around the middle of the fourth century. As a young man he went to Rome, probably about 360, where he received a classical education and, after a period of worldly living, was baptized. He began his theological studies at Trier, famous for its schools, and continued them at Aquileia. Toward 373 he set out for the East and settled first at Antioch, where he heard Apollinaris of Laodicea, one of the leading exegetes of that time.

From 374 to 379 Jerome led an ascetical life in the desert of Chalcis, southwest of Antioch, living as a hermit and learning Hebrew. Ordained a priest at Antioch, he spent 380 and 381 at Constantinople, where a friendship grew up between him and Gregory of Nazianzus.

From 382 to August 385 Jerome lived in Rome near Pope Damasus I, who commissioned him to produce a reliable Latin translation of the Bible. In 384 he corrected the Latin text of the four Gospels and made a first revision of the Latin Psalter; in 385 followed a revision of the Latin Epistles of St. Paul. When Damasus died on 11 December 384, Jerome's position became very difficult, for his harsh criticisms had made him bitter enemies, and after a few months he was compelled to leave Rome.

Traveling by way of Antioch and Alexandria, he reached Bethlehem in 386 and settled in a monastery near a convent founded by the Roman ladies Paula and Eustochium, who had followed him to Palestine. There he led a life of asceticism and study for the rest of his days.

Jerome owes his place in the history of scriptural studies chiefly to his work on the Bible. Between 390 and 405, though often interrupted by other labors, he translated the Old Testament from the Hebrew, and about 398 he revised the remaining books of the Latin New Testament. Until about 392 he had considered the Septuagint inspired, but his progress in Hebrew and his intercourse with rabbis led him to recognize only the original text as inspired. His translation, the Vulgate, became the standard Bible of the Western Church for more than a thousand years.

His other writings were equally prolific. He translated the homilies of Origen and the Chronicle and Onomasticon of Eusebius, commented on nearly the whole of Scripture, and produced the lives of Paul the first hermit, of Hilarion, and of Malchus, the catalogue of writers De viris illustribus, and a great body of letters and sermons.

He was also a fierce defender of orthodoxy and of the ascetical movement of the fourth century. Against Helvidius he wrote in defense of the perpetual virginity of Mary; against Jovinian and the priest Vigilantius, whom he regarded as mouthpieces of a reaction against monasticism and the veneration of saints and relics, he authored pointed treatises. His long controversy with Rufinus over the teaching of Origen was most bitter, though it was generally conceded among his contemporaries that Rufinus was to blame, even if Jerome's own attitude was not always above reproach. His Dialogi contra Pelagianos, written in 415, opposed the teaching of Pelagius on grace.

Jerome died at Bethlehem on 30 September 420 and is honored as a Doctor of the Church. His feast is kept on 30 September, and in keeping with a life spent translating, revising, and commenting on the sacred books, he is venerated as the patron saint of librarians.

joan-of-arc.history:
Joan of Arc, known to her contemporaries as la Pucelle, the Maid, was born at Domrémy in Champagne, probably on January 6, 1412, the daughter of Jacques d'Arc, a small peasant farmer, likely the youngest of a family of five. Although the village lay on the borders of Burgundian territory, it remained loyal to Charles VII against the Burgundians and their English allies. Joan never learned to read or write but was skilled in sewing and spinning, and the popular image of a childhood spent alone in the pastures is unfounded. Witnesses at her rehabilitation recalled a singularly pious child, grave beyond her years and tender toward the poor, who had sung and danced with other children at the so-called Fairy Tree, but from the age of twelve she held aloof from such diversions.

In the summer of 1425, at about thirteen, she first became conscious of what she called her voices: at first a voice accompanied by a blaze of light, and later the discerned presence of St. Michael, St. Margaret, and St. Catherine. Always reluctant to speak of them, she told her judges only, “I saw them with these very eyes, as well as I see you.” By May 1428 she was certain she was bidden to go to the help of the king, and the voices urged her to present herself to Robert Baudricourt, who commanded for Charles VII at Vaucouleurs and at first dismissed her.

As Orléans, invested on October 12, 1428, brought the king's cause close to complete defeat, the voices grew urgent, answering her protests that she was a poor girl who could not ride or fight with the words, “It is God who commands it.” Returning to Vaucouleurs in January 1429, she gained ground when her announcement, on February 17, of the French defeat known as the Battle of the Herrings was officially confirmed days later. She was then permitted to seek the king at Chinon with an escort of three men-at-arms, attired in male clothing at her own request as a protection to her modesty, and arrived there on March 6.

Two days later she was admitted into the presence of Charles VII, who, to test her, had disguised himself among his attendants; she saluted him without hesitation. Although a strong court party led by the royal favorite La Trémoille opposed her, a secret sign from her voices — commonly believed to have concerned a doubt Charles had conceived of the legitimacy of his birth — led the king, somewhat half-heartedly, to believe in her mission.

In 1429, at seventeen, she led the French forces that lifted the siege of Orléans, a turning point of the Hundred Years' War; the Dauphin was then crowned at Reims, the end her voices had set before her. In 1430 she was captured by the Burgundians, sold to the English, and tried by an ecclesiastical court on charges including heresy and cross-dressing. The tribunal, presided over by Cauchon, acted without reference to the pope and in defiance of her appeal to the head of the Church; condemned, she was burned at the stake at Rouen on May 30, 1431, at about nineteen.
