In 1456 an appellate court constituted by the pope reversed and annulled the sentence pronounced by the local tribunal, making the illegality of the earlier proceedings clear, to the reproach of both the King of France and the Church at large. Among her Catholic fellow-countrymen Joan had been regarded, even in her lifetime, as Divinely inspired; although England long regarded her as a witch, sympathy for her there had become general by the early nineteenth century.

The cause of her beatification was introduced in 1869 on the appeal of Bishop Dupanloup of Orléans, and the decree was published by Pius X on April 11, 1909; a Mass and Office in her honor were approved for that diocese. St. Joan was canonized in 1920 by Pope Benedict XV. Her feast is kept on May 30, and she is honored as a patron of soldiers, of those who face unjust trials, and as one of the patron saints of France.

john-of-avila.history:
John of Avila was born at Almodóvar del Campo, a small town in the diocese of Toledo, Spain, on 6 January 1500. Sent to the University of Salamanca at fourteen to study law, he conceived a distaste for jurisprudence and returned home after a year, spending the next three years in the practice of austere piety. A Franciscan journeying through the town was so impressed by his sanctity that, at the friar's advice, he took up the study of philosophy and theology at Alcalá, where he had as his teacher the celebrated Dominican De Soto.

His parents died while he was still a student. After his ordination in 1526 he celebrated his first Mass in the church where they were buried, sold the family property, and gave the proceeds to the poor. Seeing in the severing of these natural ties a vocation to the foreign missions, he made preparations to go to Mexico.

While awaiting at Seville in 1527 a favorable opportunity to sail, the extraordinary devotion with which he celebrated Mass attracted the attention of the priest Hernando de Contreras, who reported him to the archbishop and general inquisitor Don Alphonso Manrique. The archbishop saw in the young missionary a powerful instrument for stirring up the faith of Andalusia, and after considerable persuasion John gave up the journey to America. He preached his first sermon on 22 July 1529, and his reputation was at once established; crowds thronged the churches at all his sermons, and his preaching won many converts. Success also brought hatred: while living at Seville he was brought before the inquisitor, charged with exaggerating the dangers of wealth and closing the gates of heaven to the rich. His innocence was speedily proved, and by special invitation of the court he preached the sermon on the next great feast at the church of San Salvador in Seville, an appearance that was the occasion of public rejoicing.

At the age of thirty he began his career as apostolic preacher of Andalusia. After nine years in that province he returned to Seville, only to depart for the wider fields of Cordova, Granada, Bolza, Montilla, and Zafra. For the eighteen years before his death he suffered constant illness, the result of the hardships of an apostolate of forty years. He died at Montilla on 10 May 1569, the date kept as his feast. He was declared Venerable by Clement XIII on 8 February 1799 and beatified by Leo XIII on 12 November 1893; he was canonized in 1970, and in 2012 Pope Benedict XVI declared him a Doctor of the Church.

His preaching and saintly reputation drew to him many of the great figures of the Spanish Golden Age, whom he served as a spiritual guide; among his disciples were St. Teresa of Avila, St. John of God, St. Francis Borgia, and the Venerable Louis of Granada. The spread of the Jesuits in Spain has been attributed to his friendship for that body. He is credited with the founding of schools and colleges.

He wrote widely on the spiritual life. His best-known works are Audi filia, one of the best tracts on Christian perfection, and his Spiritual Letters to his disciples. His collected works were published at Madrid in 1618, 1757, 1792, and 1805; a French translation appeared at Paris in 1673, and a German translation in six volumes at Ratisbon between 1856 and 1881, while English translations of Audi filia and the Letters had already appeared in 1620 and 1631. He is invoked as a patron of the sick and of those who suffer illness.

john-of-god.history:
St. John of God was born at Montemor-o-Novo, Portugal, on 8 March 1495, of devout Christian parents. At the age of nine he was left in the care of the chief shepherd at Oropeza, Spain, where he won his master's esteem through punctuality, fidelity to duty, and earnest piety. On reaching manhood, to escape his master's persistent offer of his daughter's hand in marriage, he served in the army of Charles V and later enlisted in a regiment bound for Austria to fight the Turks. He afterwards returned to his birthplace, where he learned of his mother's death, and then worked as a shepherd at Seville and Gibraltar before going briefly with an expelled Portuguese family to Africa in the hope of ransoming captive Christians with his own liberty. On the advice of his confessor he soon returned to Gibraltar.

During these years he made an apostolate of the printed page, selling religious books and pictures in the towns and villages around Gibraltar at almost no profit, so that they might be within the reach of all. Tradition holds that during this period he received a vision of the Infant Jesus, who bestowed on him the name John of God and directed him to Granada. There the preaching of St. John of Ávila so moved him that he distributed his worldly goods and went through the streets beating his breast and calling on God for mercy. For a time he was treated as a madman, until John of Ávila directed him to another way of atoning for his past life. After a pilgrimage in which, tradition holds, Our Lady of Guadalupe revealed his vocation to him, he returned to Granada and gave himself entirely to the service of the sick and the poor, renting and furnishing a house as a hospital and searching the city for the afflicted, bearing on his shoulders those unable to walk.

For a time he worked alone, begging supplies by night and attending to his patients by day, until charitable priests and physicians came to his aid. Early accounts also relate that his labors were at times lightened by heavenly visitors. To put an end to his habit of exchanging his cloak with any beggar he met, Bishop Sebastian Ramirez of Tuy had a habit made for him that his followers later adopted as their religious garb, and the bishop imposed on him the name John of God. His first two companions, Antonio Martin and Pedro Velasco, former enemies whose quarrels and dissipations had scandalized Granada, were converted through his prayers and formed the nucleus of the congregation that became the Brothers Hospitallers of St. John of God. On his deathbed John commended Antonio to his followers as his successor, while Pedro, who called himself Peter the Sinner, became a model of humility and charity.

The miracle most closely associated with him, commemorated in the Office of his feast, is his rescue of all the occupants of the Grand Hospital at Granada from a fire; tradition holds that he passed through the flames unscathed. His charity extended also to widows and orphans, the unemployed, poor students, and fallen women. After thirteen years of this unceasing care, his final illness followed a heroic but unsuccessful effort to save a young man from drowning, and he died at Granada on 8 March 1550, mourned by all the city's inhabitants. Its magistrates and nobility gathered about his deathbed in gratitude for his services to the poor, and he was buried with the pomp usually reserved for princes.

He was beatified by Pope Urban VIII on 21 September 1638 and canonized by Pope Alexander VIII on 16 October 1690, and Pope Leo XIII named him patron of hospitals and of the dying. His feast is observed on 8 March, the anniversary of his death.

john-of-the-cross.history:
John of the Cross, born Juan de Yepes at Fontiveros in Old Castile on 24 June 1542, was the youngest child of Gonzalo de Yepes and Catherine Alvarez, poor silk weavers of Toledo, and knew hardship from his earliest years. His father, disinherited for marrying beneath his rank, died in the prime of his youth, and after the family moved to Medina del Campo John attended a poor school before serving seven years in the hospital there, caring for the poorest of the poor while frequenting a school of the Jesuits.

He received the Carmelite habit at Medina on 24 February 1563, taking the name John of St. Matthias, and obtained leave to follow the original rule of the order without the mitigations granted by later popes. Ordained a priest in 1567 after studies at Salamanca, he had intended to join the Carthusians, but meeting St. Teresa of Avila he was persuaded to remain a Carmelite and help establish a house of friars under the primitive rule; with two companions he inaugurated the reform on 28 November 1568, becoming known as John of the Cross, and as first master of novices laid the foundations of the Discalced Carmelites.

Teresa called him to Avila as director and confessor to the convent of the Incarnation, which he served, with interruptions, for over five years while the reform spread amid growing disorder and opposition. When his provincial ordered him back to Medina, he refused, holding his office from the Apostolic delegate; on the night of 3 December 1577 he was seized and carried off to Toledo. For more than nine months he endured close imprisonment in a narrow, stifling cell, receiving heavenly consolations amid his sufferings, and some of his most exquisite poetry dates from this confinement. He escaped in August 1578 in a manner described as miraculous, and thereafter was chiefly occupied with founding and governing monasteries at Baeza, Granada, Cordova, and Segovia.

After Teresa's death on 4 October 1582, a struggle arose between the Moderates under Jerome Gratian and the Zelanti under Nicholas Doria. John supported the former, and when Doria concentrated the government of the order in a permanent committee, he resisted, supporting the nuns in seeking papal approval of their constitutions and drawing on himself the superior's displeasure. Deprived of his offices and relegated to one of the poorest monasteries, he fell gravely ill, even as an adversary went from monastery to monastery gathering material for grave charges against him. Moved to the monastery at Ubeda, he was at first treated unkindly, his constant prayer, 'to suffer and to be despised', being thus fulfilled almost to the end of his life; at length even his adversaries acknowledged his sanctity. He died at Ubeda, in Andalusia, on 14 December 1591, and his funeral was the occasion of a great outburst of enthusiasm.

His teaching is set out chiefly in The Ascent of Mount Carmel and The Dark Night of the Soul, and sung in the Spiritual Canticle and the Living Flame of Love. He describes the soul's purification through the removal of what he calls the spiritual capital sins, followed by the 'Dark Night', the passive purgation in which God, by heavy and chiefly interior trials, perfects what the soul had begun of its own accord. The soul remains cooperative rather than inert, a distinction John pressed against a false quietism; emerging from the night, it enters the full light of union with God, becoming a partaker of the divine nature. Though often represented as grim, he was austere chiefly toward himself, and his writings and the testimony of those who knew him show a man overflowing with charity and kindness.

Canonized in 1726 and declared a Doctor of the Church, he is honored as the patron of contemplation, and his feast is kept on 14 December.

john-the-baptist.history:
The principal sources of information concerning St. John the Baptist are the canonical Gospels, which remain far richer than any other record. Luke is the most complete, recounting the circumstances of his birth together with his ministry and death; Matthew closely parallels Luke on the public ministry but is silent about his early life; Mark's account is meager. The fourth Gospel contributes chiefly the testimony John bore to Jesus after the Saviour's baptism, and the Acts of the Apostles add only passing allusions. The Jewish historian Josephus, though erratic in his dates and influenced by his own political aims, confirms the Baptist's popularity and bears a favorable judgment on his character. The apocryphal gospels, by contrast, either repeat the canonical material or supply idle fictions, and add nothing of independent weight.

John's father, Zechariah, was a priest of the course of Abia, one of the twenty-four priestly courses of the temple; his mother, Elizabeth, belonged to the daughters of Aaron, yet Luke calls her a kinswoman of the Virgin Mary. To reconcile the two statements, an explanation preserved by Hippolytus, perhaps drawn from an apocryphal source, traces the two families through intermarriage, so that Elizabeth was of Aaron's line through her father and cousin to Mary through her mother. Zechariah's home lay in a city of Juda in the hill-country; a tradition reaching back before the Crusades points to the little town of Ain-Karim, southwest of Jerusalem, as the home of Zechariah and Elizabeth.

His birth was heralded by an angelic message. While Zechariah was offering incense in the temple, an angel announced that Elizabeth, though aged and long barren, would bear a son to be named John. The child was to drink neither wine nor strong drink, was to be filled with the Holy Ghost even from his mother's womb, and was to go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah to prepare for him a perfect people. Because Zechariah was slow to believe, he was struck dumb until the promise was fulfilled, and Elizabeth conceived soon afterward.

In the sixth month of that pregnancy the Annunciation took place, and Mary went in haste to visit her kinswoman. At the sound of her salutation the infant leaped for joy in the womb, an event the Gospel presents as the working of the Holy Spirit in the unborn child, who seemed to acknowledge the presence of his Lord.

John lived as an ascetic in the desert, preaching repentance and baptizing in the Jordan in preparation for the coming of the Messiah. He baptized Jesus himself, and thereafter pointed his own disciples toward him with the words, 'Behold, the Lamb of God.' Jesus bore him the highest witness, calling him the greatest of those born of women. His fearless rebuke of Herod Antipas for the unlawful marriage to Herodias brought him imprisonment, and Herod had him beheaded at the request of Herodias's daughter Salome.

The Church keeps his nativity on June 24 with a solemnity long likened to that of Christmas. Its liturgy once included three Masses: the first, in the dead of night, recalling his mission as Precursor; the second, at daybreak, commemorating the baptism he conferred; the third, at the hour of Terce, honoring his sanctity. So sacred was the feast held that two rival armies which met face to face on the eve of the day in 841 agreed by common accord to postpone the battle until after it, and the custom of St. John's fires has endured in certain regions into modern times. He is venerated as the patron saint of tailors, among many other patronages.

joseph-of-cupertino.history:
Joseph of Cupertino was born on 17 June 1603 in the village of that name in the diocese of Nardò, between Brindisi and Otranto in the Kingdom of Naples. His father, Felice Desa, a poor carpenter, died before Joseph was born and left debts that drove his mother, Francesca Panara, from her home, so that she gave birth to her child in a stable. At the age of eight he had an ecstatic vision while at school, renewed several times afterward; seeing him stand gaping and staring, lost to everything around him, the other children gave him the nickname Bocca Aperta, meaning open mouth. In those same years he showed a hot and irascible temper, which his strict mother strove to overcome.

After being apprenticed to a shoemaker, he sought a religious vocation with little initial success. At seventeen he was refused admission to the Friars Minor Conventual on account of his ignorance; accepted as a lay brother by the Capuchins at Martino near Tarento in 1620, he was dismissed because his continual ecstasies unfitted him for work. His mother and uncles reproached him as good-for-nothing, but he did not lose hope, and by persevering prayer he obtained leave to serve as lay help, or oblate, in the stable of the Franciscan convent of La Grotella near Cupertino. There his humility, obedience, and love of penance became so evident that in 1625 he was admitted to the clerical state, and on 28 March 1628 he was raised to the priesthood.

His life then became one long succession of visions and heavenly favors. Almost anything that referred to God or holy things would draw him into ecstasy: the sound of a bell or of church music, the mention of the name of God, of the Blessed Virgin, or of a saint, any event in the life of Christ, the Passion, a holy picture, the thought of the glory of heaven, and above all Mass and the divine services. Buffeting, piercing with needles, even the burning of his flesh with candles left him unchanged; only the voice of his superior could bring him back and direct him. He was frequently raised from his feet and remained suspended in the air, and at times he heard heavenly music.

Because such occurrences in public caused admiration and also disturbance, for thirty-five years Joseph was not allowed to attend choir, go to the common refectory, walk in procession, or say Mass in church; a private chapel was prepared in the room where he was ordered to remain. Ill-disposed and envious men even brought him before the Inquisition, and he was sent from one lonely house of the Capuchins or Franciscans to another; through it all he kept a resigned and joyous spirit, submitting to divine providence. His mortifications and fasts were severe: he observed seven Lents of forty days each year, and during many of them tasted no food except on Thursdays and Sundays.

Nearly without human learning, since he read but poorly, he was yet able, by an infused knowledge, to answer the most intricate questions put to him; because his ordination thus came against every natural obstacle, he is invoked by students, especially before examinations. Joseph died at Osimo on 18 September 1663, and his body rests in the church there. He was beatified by Benedict XIV in 1753 and canonized by Clement XIII on 16 July 1767; Clement XIV afterward extended his office to the entire Church. His feast is kept on 18 September.

juliana-falconieri.history:
St. Juliana Falconieri was born at Florence in 1270 into the noble Falconieri family. Her uncle, St. Alexis Falconieri, was one of the seven founders of the Servite Order, and through his influence Juliana consecrated herself from her earliest youth to the religious life and to the practices of Christian perfection. From childhood she was drawn to prayer and penance, and she refused marriage in order to give herself wholly to this calling.

After her father's death, about the year 1285 and when she was about fifteen years of age, she received from St. Philip Benitius, then General of the Servites, the habit of the Third Order. The rule bound her to religious observance while allowing her to remain in her family home, and Juliana is honored as the foundress of the Servite Third Order for women and as one of the first women to wear the habit of the order. Until her mother's death she remained in her parents' house, observing the rule that St. Philip Benitius had given her. Her life there was marked by perfect chastity, strict mortification, severe penance, zealous prayer, and works of Christian charity, and she became known for her austerity and for her deep devotion to the Eucharist.

In 1305, after her mother's death, Juliana and several companions moved into a house of their own, which became the first convent of the Sisters of the Third Order of the Servites. Juliana remained superior of the community until the end of her life. The sisters wore a black gown secured by a leather girdle, together with a white veil. Because the gown had short sleeves to make their work easier, the people of Florence called them the Mantellate, the name by which the community has been known ever since.

The sisters devoted themselves above all to the care of the sick of Florence, together with other works of mercy among the poor of the city. Juliana was foremost in this service, and her heroic deeds of charity were regarded as setting a noble example to the whole community. For thirty-five years she directed the community of Servite Tertiaries, a service that continued almost without interruption from the first foundation to the end of her life.

In her final illness Juliana was unable to receive Holy Communion because of constant vomiting. According to the account mentioned in the oratio, the proper prayer of her feast day, she asked the priest to spread a corporal upon her breast and to lay the Host upon it, that she might receive in this extraordinary manner the Communion she could no longer take in the ordinary way. Tradition records that shortly afterwards the Host disappeared, and that when Juliana expired the image of a cross, such as had been on the Host, was found upon her breast.

Juliana died on 12 June 1341, after a life of more than seventy years, the last thirty-five of which had been given to the government of the Mantellate. Immediately after her death she was honored as a saint.

The Order of Servite Tertiaries was sanctioned by Pope Martin V in 1420. Pope Benedict XIII thereafter granted the Servites permission to celebrate the feast of St. Juliana, and in 1737 Pope Clement XII canonized her, extending the celebration of her feast on 19 June to the entire Church. Her canonization thus confirmed a veneration that had continued for nearly four centuries since her death.

In Christian art St. Juliana is usually represented in the habit of her order with a Host upon her breast. On account of her lifelong service to the sick, she is invoked as a patroness of the sick and of those suffering bodily illness.

lawrence-of-brindisi.history:
Lawrence of Brindisi was born at Brindisi in 1559 and died at Lisbon on 22 July 1619. Baptized Julius Caesar, he was the son of Guglielmo de Rossi and Elisabetta Masella. Educated by the Conventual Franciscans of Brindisi, he showed early piety and a gift for oratory, preaching the customary little Christmas sermon on the Infant Jesus while still a small child. Left fatherless in his twelfth year, he studied at Venice under an uncle, and in 1575 entered the Capuchins as Brother Laurence, studying philosophy and theology at the University of Padua.

With a wonderful memory he mastered the principal European languages and most of the Semitic tongues, and it was said that he knew the entire original text of the Bible; at his beatification the examiners of his writings judged that he could truly be numbered among the doctors of the Church. While still a deacon he preached the Lenten sermons in Venice, and his success brought calls to the principal cities of the peninsula and, in time, to most of Europe. The sermons he left fill eight folio volumes.

He held successively all the offices of his order. From 1596 to 1602, as general definitor, he resided in Rome, where Clement VIII entrusted him with the instruction of the Jews; by his knowledge of Hebrew and powerful reasoning he brought a great number to the Christian faith and baptized many in Rome and elsewhere. Sent also to found houses of his order in Germany and Austria, he established amid the difficulties raised by heretics the convents of Vienna, Prague, and Graz.

Elected vicar-general at the chapter of 1602, he visited the provinces and was received in Milan, Paris, Marseilles, and Spain, where crowds flocked to hear him and receive his blessing. His government joined wise firmness to fatherly tenderness; in 1605 he declined a second term, though he remained the best adviser of his successors.

In 1601, when the convent of Prague was founded, he was named chaplain of the Imperial army sent against the Turks, who under Mohammed III had conquered much of Hungary. Sent by the emperor to the German princes, he obtained their cooperation. Before Albe-Royal, the present Szekesfehervar, 18,000 Christians faced 80,000 Turks; the hesitant generals asked his counsel, and he made himself responsible for victory. Mounted on horseback for weakness, crucifix in hand, he led the army forward. The city was taken and the Turks lost 30,000 men; a second battle a few days later was won with the chaplain again at the front, and general and soldiers alike ascribed the double victory to him, his unwounded escape from the greatest danger being everywhere accounted miraculous protection.

After resigning his office in 1605 he was sent by the pope to evangelize Germany, confirming the Catholics there. In 1618 he withdrew to the monastery of Caserta, hoping for seclusion, but the leading men of Naples asked him to go to Spain and inform Philip III of the conduct of the viceroy Ossuna. He sailed from Genoa despite obstacles raised by the viceroy and carried out the mission, but the fatigues of the journey spent his frail strength, and after a few days of great suffering he died at Lisbon, as he had foretold when setting out. He was buried in the cemetery of the Poor Clares of Villafranca.

His known writings comprise eight volumes of sermons, two treatises on oratory, a commentary on Genesis, another on Ezechiel, and three volumes of religious polemics, the sermons in Italian and the other works in Latin, the polemics with notes in Greek and Hebrew. His beatification, several times interrupted, was concluded in 1783, and he was canonized on 8 December 1881. With St. Anthony, St. Bonaventure, and Blessed John Duns Scotus he is a Doctor of the Franciscan Order, and in 1959 Pope John XXIII proclaimed him a Doctor of the Universal Church. He is venerated as the patron of linguists. His feast is kept on 21 July in the present liturgical calendar; the older source's closing note records it as 6 July.

lidwina.history:
{"history": "Saint Lidwina was born at Schiedam in Holland on 18 April 1380. Her father, Peter, came of a noble family; her mother, Petronella, born at Kethel in Holland, was a poor country girl, and the family lived in poverty. Very early in her life Lidwina was drawn toward the Mother of God and prayed much before the miraculous image of Our Lady of Schiedam.

During the winter of 1395, when she was fifteen, she went skating with friends. One of them caused her to fall upon the ice with such violence that she broke a rib in her right side, and this injury proved to be the beginning of her lifelong martyrdom. No medical skill availed to cure her. Gangrene appeared in the wound caused by the fall and spread over her entire body; for the rest of her life she lay bedridden, her condition marked by sores, paralysis, and pain that seemed to increase constantly. Some looked upon her with suspicion, believing her to be under the influence of the evil spirit. When her pastor, Andries, brought her an unconsecrated host, she distinguished it at once.

At first she was bitter, but under the guidance of her confessor she came to accept her sufferings as a share in the Passion of Christ. She became known for her patience, her prayer, and the counsel she gave to the many visitors who came to her bedside. Her biographers record that God rewarded her with a gift of prayer and with visions, and that numerous miracles took place at her sickbed.

Her reputation drew notable figures to her room. The celebrated preacher Wermbold of Roskoop visited her after having previously beheld her in spirit. The pious Arnold of Schoonhoven treated her as a friend. Hendrik Mande wrote for her consolation a pious tract in Dutch, and when Joannes Busch brought it to her and asked what she thought of Mande's visions, she answered that they came from God.

From her fifteenth to her fifty-third year she suffered every imaginable pain; she was, as her biographers record, one sore from head to foot, and she was greatly emaciated. In a vision she was shown a rose-bush with the words, \"When this shall be in bloom, your suffering will be at an end.\" In the spring of 1433 she exclaimed that she saw the rose-bush in full bloom.

On the morning of Easter day, 1433, she was in deep contemplation and beheld in a vision Christ coming toward her to administer the Sacrament of Extreme Unction. She died on 14 April 1433, in her fifty-third year, after thirty-eight years of illness, in the odour of great sanctity.

Her grave at once became a place of pilgrimage, and as early as 1434 a chapel was built over it. Joannes Brugmann and Thomas à Kempis related the history of her life, and the veneration of the people increased unceasingly. In 1615 her relics were conveyed to Brussels, and in 1871 they were returned to Schiedam. On 14 March 1890, Pope Leo XIII canonized her, giving the official sanction of the Church to a veneration that had existed for centuries. Her feast is kept on 14 April.

Later medical writers have considered her one of the first documented cases of multiple sclerosis. Her life has been retold from the fifteenth-century account of Thomas à Kempis to the study published by Joris-Karl Huysmans in 1901, and she is honoured as a patron saint of those who suffer from chronic pain."}

lucy.history:
Lucy was a virgin and martyr of Syracuse in Sicily, one of the most venerated martyrs of the early Church, whose feast is celebrated by Latins and Greeks alike on December 13. According to the traditional account, she was born of rich and noble parents about the year 283. Her father, a man of Roman origin, died early, leaving her dependent on her mother Eutychia, whose name suggests that she came of Greek stock. Like so many early martyrs, Lucy had consecrated her virginity to God and hoped to devote all her worldly goods to the service of the poor.

The fame of St. Agatha, executed fifty-two years before in the Decian persecution, drew many visitors to her relics at Catania, not fifty miles from Syracuse, where miracles were wrought through her intercession. Eutychia, who had suffered a hemorrhage for several years, made the pilgrimage and was cured there. Lucy then persuaded her mother to allow a great part of their riches to be distributed among the poor. This generosity stirred the greed of the suitor to whom Lucy had been unwillingly betrothed, and he denounced her to Paschasius, the Governor of Sicily, in the year 303, during the fierce persecution of Diocletian.

The account relates that Lucy was first condemned to the shame of prostitution, but in the strength of God she stood immovable, so that she could not be dragged away to the place of shame. Bundles of wood were then heaped about her and set on fire, and again she was preserved. Finally she met her death by the sword; strengthened with the Bread of Life, she won her crown of virginity and martyrdom. Before she died she foretold the punishment of Paschasius and the speedy end of the persecution, adding that Diocletian would reign no more and that Maximian would meet his end. Later tradition holds that her eyes were torn out and that, in many versions, her sight was miraculously restored; she is honored as patroness of those with eye diseases. Her name means light, and the festivals of light with which her feast is marked, especially in Scandinavia, recall this.

The story cannot be accepted without criticism, for some of its details may be only a repetition of accounts of other virgin martyrs, the prophecy concerning Maximian was not realized, and Paschasius is a strange name for a pagan governor. No other evidence exists by which the story may be tested; it is traced back to Acta that probably belong to the fifth century and cannot be regarded as accurate. Nevertheless, the place and time of her death can hardly be questioned, and her connection with St. Agatha and the cure of Eutychia may preserve facts peculiar to her story rather than additions from a pious compiler. In any case, the great veneration shown to her by the early Church is beyond doubt. She is one of the few female saints whose names occur in the canon of St. Gregory, with special prayers and antiphons in his Sacramentary and Antiphonary, and she is commemorated in the ancient Roman Martyrology. St. Aldhelm, who died in 709, was the first writer to give a full account of her life and death from her Acts, in prose and in verse; the Venerable Bede followed him in his Martyrology.

Her relics have a recorded history of their own. Sigebert, a monk of Gembloux, says that her body lay undisturbed in Sicily for four hundred years before Faroald, Duke of Spoleto, captured the island and transferred it to Corfinium in Italy. The Emperor Otho I removed it in 972 to Metz and deposited it in the church of St. Vincent, and from that shrine an arm of the saint was taken to the monastery of Luitburg in the Diocese of Spires. After the French captured Constantinople in 1204, some of her relics were found in that city, and the Doge of Venice secured them for the monastery of St. George at Venice. In 1513 the Venetians presented the saint's head to Louis XII of France, who deposited it in the cathedral church of Bourges, though another account brings the head to Bourges from Rome.

martha.history:
Martha appears in the Gospels of Luke and John as the sister of Mary and Lazarus and a close friend of Jesus. The Gospel accounts dwell on the familiar intercourse between the Savior of the world and this humble family; John records the affection of Jesus for the household: "Jesus loved Martha, and her sister Mary, and Lazarus." Scripture speaks of her only in Luke 10:38-42 and in John 11 and 12, and all that is known of her comes from these few passages. The name itself is ancient and well attested outside the Gospels: an Aramaic form is found in a Nabataean inscription discovered at Puteoli, now preserved in the Naples Museum and dated to A.D. 5, and in a Palmyrene inscription of A.D. 179 whose Greek translation gives the form Marthein.

Luke shows Martha welcoming Jesus into her home. While she was occupied with much serving, her sister Mary sat listening at his feet; when Martha complained, Jesus gently reminded her that Mary had chosen the better part. The same active temperament appears in John, where at a supper "Martha served," and the picture of her anxiety there accords closely with Luke's portrait of the woman "busy about much serving." Commentators have long noted the remarkable likeness between the pictures of Martha drawn by the two Evangelists.

Where the family lived is not entirely certain. John represents Mary, Martha, and Lazarus as living at Bethany, but Luke seems to imply that at least at one time they lived in Galilee, though he names no town; Magdala has been suggested, an identification that would suppose Mary of Bethany and Mary Magdalene to be the same person. John's Gospel elsewhere seems to imply a change of residence for the family, and it is possible that Luke has displaced the incident he relates in his tenth chapter. The two Evangelists thus preserve complementary views of the family's home.

Martha's deepest gospel moment comes after the death of her brother Lazarus. She went out to meet Jesus, and here, too, John notes the anxiety that marks her, though her words rise to one of the clearest professions of faith in the Gospels: "I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God." Her faith was the occasion of the Lord's declaration, "I am the resurrection and the life." The Evangelist beautifully marks the change that came over her after that interview: when she had said these things, she went and called her sister Mary secretly, saying, "The Master is come, and calleth for thee."

A difficulty has been raised about the last supper at Bethany. John seems to place it six days before the Passover and, some have concluded, in Martha's house, while the Synoptic Gospels put it two days before the Passover, in the house of Simon the Leper. It has been suggested that there were two suppers, but the texts do not require that supposition. John says only that Christ arrived at Bethany six days before the Passover; he does not say that the supper took place on that day or in Martha's house. Since Matthew and Mark place the scene in Simon's house, John is best understood to say the same, and it remains to be proved that Martha could not serve there.

The Gospel record tells nothing of Martha's later life. Tradition holds that after the Resurrection she traveled to Provence in southern France, and that at Tarascon she tamed a dragon; such accounts belong to later legend rather than to Scripture. She is venerated as the patron saint of cooks, servants, and homemakers. Her feast is celebrated on July 29.

martin-of-tours.history:
Martin of Tours was born about 316 at Sabaria in Pannonia, present-day Hungary, the son of a Roman military tribune. When his father was transferred to Pavia, Martin accompanied him, and in adolescence he was enrolled in the Roman army. Drawn to Christianity from his earliest years, he was still a catechumen when his regiment reached Amiens in Gaul. At the gates of the city on a very cold day he met a shivering, half-naked beggar and divided his cloak, giving half to the poor man; the part he kept became the celebrated relic known as St. Martin's cloak. Tradition holds that he then dreamed of Christ wearing the half-cloak. He was baptized soon afterward and released from military service at Worms on the Rhine.

Freed from the army, he went to Poitiers to join the disciples of St. Hilary, whose reputation as a theologian reached beyond Gaul. Wishing to see his parents again, he crossed the Alps into Lombardy, a region troubled by Arianism; because he did not conceal his Catholic faith he was treated badly at the order of Auxentius, Bishop of Milan. Learning that the Arians troubled Gaul as well and that Hilary had been exiled, he withdrew to the island of Gallinaria. When an imperial decree allowed Hilary to return, Martin rejoined him at Poitiers in 361 and obtained leave to live as a hermit in a deserted region now called Ligugé, which became one of the first monasteries of Gaul.

He remained about ten years in this solitude, often leaving it to preach in central and western Gaul, where many rural inhabitants were still held by idolatry; numerous local legends recall these journeys. When St. Lidorius, second Bishop of Tours, died in 371 or 372, the clergy desired the famous hermit of Ligugé as their bishop. Martin resisted their prayers until a ruse prevailed: a rich citizen, Rusticius, begged him to come to his dying wife, and scarcely had Martin entered the city when popular acclamation, despite the opposition of some ecclesiastical dignitaries, constrained him to become Bishop of Tours. He was consecrated on 4 July. Unchanged in his manner of life, he settled in a small cell beyond the Loire, where other hermits joined him and formed the monastery of Marmoutier.

His simple life joined to untiring zeal sowed Christianity throughout Touraine, and he frequently left his diocese, going several times to Trier, the residence of the emperors, to plead the interests of the Church or to ask pardon for the condemned. His most remarkable intervention concerned the Priscillianists. Against Priscillian, the Spanish heresiarch condemned by the Council of Saragossa, bishops of Spain led by Ithacius had brought furious charges before Emperor Maximus. Martin hurried to Trier, not to defend Priscillian's Gnostic and Manichaean doctrines, but to withdraw him from the emperor's secular jurisdiction. Maximus at first consented, but after Martin's departure ordered Priscillian and his followers to be beheaded. Deeply grieved, Martin refused to communicate with Ithacius; later, to obtain pardon for two rebels, Narses and Leucadius, he consented to a reconciliation with Ithacius, a concession he afterward bitterly regretted.

After a last visit to Rome, Martin went to Candes, a religious center he had founded in his diocese, where illness overtook him; he died in the presbytery of the church in 397. His body was taken to Tours and enclosed in a stone sarcophagus, above which his successors raised first a chapel and later a basilica in 470. Hagiographers recorded miracles ascribed to his intercession in life and after death, and his cult was very popular in the Middle Ages. The shrine at Tours was sacked in 1562 and the collegiate church almost entirely demolished in 1793; excavations in 1860 located the site of the ancient tomb, and the feast is solemnly kept in Tours each 11 November. The Church of France has always ranked Martin among her greatest saints, honoring him as patron of soldiers and of France.

matthew.history:
Matthew, apostle and evangelist, was originally called Levi. His later name derives from the Hebrew Mattija, meaning "gift of God", and it is probable that this was the name conferred upon the tax-gatherer by Christ when He called him to the Apostolate, Levi being his original designation. The bearing of two names was common among the Jews, as in the cases of Simon-Cephas and Joseph-Caiaphas. The man "sitting in the custom house" at the moment of his summons is the same Levi whom Mark and Luke record as "sitting at the receipt of custom", and the three Synoptic accounts of the vocation are identical in terms.

A Galilean and the son of Alpheus, though Eusebius calls him a Syrian, Matthew was a tax-gatherer at Capernaum, collecting custom duties for Herod Antipas. Although a Jew, he was despised by the Pharisees, who hated all publicans. When Jesus called him with the words "Follow me", he arose at once and followed Him, afterwards tendering Him a feast in his house, where tax-gatherers and sinners sat at table with Christ and His disciples. This drew a protest from the Pharisees, whom Jesus rebuked with the words: "I came not to call the just, but sinners."

Beyond the lists of the Apostles, the Gospels make no further mention of Matthew. As a disciple and Apostle he followed Christ up to the time of His Passion and, in Galilee, was one of the witnesses of His Resurrection. He was present at the Ascension, and afterwards withdrew to an upper chamber in Jerusalem, praying in union with Mary, the Mother of Jesus, and with his brethren.

Of his subsequent career only uncertain or legendary accounts survive. St. Irenaeus relates that Matthew preached the Gospel among the Hebrews; St. Clement of Alexandria claims that he did so for fifteen years; and Eusebius maintains that, before going into other countries, he gave them his Gospel in the mother tongue. On this early testimony rests the tradition that Matthew wrote the Gospel which bears his name. Ancient writers do not agree as to the countries he evangelized: almost all mention an Ethiopia to the south of the Caspian Sea, not that of Africa, while some name Persia, the kingdom of the Parthians, Macedonia, and Syria.

Tradition holds that Matthew died a martyr. According to Heracleon, who is quoted by Clement of Alexandria, he did not suffer martyrdom, but this opinion conflicts with all other ancient testimony. The apocryphal account of his passion, judged to date from the third century and marked by Gnostic traces, is considered devoid of historic value, and other writings attributed to him, among them a sixth-century account of the birth of Mary and the infancy of the Savior, are likewise apocryphal. The place of his martyrdom and the manner of his death are disputed: it is not known whether he was burned, stoned, or beheaded. The Roman Martyrology records only that, preaching in Ethiopia, he suffered martyrdom.

The Latin Church keeps his feast on 21 September, the Greek Church on 16 November. In art he is represented under the symbol of a winged man carrying a lance as a characteristic emblem. In later popular devotion he has come to be invoked as a patron of accountants, a connection drawn from the careful record-keeping his former work as a tax collector required. He has been honored as a saint from antiquity, before the institution of the formal canonization process.

monica.history:
Monica was born of Christian parents at Thagaste in North Africa around 331. Almost nothing is recorded of her childhood. Married early in life to Patricius, an official of the town, she endured an unhappy union with a pagan man of violent temper, who appears to have been of dissolute habits and whose mother seems to have shared his disposition. Her almsgiving and habits of prayer displeased him, yet he is said to have retained a kind of reverence for her. By sweetness and patience she exercised a veritable apostolate among the wives and mothers of Thagaste, who saw in her one who suffered as they did.

Three children were born of the marriage: Augustine the eldest, Navigius, and a daughter, Perpetua. Monica had been unable to secure baptism for her children, and when Augustine fell ill she prevailed on Patricius to allow it, though on the boy's recovery he withdrew his consent. Her anxiety came to center on Augustine, who was wayward and, by his own account, lazy; he was sent to school at Madaura, where she seems literally to have wrestled with God for the soul of her son, and later to Carthage, where he fell into grievous sin and became a Manichaean. When he returned home and aired his heretical opinions she drove him from her table, but a vision she experienced urged her to recall him. A great consolation came when Patricius became a Christian; he died shortly after his reception into the Church, and Monica resolved not to marry again. A bishop whose name is not recorded consoled her with words that have become famous: 'the child of those tears shall never perish.'

Augustine then left for Rome by stealth, and Monica pursued her wayward son, arriving to find him gone on to Milan; she followed him there and through Ambrose, bishop of the city, she at last saw him yield after seventeen years of resistance. Mother and son spent six months of true peace at Cassiacum, after which Augustine was baptized in the church of St. John the Baptist at Milan. Setting out for Africa, they stopped at Cività Vecchia and at Ostia, where Monica died in 387. It was from the emotion Augustine then experienced that some of the finest pages of his Confessions were written.

St. Monica was buried at Ostia and for a time was almost forgotten; in the sixth century her remains were moved to a hidden crypt in the church of St. Aureus. In the thirteenth century her cult began to spread, and in 1430 Martin V ordered the relics brought to Rome; many miracles occurred on the way, and her cultus was thereby definitely established. Later, Cardinal d'Estouteville, Archbishop of Rouen, built a church at Rome in honor of St. Augustine and deposited her relics in a chapel to the left of the high altar. No Office of St. Monica seems to have found a place in the Roman Breviary before the sixteenth century. Her canonization belongs to the pre-Congregation era, and her feast is kept on 27 August.

In 1850 an Association of Christian Mothers under the patronage of St. Monica was established at Notre Dame de Sion in Paris for mutual prayer for sons and husbands who had gone astray; raised to the rank of an archconfraternity in 1856, it spread rapidly across the Catholic world, with branches in Dublin, London, Liverpool, Sydney, and Buenos Aires, while a similar confraternity had been established long before by Eugenius IV. Monica is honored as a model of persevering prayer and is a patron of mothers.

nicetius.history:
Nicetius was born in the latter part of the fifth century, his exact birth date unknown, into a Gallo-Roman family apparently settled in Auvergne. From youth he devoted himself to the religious life and entered a monastery, where he advanced so greatly in Christian virtue and sacred learning that he was made abbot. As abbot he came to the notice of King Theodoric I (511-534), who learned to know and esteem him; Nicetius often remonstrated with the king over his wrongdoings, yet without any loss of favor.

After the death of Bishop Aprunculus of Trier, an embassy of the clergy and citizens came to the royal court to elect a new bishop. They first desired Saint Gallus, but the king refused his consent; they then chose Abbot Nicetius, whose election Theodoric confirmed. About 527 Nicetius set out for Trier under a royal escort, and the journey gave early proof of the firmness of his administration. Trier had suffered terribly in the disorders of the Migrations, the era in which Frankish supremacy began in what had been Roman Gaul, and Nicetius became the most important bishop of the ancient see in that period.

Among his first cares was the rebuilding of the cathedral church, a restoration recorded by the poet Venantius Fortunatus; archaeological research has identified in the cathedral Frankish-period mason-work that may belong to this reconstruction. Fortunatus also mentions a fortified castellum with a chapel built by the bishop on the Moselle. Nicetius preached daily and vigorously opposed the moral evils of both the higher classes and the common people, sparing neither the king nor his courtiers. Disregarding threats, he excommunicated King Clotaire I (511-561), for a time sole ruler of the Frankish dominions, on account of the king's misdeeds; in return the king exiled him in 560. Clotaire died the following year, and his son Sigebert, ruler of Austrasia (561-575), allowed Nicetius to return home.

The bishop took part in several synods of the Frankish bishops: Clermont (535), Orléans (549), the second synod of Clermont (549), Toul (550), at which he presided, and Paris (555). He corresponded with churchmen of high rank in distant places; letters to him survive from Abbot Florianus of Romain-Moûtier, Bishop Rufus of Octodurum, and Archbishop Mappinius of Reims. The wider interests of the Church also claimed his attention: he wrote an urgent letter to Emperor Justinian at Constantinople concerning the emperor's position in the controversies arising from Monophysitism, and another preserved letter to Clodosvinda, wife of the Lombard king Alboin, urging her to do all she could to bring her husband to the Catholic faith.

In his personal life Nicetius was greatly ascetic. He fasted frequently, and while the priests and clerics of his household were at their evening meal he would go, concealed by a hooded cloak, to pray in the churches of the city. He founded a school for the training of the clergy; its best-known pupil was Aredius, later Abbot of Limoges, whose testimony, preserved by Gregory of Tours, stands among the principal sources for the bishop's life. Two treatises ascribed to him, De Vigiliis servorum Dei and De Psalmodiae Bono, are of doubtful genuineness. Nicetius died in 563 or, more probably, 566, and was buried in the church of Saint Maximin at Trier. His feast is celebrated at Trier on 1 October, while the Roman Martyrology places his name under 5 December. Remembered as a vigorous and zealous prelate who defended the rights of the Church amid the rivalries of kings and nobles, he is honored as a patron of bishops.

nicholas-of-tolentino.history:
Nicholas of Tolentino was a priest of the order of the Hermits of St. Augustine, remembered for his preaching and for his austere and meek manner of life. He was born about 1246 at Sant'Angelo, near Fermo, in the March of Ancona. His parents are said to have been called Compagnonus de Guarutti and Amata de Guidiani, though these surnames may simply indicate their birthplaces; they were pious people, perhaps gently born, who lived content with a small substance. His birth was regarded as a response to prayer, and his mother was remembered as a model of holiness.

He excelled in his studies to such a degree that, even before they were finished, he was made a canon of the church of St. Saviour. On hearing a sermon by a hermit of St. Augustine upon the text, 'Nolite diligere mundum, nec ea quae sunt in mundo, quia mundus transit et concupiscentia ejus' — that is, do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world, because the world passes away and the desire of it — he felt a call to embrace the religious life and asked the hermit to receive him into his order. His parents gave a joyful consent. Even before his ordination he was sent to different monasteries of the order, at Recanati, Macerata, and elsewhere, as a model of generous striving after perfection, and he made his profession before he was nineteen.

After his ordination he preached with wonderful success, notably at Tolentino, where he spent the last thirty years of his life and gave a discourse nearly every day. Toward the end of his life diseases tried his patience, but he kept up his mortifications almost to the hour of death. He possessed an angelic meekness and a guileless simplicity, and a tender love of virginity, which he never stained, guarding it by prayer and extraordinary mortifications.

He died on September 10, 1306. His tomb at Tolentino is held in veneration by the faithful. He was canonized by Pope Eugene IV in 1446, and his feast is celebrated on September 10.

In art he is depicted in the black habit of the Hermits of St. Augustine, with a star above him or on his breast, and in his hand a lily or a crucifix garlanded with lilies; sometimes, in place of the lily, he holds a vial filled with money or bread. He is venerated as a patron of the poor, and is also honored as a patron of souls in purgatory and of mothers and children.

pantaleon.history:
Pantaleon was a physician of Nicomedia in Asia Minor who suffered martyrdom about the year 305, during the persecution of the emperor Diocletian. He is venerated in the East as a great martyr and wonderworker, and he is counted among the great martyr physicians of the early Church. In the Middle Ages he came to be regarded as one of the fourteen guardian martyrs, better known as the Fourteen Holy Helpers, and as a patron of physicians, an office in which he continues to be invoked together with the sick, who seek his intercession for healing.

According to tradition, he was the son of Eustorgius, a wealthy pagan of Nicomedia, and of Eubula, a Christian mother who gave him his first instruction in the faith. In time he became estranged from Christianity. He studied medicine and rose to become physician to the emperor Maximinianus. The priest Hermolaus won him back to the Christian faith, and upon the death of his father he came into possession of a large fortune. He is remembered for devoting his medical skill to the service of the poor, whom he treated without charge.

During the Diocletian persecution, envious colleagues denounced him as a Christian to the emperor. The emperor, wishing to save him, sought to persuade him to deny his faith; but Pantaleon openly confessed his Christianity, and, as proof that Christ is the true God, he healed a paralytic. The emperor regarded the miracle as an exhibition of magic, and notwithstanding this, condemned him to death.

The written lives containing the details of his passion are late in date and of little historical value, and their marvels are to be read as legend. Tradition holds that his flesh was first burned with torches, and that Christ appeared to all in the form of Hermolaus to strengthen and heal him, whereupon the torches were extinguished. When a bath of liquid lead was prepared, the Lord in the same form was said to have stepped into the cauldron beside him, the fire going out and the lead becoming cold. Thrown into the sea weighted with a stone, he was borne up, the stone being said to have floated. Exposed to wild beasts, he found them fawning upon him, unable to be forced away until he had blessed them. Bound upon a wheel, the ropes snapped and the wheel broke. When an attempt was made to behead him, the sword bent, and the executioners were converted. Pantaleon implored heaven to forgive them, and for this he received the name Panteleemon, the all-compassionate. Only when he himself desired it could the sentence be carried out, and he was beheaded about the year 305.

The fact of the martyrdom itself is supported by early and widespread veneration. Theodoret, Procopius of Caesarea, and the Martyrologium Hieronymianum all bear early witness to his cult, an honor so ancient as to confirm the tradition that he gave his life for the faith. From early times a phial containing some of his blood was preserved at Constantinople, where on his feast day the blood is said to become fluid and to bubble. Relics of the saint are kept at Saint-Denis in Paris, and his head is venerated at Lyons.

As one of the martyr physicians of the early Church, Pantaleon continues to be invoked by physicians and by the sick, and his intercession is sought for healing of all kinds. In the Middle Ages he was further regarded as a patron of midwives. Like the other martyrs of the first centuries, he was never canonized by formal decree; his cult arises from the veneration of the earliest ages, before the institution of the modern process of canonization. His principal feast day is 27 July, and 28 July and 18 February are also observed in his honor.

paris.history:
Saint Paris, known as Paris of Teano from the city of his episcopate, belongs to the earliest generation of bishops who served the Church of Italy after the age of persecution had ended. Tradition holds that he was ordained bishop of Teano, a town in Campania, by Pope Sylvester I in the early fourth century. His ministry thus fell at a decisive moment in the life of the Church, which, freshly freed from persecution, was beginning to build its first churches and to establish its settled ministry in the towns of Italy. The placing of a bishop at Teano belongs to that quiet work of settlement, by which the faith took enduring root in the cities of the peninsula.

Little is recorded of his origins or of the particular labors of his episcopate, and the records do not preserve a precise year either for his consecration or for his death. The tradition of Teano honors him as the first bishop of the city and as a faithful shepherd of the people entrusted to his care. He is said to have governed the see with prudence and to have died in peace, and his memory was kept by the clergy and people of the diocese, among whom his name endured after his death. The brevity of the surviving testimony is itself characteristic of the earliest bishops of the Italian sees, whose service is often remembered chiefly through the enduring presence of the church they founded and ordered.

His feast is kept on August 5, and he is venerated in both the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches. He is honored as a patron of bishops, and the city that received his ministry honors him in turn as its patron and protector, keeping his memory in the local veneration of the diocese.

The encyclopedia article consulted for this summary concerns the archdiocese of Paris in France, which shares the saint's name, and supplies no further information about him; what may be said of St. Paris rests on the tradition of the church of Teano and on the record of his veneration rather than on any detailed ancient life.

patrick.history:
Patrick was born in Roman Britain in the late fourth century; tradition places his birth at Kilpatrick, near Dumbarton, and gives the year 387. His parents were Calphurnius, who belonged to a Roman family of high rank and held the office of decurio, and Conchessa, described in tradition as a near relative of St. Martin of Tours. In his sixteenth year he was carried off into captivity by Irish marauders and sold as a slave to a chieftain named Milchu in Dalriada, in county Antrim, where for six years he tended his master's flocks in the valley of the Braid and on the slopes of Slemish. In his Confession he recounts that during those years he prayed throughout the day and night, so that 'the faith grew in me, and the spirit was roused'; the captivity was afterward seen as a remote preparation for his apostolate, giving him a command of the Celtic tongue and, since his master was said to be a druidical high priest, an acquaintance with Druidism.

Admonished by an angel, he fled after six years, traveling some two hundred miles until he found a ship and, after some rebuffs, was allowed aboard, reaching Britain once more. His heart was now set on the service of God in the sacred ministry. He is found at St. Martin's monastery at Tours and at the island sanctuary of Lérins, and he put himself under the guidance of St. Germain, Bishop of Auxerre, at whose hands he was in time promoted to the priesthood. Tradition among the Morini holds that he labored there for some years as a missionary under Germain's direction, and when Germain went to Britain to combat the errors of Pelagius he chose Patrick as one of his companions. Amid that expedition Patrick's thoughts turned toward Ireland, and he was favored with visions of children from Focluth, by the western sea, who cried to him: 'O holy youth, come back to Erin, and walk once more amongst us.'

Pope St. Celestine I entrusted Patrick with the mission of gathering the Irish race into the one fold of Christ, a commission earlier given to Palladius, who had abandoned it before fierce opposition. It was St. Germain who commended Patrick to the pope; shortly before Celestine's death the mission was conferred, with relics and other spiritual gifts, and the name 'Patritius', understood as foreshadowing his fruitfulness as pater civium, the father of his people. Hearing at Ivrea of Palladius's death, Patrick was consecrated bishop at Turin by St. Maximus and then hastened to Auxerre before setting out for Ireland. Around 432 he returned to the island of his captivity as a missionary bishop, and for the remaining decades of his life he traveled the country, baptizing thousands, ordaining clergy, and founding churches and monasteries. Tradition holds that he used the shamrock to explain the Trinity and credits him with driving the snakes from Ireland, a legend symbolizing the end of paganism.

He died at Saul in Downpatrick on March 17, around 461, though some accounts give a later year, and his feast is kept on that date throughout the world. He is honored as the Apostle of Ireland and is the patron of missionaries. The Confession remains one of the earliest surviving writings from Britain, and other works are attributed to him: the prayer known as the Lorica, or St. Patrick's Breast-Plate, widely accepted as genuine; brief sayings preserved in the Book of Armagh; a Rule of St. Patrick; and a synodical decree directing that questions arising in the island be referred to the Apostolic See.

paul.history:
Saint Paul, known in his early life as Saul, was a zealous Pharisee from Tarsus who persecuted the early Christians. On the road to Damascus he encountered the risen Christ in a blinding vision, and the persecutor became the great Apostle to the Gentiles. What is known of him thereafter is drawn chiefly from his own letters and from the Acts of the Apostles, from which the outline of his career may be reckoned.

He visited Jerusalem three years after his conversion, and after fourteen years he returned for the meeting called to settle questions of legal observance. His second missionary journey lasted at least three years, eighteen months of which were spent at Corinth; his third occupied no less than four and a half years, three of them in Ephesus. In the course of these journeys across the Roman Empire he founded churches, preaching the Gospel in cities such as Antioch, Philippi, Corinth, and Ephesus. Taken in custody, he passed more than two years at Caesarea; the journey that followed, including a sojourn on Malta, occupied six months; and he spent two years in Rome, so that some twenty-nine years separated his conversion from the end of his first captivity.

His letters, which make up much of the New Testament, are among the most influential writings in history and form the foundation of Christian theology. He taught that justification is gratuitous, since of himself man cannot merit it; yet he insisted with equal firmness that the judgment will be universal and according to works, every one receiving the proper due of what he has done, whether good or evil. The angels themselves are not exempt, for all brought to trial must account for the use of their liberty. The final recompense of the just he describes as a crown of justice rendered by the just judge, for the man in grace is capable of merit as the sinner is of demerit.

Perhaps the most distinctive feature of his teaching on the last things is the continuity he perceives between the present and the future of the just, between grace and glory, between salvation begun and salvation consummated. Redemption, justification, salvation, kingdom, glory, and above all life are terms common to the two states, the two phases of one existence linked by a charity that never falls away.

The account in the Acts closes with him in Rome, and the circumstances of his death rest on tradition, which holds that he was martyred there under the emperor Nero, around the year 67, and that, as a Roman citizen, he was beheaded. In the early centuries imaginative narratives gathered around his name, among them the Acts of Paul, the Acts of Paul and Thecla, and a Martyrium Pauli; the cycle even included a correspondence between Paul and the Corinthians, composed to oppose the Gnostics Simon and Cleobius. Portions of these works, recovered from a Coptic papyrus and published in the early twentieth century, have confirmed the judgment passed long ago by Tertullian and Jerome: their author set his scenes in cities Paul really visited, but elsewhere gave his fancy free rein, and the accounts are fabulous rather than historical.

Paul is venerated as the patron of writers and journalists, and of all who communicate the faith. His feast is kept on June 29.

peter.history:
St. Peter's true and original name was Simon, sometimes written Symeon. He was the son of Jona and was born at Bethsaida, a town on the Lake of Genesareth, the Sea of Galilee, whose position is usually sought at the lake's northern end. Andrew was his brother, and the Apostle Philip came from the same town. Simon settled at Capharnaum, living in a house of his own with his mother-in-law at the beginning of Christ's public ministry, about A.D. 26-28, and followed the profitable trade of fisherman on the lake, possessing his own boat. He was married; Clement of Alexandria records that he had children, and the same writer preserves the tradition that Peter's wife suffered martyrdom.

Like many of his contemporaries, Simon was drawn by the Baptist's preaching of penance and was, with Andrew, among John's associates at Bethania on the eastern bank of the Jordan. When the Baptist, pointing to Jesus who was passing, said "Behold the Lamb of God," Andrew followed the Saviour and remained with him a day, then brought his brother with the announcement, "We have found the Messias." At that first meeting Jesus told him: "Thou art Simon the son of Jona: thou shalt be called Cephas, which is interpreted Peter." Cephas, the Aramaic word for rock, foretold the special place Christ had in view for Simon; the name was actually bestowed later, probably at the definitive call to the Apostolate, and was emphasized by Christ on the solemn occasion after Peter's confession of faith. After accompanying Jesus through Galilee, Judaea, and Jerusalem, Peter had returned briefly to his nets when he received the definitive command: "Come ye after me, and I will make you to be fishers of men."

From that hour he remained in the immediate neighbourhood of the Lord. Among the Twelve, Peter soon became the first, heading every list of the Apostles, speaking in their name, and specially addressed by Christ. The Gospel narrative shows both his weakness and his fidelity: rash in word and act, momentarily intimidated by difficulties, yet clinging with the greatest steadfastness and love to his Lord. He walked on the water, confessed Jesus as the Christ, on which occasion Christ gave him the name Peter and declared him the rock on which he would build his Church, and, in the hour of the Passion, three times denied his Lord. When many disciples withdrew after the discourse on the reception of Christ's Body and Blood, it was Peter who answered for the Twelve: "Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life. And we have believed and have known, that thou art the Holy One of God."

After the Resurrection, the risen Lord forgave him and entrusted him with the care of his flock. Peter preached at Pentecost, worked miracles, and led the early Church in Jerusalem and Antioch; after further journeys in the East he came to Rome.

In Rome, during the persecution of Nero, he was martyred about A.D. 64; tradition holds that he suffered crucifixion, head downward, at his own request. Venerated as a saint from the earliest Christian centuries, before formal canonization, he has always been honored as the first pope, and tradition locates his burial on the Vatican Hill, where the great basilica of St. Peter's was afterwards raised.

His chief feast, kept on June 29, is shared with St. Paul, and he is regarded as the patron saint of fishermen. In Christian art the keys, usually two, from the end of the sixth century took the place of an earlier emblem and thenceforth became his distinctive attribute as the sign of his office; the renowned bronze statue in St. Peter's, which holds them, dates from the last period of Christian antiquity.

peter-claver.history:
Peter Claver was born at Verdu, in Catalonia, in 1581, the son of a farmer, and took his first degrees at the University of Barcelona. At the age of twenty he entered the Jesuit novitiate at Tarragona. While he was studying philosophy at Majorca in 1605, Alphonsus Rodriguez, the saintly door-keeper of the college, learned from God the future mission of his young associate and thenceforth never ceased exhorting him to set out to evangelize the Spanish possessions in America. Peter obeyed, and in 1610 he landed at Cartagena, in Colombia, where for the remaining forty-four years of his life he labored as the apostle of the enslaved.

Early in the seventeenth century Cartagena, by its position in the Caribbean Sea, had become the chief slave-market of the New World, receiving a thousand captives a month from the coasts of Guinea, the Congo, and Angola. Captives bought in Africa for two ecus were sold there for two hundred, and even the death of half a cargo left the trade profitable. Neither repeated papal censures nor the voices of Catholic moralists could prevail against this cupidity, and the missionaries, unable to suppress slavery, could only strive to alleviate it. Among them none worked more heroically than Peter Claver, who was trained in the school of the missionary Alfonso de Sandoval. He declared himself "the slave of the negroes forever", and thenceforth his life was marked by superhuman charity.

Every month, when the arrival of a slave ship was signaled, Claver went out in the pilot's boat to meet it, carrying food and delicacies. The captives, cooped up in the hold, arrived crazed and brutalized by suffering and fear, and he went to each in turn, cared for him, showed him kindness, and made him understand that henceforth he was his defender and father. To instruct captives who spoke many different dialects, he assembled at Cartagena a group of interpreters of various nationalities and formed them into catechists. While the enslaved were penned up at Cartagena awaiting purchase and dispersal, he instructed and baptized them; over the course of his life he baptized and instructed in the faith more than 300,000 people. On the Sundays of Lent he assembled them, inquired into their needs, and defended them against their oppressors.

The work cost him dearly. The slave merchants were not his only enemies: he was accused of indiscreet zeal, and even of profaning the sacraments by giving them to creatures his critics claimed scarcely possessed a soul. Fashionable women of Cartagena refused to enter the churches where he gathered his people, and his own superiors were often swayed by the criticisms that reached them. Claver continued all the same, accepting every humiliation and adding rigorous penances to his works of charity. Lacking the support of men, he was given the strength of God: he came to be honored in New Granada as a prophet and miracle worker and as the oracle of Cartagena, and many were convinced that God had often spared the city only for his sake.

He died on 8 September 1654, after a long illness. He was beatified by Pius IX on 16 July 1850 and canonized by Leo XIII on 15 January 1888, on the same day as Alphonsus Rodriguez, whose exhortations had first directed him to America. His feast is kept on 9 September, and in 1896 he was proclaimed the special patron of the African missions; he is venerated as the patron saint of slaves.

peter-faber.history:
Peter Faber was born on 13 April 1506 at Villaret in the Duchy of Savoy, where as a boy he tended his father's sheep and on Sundays taught catechism to other children. An instinctive sense of his vocation as an apostle inspired in him a desire to study; he was entrusted first to a priest at Thônes and then to a school nearby, and in 1525, with his parents' consent, he arrived in Paris. There he was admitted without payment to the college of Sainte-Barbe, where he shared lodgings with Francis Xavier; the two received the degree of master of arts on the same day in 1530, and at the university Faber also met Ignatius of Loyola and became one of his associates.

After Ignatius himself, Xavier and the other companions esteemed Faber the most eminent among them, for his profound knowledge, his gentle sanctity, and his influence over souls. Ordained a priest in 1534, he was the first of the companions to be raised to the priesthood, and at Montmartre on 15 August of that year he celebrated the Mass at which Ignatius and his five companions took their vows. When Ignatius later directed the whole company to meet at Venice, Faber was charged with conducting them; he left Paris on 15 November 1536 and rejoined Ignatius there in January 1537.

After some months of preaching and teaching in Rome, the pope sent him to Parma and Piacenza, where his ministry brought about a revival of Christian piety. He was next sent to Germany to uphold the Catholic cause at the Diet of Worms, convoked in 1540, and was called to the Diet of Ratisbon in 1541. What he saw of the ruin that Protestantism had brought upon Germany and of the decay of Catholic life there convinced him that the remedy lay not in discussion with the reformers but in the reform of the faithful, above all of the clergy.

For ten months, working at Speyer, Ratisbon, and Mainz, he labored with gentleness and success, and it was above all by means of the Spiritual Exercises that he accomplished his conversions; princes, prelates, and priests opened their consciences to him. Recalled by Ignatius to Spain, he was sent back after about six months to labor for nineteen more in Germany, at Speyer, Mainz, and Cologne, gaining the clergy little by little and finding many vocations among the young. Among these was Peter Canisius, whose vocation Faber decided, for which reason he has been called the Apostle of Germany. The archbishop of Cologne, Hermann of Wied, was already won over by the new teaching and would later embrace it publicly; yet after some months at Louvain in 1543, where he implanted the seeds of numerous vocations among the young, Faber returned to Cologne, where it may be said that he extirpated all heresy.

Obliged by obedience to leave Germany in August 1544, he went first to Portugal and then to Spain. At the courts of Lisbon and Valladolid, and in the principal cities of the country, he fostered fervor and vocations, above all that of Francis Borgia, which he more than anyone else strengthened. At forty he was already wasted by incessant labor and by journeys made almost entirely on foot.

The pope thought of sending him to the Council of Trent as theologian of the Holy See, and John III of Portugal wished to have him named Patriarch of Ethiopia, but neither design was realized. Summoned to Rome and weakened by fever, Faber arrived there on 17 July 1546 and died on 1 August, in the arms of Ignatius.

Those who had known him already invoked him as a saint, and Francis de Sales never spoke of him except as a saint, while Savoy has never ceased to venerate him. He was beatified on 5 September 1872, and in 2013 Pope Francis canonized him, recognizing his holiness and his model of patient, charitable dialogue. His feast is kept on 2 August, and he is honored as patron of spiritual direction.

philomena.history:
On 25 May 1802, during the quest for the graves of Roman martyrs in the Catacomb of Priscilla at Rome, a tomb was discovered and opened. Because it contained a glass vessel, it was assumed to be the grave of a martyr, the presence of such vessels, supposed to have held the martyr's blood, being then received as a mark of martyrdom. The remains proved to be those of a young maiden of about thirteen, and the earthenware slabs closing the grave bore the name Filumena. On this basis it was assumed that these were the remains of a virgin martyr named Philumena.

The letters are painted on the plates with red paint, but the plates were evidently set in place in the wrong order, for they read LUMENA PAX TECUM FI, whereas the inscription should doubtless read PAX TECUM FILUMENA, that is, 'Peace be with you, Philomena.' The lettering belongs to the primitive class of epigraphical memorials in the Catacomb of Priscilla and dates from about the middle or the second half of the second century. The disarrangement of the plates proves that the inscription must have been completed before they were put into position, although in the numerous other examples of this kind in the same catacomb the inscription was added only after the grave had been closed; since the disarrangement can scarcely be explained as arising from an error, Marucchi appears justified in concluding that the inscription and plates originally belonged to an earlier grave and were later employed, now in the wrong order, to close another. Besides the letters, the slabs bear three arrows, either as decoration or punctuation, a leaf as decoration, two anchors, and a palm as the well-known Christian symbols; yet neither these signs nor the glass vessel found in the grave can be regarded as a proof of martyrdom, and the older view that such vessels marked a martyr's tomb has been rejected in practice since the investigations of De Rossi.

On 8 June 1805 the relics were translated to the church of Mugnano del Cardinale, in the Diocese of Nola near Naples, and enshrined beneath one of its altars. In 1827 Leo XII presented the church with the three earthenware tiles bearing the inscription, which may be seen there even today.

Philomena is not mentioned in any of the ancient sources.
