On the basis of alleged revelations to a nun in Naples, and of an entirely fanciful and indefensible explanation of the allegorical paintings found on the slabs beside the inscription, a canon of the church of Mugnano named Di Lucia composed a purely fictitious and romantic account of her supposed martyrdom, in which she appears as a young Greek princess put to death under the emperor Diocletian for refusing marriage and remaining faithful to Christ. In the absence of early testimony, nothing can be affirmed of her beyond what the name and the antiquity of the inscription suggest, and tradition holds only that she was a virgin martyr.

Devotion to the relics spread rapidly after wonderful favours were received in answer to prayer before them at Mugnano. After instituting investigations into the question, Gregory XVI appointed a special feast in honour of St. Philomena, virgin and martyr, a feast whose lessons appear in the Roman Breviary. She was never formally canonized, and her feast was removed from the general calendar in 1961, since so little about her can be established with historical certainty. Nevertheless, she continues to be widely venerated as a powerful intercessor, honoured especially as a patroness of youth and known under the title of the 'Wonder Worker'.

roch.history:
Roch was born at Montpellier in France around 1295, into a noble family; his father was governor of the city. Tradition holds that at his birth he was found marked on the breast with a red cross. Orphaned at about twenty, he distributed his fortune among the poor, entrusted the government of Montpellier to his uncle, and set out for Italy in the disguise of a mendicant pilgrim.

His route lay through towns stricken by plague. At Aquapendente he devoted himself to the sick, who were said to have been cured through his prayers and the sign of the cross. He then visited Cesena and other neighboring cities, followed by Rome, Mantua, Modena, and Parma, and everywhere the plague was said to disappear before him.

At Piacenza he himself contracted the plague and withdrew to a hut in a neighboring forest. His needs were provided for by a gentleman named Gothard, who learned of his retreat, it is said, through a miracle; tradition holds that a dog brought him bread each day and licked his wounds until he recovered. After regaining his health, Roch returned to France.

Arriving at Montpellier, he refused to disclose his identity and, taken for a spy in a pilgrim's disguise, was cast into prison by order of the governor, whom some writers identify as his own uncle. He died there five years later, in 1327. The red cross on his breast and a document found in his possession then served for his identification, and he received a public funeral, with numerous miracles attesting his sanctity.

Devotion to him spread rapidly across Europe, and he came to be honored as a protector against plague and contagious disease. In 1414, when plague broke out at Constance during the Council, the Fathers ordered public prayers and processions in honor of the saint, and the plague immediately ceased. His relics were reportedly carried to Venice in 1485, where they are still venerated.

He is honored as a saint of the pre-congregation era, before the establishment of the formal canonization process, and his feast is kept on 16 August. It is commonly held that he belonged to the Third Order of St. Francis, though this cannot be proved. Pope Urban VIII approved the ecclesiastical office recited on his feast, and Paul III instituted a confraternity under the saint's invocation to have charge of the church and hospital erected under Alexander VI; Pope Paul IV raised it to an archconfraternity, able to aggregate similar confraternities of St. Roch, and further favors were granted by Pius IV, Gregory XIII, and Gregory XIV. In art, Roch is usually depicted pointing to a plague sore on his leg, with a dog at his side.

rosalia.history:
Rosalia, venerated as a hermitess and honored as a patroness of Palermo and of the whole of Sicily, is commemorated on 4 September, with a special feast of the translation of her relics kept in Sicily on 15 July. No account of her life is known before that of Valerius Rossi, written about 1590, although churches were already dedicated in her honor in 1237. Her vita, preserved in the Acta Sanctorum, was compiled, according to the Bollandist J. Stilting, from local traditions, paintings, and inscriptions.

According to this traditional account, she was the daughter of Sinibald, Lord of Quisquina, and of Rosa, a family descended from Charlemagne. In her youthful days she left home and hid herself in a cave near Bivona, and later in another on Monte Pellegrino near Palermo, in which she died and was buried. Whether she had belonged to a religious community before her retirement is not known; the Basilians claim her as a member in their Martyrology. She is often represented as a Basilian nun with a Greek cross in her hand.

In 1624 her remains were discovered and brought to the Cathedral of Palermo, and Urban VIII put her name into the Roman Martyrology. She is venerated as a patroness of Palermo and is invoked against plague. Her feast is still celebrated in Palermo with a great procession on 4 September, and the translation of her relics is likewise kept on 15 July.

rose-of-lima.history:
Rose of Lima, virgin, was born at Lima, Peru, on 20 April 1586. Baptized Isabel, she was known as Rose from childhood, a name her mother gave her on account of her beauty; at her confirmation in 1597 she formally took the name Rose, it having been said that as an infant her face had been seen transformed by a mystical rose. From her earliest years she showed a remarkable reverence and love for the things of God, and her life came to be given over to prayer and mortification. She had an intense devotion to the Infant Jesus and His Blessed Mother, before whose altar she spent hours, and she passed long periods before the Blessed Sacrament, which she received daily. Obedient and industrious, she made steady progress in her studies and her domestic work, above all at her needle.

After reading about St. Catherine, she resolved to take that saint as her model. She began to fast three times a week and added secret penances: she cut off her hair when her vanity was assailed, wore coarse clothing, and roughened her hands with toil. Throughout she endured the objections of her friends, the ridicule of her family, and the censure of her parents.

Determined to consecrate herself to Christ by a vow of virginity, she first had to overcome her parents' wish that she marry; the struggle lasted ten years before patience and prayer won their consent. In these years temptations against her purity, faith, and constancy brought her acute agony of mind and desolation of spirit, yet, as she believed, Our Lord daily fortified her with the knowledge of His presence and consoled her with the evidence of His love.

Her fasting became perpetual abstinence from meat, and her food the coarsest sustenance, only enough to support life. By day she was occupied with charity and industry: her lace and embroidery helped to support her home, and she cared for the sick and the poor of Lima. Her nights were given to prayer and penance, often in a little grotto she had built with her brother's aid in the family garden. Later, with her confessor's consent and in spite of her parents' opposition, she lived there practically as a recluse, leaving it chiefly to visit the Blessed Sacrament. In her twentieth year she received the habit of St. Dominic as a member of the Third Order.

Thereafter her penances grew in severity to what her biographers describe as a heroic degree. She wore, concealed by roses, a metal spiked crown and an iron chain about her waist; she sometimes passed days without food, taking only a draught of gall mixed with bitter herbs; and when she could no longer stand she rested on a bed she had constructed of broken glass, stone, potsherds, and thorns, though she admitted that the thought of lying on it made her tremble with dread. This bodily rigor continued for fourteen years without relaxation, but not without consolation: she believed that Our Lord revealed Himself to her frequently, flooding her soul with peace and joy and leaving her for hours in ecstasy. At such times she offered her mortifications and penances in expiation for offenses against the Divine Majesty, for the idolatry of her country, for the conversion of sinners, and for the souls in purgatory.

Rose died at Lima on 24 August 1617, at the age of thirty-one. Many miracles were reported after her death. She was beatified by Pope Clement IX in 1667 and canonized by Pope Clement X in 1671, the first saint of the Americas. Her feast is kept on 23 August. She is represented in art wearing a crown of roses and is venerated as the patroness of single women.

rusticus-of-narbonne.history:
Saint Rusticus of Narbonne was a fifth-century bishop of southern Gaul whose life joined the monastic tradition of Lérins to the government of a troubled see. He was born either at Marseilles or in the Narbonnaise region of Gaul, and he died on 26 October 461. According to his biographers, he is the Rusticus to whom St. Jerome, about the year 411, addressed a letter commending him to imitate the virtues of St. Exuperius of Toulouse and to follow the advice of Procule, then Bishop of Marseilles; if that identification is accepted, he was corresponding with Jerome while still a young man. After completing his education in Gaul, Rusticus went to Rome, where he soon gained a reputation as a public speaker, but he wished to embrace the contemplative life. He wrote to St. Jerome, who advised him to continue his studies, and he later entered the renowned monastery of St. Vincent of Lérins.

Ordained at Marseilles, he was consecrated Bishop of Narbonne on 3 October 430, or by another reckoning 427. He shepherded the Church in a region where Roman authority was weakening and where the Christian community was still establishing its footing. With all his zeal, he could not prevent the progress of the Arian heresy, which the Goths were spreading abroad. Their siege of Narbonne, together with dissensions among the Catholics, so disheartened him that he wrote to St. Leo renouncing the bishopric; Leo dissuaded him, and Rusticus gave himself instead to the work of consolidating the Catholic body.

Between 444 and 448 he built a church at Narbonne. In 451 he assisted at the convocation of forty-four bishops of Gaul and approved St. Leo's letter to Flavian concerning Nestorianism. He was present also at the Council of Arles, attended by thirteen bishops, which met to decide the dispute between Theodore, Bishop of Fréjus, and the Abbey of Lérins. A letter sent to him by Ravennius, Bishop of Arles, bears witness to the high esteem in which he was held.

Of his correspondence, all is lost except the letter to St. Jerome and two letters to St. Leo, written either in 452 or in 458. As a monk-bishop, Rusticus carried the contemplative discipline of Lérins into the active ministry of the episcopate, and he stands with the fifth-century bishops of Gaul who consolidated the faith in the provinces of the collapsing Western Empire. His memory endures among the saints of southern France, and he is honored as a patron of bishops.

pope-silverius.history:
Silverius was the son of Pope Hormisdas, who had been married before entering the higher clergy; the date of his birth is unknown. He was a subdeacon at Rome when Pope Agapetus died at Constantinople on 22 April 536. The Byzantine empress Theodora, who favored the Monophysites, sought the election of the Roman deacon Vigilius, then at Constantinople and pledged to her cause; Theodahad, king of the Ostrogoths, unwilling to accept a pope drawn toward Constantinople, forestalled her, and by his influence the subdeacon Silverius was chosen. The election of a subdeacon as Bishop of Rome was unusual, and opposition arose among the clergy, though it was suppressed by the king. Silverius was consecrated bishop, probably on 8 June 536, after which the Roman presbyters gave their consent to his elevation in writing. A later claim that he had bought the king's support is unwarranted, resting on its author's hostility to pope and Goths alike.

His brief pontificate unfolded in an unsettled and disorderly time. Theodora sought to bring him into communion with the deposed Monophysite patriarch Anthimus of Constantinople and with Severus of Antioch; the pope committed himself to nothing, and the empress resolved to depose him in favor of Vigilius. War between Ostrogoths and Byzantines had broken out in Italy upon the death of Amalasuntha; the Gothic king Vitiges besieged Rome, the churches above the catacombs were devastated, and the graves of the martyrs were broken open. In December 536 the Byzantine general Belisarius garrisoned the city and was received by the pope with courtesy. Drawn on by his wife Antonina, Belisarius acted as the empress desired: by a forged letter Silverius was accused of treasonable agreement with the Goths, offering to leave a city gate secretly open, and in March 537 he was arrested, roughly stripped of his episcopal dress, clothed as a monk, and sent into exile in the East, while Vigilius was consecrated Bishop of Rome in his stead.

Taken to Lycia, Silverius resided at Patara, where the local bishop soon found the exile innocent and carried proofs of it to Constantinople. The emperor Justinian required a new investigation, directing that Silverius be restored to the papal see if the accusation proved forged, and allowed him to return to Italy. Silverius reentered the country, apparently at Naples, but Vigilius, evidently acting with the Empress Theodora and aided by Antonina, took charge of his unlawfully deposed predecessor and had him conveyed to the island of Palmarola in the Tyrrhenian Sea, a small and desolate place near Ponza in the Bay of Naples, where he was kept in close confinement. There he died in consequence of the privations and harsh treatment he endured. The year of his death is unknown, but he probably did not live long after reaching the island. According to the Liber Pontificalis, he was buried on the island on 20 June, and his remains were never removed.

The same account records that the faithful who visited his grave invoked him after death, and in time he came to be venerated as a saint, the earliest witness being an eleventh-century list of saints. His feast, found in a martyrology of the fourteenth century and in the present Roman Martyrology, is kept on 20 June. Honored as a martyr of the papacy, who endured imprisonment and exile rather than abandon his office, he is also invoked as a patron of prisoners.

pope-sixtus-i.history:
Pope Sixtus I was bishop of Rome in the earliest generations of the Church, succeeding Pope Alexander I and preceding Pope Telesphorus. In the oldest documents his name appears as Xystus, the spelling used for the first three popes of that name. According to the Liberian Catalogue of popes, he ruled the Church during the reign of the emperor Hadrian, from the consulship of Niger and Apronianus to that of Verus III and Ambibulus, that is, from 117 to 126. Eusebius, who followed a catalogue of popes in his Chronicon different from the one he used in his Ecclesiastical History, gives earlier dates: the Chronicon places the pontificate from 114 to 124, while the History places it from 114 to 128. All authorities agree that Sixtus reigned for about ten years. He was a Roman by birth, and his father's name was Pastor. Few details of his life survive beyond these outlines.

The Liber Pontificalis credits Sixtus with three ordinances. First, none but sacred ministers were allowed to touch the sacred vessels. Second, bishops who had been summoned to the Holy See were, upon their return, not to be received by their dioceses unless they presented Apostolic letters. Third, after the Preface in the Mass, the priest was to recite the Sanctus with the people.

The Felician Catalogue of popes and the various martyrologies give him the title of martyr. His feast is celebrated on April 6. He was buried in the Vatican, beside the tomb of St. Peter.

His relics are said to have been transferred to Alatri in 1132, though Jozzi, writing in 1900, contended that they remain in the Vatican Basilica. The cult of Sixtus at Alatri has in turn been treated in modern studies: Marini published an account of his cult there in 1884, and De Persiis, in a memoir printed at Alatri in the same year, wrote on his pontificate and on the translation of his relics from Rome. Butler, in his Lives of the Saints, states that Pope Clement X gave some of the relics to Cardinal de Retz, who placed them in the Abbey of St. Michael in Lorraine.

The Xystus commemorated in the Canon of the Mass is Sixtus II, not Sixtus I. Counted among the early popes who consolidated the Roman Church's liturgical and pastoral life in the generations after the apostles, Sixtus I is honored as a patron of church unity.

thomas-more.history:
Thomas More, knight, Lord Chancellor of England, author and martyr, was born in London in 1478, the only surviving son of Sir John More, a barrister who later became a judge, and of his first wife Agnes, daughter of Thomas Graunger. Educated first at St. Anthony's School in Threadneedle Street, he was placed at thirteen in the household of Cardinal Morton, Archbishop of Canterbury and Lord Chancellor, who sent him to Oxford about 1492, where he entered Canterbury Hall, afterwards absorbed by Christ Church. There he formed friendships with William Grocyn and Thomas Linacre, the latter becoming his first instructor in Greek; he studied also French, history, and mathematics, and learned to play the flute and the viol. Recalled to London, he read law at New Inn from about 1494, was admitted to Lincoln's Inn in February, 1496, and served three successive years as reader or lecturer on law at Furnival's Inn.

Law did not absorb all his energies. He wrote poetry in Latin and English, published an English translation of the life of Pico della Mirandola, and cultivated the friendship of learned men, among them Dean Colet of St. Paul's, who became his confessor, and William Lilly. In 1497 he was introduced to Erasmus, probably at the house of Lord Mountjoy; their friendship became intimate, and Erasmus paid several long visits to More's house at Chelsea. Having read the Fathers with care, More delivered between 1499 and 1503, in the Church of St. Lawrence Jewry, a series of well-attended lectures on St. Augustine's De civitate Dei, of which no fragment survives.

In those years his mind was occupied almost wholly with religion and the question of his own vocation. He lived near the London Charterhouse and often joined the spiritual exercises of its monks, and his biographers relate that he wore a hair shirt next to his skin. He wavered for a time between the Carthusians and the Observant Franciscans, but in the end, apparently with the approval of Colet, he abandoned the hope of becoming a priest or religious, mistrusting his powers of perseverance. Erasmus wrote that he had chosen "to be a chaste husband rather than an impure priest."

His reputation at the bar carried him into public life, and he rose to become Lord Chancellor of England under King Henry VIII; he is remembered also as the author of Utopia. At the king's request he wrote an answer to Luther's reply to the royal defense of the seven sacraments, and he engaged in lengthy printed controversies with reforming writers, among them Tyndale, Fish, Barnes, and Fryth, besides a dialogue defending the veneration of images and relics, prayers to the saints, and pilgrimage. When Henry broke with Rome and declared himself head of the Church in England, More, who had resigned the office of Lord Chancellor in May 1532, refused to take the oath acknowledging the king's supremacy and was imprisoned in the Tower of London. His Apologye, published in 1533, was written after he had given over the office.

In the Tower he remained devout and cheerful, writing prayers and letters to his family, among them a touching correspondence with his daughter Margaret. Tried for treason, he was beheaded on Tower Hill on 6 July, 1535, declaring that he died "the king's good servant, but God's first." He was canonized in 1935; his feast is kept on 22 June, and he is venerated as the patron saint of lawyers, politicians, and statesmen.

vincent-de-paul.history:
Vincent de Paul was born in 1580 to a peasant family at Pouy, in Gascony, France, though some authorities say 1576. He studied the humanities at Dax with the Cordeliers and, after a stay at Saragossa, took his degree in theology at Toulouse. Ordained a priest in 1600, he remained at Toulouse or in its vicinity, acting as tutor while continuing his own studies.

In 1605, while returning by sea from Marseilles, he was captured by Turkish pirates, taken to Tunis, and sold as a slave; he escaped in 1607 together with a renegade master whom he converted. Returning to France, he went to Avignon to the papal vice-legate, followed him to Rome to continue his studies, and in 1609 was sent back to France on a secret mission to Henry IV. He became almoner to Queen Marguerite of Valois and was provided with the little Abbey of Saint-Léonard-de-Chaume.

At the request of M. de Berulle he took charge of the parish of Clichy near Paris, then in 1612 entered the service of the Gondi family, educating the children of Philippe-Emmanuel de Gondi and becoming spiritual director of Mme de Gondi. With her help he preached missions on the family estates. To escape the esteem he attracted, he had himself appointed curé of Chatillon-les-Dombes, where he converted several Protestants and founded the first conference of charity for the assistance of the poor. Recalled by the Gondi in 1617, he resumed the peasant missions, joined by several learned Paris priests, and after nearly every mission a conference of charity was established for the relief of the poor, notably at Joigny, Châlons, Mâcon, and Trévoux.

His care then turned to the convicts of the royal galleys, who were subject to M. de Gondi as general of the galleys of France. Chained in damp dungeons and fed on black bread and water, they bore a moral misery still more frightful than their physical suffering. Vincent visited them, spoke kind words, performed every service however repulsive, won their hearts, and converted many; a purchased house served as a hospital. Named royal almoner of the galleys by Louis XIII, he lavished the same care on the convicts at Marseilles and Bordeaux, where his missions were crowned with success.

The fruit of these missions, together with the urging of Mme de Gondi, led him in 1625 to found the Congregation of Priests of the Mission for the evangelization of the country people. Believing that the good done by missions could not last without well-formed priests, he directed the first retreats for candidates to Holy Orders at Beauvais in 1628, from which the seminaries that later prevailed in France took rise. He opened a seminary at the Collège des Bons-Enfants as early as 1635, founded the lesser Seminary of St. Charles in 1642, and at his death directed eleven seminaries. From 1633 he held conferences every Tuesday at Saint-Lazare at which priests conferred on the virtues and functions of their state, and in the same year, with St. Louise de Marillac, he founded the Daughters of Charity, the first community of women devoted to serving the sick and the poor outside the cloister. He likewise organized relief for war victims and foundlings and worked to improve the care of the sick in the hospitals of France.

Vincent died at Paris on 27 September 1660, the date now observed as his feast, and at his death the poor of Paris lost their best friend. In 1705 the Superior-General of the Lazarists requested that his canonization be instituted, a petition supported by bishops including Bossuet, Fénelon, Fléchier, and Cardinal de Noailles. Declared blessed by Benedict XIII on 13 August 1729, he was canonized by Clement XII on 16 June 1737. Leo XIII gave him as patron to the Sisters of Charity in 1885, and he is honored as a patron of the sick. The letters written during his long and busy life have been estimated at not less than 30,000, though many have since been lost.

zita.history:
Zita was born early in the thirteenth century at Montsegradi, a small village near Lucca in Tuscany, into a poor family. Her earliest accounts credit a naturally happy disposition, the teaching of a virtuous mother, and the aid of divine grace with forming in her the sweetness, modesty, and conscientious application to work that would mark the whole of her life.

At the age of twelve she entered the service of the Fatinelli family of Lucca, in whose household she remained for the rest of her life. She regarded her daily duties as rendered to God rather than to men, performed them with exactness, and even supplied what her fellow servants neglected. Her piety did not win their esteem; it brought her every kind of ill-treatment from the other servants, whose accusations also turned her employers against her. This constant harsh usage failed to rob her of her inward peace or of her love for those who wronged her, and she retained her respect for her employers throughout. By such meek and humble self-restraint she gradually overcame the malice of the whole household, and at length she was placed in charge of all the affairs of the house.

In her position of command she treated the servants with kindness, exacting no reckoning for the wrongs she had so long suffered at their hands, and she showed severity only when it was necessary to check the introduction of vice among them. When any servant had fallen short, she took it upon herself to excuse or defend them before her employers. Using the ample authority the family gave her, she was generous in almsgiving, though careful to assist only those truly in need. Tradition holds that bread she carried from the house to feed the poor was found turned into flowers when she was accused of giving it away, and this token has remained closely associated with her.

Zita died at Lucca on 27 April 1271, the date kept as her feast. Numerous miracles were wrought at her intercession after her death, and she came to be venerated as a saint in the neighbourhood of Lucca. Her fame was such that the poets Fazio degli Uberti, in the Dittamonde, and Dante, in the Inferno, both designate the city of Lucca simply as 'Santa Zita'. An office in her honour was approved by Pope Leo X.

In 1580 her tomb was discovered in the Church of San Frediano at Lucca, where devotional tradition holds that her body remains incorrupt. This discovery led to the solemn approbation of her cult by Pope Innocent XII in 1696, the year reckoned as that of her canonization. The earliest life of the saint is an anonymous manuscript preserved in the Fatinelli family, published at Ferrara in 1688 by Monsignor Fatinelli. A fuller 'Vita e miracoli di S. Zita vergine lucchese', printed at Lucca in 1752 by Bartolomeo Fiorito, drew on this and other notices, especially those taken from the process drawn up to establish the immemorial cult.

Because her sanctity was attained within the ordinary labor of a servant's life, she is honored as the heavenly patroness of domestic workers and housekeepers.

therese-of-lisieux.history:
Thérèse Martin, a Carmelite of Lisieux known in religion as Sister Teresa of the Child Jesus and popularly called the Little Flower of Jesus, was born at Alençon, France, on 2 January 1873 and died at Lisieux on 30 September 1897.

She was the ninth and youngest child of Louis and Zélie Martin, a couple remembered for their holiness. Both parents had wished to consecrate their lives to God in the cloister, and the vocation denied to them was given to their children: five became religious, one joining the Visitation Order and four entering the Carmelite convent of Lisieux, where two of Thérèse's sisters had preceded her. After her mother's death the family moved to Lisieux, where Thérèse grew up with a deep desire to become a saint. Louis and Zélie Martin were themselves canonized in 2015.

Brought up in an atmosphere of faith in which every virtue and aspiration were carefully nurtured and developed, she manifested a religious vocation while still a child. Educated by the Benedictines, she applied at fifteen for permission to enter the Carmelite convent, and when the superior refused her she went to Rome with her father, as eager to give her to God as she was to give herself, to seek the consent of Pope Leo XIII, then celebrating his jubilee. The Holy Father preferred to leave the decision in the hands of the superior, who finally consented, and on 9 April 1888, at the unusual age of fifteen, Thérèse entered the convent of Lisieux.

The eleven years of her religious life were marked by signal graces and constant growth in holiness. Within the cloister she developed her 'little way' of spiritual childhood: doing small things with great love, perfectly accomplishing small duties, and trusting completely in God's mercy. Obedient to her superiors, she wrote the account of this life in her autobiography, composed in obedience to her superior.

Published two years after her death, the autobiography met with immediate success. It was translated into English in 1901, and in 1912 another translation appeared, the first complete edition of the life of the Servant of God, containing the autobiography, letters, and spiritual counsels. Passing into many editions, it spread far and wide devotion to this 'little' saint of simplicity, of abandonment in God's service, and of the perfect accomplishment of small duties. Under the title The Story of a Soul, it became one of the most widely read spiritual books of the twentieth century.

Thérèse died at Lisieux of tuberculosis on 30 September 1897, at the age of twenty-four, having promised to spend her heaven doing good on earth. The fame of her sanctity and the many miracles performed through her intercession caused the introduction of her cause of canonization only seventeen years after her death, on 10 June 1914. She was canonized in 1925, and in 1997 she was declared a Doctor of the Church. Her feast is kept on 1 October, and she is honored as patroness of missionaries and of the missions.
